#4. NPB star Teruaki Sato to be posted to MLB: What to know about Triple Crown winner, plus possible landing spots

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Hanshin Tigers will post third baseman Teruaki Sato, Japan's Triple Crown winner this season, for MLB teams this offseason, the team announced on Monday. Sato, 28 in March, slugged 39 home runs with a .306/.383/.609 batting line in 2026. A year ago, he hit 40 home runs and was named league MVP, and it seems likely he will win MVP again this year.

"I am grateful to the team for respecting my wishes," Sato said in a statement, via Kyodo News.

This past March, Sato hit second for Japan in the World Baseball Classic and was the only non-MLB player in the top six of their lineup. Shohei Ohtani hit leadoff and Sato hit second, ahead of Seiya Suzuki, Masataka Yoshida, Kazuma Okamoto, and Munetaka Murakami, in that order. Sato went 3 for 10 in five WBC games.

"He has been with us for six years, contributing to three league titles," Tigers GM Satoshi Shimamura said in a statement, via Kyodo News. "He delivered an especially outstanding performance this year."

Given his age and power, and the weak MLB free agent class, Sato figures to be among the top targets for teams looking to add a bat this offseason. Murakami's two-year, $34 million contract with the Chicago White Sox has proven to be a bargain even with his second-half fade. Sato could command more than that despite being two years older than Murakami.

Here is what you need to know about Sato now that his availability to MLB teams has been made official.

Obviously, Sato has power. His 39 home runs were one behind the league leader and came at a time when Japan is in something of a deadball era. The league hit .236/.301/.350 this year and averaged only 3.40 runs per game. For reference, MLB teams averaged 4.48 runs per game in 2026, and Myles Straw hit .241/.304/.342. Japan was an entire league of Myles Straws this season.

Sato is a left-handed hitter and not quite Murakami 2.0. He doesn't have quite as much power, won't work as many walks, will still swing and miss a bunch, and likely isn't a third baseman long-term. Here is Just Baseball's scouting report from earlier this year:

From a tools standpoint, Sato's raw power may be as close to Murakami's as anyone out of Japan, and his in-zone contact rates are sturdier than his. The glaring weakness, however, is his chase rate. It has been stagnant since his sophomore season and still sits in the bottom third of NPB hitters ... That said, Sato does immense damage on pitches in his wheelhouse, and he swings the bat at a much higher overall rate than any of those players. The result is a profile built around elite power and above-average aggressiveness coupled with swing-and-miss concerns, perhaps closer in hitter archetype to someone like Cal Raleigh or Byron Buxton.

MLB.com recently spoke to a scout who sees Sato as a corner outfielder or first baseman long-term, not a third baseman. Sato ran a 66% contact rate this season, below the 77% MLB average and in line with hitters like Brandon Lowe (67% in 2026) and Jake Burger (67%). Murakami ranked dead last among qualified hitters with a 60% contact rate in 2026.

Lowe is a reasonable offensive comp for Sato as a lefty hitter with 30-homer power and an OK walk rate. Whether Sato can stick at the hot corner is another matter. It only takes one MLB team to buy into him as a full-time third baseman, though Sato is seen as more athletic than Murakami, making the outfield a viable option. He's not necessarily destined for first base.

Players from Japan can be posted as early as Nov. 1, and, once posted, they have 45 days to negotiate and sign a contract. The entire process (passing the physical, contract signing, etc.) must be complete within the 45 days. An agreement and a handshake isn't enough. If players do not sign within those 45 days, they return to Japan, though that's unlikely for Sato.

The MLB team that signs Sato will have to pay the Tigers a posting fee that is based on the size of his contract. Here is the posting fee structure:

$5M plus 17.5% of contract value over $25M

$9.375M plus 15% of contract value over $50M

For example, the White Sox paid Murakami's former team, the Yakult Swallows, a $6.575 million posting fee on his $34 million contract. That's $5 million on the first $25 million plus 17.5% of the remaining $9 million, which is $1.575 million. The $5 million plus $1.575 million equals the $6.575 million posting fee paid to the Swallows.

Barring a surprise agreement, the owners are expected to lock out the players when the collective bargaining agreement expires on Dec. 1. The 45-day posting window was paused during the 2021 lockout, and the same strategy may be used this cycle. The Hiroshima Toyo Carp posted Suzuki on Nov. 21, 2021, his 45 days were paused when the lockout started on Dec. 1, then they resumed when the lockout ended on March 10, 2022. Suzuki signed with the Chicago Cubs on March 18.

Sato is expected to draw significant interest this offseason and not just from contending teams. Murakami's success with the White Sox, a team that went 102 losses last season to the postseason this season, means even rebuilding clubs figure to pursue Sato. He's on the right side of 30 and brings hard-to-find power potential. Some possible landing spots:

New York Mets: It seems unlikely Bo Bichette will opt out, though the Mets have an opening at first base and could also rotate Sato through the DH spot. Jorge Polanco is still under contract next season and Jared Young showed enough this year to get at-bats next year, which could perhaps steer the Mets away from Sato. Bichette opting out would change things.

New York Yankees: The Yankees received some of the worst third base production in the game in 2026 and are expected to replace incumbent Ryan McMahon this winter. They are overstuffed with first basemen (Luis García Jr., Ben Rice) and DHs (Rice, Giancarlo Stanton), so they would have to believe in Sato's ability to play the hot corner to pursue him seriously.

Philadelphia Phillies: The Phillies must replace free agent-to-be Alec Bohm at third base and they need an outfielder badly. Sato could be a fit at either position, and if push comes to shove, they can always put Bryce Harper back in the outfield and slot Sato in at first base. The only downside would be adding another lefty bat to an offense that is already heavy on lefties.

St. Louis Cardinals: St. Louis is open to adding a short-term third baseman as they wait for top prospect Jesús Báez, who slugged 25 home runs in only 59 Double-A games in 2026. Sato on a short-term contract may not be doable, but it's worth making the call. The Cardinals are a team on the upswing and the 27-year-old would fit in nicely with the rest of their core.

Washington Nationals: Washington is an arrow-up organization with the flexibility to slot Sato in at first base, third base, the corner outfield, or DH. His age lines up with their core well. Just about the only downside is adding another lefty bat to a lineup that is already heavy on lefties, but that's not a dealbreaker. The Nationals and Sato are an excellent match on paper.

#5. Jalen Hurts expected to miss rest of 2026 season after blood clots found in lungs

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Jalen Hurts is expected to miss the remainder of the 2026 season, according to multiple reports, after blood clots were found in his lungs.

The Eagles and Hurts' agent, Nicole Lynn, issued a joint statement on Monday laying out his updated diagnosis after originally announcing he had a superficial blood clot in his left calf that caused him to miss Week 6. A follow-up scan over the weekend revealed deep vein thrombosis, and he had "bilateral pulmonary emboli," meaning several blood clots were now in his lungs.

The Eagles said Hurts' prognosis is "very good" and that he is expected to make a full recovery. However, he will be treated with blood thinners, which will take him away from football activities until he is off the treatment.

"Over the last few days, Jalen Hurts has received comprehensive medical evaluations by physician experts. In the interest of transparency, we are providing additional information on the diagnosis and treatment plan related to his condition.

"Jalen was initially diagnosed by specialists in London with a left calf superficial vein thrombosis. After further testing and monitoring, the current diagnosis is a deep vein thrombosis, as well as bilateral pulmonary emboli. He is clinically stable and has no significant functional limitations. His treatment should only involve anticoagulation (i.e. "blood thinners"). During this time, he will not be allowed to participate in any contact activities, including football.

"Jalen's prognosis is very good, and we expect a full recovery. We anticipate that he will have the opportunity to resume contact football activities when off the blood thinners. In the meantime, he will remain active around the team and continue to condition. More importantly, we anticipate that he will have no long-term effects.

"We are thinking of Jalen and looking forward to a strong recovery."

No clots were found until Hurts was in London. It was initially diagnosed as a superficial blood clot. At that time, doctors advised Hurts not to sleep as a precaution, so he stayed awake for roughly 36 hours prior to the game against the Jaguars, according to reports. Despite not getting any sleep, Hurts started and threw for 220 yards and a touchdown.

It was since discovered that the blood clot was "provoked," meaning that it was caused by Hurts getting cleated in his calf during the Eagles' Week 4 loss to the Rams. That game took place a week before Philadelphia's game in London.

Hurts traveled to London that week, appearing on that week's injury report with a calf injury on Friday. He was a full practice participant that day and had no injury designation prior to the Eagles' game against the Jaguars. Hurts reportedly went to the hospital the evening prior to Sunday's game.

Philadelphia will move forward with Tanner McKee at quarterback. A 2023 sixth-round pick, McKee made his first start of the season Sunday against the Panthers. He threw for 215 yards and a touchdown in a 25-15 loss that dropped the Eagles to 2-4.

Hurts, 28, is in his seventh season with the Eagles, who selected him in the second round of the 2020 NFL Draft. During his first six seasons, Hurts earned three Pro Bowl selections and helped lead the Eagles to two NFC titles and a Super Bowl title at the end of the 2024 season. He holds the single-game Super Bowl record for rushing yards by a quarterback (72 against the Chiefs). Hurts is one of just two players (the other being Terrell Davis) to run for three touchdowns in a Super Bowl game.

Hurts was named MVP of Super Bowl LIX after amassing 293 total yards and scoring three total touchdowns in the Eagles' 40-22 win over the Chiefs. Hurts has the highest career completion percentage (73.3%) in Super Bowl history among passers with at least 40 attempts.

#6. The 76ers seem to finally have everything they need, and it makes their season both thrilling and terrifying

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

A lot has already been said about the 76ers. That isn't unusual. They tend to be one of the more talked-about teams in the NBA, just usually for all the wrong reasons. Inevitably, something tragic or comic (or both) happens, and everyone shakes their heads, has a good laugh and then waits for the next time they trip themselves up and faceplant, which often doesn't take very long.

The run-up this time has been different. The Sixers are about to begin one of their most anticipated seasons in recent memory. For the first time in a long time, there is promise. In the NBA's annual general manager survey, the Sixers received the most votes for having the best offseason. They received the second-most votes to win a vastly improved and much deeper Eastern Conference, trailing only the Knicks, the defending champions. And they were the only team other than the Spurs, Thunder and Knicks to receive a vote to win it all.

That says quite a bit about the expectations surrounding this team. So do their championship odds, tied with the Knicks (+1000 at FanDuel) and behind only the Thunder (+240) and Spurs (+270). That's the sort of elite company Philly is expected to keep after signing arguably the greatest player ever in LeBron James, and trading for Jaylen Brown coming off the best regular season of his career.

But of all the things that have been said so far about this year's version of a previously star-crossed franchise now simply laden with stars, Joel Embiid's take on the situation was perhaps the most telling. The oft-injured Sixers center has seen some stuff in his 10 NBA seasons, very little of it good, a lot of it ranging from frustrating to deeply disappointing. Technically, he's been in the league for 12 years, but he completely missed the first two seasons due to injury. That's obviously become something of a theme. Over the last three seasons, the former MVP has missed 150 games. Embiid's rash of health issues tends to pop up at the worst times, particularly around the playoffs. He's had a fractured orbital bone (twice), torn meniscus (twice), torn thumb ligament, and a bout with Bell's Palsy. Prior to last postseason, he looked to be in pretty good shape -- then his appendix quit on him and he needed emergency surgery. The man could use a break from his body.

Put all that together, and the opportunity for him to make a dent in the playoffs has been limited. He returned from the appendectomy to help the Sixers to a dramatic and unexpected first-round upset over the Celtics. The significance of that can't be overstated. No two teams have faced each other in the postseason as often as Boston and Philly. The Celtics usually beat the Sixers' heads in. This time, the Sixers won the series for the first time since 1982. It was a feel-good moment in Philly -- but it didn't last long, as the Knicks flattened them in the second round. It seems like some team or another is always giving the Sixers a proper bashing in the playoffs.

Embiid would know. He's never won more than a single series in any postseason. The closest he came was back in 2019. The Sixers had one of their best teams of the "Process" era that season. It featured Embiid, Jimmy Butler, JJ Redick (before he left for TV and eventually the Lakers head coaching gig) and prime Ben Simmons, to the extent that he had a prime, before everything went south on his game and he and the franchise went through a messy divorce. It was a good squad. They ran into the Raptors in the second round that year. The series went to Game 7, culminating in Kawhi Leonard's historic four-bounce miracle at the buzzer. That changed everything for the Raptors, who went on to win it all. It changed nothing for the Sixers, who didn't.

I was in the building that night. The ball bounced long enough on the rim that I had the time to tell the reporter next to me that it looked like the game was going to overtime. Then it didn't. The Raptors moved on and the Sixers went home like always. While Toronto celebrated, Embiid wept.

Unkind critics and online tough guys gave Embiid heat for that, but in the moment, I found it to be not just a raw, human reaction but also emblematic of how the Sixers fanbase felt as a whole. As a native Philadelphian, I've seen countless Sixers defeats. That ranks as one of the most soul-crushing, even by the standards of a team that is used to getting its heart ripped out.

In retrospect, Embiid's response to the loss also foreshadowed the agony still to come. They were close in that series. Had they won it, maybe it could have been their year. Except they didn't, and it hasn't been the Sixers year in so long that it's almost hard to remember all the way back to the last time it was.

Embiid, now 32, has been through a lot in his Sixers tenure. His new teammates might not fully appreciate just how much. Brown is a former Finals MVP and LeBron James is LeBron James. They've won it all. Embiid hasn't come close. When he was asked about everything he's been through and about the upcoming season, his reply was telling.

"I'm at the point in my career," Embiid said, "where I need to win. Between everything that's happened, that would be a good ending for the city of Philadelphia. And they deserve it."

That would be a happy ending for everyone involved, which isn't really something the Sixers are known for. That's not exclusive to Embiid or the current era. The organization hasn't made it out of the second round in 25 years. The last time they pulled it off, Allen Iverson dragged them to the Finals. That was 2001. Iverson just turned 51 if you can believe it.

The Sixers haven't won a championship since 1983 -- so long ago that it's easy to doubt if they ever will again. While the NBA was conducting that GM survey, I did some informal temperature taking of my own with people around Philly. A pair of long-time basketball writers and friends came to roughly the same conclusion and predicted the Sixers would win somewhere in the neighborhood of 50 games, then get bounced in the second round of the playoffs. Another pal was less optimistic. When I asked if there was any chance the Sixers could avoid their usual nonsense and turn in a drama-free season, he didn't have to consider the possibility at all. He just immediately laughed and shook his head. He didn't need to elaborate. A few hours later, the Sixers — always desperate for a backup center to fill the many minutes when Embiid is inevitably unavailable to play — lost Ariel Hukporti for the season with an Achilles tear. The universe has a weird way of chiming in when it comes to the Sixers.

Losing Hukporti obviously isn't ideal. For now, the Sixers will reportedly go with some combination of Adem Bona, Jabari Walker, Dominic Barlow and small-ball LeBron to back up Embiid. (And maybe a pinch of Tacko Fall, whom they signed to a two-way contract over the weekend.) There are obvious concerns there, but as Sixers-related calamities go, that's relatively minor. In fact, the usual nonsense and drama that forever surrounds the franchise have been fairly minimal in advance of the season, which does not mean they've been entirely absent.

There's been a lot of talk about James and his helicopter. People have taken videos of it leaving the practice facility and local news outlets have tracked the flights. Tyrese Maxey has joked about it. Pablo Torre, who won a Pulitzer for his investigation of the Clippers cap circumvention scheme, is now looking into James' relationship with Fanatics, which provides the helicopter for the NBA's all-time scoring leader. Carmelo Anthony came to James' defense about all that -- even though it's hardly surprising that Torre is sniffing around after former Sixers minority owner Michael Rubin, the founder and CEO of Fanatics, said so many damning quiet parts out loud.

Beyond that, there's been chatter about James commuting from New York and how he thought about going to the Knicks in free agency before ultimately signing with the Sixers. That kind of thing usually wouldn't go over well with the locals, but they're willing to give him a long runway considering he did something that almost never happens by picking Philly in the first place. There was a story about Embiid being tardy to practice, only for James to air him out -- something that was quickly denied by Embiid, James, and coach Nick Nurse, and then walked back by the original source.

And there have been the expected questions about whose team this is and how so many big-name, high-usage players are going to share one ball. Wondering about that was to be expected. Maxey is coming off the best season of his career. So is Brown. VJ Edgecombe had an excellent rookie campaign. Embiid is a former MVP. LeBron is LeBron.

But to hear them tell it, asking who's the main man is reductive. Embiid insisted that no sacrifice is necessary and no one has to take a backseat. And when Brown asked who the "alpha" is, he dismissed the notion with a curt "next question."

As Brown put it, "it doesn't have to be anybody's team."

Those are nice sentiments as far as team camaraderie goes, and they might even believe it. Of course, it's easier to believe before a single game has been played and any adversity has been faced. It should also be noted that Brown probably isn't the best messenger there, considering he and the Celtics had a pretty messy public separation this summer after spending his entire career in Boston dogged by questions of whether the team was his or Jayson Tatum's.

But if Brown and Embiid's worst indiscretions here are optimism about all this working out, they have good company. James came to town and immediately made his plans plain, promising everyone that "I didn't leave my family to lose in the second round." James has also said all the right things about fitting in with his new teammates and playing whatever role Nurse might have for him. James said he'll do "whatever they need me to do," which he figured shouldn't be difficult since "the luxury of my game is I can do everything…literally I can do everything."

An all-time quote. The man rightly does not lack confidence.

In addition to Nurse throwing James' name out as a small-ball center option, he's also mentioned running the offense through him. Nurse called James a "great offensive creator" and "table setter" and added that "if it isn't him bringing it up and starting [the possession], it's probably going to be first pass anyway to [him on] the wing."

That kind of thing provides easy fodder for skeptics of this whole experiment who wonder what trickle-down effect James will have on his teammates. How might James being the table setter impact Maxey, who made his first All-NBA team last year? Will it free up Maxey or dull his glow? How will the delicate ecosystem accommodate Edgecombe? Or Brown for that matter? How many games will the Sixers squeeze out of Embiid? How many minutes can they reasonably expect James to play when he's about to embark on his record-setting 24th season and turn 42 years old in December?

There are plenty of questions to go around, but the only good answer leads back to what Embiid said about his career and the franchise: this team has to win without delay. Anything short of a conference finals appearance will be a disaster, and even that might not qualify as a success.

Forecasts on how the Sixers will weather the season vary wildly. In the aforementioned NBA GM survey, the Sixers also got the most votes for being the toughest team to predict. That certainly tracks. As a friend and former coworker recently wrote in the Philadelphia Inquirer, the season could be great or it could blow up. That seems about right. But it's worth pointing out that everything going sideways on them is generally expected. Even considering the possibility that they might be genuine contenders is rare. When it comes to the Sixers, that's not nothing, but they still have a lot of ground to cover before it approaches reality.

#8. Brewers bash champion Dodgers to brink of NLCS sweep; CBS Sports Preseason All-America team revealed

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

This is an article version of the CBS Sports HQ AM Newsletter, the ultimate guide to every day in sports. You can sign up to get it in your inbox every weekday morning here.

One of the biggest benefits of the NIL era is that college basketball has more elite talent than ever, now that players are returning for bigger paychecks instead of bolting for NBA money at the first opportunity.

That made selecting our 2026-27 CBS Sports Preseason All-America teams especially difficult, but our experts nailed it. Each of the three teams features players who will be performing at the next level very soon, but the best of those might be Florida superstar Thomas Haugh.

As our own Isaac Trotter explains, if Haugh can improve his range shooting, he won't have to wait long to hear his name called in the 2027 NBA Draft.

When it comes to how the talent broke down by conference, it was a a pretty level playing field for the most part.

Not to spoil anyting, but Arizona freshman Caleb Holt did not make the cut. He did, however, turn some heads in the Wildcats' exhibition game.

Loyalty is an excellent quality to have in a friend or partner. It's also why we love dogs.

It should not be quite as prevalent among college football coaches, some of whom have been undone because they did what was comfortable, not what was necessarily best for the team.

Our own John Talty highlighted five high-profile coaches who have been loyal to a fault, making hires and personnel decisions that have come back to haunt them. One of those coaches is Mike Elko. After a shaky season from Marcel Reed in 2025, Texas A&M chose not to pursue an upgrade in the portal.

Instead, the Aggies gave Reed a major payday, and they'll miss the College Football Playoff because of it.

Look, it can happen to the best of us. Dan Lanning and Dabo Swinney wound up on the list, despite the success that those two have had throughout their careers.

Steve Sarkisian is another coach who has fallen into the trap of being too loyal, but he may have a huge decision on his hands in the offseason. Arch Manning has struggled enough that another year in college should be on the table. If that happens, would Sark welcome back Manning with open arms, despite his shortcomings?

Finally, one person for whom loyalty is no an issue is Missouri QB Austin Simmons. After Trinidad Chambliss won the starting job at Ole Miss last year, Simmons didn't feel the need to stick around, but there won't be bitterness when Simmons returns to Oxford this weekend.

#9. Barcelona DNA at PSG? Joan Laporta identifies similarities between Luis Enrique’s side and the Blaugrana’s iconic playing style

As the anticipation builds for the massive Champions League showdown between Paris Saint-Germain and Barcelona at the Parc des Princes, Laporta has taken a moment to reflect on the tactical identity of his opponents. The Barcelona president believes that the French side has undergone a significant transformation under the guidance of Luis Enrique, a man who knows the inner workings of the Camp Nou better than most.

"The footballing dynamics of his teams have something of the original Barca style," Laporta explained during an interview with L'Equipe. The president was quick to credit the hierarchy in Paris for their decision to appoint the Spaniard, noting the immediate impact he has made on the squad's performance and identity. "PSG's success has arrived with Enrique and he won because he gave it his personality. And when he decided to shake things up, boom! There is credit to Nasser for having bet on him, and also to Luis Campos," the Catalan chief added.

The sentiment is shared by Enrique himself, who recently commented on the tactical parallels between the two European heavyweights. The former Spain manager noted that both teams prioritize high pressing and possession-based play, making them mirror images of one another on the pitch. Enrique has been vocal about his strategy to neutralise teenage sensation Yamal by ensuring his side dominates the ball, a classic tenet of the Barcelona school of thought that he has successfully exported to the French capital.

The relationship between Barcelona and PSG has been fraught with tension for much of the last decade, fueled by the record-breaking transfer of Neymar in 2017 and the subsequent departure of Lionel Messi to Paris in 2021. However, Laporta has indicated that the ice has finally thawed between the two boardrooms.

He described a newfound mutual respect between himself and PSG president Nasser Al-Khelaifi, suggesting that the era of bitter public feuding and legal threats has been replaced by a more constructive and professional dialogue behind the scenes.

"With Nasser, I think I can say that our relationship is one of friendship," Laporta revealed, marking a stark departure from the hostilities of the previous administration. "There is a lot of respect. He manages the ECA sensationally, as does PSG."

For Laporta, this Champions League tie represents more than just a chance to reach the semi-finals; it is an "authentic" test of where Hansi Flick's rejuvenated Barcelona stand in the global hierarchy.

The Catalans have enjoyed a blistering start to the domestic season, but the Parisian test is viewed as the ultimate benchmark. Laporta believes that facing a club of PSG's stature confirms Barcelona's status as a reference point in world football, regardless of the recent financial struggles that have plagued the club's ability to compete in the transfer market.

The president remains confident in his team's ability to perform on the biggest stage, even as he acknowledges the threat posed by Enrique's disciplined side. He suggested that the upcoming match at the Parc des Princes would serve as a confirmation of both clubs' standing as elite institutions.

While Barca currently lead the way in La Liga, Laporta recently took time to defend the domestic league's integrity, even finding time to praise LaLiga president Javier Tebas for his resilience against external pressures. This focus on stability at home appears to be providing the foundation for their renewed confidence in European competition.

Week 6 gave us a handful of wide receiver breakouts that now headline the best waiver wire adds of the week. Every player in this article is available in at least half of all Yahoo leagues.

Week 6 Stock Up, Stock Down: The young receivers are here

Rivers McCown highlights four fantasy players whose fantasy football stock rose in Week 6 of the NFL season and four whose stock fell.

Rodgers is currently the QB14 on the back of the fifth-most pass attempts in the league. He finished the day with three passing touchdowns and 225 yards. It was his best fantasy outing of the year but his worst real-life performance. He gets another difficult matchup with the 49ers next week, though it also profiles as another shootout.

This is a Superflex-only add, but a rather important one. We don't yet know who the Giants will start in Week 7. Jameis Winston was pulled for McCarthy late in Week 6 and the former Viking lit the world on fire. He threw for 243 yards, a touchdown, and a two-point conversion in the fourth quarter. It's the most yards for a quarterback in the fourth quarter since 2020 and the most yards in 11 minutes of play in NFL history. In true desperation mode, McCarthy simply chucked the ball up to his superstars and let them win. His 15.6 aDOT is the highest in a game (min. 20 dropbacks) this year. McCarthy played like prime Winston after the real thing flopped. I suspect he'll get the start next week. If he plays like this again, McCarthy will be in the streaming conversation going forward.

McKee was dreadful in his first start of the year, throwing for 215 yards and a touchdown on 45 attempts. He ranked 20th out of 27 qualified quarterbacks in EPA per dropback on the week, pending Monday Night Football. Still, the news that Jalen Hurts will be sidelined for the rest of the year means McKee will make several more starts. If you are truly desperate in Superflex leagues, he's worth an add.

Travis Etienne will miss at least one more game while on IR, meaning Kendre Miller will be the Saints' lead back for another week. He saw 20-of-33 backfield carries in Week 6 and even managed two targets. Miller only went for 72 scoreless yards on his high-volume role, but the touch total was rather impressive for a member of a three-back committee. Miller will have some RB3 life when he takes on the Steelers in a week.

Johnson has seamlessly stepped in as D'Andre Swift's backup, getting on the field for exactly 40 percent of the snaps in each of his past two games. Over the past two weeks, Johnson has run a route on 37 percent of Caleb Williams' dropbacks and is being targeted on 24 percent of those routes. He also snuck in a goal line touchdown on Sunday. His role will evaporate once Kyle Monangai is healthy, but Johnson is a safe bet for a dozen touches per game until that happens.

Somehow Bam Knight returned. He made eight starts for Arizona last year but began 2026 buried behind Jeremiyah Love and Tyler Allgeier on the depth chart. With Love out for Week 6, the Cardinals simply stuck with a backfield-by-committee, giving Knight 15 carries to Allgeier's 18. Knight was far more productive, gashing the Rams for 80 yards compared to a measly 38 for Allgeier. Arizona still used Allgeier as the primary option on passing downs, but Knight managed a 40 percent route rate and saw the team's lone goal line carry. Until Love returns, Knight appears to be the 1B in his backfield.

McLaughlin and Audric Estime each saw nine carries in Week 6. Estime found the end zone but McLaughlin almost made up for that in PPR formats with four catches. McLaughlin would be a viable RB3/4 for Week 7, but the team should get one or both of Dylan Sampson and Quinshon Judkins back by Sunday. You can add McLaughlin, but the most likely outcome is that he can be cut in a few days.

Rostered in exactly half of all Yahoo leagues as of Sunday night, Bernard qualifies for this article without any caveats and is not a "Not in My League" all-star. Bernard is a perfect fit for Aaron Rodgers, operating as an easy underneath option while creating plenty of extra yards after the catch. He racked up 11 grabs on 12 targets in Week 6 and scored the game-winning touchdown to go long with 87 yards. With Roman Wilson and Michael Pittman both banged up, the second-round pick looks like a weekly WR3. If he's still out there, Bernard is the player to blow all of your FAAB on.

Cooper was activated off IR over the weekend and immediately looked like the play-making WR2 the Jets hoped they were getting at the end of the first round. The rookie reeled in six catches for 103 yards and a score.

He also had a touchdown called back via an extremely light offensive pass interference on Tim Patrick. We're working with an extremely small sample, but Cooper is averaging 4.6 yards per route run while being targeted on 28 percent of his routes. Assuming Bernard isn't available to you, this is the best waiver wire add of the week. I will be getting down 30-40 percent of my FAAB on Cooper.

Tucker blew up against a vulnerable Buffalo defense with five catches for 97 yards and a pair of touchdowns. It was his first spike week since Week 2, though he had at least four catches for 40 yards in three straight games between the spikes. Tucker has been a different player in Klint Kubiak's offense. He is on pace for a career high in yards per route run (1.96) and is posting his best season by PFF receiving grade and ESPN's Overall Score, which combines their metrics on getting open, catching the ball, and producing YAC. He isn't a true breakout bet like Cooper or Bernard, but Tucker rounds out a big three at receiver this week.

He is inevitable. Allen totaled 11 targets in Week 6. He caught eight of them for 82 yards. He has at least nine targets in three straight games. Josh Downs hasn't seen that type of receiving volume since Week 3. The ceiling with Allen is rather limited, and his role will take a hit if Tyler Warren is back from his groin injury next week. On the other hand, he has posted top-20 fantasy numbers in two of his past three starts. He should at least be rostered in most leagues.

Bourne has taken Marvin Harrison Jr.'s spot in the lineup and is already a more productive WR2 for the Cardinals. He has exactly five catches on eight targets in each of his past two games. Bourne has racked up 117 yards over the past two weeks. Bourne isn't going to threaten for a breakout season, but he's not a bad add if you desperately need WR4 points.

Noel had been percolating under the surface before Week 6 with efficient per-route numbers in a part-time role. He broke out in London with four catches for 107 yards and a touchdown. He's now averaging over 2.5 yards per route run and is on pace for nearly 1,000 yards. The bad news is that his route rate remained capped at 61 percent in Week 6, meaning the fantasy success wasn't underpinned by an improved role. Fantasy managers can hope that his role grows, but it's hard to bank on that with Tank Dell set to return and Marvin Harrison Jr. in town.

Dotson is quietly stacking games, with at least 50 yards in back-to-back-to-back weeks and two touchdowns over that stretch. His route rate climbed to 92 percent in Week 6. Dotson is more of a threat to Kyle Pitts' role than the Falcons WR3s are a threat to Dotson. He's in the FLEX mix for Week 7 against the 49ers.

Coleman has scored in three straight weeks. He has 11 catches for 182 yards over that stretch. DJ Moore left Week 4 early and missed the next two games, meaning Coleman's production has come in the absence of Buffalo's WR1. With a bye on tap for Week 7, Moore should be healthy by the next time we see the Bills. That makes Coleman a stash only in rather deep leagues.

The Jags get Week 7 off after a two-game road trip to London, so this is a stash for Week 8 and beyond. Hunter finally saw his usage on offense tick up on Sunday, catching four passes for 59 yards and a score. He only ran seven routes, but Brian Thomas Jr. wasn't far ahead with just 13 routes. Liam Coen benched BTJ in the second half and used Hunter as a part-time wideout. Whether this two-way role finally sticks is anyone's guess, but there are worse stashes in deep leagues.

Tight end is a true wasteland on waivers. Mayer is technically a backup. In reality, he's the Raiders' starting tight end and Brock Bowers is the team's WR1. Since Bowers returned in Week 3, Mayer has a 67 percent route rate with a 15 target share. He is averaging 11.5 PPR points per game over the past month. Mayer is averaging more fantasy points with Bowers healthy than he was when the star tight end was sidelined.

Pat Freiermuth was banged up in Week 6, forcing him to split snaps with Washington. The Steelers' multiple absences at wide receiver, however, put the team in 12-personnel more often, which increased the number of tight end routes up for grabs. Washington, in turn, ran 55 percent of the routes, logged a 14 percent target share, and finished the week as a low-end TE1 on the back of a short touchdown. He's nothing more than a TE2 flyer for Week 7, but that's all we're getting off waivers right now.

#11. What is Lakers' ceiling with Luka Doncic as Los Angeles' focal point?

The Los Angeles Lakers revamped their roster this offseason, officially making Luka Dončić the focal point.

As Dončić enters his third season in Los Angeles, he has already seen the legendary franchise be sold twice, but the All-Star guard has remained supportive of the ownership changes as the front office has continued to support him.

Dončić has proven he has what it takes to be a franchise star, leading a team to the NBA Finals when he took the Dallas Mavericks to the title series to end the 2023-24 season. The Boston Celtics beat the Mavericks 4-1.

It may take some time before there's a better idea of what this Lakers team can look like and what that ceiling might be, but there have been some early glimpses during the preseason.

Luka Dončić carried a heavy workload throughout the season, often playing through physical challenges as the wear of the schedule accumulated.Now sidelined for the remainder of the regular season, these images reflect moments when the strain of the year was visible as Dončić worked through injuries while leading his team.Above, Luka Dončić of the Los Angeles Lakers looks on from the bench at the end of the third quarter against the Miami Heat at Kaseya Center on March 19, 2026, in Miami, Florida.

Luka Dončić carried a heavy workload throughout the season, often playing through physical challenges as the wear of the schedule accumulated.Now sidelined for the remainder of the regular season, these images reflect moments when the strain of the year was visible as Dončić worked through injuries while leading his team.Above, Luka Dončić of the Los Angeles Lakers looks on from the bench at the end of the third quarter against the Miami Heat at Kaseya Center on March 19, 2026, in Miami, Florida.

Luka Dončić carried a heavy workload throughout the season, often playing through physical challenges as the wear of the schedule accumulated.Now sidelined for the remainder of the regular season, these images reflect moments when the strain of the year was visible as Dončić worked through injuries while leading his team.Above, Luka Dončić of the Los Angeles Lakers looks on from the bench at the end of the third quarter against the Miami Heat at Kaseya Center on March 19, 2026, in Miami, Florida.

Lakers general manager Rob Pelinka and the front office made a trade for Walker Kessler and re-signed Austin Reaves to a $185-million contract to help create a foundation alongside Dončić this offseason.

The Lakers' new big three came together for the first time against the Denver Nuggets in the preseason finale on Oct. 16, with the trio playing together in the first half.

That one half indicated it will still take some time for the trio to jell, finishing the outing at a minus-four in their 13 minutes together.

While Kessler appeared a bit out of rhythm against Nikola Jokić, he called it "a lot of fun" to play together as a trio for the first time.

Outside of the big three, Dončić showed he also has a connection building with Lakers newcomer Ziaire Williams, who was also in the starting lineup. The veteran guard found Williams for multiple lobs during the first half.

The biggest question for Dončić is whether he can stay healthy.

Dončić has continued to put in the work as well during the offseason, taking his training seriously for a second straight season.

He's come into the season in shape and looking lean to improve his on-court mobility and overall condition.

The guard had faced criticism throughout the early years of his career because of his weight and lower-body injuries.

Dončić took a step forward, playing in 64 games last season, the most he has played since the 2023-24 season when he played 70 games.

He earned his second scoring title, averaging 33.5 points per game last season. He also averaged 8.3 assists and 7.7 rebounds for Los Angeles.

Dončić will have to play like an MVP candidate again this season to help push the Lakers beyond the Western Conference semifinals.

The Oklahoma City Thunder swept the Lakers 4-0 in the conference semls last season without Dončić. He missed the Lakers' playoff run due to a Grade 2 left hamstring strain.

Dončić hosted his teammates for a minicamp in an attempt to build team chemistry after the team overhauled the roster in August.

The All-NBA player's decision to have the minicamp in the home country allowed him to remain close to his two daughters.

Dončić and his longtime girlfriend ended their engagement in March, leading to an ongoing custody battle over the daughters.

More: Luka Doncic files international petition to bring his daughters back to US

Dončić and the Lakers will host coach Steve Kerr and the Golden State Warriors at Crypto.com Arena on Wednesday, Oct. 21, in the season opener.

#14. Orioles hire new GM under Mike Elias as Baltimore tries to get back on track after rebuild stalled

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Baltimore Orioles have fortified their front office under president of baseball operations Mike Elias by hiring Jared Banner to be the club's new general manager, the team announced on Monday. Banner, who had been assistant GM of the Chicago Cubs, will "lead the organization's player development, coaching and performance efforts, while also partnering with Elias on strategy, staffing, and talent acquisition, among other duties," according to the team.

"Jared has been one of the rising talents in our league for some time now," Elias said in a statement. "He has demonstrated success running multiple different departments and has worked alongside some of the best people and front office talent in the league across multiple stops. He is a perfect fit to grow, evolve and improve the Orioles' baseball operations, and I look forward to working with him very closely as we build for 2027 and beyond."

Prior to filling that key role in the Cubs' front office, Banner had been the New York Mets' vice president of player personnel, and before that he spent some 11 years in the Boston Red Sox's front office. With the Red Sox, Banner earned World Series rings as a member of the front office for the 2007, 2013, and 2018 clubs. "I had the chance to learn from some really special people - some really great baseball minds like Theo Epstein, Jed Hoyer, Dave Dombrowski and Allard Baird. The list goes on and on," Banner told MLB.com in 2023.

Banner had recently been a candidate to become the Athletics' head of baseball operations. Instead, he'll be the Orioles' No. 2 after a search for a GM that's been ongoing for at least the past year.

Banner joins the Orioles in uncertain times. Not so long ago, the club was emerging from a deep and painful rebuild that saw them lose 115 games in 2018, 108 in 2019, and 110 in 2021. Those depths allowed them to land premium young talents like Adley Rutschman, Gunnar Henderson, and Jackson Holliday, among others. The rebuild began to bear what figured to be a lengthy harvest with a 101-win season and division title in 2023. The O's again made the postseason in 2024, but across those two seasons, they went 0-5 in playoff games. In 2025, they stumbled early on, which cost manager Brandon Hyde his job, and wound up with a sub-.500 record and last-place finish in the American League East. Hopes for a rebound in 2026 came to grief, as the Orioles went 79-82 and finished in fourth place. Now that vaunted young core is older and has stalled in certain spots, and Rutschman plays for the Boston Red Sox.

All that adds up to an uncertain future in Baltimore, and no doubt the hope is that Banner's newfound influence will shore up some of Elias' established weaknesses as a lead executive. As such, the Orioles' forthcoming offseason could be one to watch, as their winter maneuverings could signal a change in approach or at least a different means of gearing up for another run while the current core is still somewhat intact. In other words, Banner is taking on a role that may be as challenging as it is important.

#15. Jalen Hurts blood clot: Expert weighs in on Eagles' situation, and when QB could return to the field

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Editor's Note: This article was originally published on Oct. 17 after Jalen Hurts was diagnosed with a superficial blood clot. The Eagles have since announced that Hurts now has deep vein thrombosis, and multiple blood clots were found in his lungs. He is now expected to miss the remainder of the season.

Jalen Hurts' 2026 season was put on pause this week, as the Philadelphia Eagles quarterback was diagnosed with a superficial blood clot that had experienced some movement and the team placed him on IR on Saturday.

The team diagnosed the clot and informed the league of Hurts' situation last week, but he was cleared to suit up and play in their Week 5 London loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars. After a follow-up ultrasound revealed movement in the clot, the team announced that Hurts would have to sit out for at least one week while they treated him. It initially looked like the quarterback would avoid injured reserve, but ESPN reported Saturday afternoon that after consultations with doctors and experts, the Eagles decided to place Hurts on injured reserve -- meaning he will miss at least the next four games.

What is a superficial blood clot and how much time could Hurts miss? CBS Sports spoke to Dr. Henry Han at UT Southwestern to get some answers. Dr. Han is a board certified cardiologist that works at the intersection of cardiology and vascular medicine. He has seen clot-related diseases, diseases related to aneurysms, tears in blood vessels, and is very familiar with superficial vein thrombosis.

A superficial blood clot could be classified as "superficial thrombophlebitis," or a much easier term: "superficial vein thrombosis."

Dr. Han: "Basically it's a blood clot that's in one of the veins that's on the surface level underneath the skin. We typically find it in the leg, sometimes we find it in the arm. What happens is when the clot forms there, the vein gets inflamed. And so the area turns really red, it gets warm and it gets tender."

This is a situation that deserves monitoring, but it's also not the more serious "deep vein thrombosis" we've seen in sports before. Spurs superstar Victor Wembanyama, for example, was forced to miss the final 30 games of the 2024-25 season after doctors discovered deep vein thrombosis in his right shoulder. Then there's two-time NBA champion Chris Bosh, who was forced to retire early due to a clotting condition.

Dr. Han: "Superficial clots that sit near the surface on your surface veins are a lot less dangerous compared to the DVT (deep vein thrombosis). In sports we hear about the DVTs that for some athletes end up being sort of career-enders. The interesting part is that the superficial vein thromboses typically are not dangerous to that degree and the treatment for what you would need for both is a little bit different as well."

In their statement released on Thursday, the Eagles said that four days after the Week 4 loss to the Los Angeles Rams, Hurts requested treatment on his calf. He believed he was kicked or cleated in the game.

It's true that trauma to the area could have caused this clot, but we simply don't have enough information to say that definitively.

Dr. Han: "I can't speak to the exact specific case, but sort of generalities, anything that irritates a vein or slows the blood flow can trigger it. So we actually see this for people who have gotten IVs or blood draws when you have a needle in the vein that causes the irritation and damage. Other things too, like long flights. We know that certain hormone medications, pregnancy for women. But definitely trauma is one of the major causes that can cause this sort of superficial thrombophlebitis."

There are numerous cases of NFL players missing time due to blood clots. Take Carolina Panthers star right tackle Taylor Moton for example, who hasn't played at all this season because doctors found blood clots in his lung this summer. That situation required Moton to immediately be placed on blood thinners.

Moton having blood clots found in one of his lungs is a much more serious situation than superficial thrombophlebitis. It varies case to case, of course, but treatments for what Hurts has been diagnosed with can sometimes be simple.

Dr. Han: "Usually what we end up doing for standard of care is that within the first week, you can actually for a lot of patients and a lot of people, you can actually do conservative treatment, which involves things like anti-inflammatory medications, things like ibuprofen or naproxen, staying active, keeping the leg elevated, compression as sort of the first line.

"In these kinds of situations, we actually often think that the superficial thrombophlebitis is a self-contained issue. Usually what I do for my patients is that we do a follow-up scan either 7 or 14 days after the fact.  And if we see that the quality of the clot has changed, whether the clot is extended or it has moved or we do find it in deeper veins, then that kind of changes the equation for being more aggressive with treatments, which would include things as we typically do for deep vein thrombosis, the DVTs. That would be the full-on blood thinners, anticoagulants."

Dr. Han: "If it's for superficial thrombophlebitis, not every case needs to be treated with blood thinners. The cases that I treat with blood thinners are for patients that are have the clots that are getting longer or building up, so to speak, or if the patients are profoundly symptomatic with lots of pain that ibuprofen and warm compresses and elevating legs and wearing a compression garment is not cutting it. For those patients, then we do often think about reaching towards anticoagulants, blood thinners. Although the period for treatment for superficial thrombophlebitis is actually much shorter than what we would treat for DVTs. The treatment here is usually a month and a half, 45 days of treatment is sufficient, whereas the DVT sometimes is lifelong, sometimes it's between three to six months."

Everyone wants to know: when could the Eagles quarterback return to the field? Since this is not a worst-case scenario like deep vein thrombosis, we asked Dr. Han before Hurts was placed on injured reserve if there was any chance he could miss just one or two weeks

Two key factors are whether he requires blood thinners and whether this clot is indeed a self-contained issue.

Dr. Han: "It is possible. Again, just because I don't know the details of the case. The risk as I see it is being on a blood thinner and playing a contact sport would put him at extremely high risk of bleeding. And that's all bleeding complications -- blood trauma, but also internal bleeding. Oftentimes for athletics to this degree, it becomes a very strong safety consideration for being able to play or not. It's also a little hard for me to speculate if their phrasing for it -- 'It's moving' -- means that there are clots in other places, then the timeline for when he might come back is a lot harder for me to say.

"I would say the standard is if he was on blood thinners for just superficial thrombophlebitis that could be -- for symptomatic treatment -- that could be upwards of 45 days for treatment. But if there are extenuating circumstances that would have progressed or made it more dangerous or had turned into a deep vein thrombosis or something like that, then the treatment times could be much longer."

#18. The Rams might already be dead in the water

At 2-4. the season might already be over for the Los Angeles Rams.

LA may need to win 10 games in order to make the postseason. The playoffs would wipe the slate clean. All it takes it earning a spot in the tournament. The rest is a matter of taking care of business.

But getting there would mean a 8-3 record over the final 11 regular season games.

Why are 10 wins needed? Because the Silver Bulletin is projecting three NFC teams (Rams, Packers, Bears) to finish with a 9-win record. The Rams could reasonably make the playoffs with nine wins, although their chances suddenly come down to factors outside of their control.

The Packers and Bears are also 4-2 currently. Both have battled early season struggles—in Chicago's case missing Caleb Williams—to bounce back in resounding fashion. The Rams would need to keep pace with these teams and pull ahead by year's end. That isn't easy either.

So how likely would 10 wins be? It's a difficult path.

After starting 3-0, the Raiders have dropped three-straight to fall to .500. This is a game the Rams should win, although they were also expected to trounce a 1-4 Cardinals team. We know that didn't happen. Why should we be optimistic about their chances in Vegas?

The Rams would likely be favored in a rematch. Assuming Trent McDuffie and Myles Garrett play in this game after missing the first matchup, these changes would seem to favor LA. However, we can't count this as an automatic win after the Rams just suffered a disappointing loss to this team.

One of the most non-NFC West games left on the Rams' schedule. Winning the NFC West is probably out of the picture at this point. LA is instead competing against the likes of the Packers, assuming they don't win the NFC North and enter the playoffs as a division winner. The Rams will need this game for head-to-head and strength of schedule tiebreakers. In turn, losing this matchup would be catastrophic.

The Chiefs are undefeated at 5-0. Similar to the 49ers, they haven't really been challenged much yet this season. They have a point differential of 57, which means on average they are winning by more than 10 points per game.

Getting back on track means the Rams must fare well in their divisional matchups. Three games remaining against the 49ers and Seahawks gives LA upside potential. It also means three contests against formidable foes. We know Week 1 against San Francisco wasn't particularly close. LA's injury woes have only gotten worse. Why should we expect a different outcome this time?

The Rams will finish the regular season facing Seattle in two of the last three games. The currently 1-5 Tampa Bay Buccaneers are sandwiched in between.

There is a chance that Seattle already has a playoff berth locked up heading into the season finale. That could benefit the Rams if they choose to rest starters. But if the Seahawks are in full force this will likely be a close game.

#20. Thunder extend Cason Wallace on five-year, $139M deal, setting up another summer of second apron questions

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Oklahoma City Thunder have spent this offseason shedding talent, but they're ending it by retaining some. Late Sunday, they agreed to a five-year, $139 million contract extension with Cason Wallace, according to ESPN. Re-signing Wallace before the season was essential for two reasons.

First, the entire league knows how vulnerable Oklahoma City is financially, and would have jumped at the chance to sign Wallace to an inconveniently structured offer sheet in restricted free agency next summer. Second, Wallace's value may be about to rise. For the first time this season, he is expected to take on a permanent starting role.

That starting shooting guard job previously belonged to Lu Dort, who, along with Isaiah Joe and Aaron Wiggins, was traded for the sake of dodging the second apron. The Thunder opened this offseason roughly $40 million above that line and managed to sneak below it. Considering the talent in place, though, eventually going back above the line was an inevitability. Sam Presti said as much after trading Dort: "The impression I have been given is that the savings generated this summer, and from being out of the tax the last several years, will be re-allocated to future teams."

Well, one of those future teams is the 2027-28 roster, which, at this point, is essentially as expensive as this year's group was slated to be before trading away Dort, Wiggins and Joe. Let's assume Wallace's contract starts at the lowest possible figure, which would be about $23.5 million. With 13 players under contract, the Thunder are set to be roughly $25 million above the projected second apron. That doesn't take into account their three first-round picks or the possibility that they decline their team option on Ajay Mitchell in order to sign him to a team-friendly, long-term contract. In other words, the Thunder are going to be enormously expensive next season.

Now, at least according to Presti, they're prepared for that. They're also about as well-equipped to handle an enormous payroll as a team can be. This season will be Oklahoma City's first in the luxury tax of this era, so the Thunder remain years away from repeater status and the premium that comes with it. While going into the second apron once does incur some consequences, the worst of them don't come until a team's third time above the line within a five-year span. That's when a first-round pick drops to No. 30 overall. Before then, the second apron doesn't have overwhelming basketball consequences for the Thunder.

Freezing one first-round pick doesn't hurt a team that has the sort of draft surplus that they do. Restrictions relating to player acquisition through trade and free agency mean little to the NBA's best roster. The aprons make it harder to improve your team, but do little to stop teams from retaining their own players, which is what the Thunder will largely be doing moving forward.

Still, this is a small-market team that will likely have some budgetary constraints. And besides, even if the first year in the second apron wouldn't hurt that badly, the Thunder know they're going to be expensive for quite some time. They may want to delay that clock as long as possible, so the notion of ducking back under the second apron line knowing that it looms down the line isn't crazy. It's just that the Thunder have more or less trimmed any existing fat. Everyone who's getting paid on this roster now is essential.

There are rookie contracts the Thunder could move to save money. Neither Nikola Topić nor Thomas Sorber have been able to show anything yet due to injuries, and both have since been replaced internally through future draft picks. That's $12 million or so that could be dumped if neither of those players prove essential this year. There's also the matter of those three first-round picks. Ideally, the Thunder would probably like to trade one or two of them into the future. They just don't have roster spots for that many rookies, let alone money.

Still, if Oklahoma City actually does intend to duck below the second apron next summer (which, again, is no given), that probably means moving a core player. Maybe Aday Mara proves ready for a major role early enough that Isaiah Hartenstein proves expendable. Maybe Alex Caruso finally starts to show his age. Maybe someone bowls them over in an offer for Wallace, Jalen Williams or Chet Holmgren, though such a move is certainly unlikely. Until we see the season play out, we can't say for certain who, if anyone, makes sense to move. But with a big Mitchell contract looming in a year or two, the odds would suggest that someone will be.

This is the NBA's ultimate first-world problem. We've had four champions crowned since the 2023 CBA was agreed to: the Denver Nuggets, Boston Celtics, the Thunder and the New York Knicks. All four have elected to sacrifice talent at the altar of the aprons. Accumulating the sort of talent it takes to win it all today typically means giving some of it up in the name of sustainability. You can't keep everyone anymore. For now, at least, the Thunder are keeping Wallace.

#21. NBA storylines to watch in 2026-27: Can the 76ers sacrifice? Is Victor Wembanyama unstoppable?

Welcome, friends. After what has seemed like the longest offseason in basketball history, the official start of the 2026-27 NBA season tips off Tuesday.

A summer full of signings, scrimmaging and scandal has laid the runway for what should be one of the most compelling campaigns in recent memory. Here are five things we'll be paying close attention to.

Join or create a Yahoo Fantasy Basketball league for the 2026-27 NBA season

Assuming the new-look 76ers aren't on pace to break every standing NBA offensive record, someone (or multiple someones) will need to concede certain aspects of their game, contrary to what Joel Embiid boldly declared last week.

We're not going to pay too much attention to their 27th-ranked offense through four preseason games — a plethora of moving parts were at work here — but it's important to note some stylistic changes that should spill over to the regular season. Players like Embiid and Jaylen Brown, who have historically been focal points, have seen immediate changes in their usage rates (28.8 for Embiid, 26.2 for Brown) — particularly Brown, who is seeing almost 10% less of the ball than in his final season in Boston.

LeBron James #23, Joel Embiid #21, Jaylen Brown #7, and Tyrese Maxey #0 of the Philadelphia 76ers look on against the Boston Celtics during a preseason game at Xfinity Mobile Arena on October 16, 2026, in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images)

Incorporating LeBron, who I believe is still the most important piece of the equation, hasn't taken as long as I would have assumed. His whopping 42.9 assist rate this preseason is higher than at any point over the past five seasons, which isn't saying much because it's early October, but it's still clear he's trying to ingratiate himself, and the team is bending to his tendencies (Philly led the league in assist rate this preseason).

What we do have is an idea of how the 76ers will operate. They'll shoot a bunch of 3s and play at an uptempo pace to maximize how lethal James and Tyrese Maxey are in space. More focus will be put on transitional defense than on crashing the offensive glass, and expect a flurry of smart off-ball movement from the Philly 4 to account for their lack of elite individual shooting. The biggest "sacrifices" will need to come from Embiid and Brown. More screening angles, less stationary activity around the nail and blocks for Embiid, less stagnation from Brown. This experiment can work, but only with clear understanding across the board.

One of the joys about the flurry of offseason movement is when the excitement about new star duos becomes tangible. It's even more heartwarming seeing how these partnerships empower one another.

Anthony Edwards and LaMelo Ball are long-lost cousins, bringing new life to the Midwest. Paul George recently spoke about playing with Jayson Tatum and rediscovering a passion for playing that was lost previously. Social media recently captured a moment between Bam Adebayo and Giannis Antetokounmpo where the Heat center urged his new teammate to be more aggressive, taking shots he routinely does behind the scenes in practice.

But what does all of this look like X's and O's-wise once the real games start and within the context of their teams? How will the Wolves react to the potential staggering of Edwards and Ball from a defensive standpoint? Can George continue to showcase more of a role-playing spirit as he did toward the end of his 76ers tenure — and how does Boston's playmaking tree change alongside Derrick White and Payton Pritchard? In Miami, does Giannis adopt more of a lead playmaker role and does that affect Davion Mitchell's development and expectations? Is there another lever to pull when Miami's floor spacing caves in? What about up north in Toronto, where Kawhi Leonard and Scottie Barnes stem from the same defensive tree — is there enough perimeter versatility to become more aggressive in passing lanes for the others? So many new partnerships, so many new questions.

What do you do next as a 22-year-old generational talent, coming off the first unanimous Defensive Player of the Year award in NBA history and your first Finals trip? It's hard to imagine how much better Victor Wembanyama can get, but the Frenchman's humble-yet-confident nature, combined with head coach Mitch Johnson's creativity, could yield some tantalizing results.

Perhaps it's due to his sheer presence within a Spurs organization that built its reputation on shared playmaking responsibilities, but Wemby becoming a more involved (and capable) creator is exactly what San Antonio needs with their new three-guard setup. In the preseason, Wembanyama was often seen conducting traffic from the top of the key and the slot, allowing the likes of Dylan Harper and Stephon Castle to slash to the rim and affording the Spurs as much space as functionally possible. There's a clear focus to get him more centralized to San Antonio's half-court scheme, one that will improve his already impressive processor and intangibles.

Last season, Wembanyama's assist rate (17.0) and assist-to-turnover ratio (1.28) were positive and indicative of growth in a scaled-up role. His preseason figures jumped (24.5 and 1.71, respectively), and this is still without Tobias Harris, who is currently sidelined with a calf issue. Featuring Wemby at the beginning of sets as opposed to having him deploy as a finisher certainly puts more trust in the surrounding talent, but there's enough depth and versatility to raise the Spurs' floor and ceiling by some notches.

The story of the summer has been written, discussed and talked about ad nauseam, but how exactly the league plans on moving on from the Clippers' cap-circumvention scandal — and the potential trickle-down effects for other teams in their dealings — is fascinating.

Over the years, the NBA has tried to curb nefarious activity, from anti-tanking rules and new measures in place to how injuries are reported, free agency no-nos and everything in between. What hasn't been as much of a focus, at least until now, is how to effectively govern contracts.

Take Milwaukee's Gary Trent Jr., for example. The veteran wing was one of the league's bottom-40 performers last season while playing on a minimum contract. How he somehow parlayed that production into a new four-year, $64 million deal is a question only a league internal investigation can answer. But the issue isn't as much about why Trent got a payday in 2026 as it is about what went on in the previous years under the guise of smaller compensation. Did anything take place that shouldn't have?

Will every signing from this point onward be met with doubt and wonder? Are teams still willing to blur the lines between professional and personal if the outcome is adding star talent, boosting the local economy and increasing organizational valuation? It's such a murky lake to wade into, especially considering the Kawhi Leonard fallout, suspensions, fines, and, more importantly, morality and dignity.

Commissioner Adam Silver, the league office and the Board of Governors went to great lengths to curb the tanking epidemic, resulting in an expanded draft lottery, a new lottery ball setup and stricter pick rules. Will it work?

Under the new rules, teams are prohibited from selecting in the top five in three successive seasons. With these updated guidelines, teams like Utah (who selected fifth in 2025 and second in 2026) would be strongly discouraged from tanking, which is refreshing. The Jazz lost starting center Walker Kessler in free agency — and reserve Jusuf Nurkić is sidelined as well — but adding Jaren Jackson Jr. at the trade deadline last season and drafting Darryn Peterson with the No. 2 pick gives them a strong, competitive base to build on.

The general thought process here is that the more often teams show up in the draft lottery, the less they should want to return to the bottom. Let's exclude the Chicagos and Memphises of the world; we're not expecting them to suddenly flip the page and be viable franchises (although I'm much higher on the Grizzlies than the average person). But the Wizards (who had the No. 1 pick in 2026), Mavericks (No. 1 in 2025) and Hornets (No. 4, 2025) all seem to be building toward winning programs. Enough summer business has transpired within those organizations to suggest such, and diving back toward the bottom in some faint hope of landing on another top prospect — in a less-than-stellar 2027 crop — seems suboptimal.

Where it gets interesting is how the "3-2-1" rule now awards the eighth-placed team in each conference with a lottery ping-pong ball. Those teams would have a 2.7% chance at landing the top overall pick (as opposed to a zero-percent chance previously) — and could potentially alter how teams operate over the final few weeks of the regular season. Does a team sitting in sixth or seventh place, fully aware of its realistic contention chances, take a step back and try for lottery luck? This expansive approach from Silver, while bold and noble, could open up a whole different set of unknowns.

#26. Colts fire GM Chris Ballard as pressure mounts on Shane Steichen, staff after back-to-back losses

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Indianapolis Colts are in search of a new general manager. The franchise announced that it fired Chris Ballard following its 2-4 start to the season and back-to-back losses, the most recent of which came against the previously winless Tennessee Titans.

Ballard had been under pressure since the second half of last season, when the Colts lost seven consecutive games and eight of their final nine to close the year. Colts owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon, when she made the decision to retain Ballard and the coaching staff after that disappointing finish, set the expectation that improvement must come in 2026.

"I am grateful to Chris for his years of service to the Colts and for everything he poured into this organization," Irsay-Gordon said in a statement. "He cared deeply about our team and our community, and we wish Chris and his family all the best. As I said at the start of the season, the sense of urgency has never been higher. Our standard is to compete for championships, and I believe a change in leadership is necessary to meet that standard."

We have relieved Chris Ballard of his duties as General Manager. pic.twitter.com/BleD6bfTsG

This season was Ballard's 10th as the general manager. Under his watch, the Colts posted a 72-82-1 record and were 1-2 in the postseason. Time ran out on his tenure following five consecutive years without a playoff appearance, which placed Indianapolis in a tie for the third-longest active drought in the NFL. Only the Atlanta Falcons (2017) and New York Jets (2010) have waited longer for a return to the playoffs.

What's more, the Colts were the only team in the AFC South to fail to win the division during Ballard's tenure. Each of the other franchises won it at least twice.

"Making the change during the season was a deliberate decision," Irsay-Gordon said. "Waiting would only delay the important work that needs to begin now. We will conduct a thorough search for our next general manager and take the time necessary to identify the right leader for the future of the organization. I also want to be clear: this decision does not change our goals for the season. We have a lot of football in front of us, and I expect us to compete, improve, and win football games."

Ballard was in the final year of his contract and said before the start of Year 10 that he would not sign an extension prior to the start of the season. Irsay-Gordon's comments about his retention after 2025 indicated that he would have had to deliver a bounce-back season to earn another contract.

The first domino has fallen in Indianapolis, and it is now on Shane Steichen to prevent a chain reaction. The fourth-year coach entered the season on the same kind of hot seat as Ballard, because Irsay-Gordon said that he, too, understood the sense of urgency had never been higher. With one man fired, the focus now shifts to the other. Barring an in-season turnaround, Steichen could soon find the same fate.

Steichen can only operate with the players presented to him, and that Ballard was the first to go shows the Colts' issues go deeper than the coaching staff. There are clear roster deficiencies that limit the team's potential. At the same time, though, successful coaches make the most of what they have at their disposal, and Steichen is missing the opportunity to do so. The 2-4 start to the season puts Steichen on pace for the worst year of his tenure. With watchful eyes scrutinizing his every move, the team seems to have regressed.

Boos rained down from the stands inside Lucas Oil Stadium on Sunday during the 26-20 loss to the Titans. Steichen said after the game that he does not blame fans for booing "one freaking bit." While some change is clearly necessary, Steichen committed on Daniel Jones as the team's starting quarterback and said, "We've got a lot to fix, and we've got to fix it in a hurry."

When the Colts opened the 2025 season at 7-1, Ballard decided to push all of his chips forward and trade future capital for an asset that could help the team capitalize on its hot start. The move backfired.

Ballard gave up two first-round picks and wide receiver Adonai Mitchell for cornerback Sauce Gardner, and neither side of the deal worked in his favor. Gardner has struggled during his time in Indianapolis, while the New York Jets cashed in by constructing a young and promising offensive core with its newfound assets.

While that was the most glaring single failure of Ballard's tenure, his missteps primarily occurred at the quarterback position and in succession, putting the Colts in a hole they could not climb out of. In the years since Andrew Luck's retirement, Ballard was unable to find a long-term solution at the position. Only two quarterbacks started consecutive season openers, and neither of them has made it to the playoffs.

During that stretch, the Colts used a first-round pick on Richardson, who did not amount to anything more than a backup. They also gave Jones a two-year, $88 million contract extension in March despite the fact that he tore his Achilles last season. Those investments aged poorly, as did many of Ballard's moves in the latter stages of his tenure.

#32. Baltimore Orioles hire Jared Banner as general manager to work alongside team president Mike Elias

The Baltimore Orioles have hired Jared Banner as general manager to work alongside team president Mike Elias.

The Orioles announced the move Monday. Banner was the assistant GM of the Chicago Cubs, taking on that role in 2024. He's also been a vice president of special projects and vice president of player development for the Cubs.

"When I first heard Mike's vision, I knew it was something I wanted to be a part of," Banner said in a statement. "The Orioles are a storied franchise with a passionate fanbase, a historic ballpark, and an organization full of talent."

Banner's arrival comes with Baltimore's front office under increasing pressure to reverse the team's decline the past couple seasons. Elias appeared to have built the Orioles into a force when the team won 192 games in two seasons from 2023-24. Since then, Baltimore has managed only 75 wins in 2025 and 79 this year.

"Jared has been one of the rising talents in our league for some time, now," Elias said. "He has demonstrated success running multiple different departments and has worked alongside some of the best people and front office talent in the league across multiple stops. He is a perfect fit to grow, evolve and improve the Orioles' baseball operations."

Banner is a Brooklyn, New York, native. He played baseball at Amherst College and was a fellow in the baseball operations department of the Boston Red Sox in 2007. He spent 11 years with the Red Sox, working in player development and amateur scouting before becoming assistant director of player personnel in 2013.

He was Boston's vice president of player personnel in 2017-18 before becoming executive director of player development of the New York Mets. Then he joined the Cubs in late 2020.
