#33. Nets 2026-27 season preview and prediction

After two seasons of collecting top picks in the 2025 and 2026 drafts, the Nets seem ready to compete again. Brooklyn has little incentive to lose on purpose, as the Houston Rockets own swap rights to the Nets' 2027 first-round pick.

Brooklyn already has forward Michael Porter Jr., who had a career year in 2025-26. With the addition of three-time All-Star Julius Randle via trade, the Nets now have two players to rely on to create shots. But can the rest of the team's youth join them for the ride? Let's dive into what this season should look like.

The addition of Randle should help address Brooklyn's offense that ranked dead last in offensive efficiency (108.2 points per 100 possessions) last season. Over the last several years, Randle has proven that he can create his own scoring opportunities, averaging over 20 points a night six of his last eight seasons. But where he should have the most impact is creating looks for others. The power forward has averaged at least 4.1 assists in all of the past six seasons.

Brooklyn can run its offense through Randle, who is capable of initiating through pick-and-rolls as a screener or ballhandler. He should also help put Brooklyn's other players in more advantageous positions to score. A beneficiary from Randle's presence will be Porter. The small forward is coming off a strong debut season with the Nets, averaging 24.2 points, 7.1 rebounds and 3.0 assists in 52 games.

Despite the career year, Porter's efficiency dipped slightly. Adding a scorer and playmaker like Randle should allow Porter to slot into a role as second option with easier scoring opportunities. This year is important for Porter. He's eligible for a contract extension, so proving that last year wasn't a flash in the pan will be important for his future with the team.

Despite making three All-Star teams, Randle does have his flaws. He can be careless with the ball, creating turnovers. His defensive effort waxes and wanes on a regular basis. And he's a career 33.2 percent shooter from the three-point line, making him a suboptimal floor spacer.

But Brooklyn is aiming for respectability, which Randle brings as a proven veteran. And we've seen Nets head coach Jordi Fernandez excel in the past despite a limited roster.

The Nets have had seven first-round picks over the past two years. Two of those seven players seem guaranteed to receive consistent minutes: Egor Dëmin and rookie Mikel Brown Jr.

The sixth pick in the 2026 NBA Draft, Brown had a decent Summer League. He only played in Brooklyn's preseason finale after missing time with an injury. At 20 years old, Brown has potential as a shot creator and playmaker at the point guard position. But it will likely take him time to establish a consistent NBA rotation player.

Entering his sophomore season, Dëmin was spoon fed minutes in his rookie campaign, where he showed that he makes good reads as a passer. Dëmin also shot 38.5 percent from the three-point line. However, he needs to improve as a driver and finisher around the paint to be a starting caliber player. There are high hopes for his second season.

Brown and Dëmin will be given tons of opportunity. And with Dëmin's 6-9 frame, they both should be able to play in the backcourt together.

Outside of Randle, the Nets made a couple of moves in free agency, signing center Moe Wagner and guard Keon Ellis to contracts. Reserves Josh Minott and Terance Mann could also see some time.

With very few veterans on the roster there will be opportunities for the five other recent first-round picks. Nolan Traoré, Ben Saraf, Danny Wolf, Drake Powell and Joshua Jefferson will all have chances to crack the rotation. Specifically, Traoré, Saraf, Wolf, and Powell are all entering their second season. They will have to show some progress to justify a long-term roster spot past this season.

Sep 28, 2026; Brooklyn, NY, USA; Brooklyn Nets Mikel Brown Jr. (0) poses for a portrait during media day at Brooklyn Nets HSS Training Center. / Vincent Carchietta-Imagn Images

To acquire Randle, the Nets had to send mainstay Nic Claxton to the Chicago Bulls in a three-team deal. Claxton's defense and rebounding had dipped over the past few years. The center's departure creates an opportunity for Day'Ron Sharpe to start at the five. Sharpe re-signed on a two-year, $20 million deal during the offseason.

Sharpe has been a per-minute darling over the past several years, dominating opposing backup centers by feasting on the offensive boards and finishing around the basket. Over five seasons, Sharpe is averaging 16.3 points, 13.7 rebounds and 3.4 assists per 36 minutes. His work on the offensive glass will be a big help to Brooklyn creating more scoring opportunities. When Sharpe is on the floor, the Nets have played better. Teams outscored Brooklyn by 4.3 points per 100 possessions in 1,160 minutes last year, a figure far better than the -12.9 net rating the Nets had in Claxton's minutes.

The question is can Sharpe be healthy and withstand a bump in minutes? He's never played more than 62 games in a season and never averaged more than 18.7 minutes in a season. Also, he will now be matched up with the likes of Nikola Jokić, Karl-Anthony Towns and Bam Adebayo, a step up from his days as a backup.

The Nets should be better than last year. The addition of a multi-time All-Star like Randle is a step in the right direction. And the NBA's arrangement to disincentivize tanking of the draft will make the team naturally more competitive. But that also means the competition will also be trying.

Brooklyn's lack of depth and heavy reliance on unproven youngsters means it's unlikely the club will be competing for a playoff spot. Dëmin and Brown will need to wildly exceed expectations for a massive leap. Let's go with 30-52.

#34. Falcons make quarterback change, signing Andy Dalton and releasing Cooper Rush

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Atlanta Falcons are making changes to their quarterback room. The club is signing veteran signal-caller Andy Dalton, according to ESPN. In a corresponding move, Atlanta is releasing Cooper Rush, who started the first two games of the regular season.

It's been a little bit of a whirlwind for Dalton over the past two weeks. The 38-year-old had spent the entire offseason and first month of the regular season with the Philadelphia Eagles. Dalton initially won the backup job in Philly behind Jalen Hurts coming out of training camp over Tanner McKee, but was recently released on Oct. 9.

Dalton has been in the NFL since the Cincinnati Bengals selected him in the second round of the 2011 NFL Draft out of TCU. After serving as Cincinnati's starter for nine seasons from 2011 to 2019, Dalton has bounced around the league quite a bit, largely in a backup capacity. He's made stops in Dallas, Chicago, New Orleans, and Carolina on top of his most recent stint with Philadelphia.

For his career, he's completed 62.6% of his passes and has a passer rating of 87.4. The last time Dalton was on the field was back in Week 3 of this season. He made a brief appearance in Philly's loss to Chicago, throwing one pass that was picked off.

Now, Dalton joins a Falcons quarterback room headlined by starter Michael Penix Jr. and backups Tua Tagovailoa and Jack Strand.

It's not entirely surprising that the Falcons showed Rush the door. The offense was a mess over the first two weeks when he was under center, averaging just eight points per game. Rush also completed just 54.5% of his passes to go along with a 51.9 passer rating. He threw two interceptions in each of his starts this season and was even benched for Strand in the Week 2 defeat to the Panthers.

The Falcons knew what they had in Rush, and it wasn't great. With Dalton available, they get an upgrade along the QB depth chart. That cannot be overstated, given the durability concerns surrounding Michael Penix Jr.

On top of missing the first two weeks as he recovered from the season-ending ACL tear he suffered last season, Penix has also been in-and-out of the lineup with a rib injury. While he hasn't missed a game due to the injury, he was unable to finish the team's Week 5 loss to the Ravens in overtime. That thrust Tagovailoa into the fray, and he threw a game-clinching interception. If the Falcons aren't entralled with Tagovailoa, there's possibly a window for Dalton to climb up to be QB2 behind Penix.

#39. Knicks 2026-27 season preview and prediction

The Knicks entered last season with the highest expectations in recent franchise history. This year, they enter the campaign having finally met them for the first time in 53 seasons.

For many that would be enough, but this squad looks intent on repeating, which would break the NBA's streak of eight consecutive different title winners.

With the roadmap already laid out for more or less the same roster, there's no reason New York shouldn't be right there once again.

Head coach Mike Brown was brought in for one reason -- to get his team over the hump behind increased communication, a reformed offensive system, and heavier reliance on their depth. He accomplished all of the above, giving the Knicks a blueprint of a championship season they can fall back on if things get tough.

But Brown's success wasn't immediately apparent. As promised, he spent much of the regular season experimenting with schemes and rotations.

At times, that left some members of the team unsure of their roles. At others, the team was stuck in a rut. But everything clicked beginning with Game 4 of the first round of the playoffs in Atlanta.

Everybody comfortably settled into their roles at once, with the big change being how the team utilized Karl-Anthony Towns' playmaking. Each player locked in defensively and flourished as part of the team concept offensively.

Jalen Brunson continued his postseason heroics while mixing in enough off-ball play to keep him fresh. OG Anunoby put together a historically efficient scoring run.

They found basketball nirvana, entering a flow state of ball movement and abandoning any other motives. How much of this can they carry over with the ground shifting underneath them?

While the Knicks brought back most of their championship roster, this team isn't identical to the one that won it all. They lost Mitchell Robinson, their backup center who was a key man all season but especially in slowing down Victor Wembanyama in the NBA Finals.

Replacing him is Andre Drummond, another rim-runner with a knack for offensive rebounding, though generally considered a tier below Robinson overall. Drummond will bring durability, free throw shooting and a couple other skills Robinson lacked, but this potential downgrade could impact their title hopes.

While the rest of the core roster is more or less the same, the conference surrounding the Knicks has improved dramatically. Philadelphia added LeBron James and Jaylen Brown after their Eastern Conference Semifinals beatdown at the hands of New York, Indiana is getting a healthy Tyrese Haliburton back, the Heat added Giannis Antetokounmpo, and Toronto added Kawhi Leonard.

This, while contenders like Boston, Cleveland, and Detroit remain in the picture. Even if the Knicks wholly recapture their magic, facing stiffer competition makes repeating much harder.

Jun 10, 2026; New York, New York, USA; New York Knicks guard Jalen Brunson (11) reacts in the fourth quarter against the San Antonio Spurs during game four of the 2026 NBA Finals at Madison Square Garden. / Brad Penner - Imagn Images

But perhaps the biggest year over year difference is the black cloud that's hung overhead the past few weeks -- extension talks. Towns, Josh Hart, and Miles McBride can all test free agency relatively soon, with the front office shelving extension talks until later in the season.

Playing through uncertain long-term security can be a distraction, and if the Knicks re-engage on talks before the trade deadline unsuccessfully, it could open a much bigger can of worms. But all parties seem to want to come together on this, so there's reason for optimism.

Finally, how does Brown adjust to all of this? Fans shouldn't expect him to stay content with last year's playbook and approach, and to continue experimenting with options through this regular season.

He's mentioned evolving the Towns hub package as well as working in additional pick-and-roll reps for Anunoby and Mikal Bridges. There's sure to be additional twists on the winning formula as well.

The Knicks open up their repeat run against a slew of contenders, so the first month of the season will serve as an early test of the team's preparedness. How they set the pace - hangover or hunger - will tell us a lot about the season to come.

It'll be interesting to see how else Brown messes with his talent. One name that deserves added attention is Mohamed Diawara, who had an impressive though short-lived rookie season.

He's arguably the team's most tantalizing prospect, and as a big wing helps address a couple needs. If he can keep up his 40 percent shooting clip from three and show a little more consistency in his dribble and defensive games, watch out.

Then there's James Wiseman, the former second overall pick that was brought into training camp and earned himself the third string center spot. That may not seem like a crucial position, but Towns' recurring foul trouble and the scarcity of reliable backups make him a pivotal piece.

Can he shake off his injury history to recapture some of his lottery upside?

Bench ball handling is another point of emphasis, with Jordan Clarkson moving more into a wing role and McBride potentially on the chopping block. Jose Alvarado has been their go-to but can have rough stretches, leaving Tyler Kolek as the remaining option here.

Whether we see more opportunities for Kolek or a trade, getting Brunson adequate ball-handling help proved invaluable during last year's playoffs and will be this year, too.

Finally, the age old question for any contender. Now that everybody's individual sacrifices paid off, will they continue to sacrifice, or will some guys now look to cash in on their own success, especially with extensions and aprons being a hot button issue?

The Knicks have some concerns on the margins, but this group is returning healthy and largely intact, giving them some of the best title hopes in the league. The Knicks repeat as champions, 4-2 in the NBA Finals over San Antonio.

Ben Wiggins, the son of five-time Olympic champion Sir Bradley Wiggins, has signed his first professional contract with Australian team Jayco-Alula.

The 21-year-old, winner of world junior individual time trial silver in 2023, achieved a top-10 finish in the men's race at the Tour of Britain in September.

"It's a really special feeling to be joining the World Tour next year and to be racing for Team Jayco Alula is a dream come true," said Wiggins.

Wiggins began his cycling career in 2022 when he signed as a junior rider for the Fensham Howes-MAS Design team.

#42. Why Kevin Durant completely missed Mat Ishbia's point about his Suns tenure, building a championship culture

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Kevin Durant is playing the "blame KD" hashtag card on social media after Suns owner Mat Ishbia went on CNBC and said, "bringing in super talented players like Kevin Durant doesn't necessarily lead to championships." There was a bit more context to Ishbia's comments, which we'll get to, but Durant took offense to the headline and, predictably, fired back at Ishbia.

Durant: #blameKD even though KD stayed on top of his game at 36 and got u back this "culture" you love so much. Aye, Matthew acts like I got arrested for a DUI or sumn. Back to threads 😂😂😂😂😂😂😂

Ishbia: You obviously didn't watch the clip. 😂 Didn't blame you @Kdtrey5, but am happy with the culture we are building here in Phoenix. We got the right guys and right focus now and are excited for this season. ... Good luck this season in Houston.

Durant: U should be giving Thanks every chance u get. You don't have to pay me an absurd amount of money to play for another team.

So let's address this one comment at a time, beginning with Ishbia's original answer, in its entirety, when he was asked on CNBC what, with the benefit of hindsight, he had learned from the trade his Suns made for Durant two days after his purchase of the team became official in February of 2023.

"The team was I think the [No.] 8 or 9 seed [in the Western Conference] when I bought the team," Ishbia said. "We had some good young players, and [the question was]: Can we get over the top? I basically was told, 'Hey, as an owner, stay out of it. Give them some money. And so I said, 'Hey listen, we'll go into the luxury tax, go do whatever it takes to try to win a championship.

"And so, we did that," Ishbia continued. "But it was more going and getting Kevin Durant. Which ... good player, done a lot of great things, won two championships before, but it was not aligned with my vision. We had a couple years and it did not succeed, as we're well aware of at this point.

"After that year, I decided [to] trade Kevin Durant, bring in my [own] GM (Brian Gregory replaced James Jones), bring in a new coach (Jordan Ott replaced Mike Budenholzer, who had replaced Frank Vogel), and get extremely involved personally with the type of guy and type of person we want in the organization, not just on the court but off the court.

"I'm not saying [that type of person is] Kevin Durant or not Kevin Durant, but here's what I will say: It is Dillon Brooks. It is Jordan Goodwin. It is Collin Gillespie. Of course Devin Booker. I'm not going to name every one of my players, but we've defined what matters to us. We have a thing called Suns DNA. The type of player that we believe in, that we want, and it's a team that the fans will be proud of.

"Everyone thought we were going to be the worst team in the league last year. We made the playoffs. Won 45 games. We're going to build on that. So what I've learned, my biggest lesson ... it's not positive or negative about Kevin Durant. We have to define what we're about in Phoenix, and then stick with it. And believe in our vision and our path. And I didn't do that in the beginning. I kind of just threw money at the problem.

"... There was not a defined culture and North Star where we were going [as an organization]," Ishbia concluded. "And therefore, bringing in super-talented players like Kevin Durant doesn't necessarily lead to championships."

Of course he does. In fact, he didn't even really need the "necessarily" qualification. Unless we're talking about the Warriors (who had Stephen Curry, and, by extension, the sort of foundational championship culture to which Ishbia is referring, and were therefore an exception to this rule), bringing in Durant has definitively not led to championships -- or frankly even honest championship contention. Not for the Nets. Not for the Suns. And so far, not for the Rockets.

That's not the dig on Durant that it sounds like. Throughout NBA history, there are very few examples of a team without an incumbent championship superstar winning a ring by way of a hired hand. The 2016 Cavaliers and 2020 Lakers did it with LeBron James, who's the ultimate exception to this rule. He wins everywhere he goes. It's one of the brightest feathers in his GOAT-case cap.

Other than that, you've got Kawhi Leonard in Toronto, Jalen Brunson in New York, and Kevin Garnett and Ray Allen with the 2008 Celtics as the only examples this century. It just doesn't often happen that a mercenary superstar parachutes into an organization and delivers a title, and certainly not right away. Brunson needed four years and a slew of significant roster moves around him to make it happen with the Knicks.

Because Ishbia is right. You generally need an established culture with the right support system, from the role players to the coaches and the front office, in place first. Doing it the other way around is like trying to build a skyscraper on a crap foundation, and we've seen such structures fail over and over. James Harden with, well, every team he's ever gone to after Houston, including Durant's Nets, is the perfect example.

All of which is to say, when Ishbia says "bringing in super-talented players like Kevin Durant doesn't necessarily lead to championships," he's just telling the truth. It's pretty convenient, now that we all know how it turned out, that he's saying he never wanted to go the Durant route in the first place, but nonetheless, he's admitting that he messed up in trying to microwave the Suns like an overnight fantasy team.

You can't do that these days. Especially with the way the aprons are restricting expensive roster building moving forward. There's a reason we don't see teams depleting their rosters -- as the Suns did in offloading the likes of Mikal Bridges, Cam Johnson, Chris Paul, Jae Crowder and Deandre Ayton from their 2021 Finals team -- just to service their superstar fetishes anymore.

All Ishbia is saying is he has learned from his own mistakes how important roster depth, coaching and culture are to a championship pursuit, and that even an all-time talent like Durant isn't enough to overcome the absence of those organizational elements.

In this case, not really. He's right that he "stayed on top of his game at 36" and was individually spectacular in his two and a half seasons with the Suns, as he has been for his entire career, but Ishbia never attacked his personal performance. In fact, he never really personally attacked Durant at all, although you can understand the offense a Hall of Famer would take to being painted as a player with less "Suns DNA," which is code for winning DNA, than Brooks and Gillespie.

But the bottom line is the Suns, with guys like Brooks and Gillespie playing their ass off every single night, were a better team last year without Durant than they were with him the year prior when they won 36 games and missed the playoffs.

Frankly, it's almost baffling that Durant could say with a straight face that he brought the culture back to Ishbia and the Suns. In the two and a half seasons before Durant arrived, the Suns were a model franchise that had made the Finals, finished as the West's No. 1 and No. 2 seeds in consecutive seasons, and won nearly 70% of their regular-season games. In the two and a half years with Durant, they lost nearly half their regular-season games, and in the two full seasons they had him, they got swept in the first round and missed the playoffs entirely.

That's not to say any of that was Durant's fault, at least in the sense that he was always individually excellent on the court. Reasonable minds can disagree as to the additive power of Durant's particular basketball brand (it's a question of how much he raises the level of those around him), but never his own production. It's just impossible to compete for championships without all your organizational I's dotted and T's crossed.

That's the lesson Ishbia is saying he has learned. That you can't win by "throwing money" at your problems. It probably applies more to the Bradley Beal disaster than the trade for Durant, but the general point is the same. You have to fix these problems from the inside out, and the simple truth is that Durant has been parachuting in from the outside trying to save dying teams since he left Golden State. Almost nobody succeeds in that mission. Not even one of the 10-15 greatest players to ever live, as many, including myself, believe Durant to be.

The Philadelphia Eagles will be without quarterback Jalen Hurts for the remainder of the 2026 season, per reports. It is now being reported that tests over the weekend revealed that Hurts has multiple blood clots in his lungs.

Ian Rapoport is reporting that Hurts played in London against the Jacksonville Jaguars without having slept because sleeping was a risk.

That, of course, begs the question of just how much the Eagles' coaching and medical staffs knew of his condition and why they would allow him to play football if sleeping was too risky.

From the perspective of the New York Giants, the loss of Hurts is an opportunity. The Giants may have imploded against the New Orleans Saints and have fallen to 3-2-1 on the season, but they still have a 1.5-game lead in the division after both the Eagles and Dallas Cowboys lost this week.

The Eagles' season appears to be falling apart around them, and Dallas' defense is an albatross that only perfect offensive play from Dak Prescott and CeeDee Lamb can overcome. The Giants absolutely need to tighten up their own offense and stop being their own worst enemies on offense and defense. However, the path is still there to right the ship, complete the "worst to first" jump in a division in turmoil, and win the NFC East.

#47. The Brewers got it Made: In World Series for first time in 44 years, Milwaukee also has MLB's No. 1 prospect

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Milwaukee Brewers, as winners of 103 games during the regular season and the freshly minted National League champs, self-evidently have an exceptionally bright present. The future, though, is also quite shimmering, and that's because the Brewers – despite, it would seem, having notched nine straight winning seasons (2020 doesn't count) and four straight NL Central titles – have one of the best farm systems in baseball.

The Brewers' top prospect and the No. 1 prospect in all of baseball, infielder Jesús Made, reinforced this notion on Friday. On the day after the Brewers completed their sweep of the Los Angeles Dodgers to reach their first Fall Classic since 1982, Made homered in his first at-bat in the Dominican Winter League. Here's a look:

Jesús Made goes yard in his first @LIDOMRD at-bat!MLB's No. 1 prospect (@Brewers) hit 14 homers and stole 37 bases across 122 Double-A games this season. pic.twitter.com/aO8kAH14XG

As noted above, he's MLB.com's No. 1 overall prospect right now, and Made may receive that honor from multiple evaluators going into the 2027 season. CBS Sports ranked Made as the No. 2 prospect in MLB back in February, behind only Tigers shortstop Kevin McGonigle -- the overwhelming favorite to win AL Rookie of the Year honors.

Made is coming off a 2026 campaign in which he slashed .271/.344/.430 at Double-A with 44 extra-base hits and 37 stolen bases in 122 games. He did all that as a 19-year-old (he won't turn 20 until next May), which makes him exceptionally young for that level. On the tools from, Made is a switch-hitter who has thus far handled both sides, and he boasts blazing speed on the bases. He's also looking like he'll be able to stick at shortstop long-term, and manning that premium position will only raise his already high ceiling.

Made isn't the only promising prospect the Brewers have percolating down on the farm. He's one of four prospects on MLB.com's current top 100 list, and FanGraphs ranks the Brewers as having the fifth-best farm system in the game right now. Baseball America ranked the Brewers system third at mid-season and gave them an "A" grade for the year. You get the idea.

The attention right now is rightly focused on the fact that the Brewers are four wins from their first World Series title in franchise history. Made's ascendancy, though, gives Brewers rooters even more cause for hope, both now and looking forward.

#48. We asked oddsmakers to rank the 74 most important NBA players against the spread: Nikola Jokić, Wemby top the list

Over the summer, I asked a group of oddsmakers to rank all 32 NFL starting quarterbacks by their value to the point spread. While there are some other NFL skill position players — and offensive linemen and defensive players, as well — who have value to the spread, the NBA is a whole different ballgame, as only five players are on the court for a team at one time.

In a league where figuring out which players are playing on any given night is a daily challenge, an NBA superstar can have an outsized impact on the point spread — and it's valuable for bettors to know how much oddsmakers believe those players are worth.

To help determine this, I asked a group of five oddsmakers to rank the NBA's most important players against the spread.

Join or create a Yahoo Fantasy Basketball league for the 2026-27 NBA season

The prompt I gave was: "If a player wasn't on the injury report and then was declared out before the game, how much would the line move?"

There are many factors that go into making these numbers for oddsmakers, but here are a few:

Is the game in the regular season or playoffs?

Relative strength of the rest of the roster

I sent oddsmakers a list of 74 NBA players and requested that they rank the point-spread value of each one. Then, I averaged the five values together to get a final number for every player.

This is the third year I've done this exercise and Denver Nuggets center Nikola Jokić has been No. 1 all three times — and the only player worth more than five points against the spread every season. However, San Antonio Spurs center Victor Wembanyama is certainly closing the gap.

It's also the lowest LeBron James (T-32, 1.92 points ATS) has been over that time span, both due to his age and since his new team — the Philadelphia 76ers — have five players (James, Tyrese Maxey, Joel Embiid, Jaylen Brown and VJ Edgecombe) all worth at least a point against the number, diminishing James' value.

Here are the most valuable players in the NBA, ranked by their value against the spread.

1. Nikola Jokić, Nuggets (5.44 points ATS)

4. Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, Thunder (4.48)

Jokić and Wembanyama were both at the top of every oddsmakers ballot, with three favoring Jokić, one favoring Wembanyama and one tie. Every oddsmaker had them worth between four and six points against the number.

"On the same exact team, we'd have Wemby a little higher," one oddsmaker told Yahoo Sports. "But the drop-off with Jokić off the court is so massive."

Wembanyama won his first Defensive Player of the Year award last season — the first player to ever win unanimously — and became the youngest player to win the award at 22 years old. He led the league in blocks (197) and ranked fourth in rebounding (11.5 per game).

With James now in Philadelphia, Luka Doncic moved up to third, followed by SGA and Antetokounmpo. Doncic has been in the top six every year I've done this, and this is his highest value (4.58) in that time span — boosted by his outsized importance for a Lakers team that is now built around him.

SGA had the least variance among the five oddsmakers, with four valuing him at 4.5 points ATS and one at 4.4.

"There's a lot of depth on that team," an oddsmaker said about Oklahoma City, "But he's still a two-time MVP and is going to move the line quite a bit."

To his point, the Thunder have the league's highest preseason win total at 62.5 and are co-favorites at +260 with the Spurs to win the title.

The only player in the top five on a completely new team, there was a bigger range among oddsmakers as to what Antetokounmpo's value should be against the number.

"I don't know how that's going to work with Bam [Adebayo]," one oddsmaker opined. "Little bit of disagreement in the trading room — between 3.75 points and five for Giannis. I think this number is going to change early depending on how he performs with [Adebayo].

LeBron' James' value to the spread isn't what it used to be.

Despite being the clear engine on a New York Knicks team that won the NBA championship last season, Brunson had nearly an identical value ATS (3.26 this year to 3.25 last year).

One oddsmaker said he bumped Brunson's value up a half point due to his performance in the playoffs, but also noted that Brunson's value had a lower ceiling due to his lack of defensive impact and because the Knicks are a "talented team."

Haliburton was one of the tougher players to make a number for, and one oddsmaker noted that it's likely Haliburton's spread value will increase as the season progresses.

On the surface, seeing LeBron James as the 36th-most valuable NBA player against the number — tied with the Brooklyn Nets' Michael Porter Jr. — seems like a misprint, but James is 41 years old and isn't the focal point of the 76ers. Joel Embiid (2.84) and Tyrese Maxey (2.70) and the newly acquired Jaylen Brown (2.22) all had higher values against the number.

Several oddsmakers noted the difficulty of valuing players against the spread on the 76ers' new team, and Philadelphia led all NBA teams with its five players being worth a total of 10.82 points against the number.

In terms of rookies, No. 3 overall pick Cam Boozer was the player oddsmakers mentioned as likely to be the most valuable ATS as the season went along. Boozer is the favorite to win NBA Rookie of the Year (+250 at FanDuel), followed by the Bulls' Caleb Wilson (+350), the Jazz's Darryn Peterson (+450) and the Wizards' AJ Dybantsa (+450).

"Boozer and Wilson will probably mean the most to their teams this season, spread-wise," one oddsmaker told Yahoo Sports via email. "I could see them both being quite valuable by the end of the season."

#52. NBA awards picks, predictions: Luka Dončić for MVP, Joe Mazzulla for Coach of the Year among best value bets

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The advantage of betting on awards is that they are comparatively predictable. No, I cannot tell you with perfect accuracy who the 2027 NBA MVP will be... but I can tell you how the prior winners have been selected. Awards voters are humans. Humans are predictable, even if performance is not. While there will be injuries and unexpected candidates and circumstantial changes we can't yet foresee, we can at least use the history of these awards to land on the type of players who tend to win them, and then work backward from there.

So we're going to reverse engineer some best bets for NBA awards season now that opening night is nearly upon us. These are not, strictly, NBA awards picks. If you could pick one player to win Defensive Player of the Year, for example, you should pick Victor Wembanyama. But if you're trying to find the best return on investment in that category, paying minus money on the hope that Wembanyama plays 65 games seems like a high-risk, low-reward proposition.

The goal here is to find the players that best fit the prior history of these awards in a way that maximizes profit. With all of that in mind, let's begin.

The MVP formula points very clearly toward a single candidate this year. Every MVP since LeBron James in 2012 has checked two boxes: they have been between the ages of 24 and 28, and they were either a First- or Second-Team All-NBA selection in the prior season. That's essentially the criteria: a top-10 player in the previous season peaks at some point in his prime and gets a trophy. Victor Wembanyama is too young (and has the shortest odds... and carries 65-game concerns). Nikola Jokić is too old.

Only three players check both boxes. The first is two-time defending champion Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, who's facing the notable challenge of seeking his third consecutive trophy. Nobody has won three straight MVPs since Larry Bird, and that became a major topic when Jokić tried and failed to three-peat in 2023. It's not fair, but Gilgeous-Alexander is going to get held to a ridiculous standard. Michael Jordan and LeBron James couldn't go three-for-three, and there will be voters who hold that against Gilgeous-Alexander.

The second is Cade Cunningham. He has by far the longest odds of the three, but he has the most working against him as well. It's very hard to repeat as a 60-game winner. The Thunder and Celtics are the only teams to do it this century, and in addition to having superior rosters, they didn't have to deal with a tanking-free NBA. The Pistons, thanks to lottery reform, will. Win totals are going to be deflated, especially in a loaded Eastern Conference. It wouldn't take much actual decline for the Pistons to fall from 60 to 50 wins, and there's room for notable decline here. Will Jalen Duren repeat last year's performance after an offseason-long contract standoff? Can they sustain the losses of key role players like Tobias Harris and Isaiah Stewart? And of course, Cunningham isn't in the sort of offense-first environment that tends to lead to MVP stats. This is a defensive-minded team that starts two non-shooters.

That leaves us with Dončić, the seemingly perpetual offseason favorite. The Lakers have finally built him the sort of team he wants: an imposing rim protector at center (Walker Kessler), a second, star-level creator (Austin Reaves) and plenty of shooting everywhere else. The Lakers have plenty of ball-handling redundancy to keep the offense afloat when he rests. Dončić averaged nearly 34 points, eight rebounds and eight assists after Jan. 1, so the numbers should be MVP-level. LeBron is gone. The team is finally his.

We all know the Wembanyama era is coming. If it's at all close, there will be voter sympathy behind the idea of sneaking one last winner in before we assume the trophy gets its next dynastic winner. There are real 65-game fears (he needed an appeal to sneak past that threshold last season), and backup center is a concern here that could cost the Lakers games in the standings. But Dončić checks the historical boxes, will likely have the biggest raw numbers, plays for a glamour franchise and is about as due for an MVP award as any player has ever been. He might be the best player who's never won one. Now is his best chance.

Alright, let's have the Wembanyama conversation. If he plays 65 games, he wins. Any objections? No? Cool. You're paying -330 odds for the privilege of hoping he stays healthy, which implies odds of just under 77% that he wins. So what we're really asking here is if there's a 77% chance that Victor Wembanyama plays 65 games. I would lean no for a few reasons:

So if your life depended on it and you just needed to pick someone? Yes. Take Wembanyama. His odds just don't reflect his actual chances.

So, who are we looking for in the "non-Wembanyama" weight class? For starters, the responsible choice is always a center. Every decade, we tend to get one non-rim-protector winner (even if that player wins more than once). It was Gary Payton in the 1990s, Ron Artest in the 2000s, Kawhi Leonard in the 2010s, and Marcus Smart in the 2020s. We've already acknowledged perimeter play this decade, and the Smart award has aged badly enough to scare off some voters. We're also looking for a top-five defense. Every winner since 2008 has played for one except Evan Mobley in 2025... who only won because Wembanyama had a blood clot, and even he was on an anomalous 64-win team.

So who are the rim protectors on likely top-five defenses? I projected the Spurs, Thunder, Pistons, Raptors and Heat as the top-five defenses for this season. We've already covered San Antonio's candidate. Oklahoma City's Chet Holmgren has the next lowest odds at +1200, but he has the disadvantage of playing on a historically loaded defense. Assigning credit to a single Thunder defender feels reductive, and fair or not, playoff performance is absolutely held against players in this race. It's not a coincidence that Rudy Gobert lost this award in 2022, right after he was unfairly blamed for the hottest shooting night of Terance Mann's life. Holmgren is still washing the stink of the Western Conference Finals off of himself.

Detroit's candidate is a non-center, Ausar Thompson. In truth, I'd call him the NBA's second-best defender. That doesn't mean voting will reflect that, especially since the absence of Isaiah Stewart hurts the defense on balance. Besides, Thompson's fouling and offensive vulnerabilities tend to prevent him from playing the sort of minutes someone needs to win this award. Scottie Barnes does play enough minutes, but, in part because of his offensive responsibilities, he isn't quite as impactful defensively as Thompson is. The stars need to align perfectly for a non-center, and they don't in Barnes' case.

That leaves Miami's center, Bam Adebayo, who has spent years complaining about how he doesn't have one of these awards yet. Well, this is his best chance. Miami has one of the best defensive lineups in the NBA. Giannis Antetokounmpo has won this award, but he has declined just enough not to compete with Adebayo for this year's. Davion Mitchell and Andrew Wiggins are legitimate plus starters, and Erik Spoelstra might be the NBA's most creative defensive coach. Adebayo doesn't post gaudy block or steal numbers, and the all-in-ones usually nudge him below the top handful of defensive bigs, but the eye test is obviously favorable and, as with Dončić, there will be a sense that he's due if he comes close. At 40-to-1, this is one of the better value plays on the board.

Rookie of the Year is historically a counting stats award. Playing for a winning team almost never factors in, as the race between Cooper Flagg and Kon Knueppel last year, or Victor Wembanyama vs. Chet Holmgren three seasons ago, demonstrates. In the past two decades, the only Rookie of the Year winners to average fewer than 15 points per game have been Malcolm Brogdon, who only won because Joel Embiid got hurt, and Stephon Castle, who won in a historically weak class. Therefore, we're looking for opportunity first and foremost.

That immediately rules out AJ Dybantsa of the Wizards and Darryn Peterson of the Jazz. The former is on a team with two veteran stars and several younger players still trying to make their mark in the league. The latter plays with another high-usage guard who just signed a long-term extension and two veteran star forwards. They're going to be great, but they're going to have fewer opportunities.

That leaves us three viable candidates. Darius Acuff Jr. has the longest odds outside of the top four, and he's probably going to lead all rookies in shot attempts simply because he plays for the Kings. Of course, that's a bit of a double-edged sword in this respect. He'll likely be the least efficient of the candidates for the same reason, and while that doesn't matter in some races, this one will likely be too competitive for a player to get away with putting up empty numbers.

Cameron Boozer is the most pro-ready rookie in this class. He swept the National Player of the Year awards in college a season ago, and most of the analytical models pegged him as clearly the best prospect in this class. Memphis probably has the most available shots among these teams. The concern here is slight, but statistically notable. The Grizzlies simply don't play their players as many minutes as most other teams do. Tuomas Iisalo believes in limiting players to four- or five-minute bursts. If you ignore the tanking players they used at the end of the year, Jaren Jackson Jr. led the Grizzlies with only 30.7 minutes per game last year. If Boozer plays four or five fewer minutes per night than the other candidates, that could create a counting stats disadvantage.

Caleb Wilson is handling the ball quite a bit in the preseason. The Bulls are seemingly putting him through the suddenly common "what if we point guard-ified our top forward prospect" arc that Flagg endured a year ago and Giannis Antetokounmpo popularized a decade ago. That approach tends to come with growing pains, but as Flagg can attest, it is not disqualifying in the Rookie of the Year race. If anything, the volume is helpful. Wilson likely won't have the ball as much as Flagg did a season ago, but he's on a roster that makes more sense and should be more conducive to his success. You're getting slightly better odds on Wilson than you are on Boozer. It's a justifiable matter of preference between the two. Boozer is the safer pick. Wilson's upside and longer odds push him over the top for me.

Here's where we start to defy history in one notable way: nobody has ever repeated as Coach of the Year. Not Gregg Popovich. Not Phil Jackson. Not Pat Riley. Not Red Auerbach. That's why Mazzulla's odds are this long, and those odds are why he's such an easy pick. He's the NBA's best regular-season coach. I'm happy to take the 25-to-1 swing on someone this good defying history.

Mazzulla's offense has ranked either No. 1 or No. 2 in all four of his seasons at the helm for the Celtics. He maintained that excellence a season ago largely without his best player, Jayson Tatum, and with half of his 2024 championship rotation gone. His approach produces regular-season wins en masse. The Celtics shoot more 3s than almost everyone. They get more offensive rebounds than almost everyone. They protect the rim better than almost everyone. They never turn the ball over.

The Jaylen Brown trade will be enormously helpful to Mazzulla's case. It is simultaneously the narrative trigger that a coach would need to defy the "nobody has repeated" history and a move made to further mold the team in Mazzulla's image. Paul George fits much more cleanly into the whole "shoot a million 3s and never turn the ball over" scheme than Brown does. Mitchell Robinson only amplifies Boston's success protecting the basket on one end and owning the glass on the other. No roster more cleanly matches its coach's stylistic preferences than this one.

Every Coach of the Year winner since Doc Rivers in 2000 has been a top-four seed. Most of them are top-two seeds, and the formula is quite often "the most surprising of the four best regular-season teams." Well, nobody is going to be surprised when the Spurs and Thunder capture the top two Western Conference seeds. The shock of the Brown trade has worn off. Plenty of people expect the Celtics to have a very successful regular season. But it generated more than enough doubt to vault Mazzulla into a historic repeat if he pulls this off.

The favorites here are all obvious starting candidates. Payton Pritchard and Dylan Harper might be opening night starters, and even if they're not, they could force the issue relatively early. Ajay Mitchell is an injury away, but the Thunder tend to be cautious when their players get hurt. They rest key players frequently, and it's not hard to imagine a world in which Mitchell starts half of the season purely through filling in for teammates. And as is the case for Holmgren with Defensive Player of the Year, it's hard to assign too much credit to a single Thunder reserve for their bench dominance. Mitchell will score the points, but does that mean he's a better player than Alex Caruso? Jared McCain is a starting-level player. Jaylin Williams might be as well. That's a hard roster to stand out on.

Our last six winners have come from top-three seeds, so we want someone on a winning roster. We also want scoring, as 10 of the 17 winners between 2006 and 2022 were that season's leading bench scorer. We haven't had a season's leading bench scorer win since, but pure point total is always a factor in this race. You win by coming off the bench for a winner and scoring a lot of points.

The last four winners have hovered around the 13-15-point per game mark. Jenkins wasn't there most of last season, but he averaged 19 points per game in relief of the injured Cade Cunningham for a key stretch late last year. He's not going to start often this year, but think about the Pistons roster. He's really the only proven, secondary ball-handler now that Tobias Harris and Caris LeVert are gone. Unless Ebuka Okorie is ready faster than we're anticipating, the sheer volume of dribbling opportunities available to Jenkins this season is going to be absolutely enormous for a bench player. At 50-to-1, that sort of volume on a team this good is too tempting to pass up.

Most Improved Player can typically be distilled into "the first-time All-Star" award. The last two winners bucked that trend, as the Hawks won with Dyson Daniels and Nickeil Alexander-Walker. Before that? Our previous five winners were first-time All-Stars. The catch with that definition this season is that none of the obvious first-time All-Star candidates make sense through the award's other typical standards.

Austin Reaves has a great chance at making his first All-Star Team this season. He's already received votes for this award in two separate seasons. You can't be a candidate for this award every year. Cooper Flagg is another consensus pick as a possible first-time All-Star, but he's in his second season. No second-year player has won this award since Monta Ellis in 2007, but Ellis was a second-round pick. Flagg is literally the reigning Rookie of the Year. It's possible and perhaps probable that a player truly does come out of nowhere to make an All-Star Team. That player becomes the favorite. For now, we're working off of opportunity and circumstance.

Coby White has had All-Star-esque stretches. He averaged almost 28 points per game in March 2025, right after the Bulls traded Zach LaVine and handed him and Josh Giddey the keys to the offense. In the tiny, 282-minute sample he played without LaMelo Ball in Charlotte last season, White scored 33.2 points per 75 possessions on 61.3% true shooting. He won't be that good over the full season, but it goes to show that White, when entrusted to run an offense, can post absolutely bonkers numbers.

He's playing on a team with shooting everywhere. The Hornets have a real chance to break the 3-point attempt record. With Ball gone, creation is at a premium in Charlotte. White is going to be the player responsible for creating most of those 3-point attempts. He'll have a hard time actually making the All-Star team simply because Brandon Miller and Kon Knueppel are ahead of him in the team's overall pecking order and this team isn't going to be good enough for multiple All-Stars, but if the Hornets exceed expectations and White posts huge numbers in the process, a 45-to-1 ticket is going to feel very valuable.

#56. Brock Purdy and the 49ers can expect plenty of blitzing from the Commanders

Fresh off a huge Week 5 divisional win against the Seattle Seahawks, the San Francisco 49ers begin their longest stretch of games without an NFC West opponent with a Monday night date against the Washington Commanders.

Washington has already aided the 49ers this season, handing Seattle its first loss of the season with a Week 3 win over San Francisco's division rival. A Commanders loss to the 49ers on Monday night would also be a huge boost for San Francisco, with a win putting the 49ers up three games in the NFC West.

The 49ers will look to avoid a letdown spot against a lesser Washington team. Here are the numbers to know heading into the Monday night clash:

Percent. The Commanders blitz on 37.7 of opponents' dropbacks, the second-highest rate in the league.

The dam finally broke for the 49ers offense when Seattle's defense got to Brock Purdy for the first three sacks San Francisco has allowed this season. The 49ers offense will now have to face the team that sends an extra man or two at the second-highest clip in the league on Monday night.

Unfortunately, that high blitz rate hasn't done much for the lacking Washington pass defense.

Because of the blitz, Washington's defense ranks well in pressure rate (9th) and hurry percentage (6th), but that hasn't resulted in sacks. Washington ranks 24th with nine sacks, and since the pass rush can't bring down the opposing quarterback, the Commanders' poor secondary has been exposed to the tune of:

Purdy's been in incredible form to start the season, and that form should continue against the lacking Washington secondary, so long as the San Francisco offense can handle the blitzes that Dan Quinn and his Washington defense will present.

Rushing yards per game. Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels averages 67.7 rushing yards per game.

With Washington's leading rusher Jacory Croskey-Merritt (groin) out on Monday night, the onus will be on Daniels to pick up the slack in the run game, something he'll have no issue in taking on.

Entering Week 6, Daniels ranked eighth among quarterbacks with 21 rush attempts. The only reason he doesn't have more is the two games he missed, but despite the missed games, Daniels 203 rushing yards are second-most for quarterbacks behind only Josh Allen, who has 239 rushing yards on twice as many rush attempts in his five games.

Simply put, the 49ers will not face a more prolific mobile quarterback this season than Daniels.

Raheem Morris and the 49ers defense have faced one quarterback with more rush attempts so far this season than Daniels, and that was Malik Willis in Week 2 when the 49ers beat the Miami Dolphins.

Willis is a quality rusher in his own right, with the third-most at the position, 186 rushing yards on his 27 rush attempts. His 6.9 yards per attempt rank fourth among quarterbacks with 15 or more rushing attempts this season. But when the 49ers faced him, Willis couldn't get his legs going, holding the quarterback to a season-low six rushing yards on two carries.

Commanders offensive coordinator David Blough will draw up at least two designed runs for Daniels, so don't expect a Willis-like ground usage for Washington's quarterback on Monday night.

Times. The 49ers have started 6-0 four times in franchise history (1948, 1984, 1990, and 2019).

A win on Monday night would mark the fifth time the 49ers have started the first third of the season without a loss. Each of the last three 6-0 starts have meant at least an NFC Championship Game appearance (in the Super Bowl era).

1948 was the only 6-0 start in 49ers history that didn't result in a playoff game appearance (the 14-0 Cleveland Browns claimed the 1948 AAFC Championship defeating the Buffalo Bills), but the 49ers would finish 12-2. Those 12 wins came against teams like the New York Yankees, Brooklyn Dodgers, Los Angeles Dons, and Chicago Rockets.

But since the invention of the Super Bowl, a 6-0 start has meant at least an NFC Championship Game appearance for the 49ers. The 2026 49ers have the chance to do something the 1984 team did: go 6-0 with a Monday night win against an NFC East foe. 1984 saw the 49ers defeat the New York Giants to move to 6-0 with a 31-10 Monday Night Football win. San Francisco's quest for perfection in 1984 would end the next week with a loss against Pittsburgh, but the 49ers would go on to win the franchise's second Super Bowl.

The 1990 49ers would use a Week 6 win against the Steelers to move to 6-0. The streak would continue into the middle of November when a Week 12 loss to the Rams would drop San Francisco to 10-1. San Francisco would finish 1990 with a 14-2 record but fall short in the NFC Championship Game to a 13-3 Giants team that would go on to win Super Bowl XXV.

The most recent 6-0 team was Kyle Shanahan's third season with the 49ers in 2019, when San Francisco moved to 6-0 with a sloppy 9-0 win in a rainy Washington, D.C. The 49ers would stay undefeated a few more weeks before losing to Seattle to end the start-of-the-season winning streak at eight games. The 49ers would again make the Super Bowl, but fell to the Chiefs in Miami.

Now, 6-0 doesn't guarantee postseason success, but the history shines brightly on the 2026 49ers' Monday night win.

#57. 5 Sixers predictions for the 2026-27 regular season

This upcoming regular season is the most exciting and anticipated one of this era of Sixers basketball and then some. Not only has Philadelphia loaded up their roster with aspirations of winning the conference and more, but over half the East has done the same.

The word bold would normally go before the word "predictions" in a piece like this. Between the reigning NBA champions, some of the biggest offseason moves in league history, and the potential for former powerhouses to return from injured form, this is one of the hardest seasons to predict. None of these feel like particularly bold predictions, but here are five Sixers things I'm expecting to happen this season.

Though I don't expect him to qualify for any sort of scoring title. The big question for this team is how are they going to spread just the one basketball around such a talented starting five. How often that starting five actually plays together will go a long way in answering that question. At the risk of jinxing him, I do think Embiid will be on the court a lot this season barring something really going wrong (knock on every piece of wood you can see).

When Embiid is on the court, he's the one starter I see the rest of the team bending their game to the most. Working out of the free throw line area, Embiid makes as much sense as any to operate as a hub from the free throw line area. He proved last season that when he's going offensively, he's still plenty dominant to command double teams as he tries to attack the basket.

Those double teams will be deadly with the full starting five on the court — there's just not going to be anyone on the floor the defense feels comfortable leaving alone. If that premise is true, and Embiid is who the healthy starting five functions around, he will be the leading scorer on this team easily.

After wracking up multiple scoring titles, Embiid's points per game obviously took a big hit in the 2024-25 season when he was only able to play 19 games. He spent a good part of the first half of last season ramping back up into shape and only got on the floor for 38 games, but he still nearly caught up to Tyrese Maxey in points per game despite Maxey's torrid start to the season. Embiid finished last year at 26.9 points per game compared to Maxey's 28.3. With all the messaging from the team, including Maxey himself that he's going to be playing off the ball more this year, I predict the Sixers to have a new top scorer this season. Well, somewhat new.

Speaking of messaging, I'm not loving what we're hearing about Barlow out of training camp so far. He's one of three Sixers who didn't play in preseason this year with an injury. While Anfernee Simons and Adem Bona are back on the practice court, the Sixers have yet to provide a timeline on Barlow as he deals with some sort of back issue.

The sooner he's able to get back on the floor the better, as the season-ending injury to Ariel Hukporti has put stress on the backup center position before the regular season has even started. Barlow didn't play a ton of minutes at the five last season, only 10% of his minutes, according to Cleaning the Glass.

The biggest sample might have been their second round slaughter by the New York Knicks, where Barlow was thrown in there as a necessity with Embiid and Andre Drummond just unable to keep up with New York's big men. Barlow acquitted himself fairly well in that time, helping provide some of the only competitive minutes of that series.

He doesn't give you the option to stretch the floor like Jabari Walker is appearing to, he is not going to protect the rim with the springiness of Bona, but he does meet in the middle of those two in terms of rebounding prowess and athleticism. He's generally been long enough and strong enough to defend centers bigger than him. There will be nights where the Sixers wish they have a bigger look or one with more rim protection, but Barlow is currently the best option to backup Embiid on any given night, and the Sixers should hope he's able to get back on the floor sooner rather than later.

To that end, hopefully this Barlow injury isn't serious. The backup center situation is such a conundrum because the Sixers can't do much about it for quite some time. They can't sign another free agent until mid December, and then they'll only have a minimum contract to offer. They can make a trade, but those are difficult with how close the Sixers are to their first apron hard cap.

They're going to have to get creative to eat innings Embiid is not available for, especially if their supposed backup option is already dealing with an injury. Walker and Bona can hopefully fill a lot of these minutes, but they, as well as Barlow, lack the true size for the biggest matchups in the league. While Fall may not be able to provide anything else, he certainly provides that.

It may become apparent quick that Fall, who hasn't played in the NBA since 2022, was only on an Exhibit 10 contract that was converted this weekend, and missed most of training camp with a hip injury, isn't a playable option at all. When the Sixers run into some big teams early, such as the Detroit Pistons on a back-to-back in the first week of the season, they may be pulling out all the stops at the center position.

This will definitely be the one you can yell at me for. While there will certainly be some growing pains as this group figures each other out, I'm not as concerned with this as others have expressed. Despite the backup center concerns, the roster is objectively improved over the group that won 46 games last year, and there's enough infrastructure to improve on that.

The problem is the East is loaded and there could be some teams to rack up some wins. It's been hard to predict the seeding of this conference because I do think the Sixers will win a lot of games — I also think there might be some regular season machines in the East. Of these four teams, I expect three to finish ahead of the Sixers in the standings: the New York Knicks, Boston Celtics, Pistons and Toronto Raptors.

The Raptors could very well have the best defense in the league. They are going to be annoying to play no matter how many times Kawhi Leonard is in the lineup. Detroit won the most games last season and while they had a weird offseason, there's nothing to indicate they can't come close to replicating that regular season success.

The Celtics have been lock for over 50 wins, and now they're getting their best player back for what they hope is a full season of health. If there's one team in this group that might fall behind the Sixers, it might be the reigning champions. The vibes in New York haven't felt great as they've struggled to give contract extensions to some of their biggest pieces. It's also a group that has coasted through stretches of the regular season in years past.

This season I predict the Sixers to have homecourt in the first round of the playoffs, but it will be a battle to get it, which would create a whole lot of discourse around my next prediction.

This year's Sixers will come just short of matching the 2015 Hawks. Embiid, Maxey, LeBron James and Jaylen Brown are all going to have really good years. VJ Edgecombe will too, he'll make the kind of second year leap that will have everyone in the Delaware Valley thanking their lucky stars the ping pong balls fell the right way in 2025.

He'll fall just short of making his first All-Star game in his second season for one reason: the Sixers won't be high enough in the standings to justify their entire starting five making an All-Star game. For better or for worse, team record does come into account in close calls when it comes to All-Star voting. The entire starting five will make great cases this year, but voters will have a hard time putting them all in if there are a few teams ahead of the Sixers in the standings.

#58. Panthers stars on pace to break single-season franchise records

Even when Carolina Panthers quarterback Bryce Young doesn't have a great game here in 2026, his numbers still look pretty impressive.

That's what happened during Sunday's ugly win (although there may be no such thing) over the Philadelphia Eagles. Young, in the 25-14 victory, completed just over half of his passes (20-of-39) for 281 yards, two touchdowns and a 91.9 passer rating.

That brings Young's total for the campaign to 1,549 passing yards through five games. In case you're wondering, that puts him on pace to obliterate the franchise's standing record for most passing yards in a season.

In fact, if Young keeps his up, he'll break Steve Beuerlein's 1999 record by over 800 yards . . .

Young also set a new franchise record yesterday by reaching 11 touchdown passes, the most for any Panthers quarterback in the first five games of a season.

Oh, and he may be joined in the books by wide receiver Tetairoa McMillan.

The second-year pass catcher is also tracking to break a single-season franchise record, as he's on pace to surpass Steve Smith Sr.'s mark of 1,563 from 2005. Thus far, McMillan has reeled in 32 grabs for 471 yards and two touchdowns.

#59. Today's top games to watch, best bets, odds: Rays at Guardians Game 4, Washington at Purdue and more

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

I'm not a meteorologist. But I did stay at a Holiday Inn Express last night so I'm qualified to tell you that Friday's Game 4 of the ALCS between the Guardians and Rays is in danger of being affected by weather.

The forecast calls for light rain or showers until about 7 p.m. ET, one hour before the scheduled first pitch. But then the forecast shows a window of dry conditions until 11 p.m. ET.

#60. Brian Thomas Jr. landing spots: Trade rumors hits fever pitch after WR did not play in second half vs. Texans

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The writing is not only on the wall, but it's a blinding shade of neon, and it's suggesting that Brian Thomas Jr.'s tenure in Jacksonville is nearing its end. Week 6 may have been the unofficial nail in the coffin for any thought of the former first-round wideout being able to tap back into the magic from his rookie season with the franchise, as he was essentially benched in the second half of Sunday's loss to the Texans.

Thomas failed to bring in either of his two targets, including a brutal drop on the opening possession of the game. Then, after logging 15 first-half snaps in the first half, Thomas logged zero over the final two quarters. This was the second straight game where Thomas was held without a reception (five total targets).

To make matters even more dire for Thomas, Travis Hunter has started to emerge at receiver. As Thomas sat on the sideline for the second half, Hunter caught three balls for 40 yards and a touchdown over that span, and finished his day with a total of four catches for 59 yards and a touchdown. Those totals from Hunter in Week 6 are effectively half of Thomas' entire season-long production to this point (9 catches, 105 yards and a touchdown).

"Just week to week. Week to week. Guys have to step up and make plays," coach Liam Coen said postgame when asked about his confidence in Thomas, via Jacksonville.com.

In the wake of Week 6, Hunter has certainly warranted a larger share in the offense alongside fellow receivers Parker Washington and Jakobi Meyers, while Thomas is clearly fading. With Hunter's emergence, Thomas's second-half benching, and Jacksonville entering the bye in Week 7, it creates a perfect storm for the organization to truly reevaluate its receiving corps. If they come to the conclusion that they're better off elevating Hunter to a more prominent role and making Thomas' demotion permanent, they'd be better off moving him.

With that in mind, all eyes look toward the Nov. 10 trade deadline and whether or not the pass catcher will be moved by that juncture. If so, let's identify some logical trade destinations.

The Raiders are reeling a bit after losing three straight, dropping to .500 on the season. That said, this is still a competitive club that is in the early stages of its rebuild under first-year head coach Klint Kubiak. While there will always be an eye towards truly contending in the years to come, I think it'd be wise to roll the dice with Thomas here. The receiver room in Las Vegas is relatively thin, with Tre Tucker, Jalen Nailor, and Cody White currently headlining the room. Thomas would be a massive talent upgrade, and Kubiak could be the type of offensive mind capable of tapping back into something close to what we saw out of him as a rookie.

Beyond 2026, this would also be a savvy pursuit for Las Vegas. Thomas not only gives them a possible boost this season, but if he can revive his career, it's suddenly another star weapon for Fernando Mendoza whenever he steps into the starting role. A skill position group headlined by Brock Bowers, Ashton Jeanty, and Thomas Jr., with Mendoza pulling the strings, has potential.

This is another team that I think could take a calculated swing at Thomas. In any other scenario, the Dolphins are nothing close to a buyer at this trade deadline, and will likely be seen as a seller after beginning the year 0-5 and showing no signs of turning it around. That said, in a very similar vein to what we discussed with the Raiders, the Dolphins could look to try and bring Thomas in, hope that a change of scenery does him good, and suddenly the franchise has a No. 1 receiver they got on the cheap. Then, they can pair him with whichever quarterback they decide to take high atop the 2027 NFL Draft. It's a buy for the future, not for 2026.

It almost feels like a contractual obligation to include the Chiefs in any sort of fun trade rumor, particularly when it comes to someone on the offensive side of the ball. While it feels chalky, there's a reason for it. Kansas City could use another weapon at receiver, especially with Rashee Rice (hamstring) missing time. Xavier Worthy picked up the slack in Week 6 with a seven-catch, 73-yard showing in the win over the Chargers, but the next most productive receiver on Sunday was Cyrus Allen, who had two catches for 27 yards.

If there were any combination with the best shot at getting Thomas back to his 2024 version, it's Patrick Mahomes and Andy Reid. With K.C. at 5-0 and firmly in the Super Bowl conversation, it's an obvious buying opportunity.

I expect the Seahawks offense to stabilize once they get Zach Charbonnet and Jadarian Price back healthy, making the running game a more reliable part of their attack. That said, I do think the one-man show of Jaxon Smith-Njigba is a little unsustainable when it comes to their title defense.

So far this season, Smith-Njigba has accounted for 35% of Seattle's scrimmage yards, which is the highest rate by any WR in NFL history. He's also accounted for 49% of the team's receiving yards and 63% of their fourth-quarter receiving yards through six weeks. Smith-Njigba has played at an elite level and produced well with that heavy workload, but I wonder if it'd do Seattle some good to have another weapon to account for. If they pursued Thomas, maybe it would diversify the offense a bit more and make them less of a predictable pitch-and-catch unit between Sam Darnold and Smith-Njigba.

When not targeting Smith-Njigba this season, Darnold is completing 54.8% of his passes for 5.6 yards per attempt, four passing touchdowns, five interceptions, and has a passer rating of 63.8.

Whenever you think Howie Roseman is going to zig, he'll zag. Wouldn't it be just like the Eagles GM to make a move for Brian Thomas Jr. when everyone in the world thinks he's liable to start selling pieces at the deadline with his team 2-4 on the year and Jalen Hurts (blood clot) on injured reserve for at least three more games?

Even when everyone is healthy, Philly could use another receiving weapon, and Thomas is just the type of buy-low talent that Roseman has historically pounced on. Then, when Thomas is looking like his rookie self, we're all left mesmerized by how the league let Roseman land him.
