#63. P&T Round(ball) Table: 2026-27 Knicks Predictions

Greetings, Knickerbocker fans. As the 81st NBA season draws near, the Posting and Toasting crew has assembled to answer questions and offer predictions as the defending champions pursue a repeat under sophomore skipper Mike Brown.

1) Where will the Knicks finish in offensive and defensive rating, and what will drive the biggest change?

Antonio Losada: Let's do something not-so-fun and revisit last year's takes, carrying 53 years (well, not so many in my personal case) of suffering with them. I had the Knicks finishing with both a top-six offense and defense last season, and I nearly got it right, as they posted the third-best ORtg and seventh-best DRtg. Nothing other than losing Mitchell Robinson has changed, I don't expect anything to deviate a lot from what we saw last postseason, and everybody — including Mike Brown — has been together for a full season, so I'll ramp up my prediction for a top-three finish in both cats this campaign.

Michael Zeno: As Antonio said, the Knicks gave us a good baseline with third and seventh in offensive and defensive rating, respectively, so my answers will be pretty similar. I'm not sure if they can achieve Celtics-esque offensive harmony from behind the arc, but this offense will reach a new level with their new playmaking hub in the middle. On defense, I wonder if Andre Drummond will be a steep drop-off from Mitchell Robinson, but also if the strides Karl-Anthony Towns made in the postseason will carry over. Whaddya know, the man angling for a max extension is the X-factor for both. I'll say third and ninth.

Moritz Wollert: If they really wanted to I could see them finishing top three in both categories. The people in Atlanta, Philly, Cleveland and down there in Texas surely remember how dominant this Knicks group can be, even if they lost Mitchell Robinson over the summer. For a veteran championship team like our Bockers (damn, it feels good to type that) though of course there are many things a lot more important than statistical milestones. So I could see them pacing themselves, trying out some things over the course of the year and finish comfortably 5th on O and 8th on the defensive end.

Kento Kato: The Knicks have the roster and ability to be a top three team on both ends of the floor, especially if they play the way they did in the postseason. While they did lose Mitchell Robinson, a full regular season of Karl-Anthony Towns, OG Anunoby, and Mikal Bridges playing they way did en route to a championship could see them absolutely dominate the regular season. That being said, I do think some early season regression and complacency is natural, even with this group of motivated and focused core. That, along with an improved conference and the fact that teams can't possible continue putting their centers on Towns like they did at the beginning of last season makes me believe that they'll be a top five offensive team and top ten defensive team, but not quite top five in both.

Russell Richardson: I hate this question and I wrote it. Prediction: Top 15 defense, top 10 offense . . . like ninth. The loss of Mitch's gravity drops them defensively (see my A to Q6 below), and I expect Brown to limit the mileage on his best offensive players: they've already played a lot of basketball this year and this is an older team. Unless the plan is to burn through them this season and start rebuilding soon after, Mike's gonna try to keep them fresh. Which would affect the win total (also see below).

2) Which Knick will take the biggest step forward, and who could have trouble matching last season?

Losada: The fact that everybody is familiar with the system, how Brown guides his pupils, and what everyone can and can't do, I think we're facing a very real possibility of watching these Knicks level up once again. If I have to pick someone taking a step forward, that'd be Mikal being confident from game one through 82 and beyond. Someone we might start to worry about sooner rather than later is Josh Hart, if only because of what he's great at — never-tiring chaos causing — and his wheels getting so much run. Talking strictly about performance, I don't see any clear candidate to regress, roles factored in.

Zeno: I also think a big season is coming for Mikal Bridges. If anyone can benefit from the weight being lifted off his shoulders after a title, it's Mr. F— Them Picks. OG Anunoby is getting the early hype for All-Star consideration, but why can't Mikal do it if he can finally blend his scoring and defense? As for regression, it's either Jose Alvarado or Landry Shamet, just because the two were so incredible last year. I'll lean Shamet, not because I don't think he's a great bench piece for this team, but because he set some lofty expectations in the playoffs.

Wollert: I agree with Michael that Shamet could have trouble matching last season since it's hard to be a bench superstar for multiple years. My ultimate vote goes to KAT though with his contract situation lurking in the background and the reality that it is hard to keep your focus for an entire season. He gave the Knicks so much mentally in the playoffs and I have a tough time seeing that commitment in January against the Sacramentos of the world. On the other end of the spectrum I really hope Mo Diawara keeps his trajectory going upwards. So many of the other players were so close to their optimum at the end of last year that I could see him being the one guy who can really give more with a more defined role.

Kato: I'm tempted to go with Diawara just because he has arguably the most room to grow of any of the rotation players. And even though I think he'll be fine, he has had a relatively inconsistent series of exhibition games between Summer League and preseason. I also think Bridges is a fun answer given the confidence boost and the lack of worry he may be playing with. As is Towns, who is coming off of a triumphant postseason run that proved just how impactful he could be on both sides of the ball. That being said, I think Bridges is still going to more or less be the same player in the regular season. And I do think it will be difficult for Towns to be the postseason version of himself for the entirety of the regular season. My vote goes to Anunoby, who we've seen be pretty aggressive in preseason. If he can up his free throw rate like he started off preseason doing, and continues to get on-ball initiation reps, I can see him making his first All-Star appearance.

Richardson: OG will have a few more thirty point games this season, so maybe that qualifies for a leap? And Cap will have a hard time. His skills and discipline remain unchanged, but living up to expectations after a championship is a major weight. No NBA player has a bigger target on his back. And I pray every night for his ankles.

3) Which reserve will matter most to the title defense? Who needs a bigger role before the playoffs?

Losada: So much has been made of the third-string center, but right now I'd care the same about having James Wiseman or placing a broomstick on the bench. It's a clear-cut name here for me, and that's Deuce McBride. Yes, the Knicks won it all with a poor postseason run from McBride, but I don't think that can repeat itself, and hey, the better he plays, the better package the Knicks will do in return for him at the deadline, also boosting their title-defense chances! No bigger roles for nobody, status quo on the rotation.

Zeno: Yep, Deuce. I do not care how rough he looked for much of the playoff run. He barely got his conditioning back from a multi-month core injury before ramping up to high-stakes playoff games. He's a guy who needs to prove he's worth the $15 million a year that a player of his archetype deserves, and while I'm very skeptical he will be a Knick beyond this year, he is the player who can most expand this team's ceiling.

Wollert: It clearly is Jordan Clarkson with his voodoo like abilities that healed OG and kept almost the entire team healthy throughout the postseason. No matching that for any opponent. On a serious note I really hope Andre Drummond can give the Knicks a little something of what Mitch gave them off the bench for years. Not only the rebounding but a physical, gigantic presence with elbows, bumps and bruises for the opponent. If he can't provide it there probably isn't anyone else who can.

Kato: The backup center position is noteworthy. But one, Robinson wasn't necessarily a force to be reckoned with in the Finals, and two, the backup center in the postseason may not even be on the roster right now. I still agree with the others and lean McBride. I know the Knicks won it all despite a poor offensive showing from him last Finals, but he's still so valuable and has the ability to raise the ceiling of the guys he shares the floor with and ultimately, the team, unlike any other reserve.

Richardson: Landry Shamet will get votes for sixth man of the year. But I believe the most important bench player is not yet on the team. (Dun dun dunnnnnhhh)

4) Which Eastern Conference opponent poses the biggest threat, and what about that matchup worries you?

Losada: I will never not fear the Celtics the same I will never trust the Sixers to keep the puzzle together for more than short stretches of games, let alone a playoff series. Perhaps watching Toronto in the last preseason game and how tight things were, the Raps have something big in store for these Knicks when the postseason comes. KAT ate the Raptors alive on Thursday, but not the only one that matters in Scottie Barnes, so we'll see how that goes when the bright lights are on.

Zeno: If the Sixers somehow find the magic elixir that keeps LeBron youthful and gives Embiid some fresh knee cartilage, it's them, but they'll be starting Adem Bona by playoff time most likely. If Kawhi stays healthy (not as much of a guarantee as some seem to believe), the Raptors could move the needle. Maybe if the Celtics' shooting gets hot in the playoffs, or Miami gets enough from Klay Thompson and Tim Hardaway Jr. You know what? It's the Pacers. It's a WWE-esque storyline that's setting up here if these two meet for a third time in four years. The only team in the last three years to beat the Knicks in a playoff series will have that confidence every time they play them this season.

Wollert: Pacers are a good pick, even if they look vastly different this time around. Philly only worries me because the world is unfair and could have us losing to that group of not exactly likable fellas. From a pure matchup standpoint there isn't one team in the East that the Knicks can't handle, they all have major weaknesses and question marks. New York has them aswell obviously but certainly with this group have provided a lot more answers than anybody else.

Kato: The scary and the fun part about the eastern conference this season is that you can argue that eight, maybe nine, teams will consider anything short of a conference finals appearance a failure. But for, the only one I that I think has not just the talent, but the matchup, to beat the Knicks four our of seven times is the Pacers. Maybe it's just because of recency bias that I feel that way. But I can't fully trust the 76ers' ability to stay healthy, defend, or get collective buy in to sacrifice. The Raptors are scary defensively, but do they have enough offensively? The Heat are likely a year or a couple pieces away. The Pistons are still flawed for postseason basketball in my eyes. And the Cavaliers, well, they just aren't beating the Knicks in a playoff series anytime soon for a myriad of reasons.

Richardson: Everybody's sleeping on Charlotte, huh? Make mine teal!

5) What is your boldest Knicks prediction for 2026–27? Give us something we can hold against you in April.

Losada: Knowing Leon Rose and writing this against the backdrop of the Dolan-second apron summer, I'm going to go bold and say Rose completes a trade we don't ever see coming. And no, I'm not talking about the likes of Dadiet, Diawara, or Kolek. Not talking about landing a first-round pick. I'm talking about a foundation-shaking deal, involving one or multiple of KAT, OG, Hart, and Bridges.

Zeno: Josh Hart finishes the season coming off the bench. This starting lineup has been together for two years under two different coaches, has played thousands and thousands of minutes together, and has found a groove in the playoffs. That said, there are limitations, and an injury to Hart (or some complications with his gnarly finger) could push him to the bench for Shamet or McBride.

Wollert: James Wiseman will become an important rotation piece and is a major contributor come playoff time. Opponents will fear him on the offensive glass and have no answers for him as a lob threat – atleast not with their second units. Yes, that preseason kool-aid is still tasting like magic. If it ever wears off in the next few days I'd join Antonio in the "KAT might get traded" camp. Not because they don't value him but because they don't want to lose him for nothing down the road. His value is at an all time high too.

Kato: I know the Knicks recently announced that they wouldn't be negotiating extensions until later in the season. The uneasiness of hearing that have lead many fans to take that as the team saying they won't be negotiating at all this season. My prediction is that a Towns negotiation happens at some point this season. As I've done in the past in pregame and preseason predictions, this is another instance of me trying to speak something into existence. But I do think that the two sides will budge a bit and realize that they not like like each other, but are good for each other, and get some sort of deal done.

Richardson: The NBA goes on strike, not to fight for more equitable treatment of mid-tier employees, but to screw the Knicks out of their repeat bid.

6) What will the Knicks' final record and playoff seed be, and how will their season end? Would anything short of a repeat feel disappointing?

Losada: I stopped taking John Hollinger seriously or reading his content a few years ago, but I tend to agree with his prediction for the Eastern Conference's regular season. I see as many as six teams ending within two or three games' distance, and perhaps none of them winning even 50 games. The Cavaliers or the Pistons will win the 82-game circuit because that's all they win, if anything, and the Knicks will likely take it easy and finish in the 4-6 seed. Give me a 49-33 record for New York and a first-round matchup against the Raptors or the Celtics. Regarding the back-to-back title: I'm set for life with last year's chip. That's it for me.

Zeno: No idea. The East is stacked; this team is built for the playoffs, and they don't seem to be as gung-ho in the regular season. I have a hard time believing this team will regress that much from their pre-KAT hub days as a 53-win team, but what if someone gets hurt? All bets are off. I'll stake my claim on 51-31, a No. 3 seed, and a trip to the NBA Finals, where the grown-up Spurs get revenge. I will not be mad if this team doesn't repeat, especially when I spent much of my life thinking they'd never win one, but if they lose to someone like Indiana or Philly or even Boston? I'll be annoyed.

Wollert: Top seed in the East, baby, 55 wins and not looking in the rearview mirror. I've never been as pleased and happy going into a season, just cool, calm and collected. In due time that will wear off, plenty of things will go wrong and the all out pessimist in me will kick the little angel off my shoulder. But before it's pitchfork time I believe that these Knicks can do no wrong, will get back to the Finals and beat the Spurs for the repeat. If they fall short I definitely will be dissapointed but will surely get over it quicker than in the past. I should, right? Maybe? No, it will still be awful.

Kato: The east is back to being a beast. The team is one year older and coming off of a championship. And they lost Robinson. I do think a lot of that will be offset with the fact that they unlocked a level of basketball perfection that the team had never previously sniffed. But it's hard to keep that up for all 82 games, especially when finishing first in the regular season does not mean much for them. They've proven they relish playing on the road, and I can see them coming out the gates a bit slow, and taking the regular season slightly lightly. They'll still be great, but I expect them to win 51 games and finish as a third or fourth seed after the 76ers, Celtics, and maybe the Pistons.

Richardson: Under 50 wins, sixth seed. A winner hasn't repeated in seven or eight years, and this team won't break the streak. NY was blessed with health last season. Making Towns an offensive hub in the playoffs added a complexity that opposing teams had no time to prepare for. Mitch was more important in five minute stints than we fully understand. And by confronting the team about their petty dislikes, Brown got everyone pulling in the same direction for the playoffs. Staying healthy is hard, especially with a so-so second unit forcing the starters to play longer; rival teams have added players to counteract NY's offense; Drummond is good, but will not alter opposing strategies the same way Mitch does; and winning has a way of distorting egos. I could see an ECF. I can't see the Finals again. And based on my optical prescription, it's clear I can barely see at all.

#66. Likely 24-team CFP expansion could reshape college football (again) in 2027

The College Football Playoff is moving closer to expanding its current 12-team field to a potential 24-team field in 2027, a change that could dramatically alter the postseason for Texas Longhorns football, the SEC, and beyond. But despite reports of a preliminary agreement with ESPN, expansion has not been formally approved, and key details remain unresolved.

Late last week, the Associated Press reported that the CFP and ESPN had reached a "handshake agreement" on a framework to help offset the revenue conferences could lose by eliminating their championship games. The report, which cited an anonymous source familiar with the negotiations, said an official contract and other details remained unfinished. The CFP's own Oct. 15 statement confirmed that discussions with ESPN were ongoing.

However, the statement did not announce that an official deal had been struck.

Big Ten pushes for 24 teams, while SEC weighs the costs

Big Ten commissioner Tony Petitti has emerged as one of the proposal's strongest advocates, arguing that a larger playoff would make more regular-season games meaningful by keeping additional programs in contention into November. The Big Ten, ACC, and the Big 12 have supported a 24-team field, while the SEC has expressed skepticism.

SEC commissioner Greg Sankey previously favored expanding from 12 teams to 16, citing the potential financial and competitive consequences of a larger bracket (expanding to 24 teams, in other words.) In May, Sankey said the SEC did not have consensus on the size of an expanded playoff. He also emphasized the risks tied to eliminating conference championship games.

Georgia president Jere Morehead also publicly opposed jumping directly to 24 teams. In May remarks reported by The Athletic, Morehead said he preferred trying a 16-team format first. Morehead argued that a 24-team field could diminish the importance of major regular-season matchups.

The SEC's position remains a key variable. Although Sankey has acknowledged growing interest in 24 teams, that does not amount to formal approval of a finalized format amongst the league's official movers and shakers.

The proposed model described by the AP would feature 24 teams: four automatic bids for Power Four conference champions, one automatic bid for the highest-ranked Group of Six champion, and 19 at-large selections. The top eight teams would receive first-round byes, with early-round games played on campus, which has been a selling point amongst many programs thus far. These details remain part of the reported framework, rather than an officially approved bracket.

For Texas, expansion could provide more margin for error in a demanding SEC schedule and another route to a national championship after a disappointing regular season result, such as the 2026 regular season is shaping up to be after the Longhorns dropped consecutive matchups versus Oklahoma and Florida.

Even so, the potential benefits come with trade-offs.

Eliminating or restructuring conference championship games would affect both tradition and revenue, opponents of CFP expansion have argued. The SEC's championship game in Atlanta is a major athletic event; replacing it with additional playoff contests would require the conference to weigh financial returns against the value of its existing postseason, now.

The reported ESPN framework puts a 24-team playoff closer to reality — as near as we get without ink meeting paper — but the CFP has not formally approved the change. The Big Ten, ACC, and Big 12 have advocated expansion, while Georgia's Morehead has led the for those who have argued for a more cautious approach for any continued CFP expansion.

If approved by the Dec. 1 deadline for the 2027 season, a 24-team bracket would represent another major postseason overhaul just three years after the CFP expanded from four teams to 12. For Texas, more access would be welcome. Whether the change creates a better postseason — or simply a bigger, more lucrative one — remains to be seen for now.

#70. Who is MLB's next superteam? Why possible Dodgers decline could open door for Brewers, Yankees, others to rise

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

It was the end of a season and maybe the end of a dynasty. The Los Angeles Dodgers were unceremoniously swept in four games in the NLCS by the Milwaukee Brewers. The Brewers erased an early 4-0 deficit to win Game 4 on Thursday (MIL 6, LAD 4). It is Milwaukee's second-ever pennant and first since 1982. The Dodgers, for the first time since 2023, are going home ringless.

"Extremely proud," Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said when asked how he felt about his team's recent run. "It never feels good to lose and not accomplish a goal to win the World Series. It started back in the early part of February. I love this team and what we had to go through. It's one of those things that every night we take the field, people are bringing their best to beat us."

Even with the NLCS loss, the Dodgers are undoubtedly the team of the 2020s thanks to their three World Series titles (2020, 2024-25), and they are the closest thing baseball has had to a "superteam" since the late 1990s/early 2000s New York Yankees. There was an air of invincibility surrounding the Dodgers right up until the Brewers sent them home for the winter.

Baseball is hard. It's a grueling sport with a long regular season, and an increasingly long postseason subject to more randomness than any other sport. Building a superteam is almost impossible, which makes L.A.'s recent run all the more impressive. Yes, they spent A LOT of money, but so did many other teams, and none came close to this level of success.

Which teams have the best chance to emerge as baseball's next superteam? We can debate exactly what we mean by "superteam" (multiple World Series titles? perennial contention?), but it is one of those things you know it when you see it.

The best of the best. The teams that, if they win the World Series next year, no one would bat an eye and consider themselves surprised. These are the teams with the best chance to be baseball's next superteam.

Los Angeles Dodgers: As poorly as they played in the NLCS, and as old as they looked in the NLCS, there's no reason to think the Dodgers won't enter 2027 as the NL West favorites and on the short list of World Series contenders. They're talented, they're smart, and they have unmatched resources (money and tradeable prospects). A salary cap or stiffer competitive balance tax penalties may rein the Dodgers in a bit, but their player development is so good that I suspect they would continue to dominate the sport anyway.

Milwaukee Brewers: They have been baseball's best team the last two seasons and almost their entire core is either signed long-term or under team control with little service time. Milwaukee's farm system is also regarded as one of the game's best, if not the best. Infielder Jesús Made is arguably the top prospect in baseball and he should make his MLB debut in 2027. Small market teams are always at a disadvantage when it comes to putting together dynastic runs because money equals margin of error. The Brewers can't plug a roster hole or paper over a mistake with money the way big spending teams can. Salary cap or no salary cap, the next collective bargaining agreement figures to include increased revenue sharing, which would level the financial playing field somewhat.

New York Yankees: The Yankees are a metronome. They haven't had a losing season since Wayne's World was in theatres, their "bad" seasons are usually pretty good, and they're in the postseason just about every year. Free agency can be a minefield, but the Yankees tend to nail their biggest signings (Gerrit Cole, Max Fried, etc.), and their player development has improved. The Yankees are here because they give themselves a bite at the apple every season. They're in the postseason every year, and any year could be the year things fall into place for a parade down the Canyon of Heroes.

These teams are in the postseason more often and not, and they usually find themselves near the top of the standings. They're all just a few breaks and fortunate bounces away from superteam status.

Atlanta Braves: Other than an injury-plagued 2025 season, the Braves have been to the postseason every year since 2018. They have a prime-aged core on the position player side (Ronald Acuña Jr., Drake Baldwin, Matt Olson, etc.) and the ageless Chris Sale fronting the rotation. The Braves have been held back by depth issues the last few years, however, which prevents them from moving up into Tier 1. They looked like a potential dynasty following their 2021 World Series win. That's a pretty good reminder of how hard it is to win a championship and stay championship-caliber in this game.

Boston Red Sox: The Red Sox must figure out how to break through the ceiling they've hit the last two years (losing the Wild Card Series at Yankee Stadium), but gosh, what a core. Roman Anthony, Garrett Crochet, Ceddanne Rafaela, and Payton Tolle are an enviable quartet to build around, and there's a strong supporting cast in place. The Red Sox are one or two big bats away from being a serious problem for the rest of the American League. Even without that big bat(s), they're good enough to reach the postseason and capable of going on a run.

Chicago Cubs: They have some heavy lifting ahead of them this offseason, given the state of the rotation and the fact that both corner outfielders (Ian Happ and Seiya Suzuki) are free agents. When you start your roster with Pete Crow-Armstrong, though, and have a supporting cast that includes Alex Bregman, Michael Busch and Nico Hoerner, you're about 80% of the way to World Series contention. The Cubs are stuck playing in the same division as the Brewers and that makes life challenging, but in no way does it doom them.

Cleveland Guardians: Yes, they play in a crummy division, but the Guardians win that crummy division every year and work their way into the postseason. That's more than half the battle when it comes to establishing yourself as a superteam. Cleveland will never run high payrolls, which lessens their margin of error, though the upcoming collective bargaining agreement could improve things for tiny payroll teams. Bottom line, the Guardians keep pumping out quality pitching, and when you do that, you have a chance to win a lot of ballgames.

Philadelphia Phillies: The Phillies are getting long in the tooth and they're closer to the end of their World Series window than the beginning, but that window is still open. It will remain open as long as they have Jesús Luzardo and Cristopher Sánchez leading the rotation, and Bryce Harper and Kyle Schwarber anchoring the middle of the lineup. You have to squint to see a potential superteam here, yes, though the foundation of a World Series-contending roster is in place. Improve the supporting cast and the Phillies are right there with any team.

San Diego Padres: I am curious to see how the Padres approach their first offseason under their new ownership. José Feliciano and Kwanza Jones, the new owners, insist they will spend to keep the team in contention. OK, so why shouldn't the Padres be in on Tarik Skubal on Day 1 of the offseason then? The Padres have to figure things out on the pitching side, for sure. They badly need more depth. They do have a strong blend of 20-somethings (Jackson Merrill, Ethan Salas, Fernando Tatis Jr.) and veterans (Manny Machado) to build around, though.

Tampa Bay Rays: Tampa's status as a perennial contender is a wee bit overstated (this is their first postseason appearance since 2023), but they are inarguably one of the smartest teams in baseball, and they have a capital-S Superstar in Junior Caminero. Also, they have a new ballpark coming in the next few years, one that will be located in Tampa rather than St. Petersburg. That should boost revenues and thus payroll, and improve their World Series chances.

This tier is reserved for teams that should have been better than they were in 2026. These teams could be on the cusp of superteam status a year from now, but right now, they're all well short for one reason or another.

New York Mets: The Brewers having the success they've had while the Mets have authored back-to-back disaster seasons begs the question: Is POBO David Stearns really all he's cracked up to be? The silver lining of their lost 2026 season is that several young players emerged as long-term building blocks, most notably Carson Benge and Nolan McLean. Those two, plus Juan Soto, who will turn only 28 later this month, are the makings of a championship-caliber core, plus owner Steve Cohen is very willing to spend. Are the Mets a potential superteam? Yes. Have they earned the benefit of the doubt? Absolutely not.

Seattle Mariners: Expectations were sky high coming into the season and then the Mariners fell flat and finished five games back in what was arguably the worst division in baseball history. More distressingly, franchise players Cal Raleigh and Julio Rodríguez took big steps back. It feels like the range of potential outcomes for the 2027 Mariners is massive. You could tell me they'll win 102 games and storm to the World Series, and I'd believe it. You could also tell me they'll stumble to 75 wins and Rodriguez's name will pop up in trade rumors, and I'd believe that too.

Toronto Blue Jays: Last year, the Blue Jays came as close to winning the World Series as you can without actually winning the World Series. If Vladimir Guerrero Jr. continues to be this moving forward, that's an enormous problem and puts a serious dent in Toronto's World Series hopes. I'm willing to give Guerrero and the Blue Jays some benefit of the doubt and assume 2026 is not their new normal, but not so much that I'll move them into Tier 2. They have won a postseason series in just one of the last 10 seasons, after all.

At best, these teams are a year away from being a year away from possible superteam status, but they are arrow-up organizations rapidly approaching contention. If they were a stock, I'd say buy buy buy.

Chicago White Sox: I thought the White Sox were a year away entering 2026. Instead, so many of their young players took a step forward at once, and they were able to contend for the AL Central title. Making the jump from rebuilder to contender is the easy part. The hard part is staying in contention. To do that, the White Sox must come up with more pitching, and we need to see some more commitment (i.e. raise payroll) from owner Jerry Reinsdorf, who treats the ChiSox as the smallest big market team in baseball.

St. Louis Cardinals: The transition from John Mozeliak to new POBO Chaim Bloom is complete, and now the farm system and player development apparatus is on the rise. The Cardinals have several building-block position players in place (Masyn Winn, Jordan Walker, JJ Wetherholt) with more on the way (Jesús Báez, Rainiel Rodriguez, etc.). Now the pitching must catch up to the position player side of things, and pitchers are wizards these days. Anyone could break out at any moment. The Cardinals are on the cusp of a return to sustained contention.

Washington Nationals: The new front office, led by POBO Paul Toboni, is getting rave reviews. The results are already showing up on the field, too. CJ Abrams, Cade Cavalli, and Jacob Young all made leaps this season. They turned low-cost pickups Foster Griffin and Curtis Mead into a bounty of young players at the trade deadline. The farm system is robust. The Nationals are in a brutal division, but the third wild card spot is very forgiving. All indications are that they will compete for one of them soon, and the NL East title not long after that.

#74. 2026-27 Forecast: Improved Wizards will compete for a play-in spot

For the first time since the 2022-23 season, the Washington Wizards will be trying to win games. That's not an innovative endeavor in professional sports, though it's not one the franchise has successfully implemented for…well…decades.

The team made a series of moves during the 2025-26 season and in the offseason to boost the overall talent level. The big additions are Trae Young (who appeared in five games last season before getting parked), Anthony Davis (zero games last season), and AJ Dybantsa, the No. 1 overall pick in the 2026 NBA Draft.

Those three are — at least theoretically — massive talent upgrades. I say "theoretically" because of the health histories of Young and Davis and the perfectly normal "how soon does he get it?" questions about any 19-year-old, even enormously gifted ones like Dybantsa.

They further improved their big man rotation by trading for Deandre Ayton.

The front office made sure they had strong veteran leaders by bringing back Khris Middleton and Anthony Gill. And they shuffled some names at the end of the bench with a trade to absorb the contract of Tre Mann and the selection of Felix Okpara in the second round.

The roster is…interesting. In Davis, Young, Ayton, and Middleton they have a group that might have formed the nucleus of a good team 3-5 years ago. In Dybantsa, Alex Sarr, Kyshawn George, Bilal Coulibaly, Tre Johnson, and Bub Carrington they have a group of youngsters who could form a good team 3-5 years in the future.

The new try to win strategy will increase scrutiny on Brian Keefe, who sports one of the worst winning percentages in league history. The team made some changes to the coaching staff, promoting Adam Caporn (well respected around the league, and also coach of the Australian national team) to lead assistant, Cody Toppert from his role coaching the Capital City Go-Go, adding Patrick Ewing as a big man coach, and former NBA head coach Steve Clifford as an advisor.

David Vanterpool, who'd been the lead assistant the past three seasons, moves into a front office job.

This year's forecast presented some unique challenges. Biggest of these was guesstimating minutes. For the holdover Wizards, past may not be prelude. More productive youngsters (Sarr, Coulibaly, George) likely missed games and saw reduced minutes because of the team's commitment to losing — not because the various injuries and ailments would have kept them out of games if they'd been trying to win.

On the other hand, Carrington played more than 2,200 minutes (and all 82 games) in each of his first two seasons. Odds of him playing another 2,000+ minutes this season are minuscule.

Veterans like Young and Davis have missed time throughout the past few seasons due to injury, including huge chunks of last season. Both could have played more last season…if the Wizards had been trying to win. Both have fairly recent seasons with high minutes.

Davis played 2,700 regular season minutes in 2023-24. But he's missed a lot of time since. Compounding the challenge is that he's 33-years-old, which is when NBA players typically do two things: get injured and get worse. So, while I anticipate Davis will play more than he has the past couple seasons, I'd be surprised if he cracks 2,000 minutes. My guesstimate for him is 1,650.

Young, on the other hand, has been reasonably healthy. He played 2,739 minutes in 2024-25, and has appeared in less than 2,000 minutes just twice in his career. In one of them, he played 1,942 minutes. He surely would have played much more last year if wasn't for The Tank. Bottom line: Young has been reasonably healthy throughout his career, and can probably be counted on to be available. I have him guesstimated at 2,375 this season.

These forecasts use my Player Production Average (PPA) metric. PPA is an all-around rating tool that credits players for things they do that help a team win, and debits for things that don't — each in proportion to how individual players contribute to NBA wins and losses. PPA is pace neutral and includes accounting for defense, role and the level of competition a player faces when he's on the floor. In PPA, average is 100, higher is better, and replacement level is 45.

Below are results from four different forecast approaches: one using my Statistical Doppelgänger Machine (DOPP), another using a predicted PPA based on an age-adjusted career curve (dubbed MILK in honor of sports economist David Berri, who wore that NBA players, "…age like milk…"), a simple weighted three-year average PPA (SIMP) and another that applies an aging adjustment to that weighted three-year average (SAGE).

I estimated minutes by using a weighted average of each player's minutes in recent seasons, as well as my best guess at each player's role in the team's rotation this season.

DOPP = forecasted PPA using the Doppelgänger approach

MILK = forecasted PPA using last season's PPA and an age adjustment

SIMP = forecasted PPA using a "simple" weighted three-year average PPA

SAGE = forecasted PPA using a "simple" weighted three-year average and an age adjustment

BLEND = forecasted PPA using an average of the four approaches above

The *** represents my best guess of which forecast is most probable for each individual.

Before getting into the forecasts, I'm dubious about the SIMP and SAGE approaches, at least for younger players. The SIMP approach (weighted three-year average) forecasts lower scores for young guys, who typically play their worst as rookies and then improve. The age adjustment in the SAGE method improves that estimate somewhat, but still has the same underlying issue.

My feeling based on having done these for a few years is that DOPP and MILK are probably going to be better for players in their first 3-4 seasons, and that SIMP and SAGE will be applicable to established veterans.

Sublime and inventive passer with a ton of skill and craft across his offensive game. Young's penchant for jacking up long threes is something of a drain on his offensive efficiency, and his adventurous passing leads to a lot of turnovers. Still, he's a dynamic offensive player, who has a history of generating a high number of trips to the free throw line.

He's been one of the NBA's worst defenders for eight seasons because he's small, slender, and hasn't played with much alertness or effort on that end. In Washington, he says he's going to work harder, which seemed to be the case in preseason.

Skillful and competitive player, who improved his shooting last season. He tries hard on defense, and he's huge — at least 6-8 and getting stronger because of a borderline psycho offseason regimen.

The competitiveness has led to excessive fouling and turnovers, which have undermined his overall impact. He was named a starter at the beginning of trainging camp, and he had a great preseason.

Players most like George tended to improve at this point in their careers, though the improvement was somewhat modest. George seems primed for a major leap, however.

The uber talented, hyper-athletic forward was Washington's prize for sustained losing. He was the No. 1 overall selection in a historically good draft, and he has all the tools to be an elite scorer for the next dozen years.

The Wizards may have to wait to see him in regular season action — he turned an ankle in the final preseason game and is listed as day-to-day. (My guess: he plays. He's 19-years-old and is probably already fully healed.)

For forecasting rookies, I use a system based on production over the past decade from players in a similar draft position.

Davis has been a great player, especially on the defensive end in the postseason. His regular season defensive impact has been more hit or miss, which could be said of his shooting away from the basket (though more miss than hit). And he's tended to get hurt a lot. And he's aging. And he wants a massive contract extension.

My guess is he'll miss time again, though not as much as previous seasons. I don't think he'll appear in enough games to qualify for awards. The hope is that he's healthy enough for long enough that Sarr and the other youngsters can learn from his defensive communication.

Don't be shocked if he's elsewhere by the trade deadline.

The No. 2 overall selection in the 2024 NBA Draft, Sarr is another of Washington's tanking prizes. After one of the least efficient offensive seasons in NBA history as a rookie, Sarr improved significantly at that end. He showed off a much improved post game, better shooting from everywhere, and even some passing chops.

His strength seemed to be on defense, where he held his own switching onto perimeter players and was a busy and effective rim protector. The presence of Davis and Ayton should alleviate some of the burden he had to shoulder, which could result in a more efficient and effective player.

Still just 21-years-old, Sarr could develop into a truly great player over the next few seasons. The next two are when NBA players typically make their biggest leaps.

This is a make or break season for French wing. Coulibaly is long, quick, fast, and bouncy, which helps make him into an effective and disruptive defender.

His offensive game has been an adventure. Passive at times, over-aggressive at others. His three-point shooting has been deficient, though defenders have had trouble staying in front of him when he decides to drive.

He's improved each season of his career and is at a crossroads — he's a restricted free agent at the end of the season, unless he unexpectedly reaches an agreement on an extension.

Acquired to be a backup big and an insurance policy against Davis' frequent outages, Ayton is also at a career crossroads. He's talented and fairly productive, and his teams keep wanting to get rid of him.

In Washington, he'll primarily come off the bench for the first time in his career (assuming Davis plays) but should get plenty of minutes. If he buys in and produces, he'll likely command at least an MLE-level deal going forward. If not, he could be relegated to minimum salary deals.

Carrington has yet to miss a game in his two NBA seasons. He's competitive and shot above 40% on threes last season. He's likely to play less this season, and probably wouldn't have played so much on a better team.

The quality of his play didn't tick up despite the better shooting. He'll need to get better at both ends to maintain a spot in the rotation.

Good-maybe-great shooter. The question on Johnson is whether he can show more dimension to his game — some playmaking, a few more rebounds, better defense. It wouldn't hurt to get a lot stronger, which may take some time since he's still just 20-years-old.

Entering his age 35 season, Middleton figures to be at the end of the team's rotation. He's the team's elder statesman, and he's seen it all — winning a title with the Milwaukee Bucks, missing huge chunks of seasons with a series of injuries, battling back to be productive even as he's aged.

Odds are, Middleton's days as a productive player are in the rearview mirror. He still has a lot of veteran savvy to contribute, and there will probably a game or three or five where he comes through big time for the team.

Good player the past couple seasons, but he appears to be the odd man out of the rotation — at least to start the season. My guess is he'll still get more than a thousand minutes this season, and that he'll be pretty good again. I would not be surprised to see him end up elsewhere as part of a multi-player and draft pick trade.

The good news: this year's Washington Wizards will be more competitive this season. At least some of the youngsters will improve — perhaps significantly — and the team has some skilled veterans with histories of high-level performances.

The bad news: they're still not ready to be good. The youngsters are still a few years from their primes. The oldsters are likely past their primes already. That's a statement that includes Young and Ayton, who are both entering their age 28 season, by the way.

The years of tanking have given the Wizards two potential stars in Dybantsa and Sarr, though both are likely several seasons from achieving that status. George and Coulibaly seem like probable rotation-level players. Davis, Young, and Ayton will outproduce guys previously on the roster, even if they fall short of their previous heights.

The various forecasting approaches yield the following forecasted wins totals:

While the above feels kinda disappointing, even the worst of these would mark significant improvement for the Wizards. Last season, they managed just 18 wins.

If everyone reaches their best-case forecast, I guesstimate the team could reach 36 wins. In an all-peaks scenario, they could get to 41.

My prediction is a season of significant improvement. I anticipate the older players will be good, though well short of their previous peaks and that the youngsters will continue improving. I would not be surprised to see a veteran or two departing midseason as the front office tries to position the team to arrive in the postseason as a contender.

Final Prediction: 34-48 and 11th in the Eastern Conference.

#75. Peyton Manning a favorite candidate for Colts’ GM job

The Indianapolis Colts fired general manager Chris Ballard on Monday, one day after blowing a 13-0 halftime lead in a 26-20 loss at Lucas Oil Stadium to the previously winless Tennessee Titans. The move came after a 2-4 start to Ballard's 10th season.

Ballard, 57, had held the job since January 2017, signed a five-year extension in 2021 and led Indianapolis to two playoff appearances, in 2018 and 2020. Owner and CEO Carlie Irsay-Gordon said "a change in leadership is necessary" to meet the franchise's standard of competing for championships. A familiar name from the franchise's past has already entered the conversation.

MORE: 3 NFL teams that should be worried after Week 6

Peyton Manning in field before Miami Dolphins and the Indianapolis Colts game. Credit: Grace Hollars-USA TODAY Network via Imagn Images.

The Colts are considering Peyton Manning for the general manager vacancy, according to Dan Patrick on The Dan Patrick Show.

Indianapolis is exploring whether Manning would be interested in the job and a potential ownership stake down the line.

Before his retirement, Manning spent 14 seasons with the Colts, throwing for 54,828 yards and 399 touchdowns and winning Super Bowl XLI before Indianapolis released him in 2012.

Irsay-Gordon called the in-season timing deliberate and said the Colts will conduct a thorough search, taking the time necessary to find the right leader.

He has. Then-owner Jim Irsay said in 2019 that he and Manning came close to an agreement on a president or general manager role before the 2017 season. Manning ultimately passed.

Assistant general manager Ed Dodds, who joined the Colts in 2017, also remains with the team and has interviewed for GM jobs elsewhere.

Indianapolis visits the Minnesota Vikings on Sunday, Oct. 25, at 1 p.m. ET on CBS. Head coach Shane Steichen will lead the team without the GM who hired him, and Irsay-Gordon said the firing does not change the Colts' goals for the season.

#78. Aaron Glenn: No confusion about who got the ball to start the second half

Jets head coach Aaron Glenn's on-field interview before the start of the second half on Sunday went viral, but Glenn said on Monday that his comments were misinterpreted.

Glenn told Aditi Kinkhabwala of CBS that the team would be ready to go despite being down 17-3 and that "the good thing is we get the ball, we get a chance to go move it and finish." That was widely interpreted to be Glenn saying that the Jets would receive the kickoff to start the second half, which was not the case, and Glenn said on Monday that he was talking about what would happen after the defense forced a stop.

"No, I actually talked about just the offense," Glenn said on Monday, via Howie Kussoy of the New York Post. "I think they were talking about sustaining drives, and my conversation with them is when the offense gets the ball back, man, we want to be able to sustain a drive and go score. Then when the defense gets back on, we want to make sure we stop them and get the ball back to our offense. That's what I was talking about when it comes to that. The conversation was talking about the offense at that time."

Things actually did work out as Glenn hoped as the Jets forced a punt and then scored on a touchdown pass to rookie wideout Omar Cooper. They would eventually pull within 17-13, but the Patriots went on to win 26-19.

#79. The Spurs will start Dylan Harper on opening night, so where does that leave De'Aaron Fox?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

For opening night, at least, the San Antonio Spurs have answered the single biggest starting lineup question of the 2026-27 season. Dylan Harper, the No. 2 pick in the 2025 NBA Draft and the second-best player in San Antonio's NBA Finals loss to the New York Knicks, will officially join the starting five alongside Victor Wembanyama, Stephon Castle, Devin Vassell... and De'Aaron Fox, the expensive veteran whose injured ankle and ensuing struggles loomed large over that Finals defeat.

San Antonio barely used the three-guard lineup last season, and for good reason. It was outscored significantly in both 54-possession regular-season and 83-possession postseason samples last year. The lineup outscored the Phoenix Suns by 10 points in 25 possessions in a recent preseason victory, but the Spurs shot just 2 of 9 on 3s when all three guards played together in that game.

That is the primary concern here. Harper, Fox and Castle are all strong drivers with questionable 3-point shots. Such players typically do best when surrounded by other shooters. The Spurs can get away with having two of them on the floor at once because their center, Victor Wembanyama, is game-breaking in dozens of ways, including his ability to space the floor. San Antonio took off last season when it upgraded its shooting by inserting Julian Champagnie into the starting lineup.

With all three guards playing together, though, the delicate balance between shooting and ball-handling has tilted too far toward the latter. Ball-handling doesn't have nearly the amplifying effect that shooting does, and opponents will inevitably cheat off of the two guards without the ball in their hands whenever one of them is trying to create shots with it. The trio is so talented, and comes with the inherent advantage of playing with Wembanyama, that the Spurs will almost certainly win most of the games it plays with this starting lineup.

But it's certainly suboptimal. We all know where this is probably heading. Harper was simply too good to keep coming off of the bench, and Castle is too good to ever move there. Eventually, the best version of the Spurs likely has Fox, the oldest and most expensive of the three guards, coming off of the bench as Harper did a season ago. San Antonio's starters with Champagnie playing alongside two of the guards outscored opponents by 17.6 points per 100 possessions a season ago. The formula of two guards, two shooters and Wembanyama is this team's endgame.

Yet even if that's the case, the Spurs are slow-playing this. In the long run, that's probably the sensible approach. Benching a reigning All-Star on a max contract is fraught. Fox very intentionally steered himself to San Antonio through a direct trade request, presumably expecting to be the starting point guard on a dynasty. Players of his stature and age are rarely eager to come off of the bench. Asking him to do so on opening night based off of a poor Finals series in which he was injured risks alienating a key player and, cynically, destroying what little trade value he might have left.

Even if the Spurs do plan to bench Fox down the line, easing him into it seems like the safest approach. He still has a chance to prove that this three-guard lineup can work, and if it does, well, maybe there's less of a problem here than we're assuming. If it proves uncomfortable or if the lineup data suggests it's flopping, the Spurs at least have empirical data supporting a change. They can at least tell Fox that they tried.

They'd hardly be the first team to try this approach to benching a star. Russell Westbrook went through it with both Los Angeles teams, for instance. The Lakers benched him after an 0-3 start in the 2022-23 season. The Clippers let him and James Harden start five games together a year later, lost all five, and then went 27-7 in their next 34 after benching him. Sometimes, you have to sacrifice a few games for the greater good. Players of this caliber tend to expect a certain degree of respect that the attempt at least affords.

The notion of sacrificing games is going to be a bitter pill to swallow in this case, specifically, because San Antonio's competition for the No. 1 seed in the Western Conference practically never does so. The Oklahoma City Thunder churn out 60-win seasons in their sleep, and home-court advantage in the practically preordained Western Conference Finals between them, despite San Antonio's road victory a year ago, is meaningful. But that same road victory showed the Spurs that what matters isn't October or November. It's May and June.

If the Spurs have to take the long road to optimized lineups and locker room harmony, so be it. For now, they're giving Harper the starting job he so clearly deserves and tabling the Fox end of the equation until the issue is forced.

#80. Rangers lose star goaltender Igor Shesterkin for season with lower-body injury; what's next for New York?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

New York Rangers goaltender Igor Shesterkin will miss the remainder of the season with a lower-body injury, the team announced on Saturday.

Shesterkin suffered an apparent leg injury in the Rangers' loss to the Washington Capitals on Friday night as his right leg slid awkwardly into the post while scrambling to get back in position. Shesterkin fell to the ice immediately, and he needed assistance to get down the tunnel.

Prior to that loss, the Rangers were off to a terrific 4-1-0 start, and Shesterkin was a driving force behind that success. In just five appearances, Shesterkin posted 3.90 goals saved above average with a .900 high-danger save percentage, according to Natural Stat Trick.

The 2022 Vezina Trophy winner, Shesterkin has put up sparkling numbers since he entered the NHL in 2019-20. In 330 games, Shesterkin boasts a .917 save percentage, a 2.51 GAA and 22 shutouts. Over the last three full seasons from 2023-26, Shesterkin ranked third in goals saved above average with 45.4. Only Connor Hellebuyck and Andrei Vasilevskiy were better in that category.

Shesterkin was a big reason why the Rangers felt they could bounce back from a disappointing 2025-26 season, and losing the star goaltender puts a huge dent in the team's playoff hopes. It doesn't help that backup goalie Joonas Korpisalo is also hurt.

Dylan Garand replaced Shesterkin on Friday night, and Spencer Martin will be recalled from the AHL after recovering from his own injury. With the Rangers playing well early, it wouldn't be a shock to see them explore better replacement options for Shesterkin.

New York won't be able to replace Shesterkin's impact because he's one of the five best goalies in the world. However, the team should be able to upgrade its current goaltending situation, which is a fairly low bar to clear.

First, there are unsigned veterans still on the open market in Petr Mrazek and James Reimer. Neither one was great last season -- hence their availability at the moment -- Reimer and Mrazek could provide a level of stability in the crease that the Rangers simply don't have right now.

New York could also explore trade possibilities, and Minnesota Wild netminder Filip Gustavsson could be a solution there. Jesper Wallstedt is the future of the crease in Minnesota, making Gustavsson more of a luxury. Would the Wild send Gustavsson to New York in exchange for some draft capital it could use to acquire a center?

The one snag in a potential Gustavsson deal is his contract. Gustavsson is in the first year of a deal that pays him $6.8 million over the next five seasons. That's a big commitment for a player who will become a backup when Shesterkin returns.

Obviously, Connor Hellebuyck has been on the trade market for months now, but that trade wouldn't make sense for the Rangers. Hellebuyck is on an expensive long-term deal, and New York would have $20 million tied up in goalies if they made that move, not to mention the astronomical acquisition cost.

However, if you'll allow me to get creative here, it's no secret that the Florida Panthers have pursed Hellebuyck. What if the Panthers traded Jacob Markstrom -- just acquired in the offseason -- to the Rangers in order to make room for Hellebuyck?

Markstrom does have a 20-team no-trade list, so the question is whether New York would be one of his 11 approved teams. Florida flipping Markstrom so quickly seems like a long shot, but the team has taken plenty of big swings in recent history.

#81. Bills' C.J. Gardner-Johnson apologizes for spitting at Brock Bowers

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Buffalo Bills safety C.J. Gardner-Johnson apologized for an incident in the second quarter of Sunday's game against the Las Vegas Raiders in which he spit at Raiders tight end Brock Bowers.

Gardner-Johnson, who was ejected on the spot, addressed "my opponent, my teammates, my organization, and everyone who supports me" in an Instagram story.

C.J. Gardner-Johnson spits in the direction of Brock Bowers, leading to disqualification pic.twitter.com/8zW4OYIP7o

"My passion and competitive nature have always been a huge part of who I am, but I also understand that there is a line that should never be crossed," Gardner-Johnson said. "The gesture I made toward my opponent was inappropriate, unnecessary, and not a reflection of the respect I have for him or this game. There is no excuse for my actions, and I take full accountability. No matter how emotional or intense the competition gets, I have to hold myself to a higher standard."

Both players involved in the scuffle said in their postgame media availability that they were jawing at each other when the incident occurred. Gardner-Johnson said he expects to receive a fine from the NFL.

"I love this game, I respect this game, and I will always protect the integrity of this game," Gardner-Johnson said. "My actions will speak louder than words moving forward."

Spitting is an automatic ejection. Last year, Eagles defensive tackle Jalen Carter got ejected six seconds into the first game of the season for spitting on Dak Prescott, and later in the season, Ja'Marr Chase got suspended one game for spitting on Jalen Ramsey (who got ejected for punching Chase after the alleged spitting incident). Initially, the refereeing crew did not see Chase spit, which is why only Ramsey was ejected, but the NFL determined after the game that Chase indeed spat on Ramsey, resulting in the suspension.

It's the second ejection of Gardner-Johnson's NFL career; the other came in 2024, when he accrued two personal foul penalties in the same game. He then gave middle fingers to the Commanders' crowd on the way out.

Gardner-Johnson is in his first season in Buffalo — his sixth different team and fourth in the past three years. One of the game's most fiery competitors, he has been a key part of the Bills' defense thanks to his versatility in the secondary, so it's a big loss Sunday and potentially beyond, should the NFL choose to suspend Gardner-Johnson.

#82. Milwaukee Bucks change time of home opener with Brewers hosting World Series Game 1 on same night

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Milwaukee Bucks have moved their home opener against the Chicago Bulls on Friday, Oct. 23 to the afternoon to accomodate Game 1 of the World Series, which will be hosted by the Milwaukee Brewers.

The Bucks' matchup with the Bulls, which was scheduled for 7 p.m., will now tip off at 3 p.m. local time. Major League Baseball has not yet officially announced a start time for Game 1 of the World Series, but it is likely to start around 7 p.m. CT.

Here is a statement from the Bucks regarding the schedule change, which will create a unique sports doubleheader in Milwaukee:

"The Brewers' return to the World Series for the first time in 44 years is a special moment for Milwaukee and sports fans across Wisconsin. Congratulations to the Brewers and the entire organization on this tremendous achievement, and we'll be cheering them on as they begin their World Series run. The Bucks are proud to move our home opener to 3 p.m. in recognition of this historic occasion and thank the NBA for making this schedule change possible."

The Brewers, who won a franchise-record 103 games this season and had the best record in baseball, advanced to the World Series for the first time since 1982 by sweeping the Los Angeles Dodgers in the National League Championship Series. The Dodgers had won the last two World Series, and had been vying to become the first team to threepeat since the New York Yankees from 1998-2000.

The Brewers will play either the Tampa Bay Rays or Cleveland Guardians. The Guardians currently lead the American League Championship Series, 2-1. Should the World Series go the distance, there could be another scheduling conflict between the Brewers and Bucks. Game 7 of the World Series is set for Oct. 31, and the Bucks are hosting the Cleveland Cavaliers that night.

The Bucks, who won the NBA championship in 2021, will begin a new era when their season tips off next week. During the summer, the team traded two-time MVP Giannis Antetokounmpo to the Miami Heat, ending the Greek Freak's 13-season run in Milwaukee, where he had become an icon.

#83. 2026-27 NBA News, Injury Updates Oct 19: Ben Simmons tears Achilles, Stephen Curry tweaks ankle

Welcome to our weekly Monday Morning NBA notebook, a quick hit of NBA news and injuries from around the league to catch you up on what happened in the past week. If you've been focused on football — or going to a Doja Cat concert, or just enjoying life — and not been paying much attention to the NBA, we've got you covered. Here's what you need to know.

This is just devastating news: Sacramento's Ben Simmons suffered a torn right Achilles in a practice on Sunday, will undergo surgery and miss the entire 2026-27 season.

Simmons was out of the league last season, focusing on getting his body healthy — after years of lingering back issues and multiple surgeries — and his mind in a good place. It appeared to have worked. Reports out of Sacramento had been overwhelmingly positive, and Simmons, 30, averaged 10.5 points, 4 rebounds and 4 assists in 17.4 minutes per preseason game. He was expected to be a starter. Now a fluke injury has sidelined him.

It also leaves Kings' coach Doug Christie scrambling to round out his rotations.

Golden State's Mr. Everything Stephen Curry gave everyone a scare when he limped straight to the locker room during a public practice on Sunday.

After practice, coach Steve Kerr said Curry was "fine" and downplayed it as a tweaked ankle. Officially, the Warriors have said it's a sprain, although it doesn't appear to be severe.

The Warriors open the season on Wednesday against the Lakers. Curry's status will be worth monitoring.

Warriors big man Kristaps Porzingis came in this week and met with general manager Mike Dunleavy and vice president of player health & performance Dr. Rick Celebrini about his still-undisclosed ailment. There is no timeline for his return, but Porzingis said he is improving, is frustrated, and shot down some of the most ridiculous (but somehow gaining traction) speculation among Warriors faithful.

This is a good bit of work by both sides. The Oklahoma City Thunder lock up now-starting guard Cason Wallace with a five-year, $139 million contract extension. With that, the Thunder now have their starting five, plus bench star Alex Caruso, under contract for multiple years.

Wallace, 22 and Second Team All-Defense last season, will step into a larger role as a starter for the Thunder this season, stepping into Lu Dort's role (Dort was traded to Atlanta in a cost-cutting move). Wallace could have bet on himself and a big restricted free agent market next summer, but surveyed the landscape and decided to stay with the only team he has known on a healthy contract.

Welcome to the start of the NBA season — and it all begins with an epic triple-header on NBC and Peacock.

• Boston Celtics at Detroit Pistons, 3 p.m. Eastern. For all the focus on other teams in the East, these were the top two seeds in the conference a year ago and with Jayson Tatum and Cade Cunningham, they are going to be back near the top again.• Philadelphia 76ers at New York Knicks, ring ceremony at 6:30 p.m., game at 7 p.m. Eastern. Newcomers LeBron James and Jaylen Brown lead Philadelphia into Madison Square Garden as the 76ers look to spoil ring night for Jalen Brunson, Karl-Anthony Towns and the rest of the Knicks.• Oklahoma City Thunder at San Antonio Spurs, 9:30 p.m. Eastern. Game 8 of last year's epic Western Conference Finals, with a showdown between two MVP favorites: Victor Wembanyama and Shai Gilgeous-Alexander.

You can catch all the games on NBC or stream them on Peacock.

• Nuggets wing Julian Strawther suffered a sprained left knee and is out indefinitely, he will be re-evaluated in six weeks. Strawther suffered the injury in a preseason game against the Clippers, and it looked worse than it turned out to be. With Peyton Watson no longer in Denver, Strawther, the 24-year-old fourth-year player out of Gonzaga, is poised to take on a bigger role with the team, but that is now on hold.

• The New York Knicks waived veteran guard Bruce Brown. As reported a few days before, the Knicks coaching staff and front office wanted to keep Brown on the roster this season, but to do so and stay under the second apron of the luxury tax — as mandated by owner James Dolan — they would have needed to trade Pacome Dadiet or Tyler Kolek, and no deal was available, so Brown was waived. Reserve big man James Wiseman gets the final roster spot. Don't expect Brown to be out of a job for long.

• The Philadelphia 76ers are keeping fan favorite, 7'6" Tacko Fall around on a two-way contract to start the season. For a team with depth questions at center, there are good basketball reasons for this, but it just makes a lot of fans happy to see him play.

• The good news for the Kings was that reserve center Maxime Raynaud suffered "only" a right patellar subluxation that will keep him out a couple of weeks. It looked a lot worse when it happened. While there is no timeline for a return, Raynaud — Second Team All-Rookie last season — should be back early in the season.

On top of that, another Kings center, Dylan Cardwell, suffered a left calf strain and will miss a couple of weeks at the start of the season. That leaves the Kings thin at center. Domantas Sabonis will start at the five, but after him it's now Precious Achiuwa (more of a four) and two-way player Jonathan Mogbo.

• The Charlotte Hornets chose to waive veteran guard Pat Connaughton — who was on a non-guaranteed contract — which means they keep former No. 6 pick Tidjane Salaun (current GM Jeff Peterson's first pick).

• The Clippers' Brandon Ingram is back to doing on-court work and getting closer to a return, but he is still going to miss the start of the season and there is no timetable for his return. The Clippers need his shot creation.

• Also with the Clippers, they waived Cam Christie, but then brought him back on a two-way contract. For two seasons after the Clippers drafted him in the second round, Christie — brother of Dallas' Max Christie — has teased fans and the organization with his potential, but he never seemed to develop. The Clippers had to make roster cuts, and after a rough preseason Christie was the guy not making the final 15, but keeping him around is smart.

• Thunder rookie Otega Oweh, the No. 41 pick in last June's NBA Draft out of Kentucky and on a two-way contract, suffered a torn Achilles and is out for the season.

• The Suns and young center Oso Ighodaro agreed to a three-year, $29 million contract extension that will keep him with the team through 2031. Ighodaro played 82 games with Phoenix last season, was solid, and will have a real opportunity to grow that role this season.

#84. Jota 'met some demons' during long injury absence

Jota admits he "met some demons" during his long injury absence but believes there is no need to "rush" his return to full match fitness at Celtic.

The Portuguese winger, 27, sustained cruciate ligament damage in April 2025 and made his first-team return last weekend in the 2-0 win at Motherwell.

And, after coming off the bench again in Sunday's 7-1 Scottish Premiership victory at home to Hearts, Jota believes the ordeal has strengthened his character.

"I've met some demons and I've had some good talks with them," he said. "We developed a good relationship and we are all on the same table nowadays and we can laugh about everything that happened.

"If you don't grow from a situation like this, it's because you didn't learn anything.

"I could step away, see different things from other perspectives and value some stuff that maybe I wasn't valuing before.

"I have a clear idea of what I want, what I am. There's no lost time because I grew a lot. It had to be what it had to be and I didn't lose. I actually gained because I'm way stronger nowadays."

Hearts roll out red carpet ... and Celtic walk all over it

#87. Six Other Heroes From BYU’s Momentous Win Over Notre Dame

We all know the name Bear Bachmeier. If, by some miracle, Bachmeier were to become the second ever Heisman Trophy winner in BYU history or at least get invited to the ceremony, the path to that moment truly gained traction against the Fighting Irish on Saturday night. He was clearly the biggest hero from the 28-24 win by No. 8 BYU over No. 2 Notre Dame. Per Kirk Herbstreit on X, "(Bachmeier is) the FIRST FBS player in the past 30 years to throw, catch, and rush for TD against an AP TOP 5 opponent in the same game."

He deserves all the praise and possible accolades that come with that special win and so far, special season for Bachmeier and BYU. But this is a moment to allow others into the spotlight. Let's highlight six other players who played a massive role in BYU upsetting the Irish in the biggest win at LaVell Edwards Stadium maybe ever.

What if I told you that BYU would out-gain Notre Dame on the ground without reigning Big 12 Offensive Player of the Year LJ Martin at running back? I would have been checked for signs of hallucinations or hypnosis. BYU did exactly that. Credit to offensive coordinator Aaron Roderick for getting creative. Of course, Bachmeier did his portion on the ground with 44 yards on 14 attempts and two touchdowns. But Rex needs his flowers. Most discounted the run game outside of Bachmeier against this vaunted Irish run defense. Instead, Rex averaged 6.6 yards per carry on 10 totes for 66 yards. He had two runs of at least 10 yards and gained three first downs. He provided enough of a variety in the run game for the Irish to have to think about someone other than Bear.

I almost listed Kasper as "WR/QB." The double pass from Bachmeier to Kasper, who tossed it back to Bachmeier for a touchdown, was a thing of beauty. Not only was that a dime of a pass from a 6-foot-6 receiver, but Kasper was a huge player in the passing attack at his traditional receiver role as well. Getting eight targets, he hauled in six passes for 66 yards. He was clearly Bachmeier's most reliable weapon in key spots as four of his six catches earned first downs. His passing touchdown combined with his skills as the tall receiver option for Bachmeier earned himself kudos here. What a pickup for Kalani Sitake, getting Kasper from Oregon in the transfer portal.

The offensive line never gets the love they deserve. All-Big 12 center Bruce Mitchell played one of his finest games as a Cougar. Per Pro Football Focus, Mitchell was BYU's highest graded offensive lineman in the winning effort. in 38 pass blocking snaps, he didn't even allow a single quarterback pressure, let alone sack or hit. He had a perfect day at the office in pass protection. He also provided a key block to spring Bachmeier free after he caught the double pass from Kasper. Mitchell's block after getting to the outside gave Bachmeier a lane to run into the endzone.

Uluave was BYU's most important transfer this offseason. After earning All-ACC honors at Cal, Uluave came to Provo to essentially replace Jack Kelly, now in the NFL. He hasn't just replaced Kelly on the field. He has been one of the biggest veteran leaders and most important locker room pieces for Sitake as well. All that was on display on Saturday night. He collected nine tackles, which led the team. He added a tackle for loss as well. He wasn't just your typical off-ball linebacker either. He was BYU's most effective pass rusher as well, leading the team with five QB pressures. He was everywhere, flying sideline-to-sideline.

BYU might have the best linebacker duo in at least the Big 12 Conference with Uluave and Glasker. Glasker got hurt against TCU and missed the game against Iowa State. His status for the game was in doubt during the week. He played and made an enormous impact. He ended up being BYU's highest graded defender per PFF. With six tackles and three pass breakups, Glasker was a menace.

Getting Damuni back from injury after he got hurt against Utah Tech was a huge boost to the defense. He didn't miss a beat. In fact, he looked better than ever. Pro Football Focus has a stat called "stops" which is described as " tackles that constitute a 'failure' for the offense." Damuni led the team with six stops. That is twice as many as the next closest BYU defender. In coverage, he faced six targets from Notre Dame's talented quarterback, CJ Carr. Damuni allowed just three catches in those six passes, totaling in a meager 12 yards for the Irish. Damuni was a big reason why the Notre Dame passing offense was limited for much of the game. He held their talented wideout Micah Gilbert to zero catches when the two were matched up, including Damuni's lone pass breakup.

#88. Joel Embiid explains why he's 'against the concept of sacrificing' for the star-studded 76ers

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Philadelphia 76ers are the latest NBA organization to build a superteam, adding Jaylen Brown and LeBron James this offseason to create a starting lineup with four All-Stars alongside Tyrese Maxey and Joel Embiid.

James. in particular, knows exactly what it takes to get a team of stars to accomplish their ultimate goal of winning a championship, but this 76ers squad is approaching things a little bit differently than James' Big 3 Heat.

Where Chris Bosh was the player to clearly sacrifice his role for the betterment of the team alongside James and Dwyane Wade in Miami, Embiid said after Friday's preseason finale that he believes the Sixers can thrive without needing anyone to take a back seat to anyone else, via ESPN.

"I'm against the concept of sacrificing," Embiid said. "I think the way I explained it was you do what you do best, and we're going to support you. ... I don't think anybody has to take a back seat."

The Sixers can certainly structure their rotations to where each of their four stars has moments throughout a game where they get to be the focal point. However, when all four share the court together, there will need to be a hierarchy in place, particularly come crunch time in close games.

That's going to require some give-and-take from the four stars, and it could be dependent on their opponent as to which of their stars has the biggest advantage. Embiid may prefer to call it support rather than sacrifice or a back seat, but the Sixers are going to have to learn how to work together and play secondary roles to make this all work.

What may help the Sixers the most is that no one understands that more than James, and the 42-year-old taking a minimum to sign in Philly signaled he's happy to play that supporting role and pitch in as a lead option when needed.

Jaylen Brown also has experience playing off a fellow star and winning a championship, so there shouldn't be any shortage of understanding of what it takes to succeed. The bigger question is whether everyone can come to an agreement on how that works best, making Nick Nurse's biggest task ego management

While Embiid and the Sixers stars figure out how they can all maximize each other's strengths, the organization is still trying to piece together a center rotation behind Embiid. After Ariel Hukporti suffered a season-ending Achilles injury, Philadelphia found itself extremely thin at the five behind Embiid, with Adem Bona -- who has missed the preseason with a foot sprain -- as the only reserve center on the roster.

On Saturday, the Sixers addressed their issues in the short term by converting Tacko Fall to a two-way contract after having him signed to a camp deal. The 7-foot-6 big man has missed the preseason with a hip strain, but the Sixers must feel confident he'll be able to help them fairly soon to bolster their rotation.

Fall has been out of the NBA since the 2021-22 season when he played 11 games with the Cavaliers. In his career he's only played in 37 games in three seasons, but the Sixers must believe he can be a contributor to their rotation to convert him into a two-way spot.

With their first apron hard cap, Philadelphia couldn't even add a vet minimum full-season deal after Hukporti went down, and Fall could be a relatively short-term stopgap until their cap situation allows for a partial-season deal.

Between stars learning how to work together and Nurse trying to cobble together a center rotation behind Embiid, there will be no shortage of intrigue in Philly at the start of the season.
