#90. MMBets: The Golden State Warriors are firmly mid

Five years ago, the Stephen Curry led Golden State Warriors won a fourth title together over the Boston Celtics. Steve Kerr, Draymond Green, and Curry are all still in place, and yet these Warriors are perhaps as far off as they've ever been from their championship winning days. Father time is undefeated, and often times the end of an era can be a bit unceremonious. The Warriors are a dying dynasty at best, or in reality, a dynasty that'd been dead for a few seasons now. As they look to what's next, can they give the Curry era an ending that it deserves?

PHOENIX, AZ – APRIL 17: Stephen Curry #30, Draymond Green #23 and Steve Kerr of the Golden State Warriors huddle up after the game against the Phoenix Suns during the SoFi NBA Play-In Tournament on April 17, 2026 at PHX Arena in Phoenix, Arizona. Of course, Lendeborg won a national title at Michigan with Dusty May, Morez Johnson Jr. and the rest of their group, so he knows how to be a part of winning basketball. I just wonder what the long term path is here. I get giving Curry all the tools he deserves to give it an earnest shot, but there is very little in the way of future assets to build around. In the immediate, the Warriors figure to be around the same as they were last year. But in the long term, there's many reasons to be concerned about the long term viability of this franchise.

#94. Orioles' David Rubenstein admits what MLB owners don't want fans to know: They're making a ton of money

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

David Rubenstein said the quiet part out loud. This week, the Baltimore Orioles owner admitted that yep, team owners make a ton of money, which is perhaps not the message the league wants to convey weeks before the owners are expected to initiate a lockout and work stoppage. The collective bargaining agreement expires at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1.

"A lot of my friends were buying teams, and I realized they're making money. They're making more money than I'm making in private equity," Rubenstein said Thursday at a forum with other pro sports owners at the Economic Club of Washington, D.C., per Baltimore Baseball. "I thought I should look at it as a financial thing, but ultimately I bought the Orioles for a philanthropic purpose. I grew up in Baltimore, as people know. I didn't think I'd done enough for Baltimore, so I bought the team to help revive the team a bit and ultimately revive Baltimore because Baltimore had some challenges."

Rubenstein also said the "owners care more about winning than making money (but they're) not against making money."

This is refreshing honesty from Rubenstein, really. It wasn't too long ago that MLB's owners were telling fans that owning a team "isn't very profitable," something that isn't even the tiniest bit believable. MLB has since shifted its rhetoric away from "owning a team isn't profitable" to "we need a salary cap for competitive balance," which has a better chance of resonating with fans.

No matter which team wins the ALCS, we're in for a small-market World Series. The Milwaukee Brewers swept the two-time defending World Series champion Los Angeles Dodgers (the villain in most of MLB's salary cap messaging) in the NLCS and will face either the Cleveland Guardians or Tampa Bay Rays in the World Series. All three teams are in the bottom 12 in payroll, per FanGraphs.

The small market World Series matchup may force MLB to change its messaging a bit, but it won't end the league's salary cap pursuit. The owners have wanted a salary cap since the dawn of the sport to control costs and boost franchise values. The current sales pitch is "the only way to achieve competitive balance is to give us this thing we've always wanted."

Rubenstein went on to acknowledge his failings with the Orioles. He purchased the team in March 2024. The O's were coming off a 101-win season in 2023 and won 91 games in 2024, but they have since slipped to 75 wins in 2025 and 79 in 2026. The rebuild has yet to yield much success.

MLB and the MLB Players Association have publicly traded proposals in the last several weeks. They could reach an agreement before Dec. 1. More likely, the owners will lock out the players for the second time in five years.

#97. The Cleveland Browns are good. What do we all do now?

There are certain truths we hold to be self-evident: The sun rises in the east. Star Wars movies were better when you were a kid. And the Cleveland Browns will always, always be terrible.

So what happens when one of our bedrock truths turns out to be wrong? What happens when — I can't believe I'm writing this — the Cleveland Browns turn out to be good?

As of Week 6, the Cleveland Browns lead the AFC North — by tiebreaker, at least — with a record of 4-2. That's better than the defending champion Seahawks, better than the supposed super-team Rams, better than the entire NFC South and East. This is the latest the Browns have been in first place in a season since 2014, one of those stats that makes you cringe because it even has to be said.

How did this happen? Well, nobody's going to like the answer. Coming into the season, the verdict on Cleveland was that this was a donut of a team, blessed with talent on both sides of the ball but lacking that essential core — i.e., a quarterback. This problem has haunted Cleveland for decades, of course, but it became particularly acute when Cleveland's front office piled up draft picks and then, shockingly, used them wisely.

Shedeur Sanders wasn't the one. Dillon Gabriel wasn't the one. Joe Flacco wasn't the one. As it turned out, the one quarterback able to lead the Cleveland Browns to victory is the quarterback nobody wants to lead the Cleveland Browns to victory.

Deshaun Watson, it turns out, is the answer to Cleveland's quarterback troubles. Of course.

Watson, who's been accused of dozens of counts of sexual assault and settled 20 claims, is just about the last person any organization would want as the face of their team. Were this virtually any other workplace, Watson would have been kicked to the curb and forgotten years ago. But the NFL has a forgiveness blind spot for players who are just too talented to disregard, and Watson has set up camp in that blind spot.

Cleveland Browns quarterback Deshaun Watson walks off of the field after defeating the Baltimore Ravens.

Regardless of the court of public opinion — and the Browns, among other teams, made it clear they don't recognize the authority of that court when they pursued Watson in the first place — Watson has met all the terms of his employment with the NFL. That means all his past "adversity" — the euphemism announcers are now employing to sanitize the many allegations against him — will remain in his past. And as distasteful as it may be to a swath of NFL fans, Watson is forcing the league to consider him in football terms, not social ones.

From a football standpoint, Watson has been a qualified success this season. He's not dominating games, but he's not losing them, either, which in the current NFL is enough. He has seven touchdowns against two interceptions this season, with a passer rating of 92.0 and a completion rate of 63.8 percent. That's not good enough to reign, but it's good enough to survive.

The Browns are coalescing around Watson. The defense lost Myles Garrett via trade, but remains strong enough to contain opposing offenses. Against Baltimore on Sunday, for instance, Cleveland's defense gave up 10 points in the first quarter, but nothing the rest of the game. That allowed Watson and the offense to plod along, turning a crucial Derrick Henry fumble into a touchdown and kicking just two field goals, including a walkoff game-winner.

The Browns are reveling in the moment … for the moment. "I'm going to enjoy tonight," first-year head coach Todd Monken said after the win. "And that's what you have to do in the NFL. These are the nights that you don't ever want to end, because tomorrow it's on to the next game."

Here's the good news for Cleveland: the "next game" is woeful Tennessee. After that, the Steelers, the Saints, the Texans — on and on, winnable game after winnable game. The only current division leader on the Browns' remaining schedule: the NFC East's Giants. Not exactly a fearsome slate.

This most definitely isn't the way you want to build a team, with a radioactive quarterback and a defense that relies more on opportunity than overwhelming force. But it's working for Cleveland, and in a year where there's no one dominant team, slow and steady keeps you in the race.

No, we're not saying the Cleveland Browns will go 15-2 this season. But we're saying there's a non-zero chance they could. And that should concern all of us. Because if the Cleveland Browns are now good, what can we even believe in anymore?

#98. How LeBron James, in his 24th season and first with the 76ers, can pass Michael Jordan in NBA GOAT debate

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Time is a thief that can rob you of youth before you realize it. That is the case for all of us ... except if your name is LeBron James.

James, 41, is and is entering his 24th season in the NBA. When James' new team -- the 76ers -- plays its season opener on Tuesday night against the reigning champion Knicks at Madison Square Garden, it will be nearly 23 years to the day since James stepped on the floor in Sacramento to play in his first regular-season NBA game.

I first wrote about James in the fall of 2003, when I was an 18-year-old high schooler in Ohio. As a college sophomore, I wrote about him again in 2006. Like many to come over the following years, the focus of that story was about whether James could one day surpass Michael Jordan, the sports icon of my childhood.

And now here we are, two decades later. Like James, I am 41, a father and have been bitten by the golf bug. That's where comparisons between James and I end. But the comparisons between James and Jordan? As the past 20 years have shown us, they're not going anywhere.

Long ago, James answered the question as to whether or not he could live up to his unprecedented hype. He has, 10 times over.

His laundry list of accomplishments includes four NBA titles (with three different franchises), four league MVPs, playing in an unfathomable eight straight Finals, being part of the NBA's first father-son duo, and being the catalyst behind the greatest comeback in NBA Finals history.

From a longevity standpoint, James stands alone. He is the NBA's all-time leader in points and games played. He is the charter member of the 40K/10K/10K club (40,000 career points, 10,000 rebounds and 10,000 assists).

Ironically, James' most famous play is not a basket, rebound or an assist. It's his block that helped end Cleveland's 52-year title drought.

Lebron James chase down block on Iguodala vs 73-9 Warriors. Finals, game 7.June 19th, 2016. pic.twitter.com/7xERK8F6JG

And he's still playing at a high level. He finished sixth in the MVP voting during his age-40 season. Last year, James led the Lakers to playoff series win after injuries sidelined Luka Dončić and Austin Reaves. James is ranked No. 19 on CBS Sports' list of the top 100 players entering the new season. The only NBA player who can remotely compare to James in terms of longevity is Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, who was still a quality starting center when he won his last two NBA titles at ages 40 and 41.

There is usually a generational divide when it comes to the James-Jordan debate.

NBA fans who watched the Jordan era usually struggle to hand away the crown to James or to anyone else. We believe that we saw the greatest player who played the game at a level that had never been seen before and will never be seen again. Watching Jordan was just ... different. Otherworldly, even.

Allen Iverson may have said it best during his Hall of Fame induction speech: "I remember the first time I played against him. I walked out on the court, I looked at him and for the first time in my life, a human being didn't look real to me."

It's more than that, though. Jordan had more "moments" that any athlete in history. There's the 63-point game in Boston in '86, the slam dunk titles (back when that mattered), the game-winning shot in Cleveland in '89, the jaw-dropping layup in the '91 Finals, the 35-point first half points in the '92 Finals, the 55-point performance in the '93 Finals, his first championship after baseball and the tragic death of his father, the Flu Game, and my personal favorite, his 45-point performance in the '98 Finals that was punctuated by his title-clinching shot.

Michael Jordan goes off against Utah in Game 6 of the 1998 Finals.45 points and the iconic game-winner to secure his 6th ring. 🏆 pic.twitter.com/hpdJuoxwr5

Jordan wasn't just superhuman, so was his team, the Chicago Bulls, who ran the NBA for the majority of the '90s.

No one knows this better than James, who was one of the millions of kids back then who grew up idolizing Jordan. To James' credit, he seems at peace with his legacy, both on and off the court, and he should. He doesn't need to prove anything to anyone. He really never did, but his drive to do so undoubtedly helped make him what he is today.

For the younger generations, James is their Jordan. But for those of us who remember Jordan and still refer to him as the GOAT, even we will have to concede that unofficial title to James if he -- at 42 years old -- wins a fifth title with a fourth franchise that hasn't won it all since 1983, the year before James' birth.

James won't take solace in winning one playoff series in Philly. He said as much during the 76ers' media day.

"I didn't leave my family to lose in the second round," he said. "I know that for sure."

It's a good thing James feels that way, because if he is going to definitively pass Jordan as the greatest of all-time, it'll take more than just winning a playoff series or two. It will take him and the 76ers winning it all.

James would still be one championship behind Jordan, of course. But five championships with four different franchises, plus the unprecedented longevity, would make James' GOAT case as strong as it's ever been.

The debates James and Jordan will likely never end, but the 2026-27 season gives James the best chance to add to his GOAT case that he's had in quite some time.

#100. Laporta launches fierce attack on Real Madrid: ‘They chose the wrong path, and are paying the price’

FC Barcelona president Joan Laporta has delivered a series of pointed remarks about Real Madrid, Paris Saint-Germain, Lamine Yamal and his club's ambitions in an interview with French newspaper L'Equipe.

Laporta described the relationship between Barcelona and Real Madrid as effectively over, accused their rivals of prioritising individual talent and expensive signings over team cohesion.

He also insisted that Barcelona are moving in the right direction under Hansi Flick and sporting director Deco.

Asked about Barcelona's relationship with Real Madrid, Laporta did not hold back.

"No, there is no relationship between us anymore. I would go even further and say that it has become a confrontation between us.

"Real Madrid have lost credibility, both institutionally and in sporting terms. They no longer have any presence within the institutions. They chose the wrong path, and now they are paying the price.

All out war between Spain's biggest clubs. (Photo by Angel Martinez/Getty Images)

"They opened their chequebooks and spent huge sums on very expensive players, but those players have not delivered the results they expected."

Laporta also Real accused Madrid of attempting to justify their shortcomings by focusing on the Negreira case, which concerns payments made by Barcelona to companies linked to former refereeing official Jose Maria Enriquez Negreira.

"In Madrid, they preferred individual brilliance and big-name signings," he said.

"They are trying by every possible means to justify their failures by lying about the Negreira case because they have not won anything for two years. We are winning, and we are candidates to win everything."

Laporta was also asked about his previous warning that Kylian Mbappe's arrival at Real Madrid could create problems within the dressing room.

"Yes, I said that. Having more than one rooster in the coop can never work. The priority in football must be the team and the team spirit. Without those things, the project will not succeed," Laporta explained.

Laporta criticised Real Madrid's methods. (Photo by Denis Doyle/Getty Images)

"That is one of Barcelona's strengths. We have great talents, players from La Masia and players from other footballing cultures, and we manage to build a team in which they work together harmoniously.

"That is thanks to a great coach, Hansi Flick, and a sporting director, Deco, who is working to make the team better."

Apart his criticism of Real Madrid, Laporta spoke positively about Barcelona's relationship with European football's governing body following the fallout in the past due to the Super League.

"We have returned to the football family with UEFA. Nasser, the president of Paris Saint-Germain, played a role in all of this, as did Aleksander Ceferin, whom I have known for a long time. I believe he is the best president UEFA could have.

"This is an important moment for football, which is changing in scale, and it is important to have a president like Ceferin."

#102. Aaron Glenn: No confusion about who got the ball to start the second half

Jets head coach Aaron Glenn’s on-field interview before the start of the second half on Sunday went viral, but Glenn said on Monday that his comments were misinterpreted.

Glenn told Aditi Kinkhabwala of CBS that the team would be ready to go despite being down 17-3 and that “the good thing is we get the ball, we get a chance to go move it and finish.” That was widely interpreted to be Glenn saying that the Jets would receive the kickoff to start the second half, which was not the case, and Glenn said on Monday that he was talking about what would happen after the defense forced a stop.

“No, I actually talked about just the offense,” Glenn said on Monday, via Howie Kussoy of the New York Post. “I think they were talking about sustaining drives, and my conversation with them is when the offense gets the ball back, man, we want to be able to sustain a drive and go score. Then when the defense gets back on, we want to make sure we stop them and get the ball back to our offense. That’s what I was talking about when it comes to that. The conversation was talking about the offense at that time.”

Things actually did work out as Glenn hoped as the Jets forced a punt and then scored on a touchdown pass to rookie wideout Omar Cooper. They would eventually pull within 17-13, but the Patriots went on to win 26-19.

#103. Steelers PFF grades: Germie Bernard shines; Troy Fautanu stagnates

The Pittsburgh Steelers erased a 16-3 fourth-quarter deficit to beat the Tampa Bay Buccaneers 26-19 in overtime Oct. 18.

The comeback was fueled by a defense that started forcing Tampa Bay quarterback Jalon Daniels into costly mistakes, along with a passing game that overcame an ugly first half in which quarterback Aaron Rodgers and Co. could not move the ball with any consistency.

Here's a look at some notable numbers from the outing via Pro Football Focus, the scouting website for whom evaluators grade players for every snap of every game on a 1-100 scale.

Required reading: Steelers win first 'Tomlin game' of the Mike McCarthy era with comeback

The thing that stands out most from the rookie's career-best performance of 11 catches for 87 yards and the game-winning touchdown against Tampa Bay is how much of it was in his hands. Literally. Bernard's average depth of target (ADOT) for the day was a miniscule 1.8 yards. On average, that shouldn't translate to much production at all, because it puts the onus on the receiver to gain meaningful yardage after the catch. Bernard managed to pick it up in chunks all day, though, to finish with a YAC total of 68. The Steelers would probably prefer for him to become more of a downfield threat – his ADOT of 5.1 yards is a major reason his season grade is a pedestrian 61.2. If he can continue to build chemistry with Rodgers, however, he could be a valuable weapon in this Mike McCarthy offense that is increasingly leaning on short, quick passes.

The 37-year-old got off to a slower start than we're used to with just five pressures in the first three games of 2026. He also had just three stops – defined by PFF as plays that result in failure for the opposing offense – in that span. In the past three games, however, he's turned it on with 11 pressures, five stops and two performances graded at 85.8 or better. Heyward has finished with a season grade of at least 84.4 in eight of the past nine seasons, so he's taking major steps back toward the level of dominance that may some day lift him to the Pro Football Hall of Fame. If there's a lingering concern, it's that Heyward hasn't found a way to get home against opposing quarterbacks nearly as often yet. He has just one sack so far, putting him on pace for three over the course of the season. That would be his lowest output ever over a fully healthy season in which he held a starting role throughout.

Four more pressures allowed against Tampa Bay, including a sack and quarterback hit on Rodgers, brought the third-year tackle's total to 17 this season. Only 11 tackles league-wide have allowed more. Granted, only two tackles have taken more pass blocking snaps, so some of that leakiness is a product of the pure volume of passing that coach Mike McCarthy's offense is doing right now. Still, Fautanu hasn't taken that next step toward being a cornerstone as the Steelers hoped he might be when they invested a first-round NFL draft pick in him back in 2024. That's especially true when you consider that his pass blocking grade of 69.6 is well ahead of his run blocking grade of 57.7. He's shown virtually no growth in either category since his rookie season. He's less volatile than former teammate and 2023 first rounder Broderick Jones was, but it's hard to see the upside that matches the draft capital used to acquire him right now. Rookie Max Iheanachor (68.9) is already grading better.

The Steelers have had a major problem getting production from veteran cornerbacks they've signed or traded for in recent years. From Patrick Peterson to Steven Nelson to Donte Jackson to Darius Slay last season, they've been ordinary at best and flat-out bad at worst after joining the team. Dean's trajectory wasn't promising either before Sunday. He'd missed most of two of the previous three games with an injury and was picked on by Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow in the third. It wasn't what the Steelers hoped for when they signed him to a three-year, $36.7 million contract in March. He rose to the occasion against Tampa Bay, though. It wasn't just his interception that set up the game-tying field goal in the fourth quarter. Daniels tested Dean in his return from injury with 11 targets on the afternoon. He allowed just four catches for 48 yards on those plays and permitted just five yards after the catch. It was a great outing that lifted his season grade to a very solid 86.2. If he can stay healthy, he may be the veteran to break the front office's streak of bad luck at this position.

Former Cincinnati Bengals quarterback Andy Dalton is signing with the Atlanta Falcons, according to multiple reports.

NBC Sports reported Oct. 18 that Dalton said "no thanks" when the Eagles asked him to return. Dalton was released Oct. 9 by the Eagles.

Dalton turns 39 years old later this month.

In September, Dalton entered the Eagles' Monday Night Football game against the Chicago Bears in relief of starting QB Jalen Hurts, and threw an interception in the end zone in the second quarter. It's Dalton's only pass attempt of the 2026 season.

#110. 2027 NBA Mock Draft: Tyran Stokes, Jordan Smith Jr., Stefan Joksimovic headline top picks before season starts

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The ongoing theme of the 2027 NBA Draft is how wide open it will be. Amidst the backdrop of college basketball's NIL market, the upcoming draft, particularly at the top, is more unpredictable than previous years. With eight months still to go, nothing is a sure thing, a drastic shift from what we experienced in last year's cycle.

That includes the draft order itself. The 2027 NBA Draft will mark the first year of the league's lottery reform, or what is called the "3-2-1" lottery system. The new system is designed to discourage tanking.

There will now be 16 teams in the lottery (up from 14): the 10 teams that miss the postseason entirely, the No. 9 and 10 seeds in both conferences, and the losers of the No. 7 vs. No. 8 Play-In Tournament games.

There will be a new distribution of lottery balls. The teams with the three worst records would fall into the so-called "relegation" zone. They would receive only two lottery balls each. The seven remaining teams that miss the postseason entirely would receive three balls. The No. 9 and No. 10 seeds would receive two balls, and the loser of the No. 7 vs. No. 8 game would get one ball each. In total, this means there would be 37 lottery balls assigned to 16 teams.

Because that new system makes it much more difficult, if not impossible, to forecast the order, this first mock is reverse-engineered based on Tankathon's predictive win totals and is thus more based on the players than on team needs.

#111. Josh Allen on flicked TD pass to Keon Coleman: "I was just trying to make a play"

Midway through the third quarter of Sunday’s victory over the Raiders, Bills quarterback Josh Allen made another signature play for a touchdown pass.

It was third-and-8 when Allen was pressured, moved to his left, then sent a backhand flip about 15 yards into the end zone to an open Keon Coleman, who made the catch for the score.

It’s nothing new for Allen, who has been an improvising playmaker for years now.

“It’s who he is,” head coach Joe Brady said in his postgame press conference.

Allen noted that he saw Coleman flash open, but it was the crowd — that was full of Bills fans — that really indicated the play’s success.

"[O]nce it comes out, you kind of get hit and tumble around, and it’s so hard in these away games, which feel like home games, once you hear the crowd go crazy, you’re like, ‘I don’t know if it’s a touchdown, I don’t know if it’s an interception,’” Allen said. “So again, he finds himself in the right place at the right time and finds a way to get open.”

Before Allen flicked it to Coleman, there was a moment where it looked like he could run.

“Again, I was just trying to make a play,” Allen said. “They played really good defense. I stepped up in the pocket, felt somebody coming from the left side there, stepped back, and again, quick eyes, saw our guy open and gave him a chance.”

For his part, Coleman said he was just trying to find space where Allen could see him and he wasn’t surprised by the result.

“I watched it, I was right there. I saw him flicking like that,” Coleman said. “I might have robbed Skyler [Bell]. He appeared behind me. He thought that ball was coming in when I just came out north. I just saw him in trouble, bro. Trying to make a play.

“He threw it around the dude. It’s just him, bro.”

That’s just part of the experience of playing with Allen.

“Play [is] never dead until the whistle blows,” Coleman said. “With him, even if a guy comes free hard to get him down — you might get there, but attacking him is a whole different obstacle. So, my job is when I feel that’s going on, you have to get your eyes back to the quarterback and find what we’re doing.”

#113. What's next for the Dodgers? Futures of Shohei Ohtani, Tarik Skubal uncertain after elimination

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Los Angeles Dodgers dynasty is over, or has at least hit a major bump in the road. Thursday's Game 4 loss to the Milwaukee Brewers completed the four-game sweep and sent the two-time defending World Series champions home for the winter. Los Angeles' season is over, as is its stretch of eight consecutive postseason series wins dating back to 2024.

There is no getting around it: The Dodgers looked old in the NLCS. They are old too. Weighed by playing time, they had baseball's oldest collection of position players this season. Will Smith is 31. Shohei Ohtani is 32. Mookie Betts and Teoscar Hernández are 34. Freddie Freeman is 37. The team's core hitters are getting long in the tooth. It was obvious in the NLCS.

That said, the Dodgers remain extremely talented and have the resources (money and tradeable prospects) to improve their roster in the offseason, and again contend in 2027. As bad as they looked in the NLCS, there is no reason to think the Dodgers won't be among baseball's best teams next year -- and on the short list of legitimate World Series contenders.

Here now are three questions facing the Dodgers following their unceremonious NLCS sweep.

In fact, let's talk about his future both short- and long-term. Ohtani was clearly diminished late in the regular season and into the postseason. He played through knee and biceps injuries and simply did not look like himself at the plate. His swing was all arms and there was little hard contact. Before his second-inning home run in Game 4 on Thursday, Ohtani hadn't gone deep since Aug. 18. His power vanished.

Here is Ohtani's expected slugging percentage, which is based on contact quality (exit velocity, launch angle, etc.), throughout this season. It slipped significantly late in the year:

Ohtani did not pitch after July 3 and had a start-and-stop in late August. He rehabbed his injuries, threw bullpen sessions and live batting practice, then had to shut it down before getting back on a mound in a game. Ohtani was playing like his usual MVP self until his injuries popped up in the second half. Once that happened, his season began to circle the drain.

The Dodgers now face two questions with Ohtani. One, does he need offseason surgery on the knee and/or biceps? And if he does need surgery, will the recovery cut into his 2027? Keep in mind that it is a near certainty there will be a lockout this offseason once the CBA expires on Dec. 1, and teams will be banned from communicating with their players. Ohtani would have to rehab on his own, without the team's input.

"It's hard to tell" if he'll require surgery, Ohtani said through an interpreter after Thursday's loss. He does, however, plan to pitch next season, he said.

Offseason surgery is the short-term question. Long-term, regardless of what he said in the shadow of the NLCS sweep, are Ohtani's days as a pitcher numbered? This has been a question since Day 1 of Ohtani's MLB career. His ability to be and remain a two-way player has long been doubted, but he has kept doing it, even if there have been some speed bumps along the way. Ohtani has made a career of doing what people said he couldn't.

The man is 32 now, though. He'll turn 33 next summer and the physical ailments (the knee, the biceps, two UCL surgeries, etc.) are beginning to add up. At some point, Ohtani won't be able to continue as a two-way player, and with each passing season, that point draws closer. Are we there now? Is this it? Is this the end of Ohtani's time as a pitcher? It could be, sure.

My guess is that Ohtani will continue to pitch next season and the Dodgers will happily let him because there is so much value to be gained even if he throws only 75 innings a year. You can't be as good as Ohtani without being stubborn. He's been stubborn in that he insists on playing both ways, and he has continued to do it well. I don't see him dropping it this winter.

It should surprise no one if Ohtani comes out next year, hits 40 home runs, makes 15 ace-caliber starts and wins his fifth MVP unanimously. Do not forget that he was playing at that level as recently as July. The recovery times for the knee and biceps injuries are an offseason question, for sure, and the bottom line is the "will he continue to pitch?" questions will always exist.

The Dodgers are locked into so much of their core: Betts, Freeman, Ohtani, Smith, Kyle Tucker, etc. They aren't going anywhere. That said, there are a few members of the supporting cast, players who have been around for all three recent World Series wins, who might have to be shown the door this offseason for the sake of diversifying the lineup and getting younger and more athletic.

Finding a taker for the final season of Teoscar Hernández's contract and then plugging the precocious Josue De Paula into left field next season is a worthwhile move. It's difficult because Hernández is popular in the clubhouse, but, on the field, De Paula figures to give the Dodgers a better chance to win ballgames moving forward. (De Paula is a poor defender, but so is Hernández.)

The Enrique Hernández era has run its course. He hasn't been even an average regular-season player since 2022, and, for all his postseason heroics, he's barely scraping a .600 OPS in the last two Octobers. Tommy Edman is a better version of the same player. There's no need to carry both on the roster, plus Edman's injuries suggest a smaller role is needed. Less could be more.

Max Muncy stayed healthy this season, hit 29 homers and posted 4.1 WAR, and is owed an affordable $10 million in 2027. Plus, it's a bad offseason to need an infielder. The free-agent market is very thin and you're not likely to find better than Muncy on the trade market. Still, he is 36. Keeping Muncy is justifiable, but it also makes sense to explore alternatives. It never hurts to look.

Blake Treinen has not been healthy and effective at the same time in two years. Alex Vesia's fastball sat 91-92 mph over these last few weeks. Both are free agents and the Dodgers have so many young hard-throwers in Triple-A that I think it's worth turning the page and injecting some younger arms into the bullpen. Evan Phillips may be in this camp, too.

Then again, who am I to doubt the Dodgers and their process? Disappointing NLCS aside, they have been baseball's most successful team of the 2020s, and if they want to remain in the Hernández and Muncy and Treinen business, I won't say they're wrong. It does appear that things are getting a bit stale, though. Incorporating youth would be sensible, and it isn't difficult to find ways to do it.

There's no sense in asking if the Dodgers can retain Tarik Skubal. Of course they can. They are baseball's biggest spenders and he is a Scott Boras client. Typically, all you need to do to get a Boras client is make the biggest offer, which the Dodgers can do. Maybe there's a salary cap that changes the equation. Based on what we know right now, yes, the Dodgers can, of course, re-sign Skubal.

Will they is a different matter. Tyler Glasnow, Blake Snell, and Yoshinobu Yamamoto will return next season. Ohtani could be back on the mound as well, as he indicated is the plan. Emmet Sheehan and Justin Wrobleski both pitched well for long stretches this year and are among the very best No. 5 starter options in the game. Gavin Stone, the team's 2024 innings leader, should return from shoulder surgery as well.

There is never a bad time to sign a pitcher like Skubal, and the Dodgers, with their World Series window still open, are well-positioned to bring him back. They have the money, they can easily clear rotation space, and all indications are that Skubal enjoyed his time with the team after coming over the trade deadline. This feels like a match made in free-agent heaven.

Now it's just a matter of whether the Dodgers can get it done. Perhaps a salary cap or increased competitive balance tax penalties limit their spending; maybe they opt to spread their money around to multiple players; maybe another team just won't be denied. The Dodgers don't absolutely need Skubal. Re-signing him would up their odds of returning to the World Series, though, and help ensure their dynasty didn't end on Thursday night.

For his part, Skubal declined to comment on his impending decision after Game 4.

"I'm not going to comment on my future really at all," Skubal said, via MLB.com. "Today sucks, you know, and that's kind of where my head's at."

#114. NHL Power Rankings: Flyers flounder to start new season as Rick Tocchet searches for answers

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

I hate to get so negative just one week into the season, but the Philadelphia Flyers have forced my hand. After a magical run to the second round of the 2026 Stanley Cup Playoffs, the Flyers have fallen on their face through four games.

Philadelphia opened the season with a 7-0 loss to the rival Pittsburgh Penguins, and coach Rick Tocchet described his team's play as "disturbing." There was only one way for the season to go after that, right? Wrong.

The Flyers are off to an 0-2-2 start, and the underlying numbers aren't pretty. Per Natural Stat Trick, they have a five-on-five expected goals share of 26.0%, which ranks last in the NHL. Their 4.57 xGA/60 also ranks last. Their 1.94 xGF/60? You guessed it. Last.

Tocchet's bunch entered the season with a lot of well-earned optimism. Even with subpar play from Matvei Michkov last season, the Flyers managed to reach the Eastern Conference Semifinals. Rookie Porter Martone asserted himself as a budding star with six goals and nine assists in 19 games between the regular season and playoffs.

There's still plenty of time -- 80 games exactly -- for the Flyers to get back on track and restore that optimism, but to say this has been a discouraging start would be an understatement.

#116. Why Paul George Is Ready to Rediscover All-Star Form After Celtics-76ers Trade

Why Paul George Is Ready to Rediscover All-Star Form After Celtics-76ers Trade originally appeared on NESN. Add NESN as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

Paul George reminded the Boston Celtics of what he can do when healthy during the 2026 NBA Playoffs.

Now, George will look to carry that production into his first season with the Celtics.

At 36, George has plenty to prove following two injury-plagued seasons. But don't get it twisted. He's still capable of being a difference-maker on a contender.

In fact, Boston is the perfect place for George to rediscover his All-Star form.

MORE:Paul George Hints at How Long He Wants to Stay With Celtics

It wasn't long ago that George was an All-Star.

George earned his ninth career All-Star selection in 2023-24, his final season with the LA Clippers. He appeared in 74 games that season, averaging 22.6 points, 5.2 rebounds, 3.5 assists and 1.5 steals per game as Kawhi Leonard's co-star.

The problem is George then appeared in 78 games over two seasons in Philadelphia. Injuries limited him to 41 games in 2024-25. He dealt with more injuries and served a 25-game suspension in 2025-26, limiting him to 37 games.

The good news for the Celtics is George feels like his body is healthy again. He said during Media Day that he believes his recent struggles have been more about injuries than a decline in ability.

"To hear that he's not capable of this or he's 'washed,' it's frustrating just because it's like, I'm still capable of doing those things when healthy and I feel like my body is back healthy," George said. "I feel I'm capable of doing those things again."

Staying healthy is the first step toward him looking like an All-Star again.

MORE:Jaylen Brown Details His Full Range of Emotions After Celtics Trade In Candid New Interview

George doesn't even need to replicate Brown's production on his own. Jayson Tatum will return to being Boston's No. 1 option, leaving George to help the Celtics replace Brown's contributions by committee.

To do that, George will need to be a reliable shooter who can provide secondary playmaking and add to Boston's already stout defense.

George has shown he can still contribute in all three areas. He played an important role in Philadelphia's comeback win over Boston in the 2026 NBA Playoffs, and he gave the Celtics a taste of his two-way impact in the preseason.

George's defensive impact could be particularly valuable in Boston.

George led the league with a whopping 3.5 steals per game in the preseason. That number won't hold over a full season — that would be the third-most steals anyone has ever averaged — but his length and anticipation could help the Celtics force more turnovers and generate more transition opportunities.

The Celtics have room to improve in that area. They've been an excellent defensive team under Joe Mazzulla, but they ranked 28th in steals per game and 25th in points off turnovers last season.

George's ability to disrupt passing lanes gives the Celtics another weapon on a defense that already ranked among the league's best.

MORE:Jayson Tatum's Connection to Paul George Goes Back Even Further Than You Think

The Celtics don't necessarily need George to return to his Clippers-era form to have a successful season.

If he can stay healthy, knock down open 3s and help the Celtics become even feistier defensively, George could become an important piece of a team with legitimate championship aspirations.

A 10th All-Star selection might be an ambitious goal for George at this stage of his career, but if he can consistently contribute on both ends of the floor, he could silence some of the doubters who questioned the trade.

#117. Rulebook: 2026-27 NBA points of emphasis and areas of focus

In late September, the NBA announced its points of emphasis and areas of focus for officiating, which included videos with narrated examples of the league's new "points of education." A week later, NBA.com's Jeff Zillgitt broke them down in prose. So, with NBA Opening Day on October 20—and the Bucks' season officially starting on October 21—it's time fans hit the books. Of course, that's arduous. So here, condensed for your convenience, are the "Cliff Notes."

The point of emphasis: The league is cracking down on offensive players using their off arm to push off and create space.

Why you should care: Defenders might finally be able to, you know, have some semblance of a chance to defend again. And with Taylor Jenkins prioritising a return to defensive aptitude—and Bucks fans wanting a return to the dawg days—this could work in their favour. Then again, as Zillgitt wrote, "There is some leeway, a fine line in which the player can use his off arm against the defender as the player with the ball uses his off arm to firm up or feel for the defender."

Need more? Check out the NBA's official video:

The point of emphasis: Screeners better do so legally—and that means without two hands.

Why you should care: Jericho Sims committed 28 offensive fouls last year, tied with Victor Wembanyama for the 10th most in the entire league. But Sims isn't called for the same type of offensive fouls that Giannis was—he's not barreling through opponents on his way to the cup. No, Sims' come mostly from illegal screens. Don't believe me? Just ask the Gyro Step podcast's Rohan Katti:

Get your nose in the books and your reps in the lab, Jumpman!

The point of emphasis: Players called for flopping will receive a non-unsportsmanlike technical foul and the opposing team will be awarded a free throw. But for such a foul to actually be called, it has to meet the STEM criteria:

Head snaps do not. They are embellishments, drawing attention to something that is illegal, so they are permissible.

Why you should care: Call me defeatist, but you probably shouldn't. How can a referee possibly process a call that has its own set of four criteria in an instant? This will likely go the way of past points of emphasis—called several times early in the season only to be forgotten by December.

The point of emphasis: Don't be reckless when closing out. Simples.

Why you should care: If the Bucks' preseason is anything to go by, they'll be hoisting up a lot of long-range bombs this season. With that, they'll face an increased number of closeouts. And with that, they'll (potentially) face an increased number of reckless closeouts. Notably, "the shooter can fall to the floor in a sitting motion if he feels he's protecting himself on a closeout." Moreover, doing so "is not considered a flop." So, pull up a pew, fellas. Stay safe!

Want more on these? Check out the NBA's official video:

The point of emphasis: This one's on the defensive team. They—players and coaches—need to stop time-wasting once a foul is called. Either challenge the call or don't. Any filibustering will result in a delay of game violation.

Why you should care: For all the joy that NBA games bring, at times they drag on so much that it's as if you're back in the year 2000 listening to The Opposite of H20. This point of emphasis, then, might give you a few of those oh-so-precious minutes back. Paired with the absence of Giannis' free throw routine, you might even find yourself looking for things to do!

And, just in case you truly are a sicko and want the tape, here it is:

What do you think, Brew Hoopers? Has the NBA got its points of emphasis right? And if you were in charge, what rules would you like to see emphasised?

#118. Jalen Hurts has deep vein thrombosis, multiple pulmonary embolisms

The 2026 season of Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts is most likely over.

Hurts, who played eight days ago with a blood clot in his leg, has been diagnosed with a deep vein thrombosis and a pulmonary embolism in each lung.

A pulmonary embolism is a very serious health condition. From the Mayo Clinic’s website: “A pulmonary embolism can be life-threatening. About one-third of people with an undiagnosed and untreated pulmonary embolism don’t survive.”

The Eagles and agent Nicole Lynn issued a statement on Monday morning disclosing the change in Hurts’s condition.

“Over the last few days, Jalen Hurts has received comprehensive medical evaluations by physician experts,” the statement explains. “In the interest of transparency, we are providing additional information on the diagnosis and treatment plan related to his condition.

“Jalen was initially diagnosed by specialists in London with a left calf superficial vein thrombosis. After further testing and monitoring, the current diagnosis is a deep vein thrombosis, as well as bilateral pulmonary emboli. He is clinically stable and has no significant functional limitations. His treatment should only involve anticoagulation (i.e. ‘blood thinners’). During this time, he will not be allowed to participate in any contact activities, including football.

“Jalen’s prognosis is very good, and we expect a full recovery. We anticipate that he will have the opportunity to resume contact football activities when off the blood thinners. In the meantime, he will remain active around the team and continue to condition. More importantly, we anticipate that he will have no long-term effects.

“We are thinking of Jalen and looking forward to a strong recovery.”

It’s good that a serious health condition is being taken seriously. There’s still a very real question as to whether it was taken as seriously as it should have been from the outset.

We’ll have some more thoughts on that later. For now, we wish Jalen the best as he focuses on resolving a serious health condition.

#119. NBA over/under predictions for every Western Conference team: Lakers undervalued, Warriors in for a long year

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

In the 2007-08 NBA season, all eight Western Conference teams won at least 50 games. That will not be the case again this season. There is a pretty big falloff after the top six West teams (Spurs, Thunder, Nuggets, Timberwolves, Rockets and the Lakers), with the middle class teams looking like the Trail Blazers and Jazz.

From there, the lower-tier teams are going to face added struggles of a more competitive nightly schedule, thanks to lottery reform removing the incentive to lose for a third of the league. Factor in how tough the East is (everyone has to play those teams twice), and wins are hard to come by for everyone. It makes picking the over/under win totals an especially difficult exercise, as it is every year.

Still, we'll give it our best with the information we have available to us. Earlier this week, we put out our Eastern Conference over-under predictions. Now let's get to the West.

This is a stay-away line because the Mavericks' season could go so many different ways. They could trade Kyrie Irving and bottom out, relatively speaking, or they could keep Irving, P.J. Washington and Daniel Gafford, get Dereck Lively II back in a timely manner, and with Cooper Flagg profiling as a potential All-NBA player and a bunch of wings and size all over the floor, win north of 40 games pretty easily.

Deep down, I just don't think Irving makes sense on the team's timeline and they'll ultimately find a way to trade him. And if he goes, why not Washington, Gafford and/or Naji Marshall? I'll go under, but it'll be close.

Another tight one. This largely comes down to Aaron Gordon's availability. When he plays, they still kill people. When he's out, much different story.

Given that Gordon is healthy right now and has looked good in preseason, I'll give him the benefit of the doubt and err on the side of the Nuggets' pretty much unmatched continuity with its starting lineup. Cameron Johnson caught a lot of flak last year, but look at the numbers. He shot 43% from 3 and was lights out after a terrible start, and he's going to be more comfortable in year two. DeMar DeRozan doesn't seem like a great fit, but he could theoretically help keep the non-Nikola Jokić minutes above water.

Bottom line, there's still a lot of talent here and one of the best starting fives in the game, and with that at his disposal, I just can't see Jokić not winning 50 games.

This pains me to say as a Northern California native, but Golden State is going under this number. It's always going to be tempting to talk yourself into the idealized version of a Stephen Curry team. Yaxel Lendeborg is going to be awesome! Brandon Williams is going to be a bench spark plug! Gui Santos is slept on! Al Horford can still play! So can Draymond Green!  All we gotta do is keep Curry healthy and stay relevant until Jimmy Butler gets back and take off from there!

Sorry, folks. It ain't happening. The far more realistic scenario is Curry, who only played in 43 games last year and is fighting an old-man knee that seems like it's going to bug him off and on for the rest of his career, misses a lot of time again as the decision comes down to pushing a 38-year-old to his breaking point to maybe sneak into the play-in tourney or erring on the side of keeping his fresh for next year, when they have substantial cap space and are planning (as they always are!) to make a big addition.

Who knows when or if Kristaps Porzingis will even be able to play. Banking on Butler coming back after a torn ACL and a year off to just be, well, Jimmy Butler in February is a fairy tale. Too many things would have to go perfectly for this to even be a .500 team, and I mean perfectly. It's just not likely. The West is too good, too deep, and the Warriors, frankly, are neither. Take the under.

I don't understand this number. Yeah, the Rockets went in the tank at points last year and looked bad in the playoffs, but they won 52 games with no point guard and Steven Adams, a major part of their major offensive rebounding advantage, out for the entire second half of their schedule. Now the Rockets get Adams and their point guard, Fred VanVleet, back. This is a better team than the one that finished last season with the sixth-best net rating in the league.

If you're waiting on the Kevin Durant decline, get comfortable. The guy averaged 26 points per game last season on damn-near 52/41/87 shooting splits with almost zero structural offensive assistance. To that point, Houston needs to improve its possession quality and find some semblance of dependable late-game offense other than giving the ball to Durant and spectating. VanVleet should help immensely with that aspect.

Also, don't get too caught up in the lottery-reform narrative as it pertains particularly to the Rockets, who were not a team feasting on tankers last season. Among the top-10 Western Conference teams, only the Clippers lost more games to below-.500 opponents. During an extended December-January stretch, the Rockets lost games to the Jazz, Pelicans, and the Mavericks, Kings and Blazers twice each. They were also 1-7 in overtime games. Chances are, at least half those games swing their way this season.

There's a strong case to be made that 52 wins was about the lowest possible outcome for Houston last season. Based on their point differential, Cleaning The Glass pegged them as an expected 56-win team. And again, they are better this season. This 48.5 number is a comfortable over for me.

There are some names on this Clippers team, notably Darius Garland and Brandon Ingram. But Ingram has a partially torn Achilles, and there's no telling when he'll be ready to go.

Max Strus is also hurt to start the year, and the most important factor in this line is that the Clippers almost have to trade some guys to recoup some of the future draft picks they forfeited to the Kawhi Leonard cap-circumvention cause (Rui Hachimura, Kris Dunn, and Derrick Jones Jr. are prime candidates).

Ultimately, Ty Lue's coaching might be enough to keep the Clippers out of the bottom-three relegation zone, but they'll still go under this number as they devote most of the season's focus to developing Keaton Wagler.

The Lakers were looking like a shadow contender until Luka Doncic and Austin Reaves got hurt last year. Yes, they lose maybe the best player ever, but the numbers with Dončić and Reaves on the court without LeBron James still paint a rosy picture.

With those two on the court without James, the Lakers outscored opponents by 8.3 points per 100 possessions with an 80th percentile offense and defense last season. Rob Pelinka might have paid a bit too much for Walker Kessler, but that's a major addition. If he gets hurt for a significant stretch, the Lakers' defense is shot, but that's the only thing that gives me even brief pause on this number. Assuming Kessler plays in 60-65 games, he will be a possession monster for them on the offensive glass and give Dončić a functional roll partner.

This team is just built to win regular-season games. The postseason is a different story when teams start looking to hunt Dončić and Reaves, but night in and night out, having Dončić and Reaves is such guaranteed high-level offense, it's hard to see the Lakers going under 50 wins, let alone falling down to 46, on the strength of that duo alone with Kessler in the middle.

Now add in some sneaky depth. There are a lot of guys who can catch and shoot 3 off Dončić's gravity. The Lakers can play a pretty mean five-out lineup with Sandro Mamukelashvili at center. Quentin Grimes is a player, and the addition of Collin Sexton maintains creative capacity when Dončić sits and/or misses time. To me, 55-57 wins is in play for the Lakers. Have you forgotten how great Dončić is? This is a wildly low number.

I think rookie Cameron Boozer is ready to average 20 and 10 out of the gate. Playing alongside Zach Edey, who was a top-10 offensive board guy as a rookie and is a problem with his size inside (the Grizzlies killed teams in his minutes last year, albeit in almost an irrelevantly small sample as he only played 11 games), he should be able to overpower matchups against smaller defenders.

Those two guys and Isaiah Stewart are the frontline foundation of a team that is going to play extremely hard every night. Ty Jerome, who played in just 15 games last year, is very good and will create pick-and-roll offense. Quinten Post gives them size and stretch shooting behind Edey. Cedric Coward, who can really defend and attack the basket with force and has a sweet shooting stroke, is a guy to watch for a big sophomore leap after a strong rookie season. I love Jaylen Wells (in part because I went to the same college as him!). Jerami Grant averaged just under 20 points and shot 39% from 3 on volume last year.

I just think Jerome and Edey basically not playing last year and the Grizzlies still winning 25 games (with an incentive to tank) is the profile of a team that can win five more games this season.

Shooters convert shots at one of the highest rates in the league off LaMelo Ball passes. He's an extraordinarily gifted passer who hits his in rhythm and on target. Anthony Edwards shot 48% on catch-and-shoot 3s last season. This has the makings of a truly dynamic offensive duo, with Ball relieving some of Edwards' on-ball stress and juice in an offense that, in general, could get a little bogged down running through Julius Randle in the past.

You can have your concerns about Ball staying healthy or surviving defensively in a playoff series, but there is a lot of defensive infrastructure in Minnesota with Rudy Gobert and Jaden McDaniels (one of the better true two-way players in the league), and this team is going to play with a lot of energy and swagger. Jonathan Kuminga should really benefit from Ball's hit-ahead passing and general pace pushing. Naz Reid will be missed, and the frontcourt depth could be a pain point. Give me the over.

Zion Williamson is a round peg in a square hole. He doesn't fit next to Derik Queen because neither can shoot nor defend. Williamson needs the ball to really make an impact, but you can't justify not playing through Queen and Jeremiah Fears.

There are teams that are better than the sum of their parts and teams that are worse than the sum of their parts, and the Pelicans are the latter. They have good players. Herbert Jones. Trey Murphy III. Dejounte Murray. All these guys can play and therefore should be traded because this team, as constructed, is going nowhere and has too many overlapping skill sets with the same flaws.

The only question with this team is whether the front office will do the right thing and make some of these trades (notably Murphy III) at a reasonable price, rather than holding out for the Danny Ainge train-heist package. Either way, this team is going under.

I'm telling you right now, do not mess with this bet. The Thunder could very easily go over this number. They won 64 last year and Jalen Williams only played 33 games. But in a league this deep, I'm banking on just one 60-win team and it won't be OKC. The Thunder just have the motivation to really put their pedal to the floor.

That doesn't matter a ton because their floor is so high, and they have so many deep, guaranteed sources of offense and defense, individually and collectively, but it's just enough of a factor for me to say this team to finish under 63 wins, if only slightly.

Phoenix is definitely going to regress from its 45 wins last year. The question is how much? Personally, I think this is a 36-38 win team because they won last year by flat-out playing harder than their opponents.

That won't catch as many teams by surprise this season, and it's just tough to sustain that winning blueprint over multiple seasons when you're at a talent deficit against two-thirds of the league. Lottery reform stands to punish this team considerably, too. The Suns killed the bad teams last year: 23-4 against bottom-10 opponents, per Cleaning the Glass. Those are teams that are no longer incentivized to concede defeat.

Also, can Dillon Brooks really repeat his 2025-26 season? It wasn't the most efficient, but this guy was a flat-out stud second scorer. Maybe he really is that. But a Brooks regression is certainly on the table. Combine all of this with the strength of the West and the league overall, and I just don't see a 40-win roster in Phoenix.

I like this over quite a bit. I have the same concerns about the Ja Morant/Damian Lillard pairing as everyone else, but I don't think it'll take Micah Nori -- who's on a one-year contract and doesn't have time to mess around with losing lineups -- long to move Morant to the bench. From there, the upside of his scoring becomes much more of a bonus play.

Outside of that concern, I love this team. Lillard feels so right back in this uniform and I have no reason to think he'll be anything less than very good. They'll have to figure out the balance of on-ball creation as Deni Avdija is probably the guy that deserves the most usage and Lillard, though obviously capable, was never the best version of himself off the ball in Milwaukee.

Still, we're not talking about a contender here. We're just talking about finishing a little above .500 for a team with a potentially still-elite shot creator Lillard, an All-NBA-level player in Avdija, a top-shelf rim protector in Donovan Clingan, a first-class wing defender in Toumani Camara, and the wing depth of Jrue Holiday, Morant and Scoot Henderson -- who's in a contract year and coming off a pretty quietly solid third season -- to cover for the six-month loss of Shaedon Sharpe, who will be back hopefully for the post-All-Star stretch run. This is a good team unless Morant completely screws it up.

This is the worst team in the league. The 21.5 total reflects that (by far BetMGM's lowest line), but it's not low enough. Darius Acuff Jr. is going to put up a barrelful of empty stats, which will hopefully be a fun reason to watch the Kings, but there isn't a defensive bone to be found on this team.

Zach LaVine has to get traded or bought out or something. Domantas Sabonis, too. I mean, this team could very likely be starting Ben Simmons on opening night. If you think they're going over this line just because it's so low, fine. But I can't bring myself to endorse any sort of winning wager on a team this bad.

There's a blueprint for winning 60-plus games. It starts with talent, which, of course, the Spurs are loaded with. Then it's about depth, because guys are going to miss games and winning 60 necessitates putting a high-level NBA team on the floor every night.

And then there's the "something to prove" factor. Victor Wembanyama sets this tone. He openly talks about wanting to win the MVP, so he's going to play the 65 games at least, and he's going to play them hard. Dylan Harper is pushing to prove worthy of all the hype. The Spurs believe they are on the cusp of a dynasty. In the initial stages of championship development, teams like the 2014-15 Warriors and 2024-25 Thunder play the regular season with the fervor of a team announcing the true beginning of its reign.

Last season, the Spurs sort of crashed the party. This season, they're throwing the party. They're going to be out to dominate every single night, and with the baseline defense of Wembanyama and so many viable creators that can cover for each other's injuries and/or off nights, the baseline here is just too high with this kind of motivation to see the Spurs going under 60 wins. I think 65-67 wins is the real number.

The Jazz are finally ready to start playing games with the actual goal of winning. They've traded for Jaren Jackson Jr. and kept Lauri Markkanen all these years. They've seen Keyonte George develop into a lethal weapon. They drafted Darryn Peterson at second overall. And with the spacing this team has with its bigs, those two could combine for 40 a lot of nights. Utah's offense will be very good.

The defense is another story. Walker Kessler is gone, and Jackson Jr. is an almost unbelievably poor rebounder for his size. Jusuf Nurkic being out to start the year (listed as a four-week injury, but we'll see) really hurts Utah's rebounding prospects and he is a passer who can tie a lot of this offense together. The bottom line is Utah was competitive in a good amount of games last year until it decided not to be, and there is real talent on this roster. Give me the over as this team fights for a play-in berth.

#123. Colts fire GM Chris Ballard

The Colts have made a major change in the wake of Sunday’s loss to the Titans.

Owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon announced that they have fired General Manager Chris Ballard. Ballard had been in the job since 2017 and made the playoffs twice in his first four seasons, but have not been back since 2020 while cycling through a number of different quarterbacks.

That led Irsay-Gordon to say this offseason that improvement was needed, but Sunday’s loss dropped the Colts to 1-5 on the season and became the final act of his tenure.

“I am grateful to Chris for his years of service to the Colts and for everything he poured into this organization,” Irsay-Gordon said in a statement. “He cared deeply about our team and our community, and we wish Chris and his family all the best. As I said at the start of the season, the sense of urgency has never been higher. Our standard is to compete for championships, and I believe a change in leadership is necessary to meet that standard. Making this change during the season was a deliberate decision. Waiting would only delay the important work that needs to begin now. We will conduct a thorough search for our next general manager and take the time necessary to identify the right leader for the future of this organization. I also want to be clear: this decision does not change our goals for the season. We have a lot of football in front of us, and I expect us to compete, improve, and win football games.”

Head coach Shane Steichen remains on the job, but he’s clearly on thin ice moving forward with Ballard already gone.

#124. ‘I know your dad and he was better’: Aaron Rodgers roasts Bucs rookie Josiah Trotter

Pittsburgh Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers is in his 22nd NFL season, which means he's been around long enough to have played against the fathers of some of the players now chasing him. And on Sunday, he made sure one of them knew it.

After Tampa Bay Buccaneers rookie linebacker Josiah Trotter got in his face during the first half of Sunday's game, Rodgers responded with a smile and dished out some brutal trash talk, telling Trotter that he knew his dad, and that his dad "was better."

Rodgers had the last laugh on the scoreboard, too. The Steelers trailed 16-3 in the fourth quarter, but they rallied to force overtime before Rodgers hit Germie Bernard for a game-winning touchdown in a 26-19 victory at Raymond James Stadium.

Rodgers finished 33-of-49 passing for 253 yards, two touchdowns, and an interception. The win moved Pittsburgh to 4-2, while the Bucs fell to 1-5.

After the game, Rodgers also called the grass at Raymond James Stadium "one of the worst surfaces in the league."

Trotter came after Rodgers following a pass rush during the first half, but the 42-year-old quarterback didn't seem bothered. Instead, he smiled and fired back.

"I know your dad and he was better," Rodgers told Trotter, in a clip shared by Pardon My Take.

Trotter's father, Jeremiah Trotter, was a four-time Pro Bowl linebacker who played in the NFL from 1998 to 2009, mostly with the Philadelphia Eagles. He was a first-team All-Pro in 2000, and he even spent the 2007 season with the Buccaneers.

Rodgers entered the league in 2005, so he overlapped with the elder Trotter for several seasons.

Josiah Trotter, meanwhile, was a second-round pick by the Bucs in the 2026 NFL Draft, going 46th overall out of Missouri. His older brother, Jeremiah Trotter Jr., is a linebacker for the Eagles.

The clip quickly went viral on social media, racking up more than 1.6 million views on Pardon My Take's post alone.

#126. NBA instructs sportsbook partners to ban certain bets ripe for manipulation, per report

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

In the aftermath of multiple high-profile gambling scandals, the NBA will no longer allow certain types of bets that would appear to be the lowest-hanging fruit for potential conspirators.

Citing a memo distributed to the league's sportsbook partners on Friday, ESPN is reporting that "bettors will not be able to include the under on the same player's statistics in parlays, in addition to other betting markets the league considers problematic."

The NBA and prominent sportsbooks have agreed to ban multiple types of bets, per me and @DavidPurdum, such as:- Parlay bets involving the under on the same player's statistics - "First of" market; examples: winner of opening tip, an individual's specific shot, rebound, assist,…

The league also directed its authorized gambling operators, including DraftKings and FanDuel, not to offer bets on the winner of the opening tip, players to miss specific shots and under bets on players who are expected to play fewer than 12 minutes in a specific game.

The NBA has the authority to restrict what partner sportsbooks offer through its agreements. The NBA estimates its partner sportsbooks account for upward of 99% of the U.S. betting market.

These bets on an individual player's over/under lines are particularly ripe for fixing because the player can control the outcome. These were the bets exploited by Jontay Porter, who received a lifetime ban in 2024 for disclosing inside information to bettors and wagering on games. Porter admitted in court that he took himself out of games early to make sure his under bets hit.

If you're not familiar with how these lines work, let's say a player's rebounding line for a game is set at 3.5. If you bet the under, you are betting that the player will finish with three or fewer rebounds. Obviously, a player can largely control that by simply not pursuing rebounds, and he can eliminate the possibility of even accidentally running into a loose rebound or two by simply removing himself from the game for a fake injury once he has logged the time to make the game and bets on his lines official.

He relays this information to bettors beforehand, and they put a bunch of money on him to go under the projected total. ESPN notes that in the Porter criminal complaint, federal prosecutors pointed to one bettor placing an $80,000 parlay bet on Porter going under his line for assists, rebounds, points, 3-pointers, steals and blocks for a March 2024 game between the Raptors and Kings that stood to pay out more than a million dollars. Porter left that game after playing just three minutes.

The same type of scandal has been alleged involving Terry Rozier, who removed himself after playing just nine minutes in a 2023 game that was called into question for the same conspiratorial reasons, and Malik Beasley.

The NBA knows how bad a look this is for a league now so deeply connected with gaming partners, and these measures are a clear indication that it is trying, to whatever extent possible, to put the genie back in the bottle regarding the bets most ripe for manipulation.

#127. NBA predictions: Picks for 2027 champion, MVP, Rookie of the Year, and more

It might be harder to predict the NBA right now than it has been at any point in league history. The last eight years have produced eight different champions, and no team has even made back-to-back NBA Finals appearances over that time. The second-apron is breaking up contenders early, and an added emphasis on pace-and-space is leading more injuries that make it so much harder to sustain success year-over-over.

The NBA season rarely plays out how we think it's going to. The New York Knicks weren't exactly a popular preseason pick to win it all last year, and absolutely no one saw the San Antonio Spurs morphing from a 44-win team to the Western Conference champions. The Indiana Pacers made a darkhorse NBA Finals run in 2025, the Dallas Mavericks did the same in 2024, and Miami Heat got all the way there as an 8-seed in 2023. You might think we can already fast-forward to a Thunder-Spurs rematch in the Western Conference Finals this year, but there tends to be a lot more chaos in this era of the league than ever before.

With the 2026-27 season here, let's make our picks for the 2027 NBA Finals and every major award. For more NBA preview coverage, check my list of breakout player candidates, preseason standouts, and preseason rookie rankings.

I think it's fair to frame the East as the Knicks vs. the field. I respect the Knicks, but I'd still take the field in that equation, just because it's so hard to put together consecutive Finals runs in this era. I was choosing between the Raptors and Celtics for my East pick, and I'm going with Toronto for a few reasons. You usually need a top-5 player to make a Finals run, and Kawhi Leonard looked like that type of player last year. I'm well aware of his constant injury issues late in the season, but hey, Toronto did a good job pacing his body last time he was there in 2019, and I think they can do it again. Scottie Barnes is going to have a monster year as Leonard's sidekick, and when the two share the floor with sophomore Collin Murray-Boyles, it's going to be impossible to score on Toronto. Ja'Kobe Walter and Jamal Shead are very good role players for this team, and I think Allen Graves can be a contributor off the bench as a rookie, too. Toronto games won't be pretty, but Kawhi gives them the halfcourt scoring they lacked a year ago, and the rest of the squad should be ready to win a rock fight every night out.

The Spurs won 62 games and were the only team in the league to place in the top-3 of both offensive and defensive efficiency last year. The scary thing is I think they will be even better this year. Obviously, it all starts with Victor Wembanyama, who is in the rare position of already being the best player in the world while still having so much room left to improve. Wemby's defense is multiple levels above any other player on the planet, and I expect we'll see a more well-rounded offensive game from him this year. Dylan Harper's sophomore leap is coming, and he's going to be one of the best guards in the Western Conference before you know it. I'm fascinated to see how San Antonio handles the dynamic between Harper and De'Aaron Fox, but Fox should be better than he was in last year's playoffs on a bum ankle, and his bloated salary is a problem for another day. Even if I'm not the biggest Stephen Castle guy (cut down the turnovers, man!), San Antonio still has some other great role players, led by Julian Champagnie and Devin Vassell. I think Tobias Harris' scoring can help out in the halfcourt in a pinch, and I liked their draft haul, too. If any team can sustain consecutive title runs in this era, it's the Spurs.

Kawhi vs. the Spurs for a championship would be absolute cinema. Get me an alternate feed with Uncle Dennis' color commentary! Toronto's defense will be nasty, but Wemby is a problem without a solution. I have Wemby getting his first chip at 23 years old.

Boring answer, I know. Luka Doncic was my backup choice. Shai Gilgeous-Alexander in 2025 is the only NBA MVP to win the championship in the last decade, so it won't be easy, but it feels like Wemby is destined to pull off a few of these double-dips in his career. Might as well start now.

It's a lock if he plays 65 games. If he doesn't, I'd go with OKC's Chet Holmgren, who is fantastic when he plays anyone but Wembanyama.

Pick a play type, any play type, and Boozer is already excellent at it. He can body people in the pick-and-roll as the handler or screener, he can nail three-pointers off the dribble or the catch, he can drive, he can clean the offensive glass for putbacks, he can crush the offensive glass like a traditional big man, and he's an expert decision-maker with the ball in his hands. The former UC Santa Barbara product can provide everything teams want from a secondary ball handler with airtight driving ability, improved outside shooting, and a knack for finding teammates without turning the ball over. #130. Eagles QB Jalen Hurts Out for Season as Blood Clot Spreads to Lungs

Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts will miss the remainder of the 2026 NFL season after doctors discovered blood clots in his lungs.

The news, first reported Monday by ESPN's Adam Schefter and NFL Network's Ian Rapoport, marks a major escalation in a medical situation that developed late last week.

On Thursday, October 15, the Eagles announced that Hurts would miss Week 6 due to a superficial blood clot in his calf, stemming from an injury suffered against the Los Angeles Rams in Week 4. By Saturday, after consulting with medical specialists, Philadelphia placed the athlete on injured reserve, initially sidelining him for at least four weeks.

However, follow-up testing revealed that the clot had progressed into deep vein thrombosis and bilateral pulmonary emboli—forming clots in both lungs.

— Philadelphia Eagles (@Eagles) October 19, 2026

Hurts hasn't spoken out about the health update, but his agent, Nicole Lynn, along with the Eagles, released a joint statement regarding his diagnosis and expected treatment plan, which was shared across all official social media accounts.

While Hurts remains "clinically stable and has no significant functional limitations," he must undergo a blood-thinning regimen lasting at least three months. League and medical guidelines strictly prohibit players from participating in contact sports while taking anticoagulation medication.

While many fans in the comments expressed support, a few expressed anger about why Hurts wasn't taken out sooner. The Go Birds News account on Twitter commented: "Why was he ever allowed to play in the London game? Complete malpractice." Another user commented, "JFC, how can you let our star player fly with such a condition. Get better Jalen. go birds."

Despite the sudden end to his season, medical experts expect a complete recovery for the 28-year-old player.

"Jalen's prognosis is very good, and we expect a full recovery," the joint statement concluded. "We anticipate that he will have the opportunity to resume contact football activities when off the blood thinners. In the meantime, he will remain active around the team and continue to condition. More importantly, we anticipate that he will have no long-term effects."
