#132. What Tarik Skubal said about his pending free agency after Dodgers' playoff elimination

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Ace left-hander Tarik Skubal watched his Dodgers get eliminated in the NLCS from the dugout in Game 4 on Thursday night. Now, Skubal's next stop is free agency this coming offseason. He will be the top free agent on the market and command an absurd amount of money before signing on the dotted line.

Unsurprisingly, Skubal didn't have much to say on the matter after Game 4.

"I'm not going to comment on my future really at all," he said, via MLB.com. "Today sucks, you know, and that's kind of where my head's at."

Skubal heads to free agency having made the playoffs for three straight years and posted a 2.13 ERA in eight playoff starts, but his teams have been unable to make the World Series. In fact, the trip to the NLCS this year with the Dodgers was the deepest he's ever been in the playoffs. The Tigers made the ALDS in both 2024 and 2025 before being eliminated.

The 29-year-old Skubal was the American League Cy Young winner in both 2024 and 2025. This season, he suffered an injury to his pitching elbow that required surgery, a new procedure called NanoScope surgery. He healed remarkably quickly, only missing starts between April 29 and June 13.

Nine starts later and the Tigers -- despite only being 2 ½ games out of a playoff spot -- decided to get in front of missing the postseason and losing Skubal to free agency. They traded him to the Dodgers at the deadline for a package that included top prospect Zyhir Hope.

Between the two teams this season, Skubal made 26 starts and went 12-7 with a 2.72 ERA (155 ERA+), 0.96 WHIP and 186 strikeouts in 158 ⅔ innings. His 4.6 WAR was down from 6.7 and 6.4, respectively, in the previous two seasons, but he made five fewer starts.

Normally, a pitcher like Skubal hitting free agency would mean bidding into the mid-nine-figure range, but there's uncertainty this time around with the CBA expiring and the ownership side driving hard toward a salary cap. It's possible that Skubal's contract needs to wait until after a deal is made between the two sides and teams know what they have to work with in their finances. Conversely, a team could be incredibly aggressive in trying to get his deal grandfathered under the previous CBA. Time will tell.

For now, Skubal and the rest of the Dodgers head home for the winter.

#134. Spanish club Basket Zaragoza attempting to block Thunder rookie Aday Mara from making NBA debut

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The organization Aday Mara began his professional basketball career with is publicly challenging his move to the Oklahoma City Thunder. Basket Zaragoza, the Spanish club that Mara played for from 2021-23 before he played college basketball at UCLA and Michigan, released a statement on Friday saying Mara is still under contract for the 2026-27 season and it will oppose him suiting up for the Thunder, who chose him with the 12th pick in the 2026 NBA Draft.

In a statement, Zaragoza said it has not received a formal request for Mara's international transfer and would oppose such a request if one is made. The club said it has relayed its position to multiple parties, including the Thunder, the NBA, FIBA and the Spanish Basketball Federation. FIBA does not require an international transfer for players to play in the NCAA, but it does for other professional leagues.

Spanish newspaper Heraldo de Aragon reported Friday (via Eurohoops.net) that Zaragoza is seeking a financial settlement:

As the local newspaper Heraldo de Aragon reported first his former team claims to hold his playing rights and plans to block any international clearance until a financial settlement regarding his departure is reached. This case had initially progressed to litigation and remains without a legal resolution. Therefore, the club has reportedly warned the NBA, the Thunder, FIBA, and the Spanish Basketball Federation that the 7-foot-3 big needs a formal Letter of Clearance to be eligible to play in the 2026–27 Regular Season.

In response, the Thunder said Friday that "no clearance from the Spanish team is required" for Mara to play in the NBA.

"Aday last played three years of NCAA college basketball and therefore, as advised by the NBA, no clearance from the Spanish team is required for him to play in the NBA," a team spokesperson said.

The 7-foot-3 Mara left Zaragoza, his hometown club, to begin his college basketball career at UCLA in 2023. He played for the Bruins for two seasons before transferring to Michigan, where he became a crucial cog in the Wolverines' national championship run. Mara was one of the best shot blockers in college basketball and vaulted into a first-round pick, landing with Oklahoma City.

Mara, 21, has been one of the stars of the preseason and is expected to play a significant role off the bench for the Thunder this season. In Mara's third preseason game against the Hawks, he played 33 minutes and finished with 17 points, 10 rebounds, six assists and four blocks.

Oklahoma City opens the 2026-27 season against the San Antonio Spurs on Oct. 20.

#135. Do the Raptors have enough shooting to contend?

Last year's Toronto Raptors were one of the most fun teams in the league, a whirling dervish on defence that could be absolutely devastating in transition. But, the team's lack of shooting hamstrung its halfcourt offence, forcing athletic slashers like Scottie Barnes and RJ Barrett to operate in a phone booth, leading to some close losses at the end of fourth-quarter slogs. While swapping Brandon Ingram for Kawhi Leonard will undoubtedly give the offence a boost, the question remains: have the Raptors done enough to address their shooting deficiency?

Outside shooting is a force multiplier in today's NBA. Not only can a hot shooter flip a scoreline in an instant, but the threat of a marksman with a quick trigger pulls defenders away from the paint, giving his teammates more room to attack the paint, especially important for teams like Toronto who are built around a young star who lives at the rim.

Leonard, the headline-grabbing new addition, knocked down 38.7% of his outside shots last year and was above 41% the three seasons before that. He's an excellent three-point shooter, but he really makes his money in the midrange, where he's one of the game's premier iso scorers. In some ways, he's a more physically strong and deadlier version of Brandon Ingram. His shooting skill will be a boon and he shot more threes (6.8 per game) than ever last season, but, for the Raptors, whether or not his teammates can space the floor for him is just as vital as whether or not he can space the floor for others, since he'll have plenty of the ball at the end of the shot clock.

If we assume that the Raptors' last preseason starting lineup (Leonard, Barrett, Barnes, Immanuel Quickley, and Jakob Poeltl) will be their regular season starting unit, only two of those players (Leonard and Quickley) shot above league average from three last year. Barrett has had a 40% season in his past, but has only shot 36% or better one other time in his seven seasons in the league and, like Leonard, he doesn't toss them up at particularly high volume. Barnes is a career 30.1% shooter from beyond the arc and will be treated as a non-shooter in the playoffs, and Poeltl's range barely extends beyond the basket. Quickley has a fast release and is unafraid to pull up from well beyond the arc, but he's more streaky than automatic. He'll probably need to up his three-point volume even more (he was at 6.8 attempts per game last year, the same as Kawhi) to really move the needle for a team that was just 26th in three-point attempts and 21st in percentage last season.

In fact, of the top eight Raptors in minutes per game last season, only Ingram (gone, but accounted for by Kawhi's arrival), Quickley, and Sandro Mamukelashvili (also gone) shot better than league average from deep and only one other regular (Ja'Kobe Walter, at a sizzling 40.9% on 3.7 attempts per game) did so. Even if the Raptors opt to finish games with Collin Murray-Boyles at centre instead of Poeltl, CMB is still an unproven shooter who hit 34% last year on less than one try per night. Even a super small-ball lineup with Barnes at the five might not have particularly great spacing, unless Walter has a breakout season or Barrett finds consistency from deep. Jamison Battle can really shoot, but it's not clear he'll have a big enough role to make a significant impact and their best defensive guard, Jamal Shead, has only made 32.2% of his threes in the NBA.

This year's Raptors team will still be plenty dangerous and they'll be an absolutely miserable team to have to play against, whether in the regular season or the playoffs, but it may take another roster move, or a breakout shooting performance from CMB, Walter, or Shead, for them to have enough offence juice to take down the league's elites in a playoff series.

#136. UNC beats Duke — Winners, Losers, & Honorable Mentions

Carolina fans had seen this story before: the quick 17-0 lead on the road, a sinking feeling of when things would start to crash, and then the torture of the lead disappearing. The first sign was an unfortunate fumble, and yet the defense just kept giving the Tar Heels chances to run away with it. The offense couldn't convert, and then special teams just seemed to make the inevitable happen.

Then a funny thing happened — the offense came back to life just in the nick of time. Once again, the Tar Heels didn't completely fold, and between a game-winning drive and a great interception, Carolina rode back to Chapel Hill with the Victory Bell for the first time in a couple of years.

So let's dive right into the winners, losers, and honorable mentions for UNC's 24-20 win over the Blue Devils.

Jaylen McGill – One huge problem for the UNC offense was how early Benjamin Hall went down. Hall was trying to stretch out a play and basically got pulled in opposite directions on the tackle. All of a sudden, Carolina's deep running back corps suffered a huge hit. McGill took some time to get warmed up, but he's someone that the staff has had their eyes on. On the last drive, though, he had his signature moments. On a fourth and four he rushed for 16 to keep things moving, and then right out of the two minute timeout he took the ball and scampered 24 yards for the go-ahead score. That he was able to not only extend the drive but win the game turned what could have been a disaster for Carolina into arguably the biggest win of the Belichick Era.

Jordan Shipp – As amazing as he's been for Carolina this year, it took into the sixth game for him to finally get a touchdown. What he had to do to actually get that touchdown will have that clip being shown when his name is called in the NFL Draft. It's one thing to make some hay as a receiver when you have a great quarterback, but it's another when you take — we'll call them rough — passes and haul them in for scores. Even his mistake is one that comes with a silver lining. When Shipp fumbled on the play that led to Duke's first score, instead of yelling at teammates or an official, he just walked to the sideline with his head up and tapped himself on the chest, raising his hand to say "that's my fault." He clearly didn't let it eat at him as he finished the day with 75 yards, and when he's the main target life is not going to be easy for him.

UNC Defense – Just a Herculean effort. This squad bowed up and bailed out the UNC offense time and time again. The only touchdown Duke scored on them was the drive on which they took the lead, and even that came on a very short field when the punting team couldn't get a kick off and gave the Blue Devils the ball at the UNC 34. That sudden change is hard on a defense to stop, and they had managed to keep Duke to just two field goals up to that point. They also didn't fall for the myriad of gadget plays that Manny Diaz seemed to want to try to consistently throw at them, almost as if he wanted to really show he could once again outcoach the great Bill Belichick. Diaz overthought it and the UNC defense made them pay. Yes, you'd love more tackles for losses, and the turnover didn't happen until the last play of the game, but the defense is the reason Carolina won that game.

Turnovers – Duke went, effectively, 1-2 on the two fumbles lost for Carolina, and the first one was the only real reason Duke was in the game in the first place. While Carolina was deep in Duke territory, the offense had been effective and another sustained effort that turned into three or seven points might have completely deflated Duke for the rest of the evening. Instead, Shipp's fumble reignited the Devils and completely killed Carolina's momentum basically for the rest of the game until the final drive. The Tar Heels also couldn't force a turnover until the very last drive. That's not really a sustainable formula for the rest of the season, so Carolina needs to be better at protecting the ball, forcing turnovers, or both going forward.

UNC Punters – Aeron Burrell did not have a good day kicking, only averaging 41.7 yards on the day (and his longest was 43, so it's not like there was one kick that killed his average). He ultimately was hurt at some point in the game, and so Adam McCann-Gibbs had to come in cold. The snap to him didn't go well, and his indecision gave Duke the ball with outstanding field position. The Carolina defense just couldn't respond — and honestly, who can blame them? — and put the offense in a difficult position.

UNC Offense (Post First Quarter) – Until the drive that started with 4:34 left in the fourth quarter, the offense that scored on their first three possession managed three punts, two fumbles, and a turnover on downs — which, technically, what that messed-up punt was called. The defense was playing their guts out consistently, keeping Duke at arm's length, begging for the offense to get one more score so that they could get some space between them. The offense, arguably, was responsible for the same amount of Duke points as the UNC defense. A lot of it is at the quarterback position, as Billy Edwards, Jr. is just not a good quarterback. He's fine. He's better for UNC than Gio Lopez was for UNC — again, you wonder if Carolina hadn't nuked that bridge what Lopez would have done in the Petrino offense — but there's no reason why an open Shipp in the end zone should have to go through what he did to catch the ball. Also, Duke quickly realized just how important Shipp was to the team, and Edwards was so locked into him that when he couldn't connect it just dried up. If Petrino and Carolina are going to stick with Edwards the rest of the season, they need to do more with his obvious limitations.

Kenton Dobson III didn't just have the big pickoff for the Tar Heels, he was also fourth on the team in tackles with two solo and seven total. Not bad numbers…Jelani Thurman had another solid day with 52 yards in catching but he had the other highlight of the day by laying one of the toughest stiff arms you'll see on a defender and then ultimately getting hit out of bounds. He continues to shine as a portal addition….Demon June had the other touchdown for the Tar Heels with just a great red zone run. While he hasn't put up the gaudy numbers, he's put up great work deep on the field, and he's settled into his role nicely.

This stretch of games rolls on as the Tar Heels finally return to Kenan Stadium for the first time since the Notre Dame loss to take on Syracuse. Carolina enter the second half of the year with a 4-2 record and only have to hit the road two more times this season. Can this squad keep the momentum rolling? We'll see under the Kenan Stadium lights with the first night game of the season.

#139. Rams' Kyren Williams questions playing time after offensive issues: 'Probably because I'm not out there'

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Los Angeles Rams, the preseason darling and the offseason's crowned superteam, have nothing super about them so far in 2026. The hype around the franchise has quickly dissipated after a 2-4 start through the first six weeks of the regular season. Rock bottom — to this point at least — hit on Sunday with a home loss to the Arizona Cardinals, who were 13.5-point underdogs heading into SoFi Stadium. That defeat dropped L.A. to last place in the NFC West.

To make matters worse, there appears to be some discontent sprouting in the locker room when it comes to certain roles, particularly in the backfield. Following Sunday's game, running back Kyren Williams was asked about the Rams' inability to find any consistency on offense.

"I can't tell you, bro," Williams said, via The Orange County Register. "Probably because I'm not out there."

Williams totaled 10 carries for 50 yards in Week 6, while also catching three of his six targets for 17 yards. Those 13 total touches were his lowest of the season. While he didn't see a lot of touches for his standards, Williams was on the field for 72.4% of the snaps on Sunday, which was his third-highest snap rate of the season. Meanwhile, fellow Rams back Blake Corum saw 11 touches (nine carries and two receptions), which were the second-highest of the season for him. He played 27.6% of the offensive snaps.

While Williams still has the lion's share of the snaps, the margin of opportunities between him and Corum was closer than the snap rate would suggest. Over the previous three seasons coming into 2026, Williams averaged 17.8 carries per game. Through six games this year, he's averaging 13.3 rushing attempts per game.

"I can't really call that. It's not on me," Williams said when asked if he wanted a bigger workload like he's had in seasons past. "But I just think no matter what, we gotta continue to have the energy. You gotta continue to, when plays are made, be excited, be happy so we uplift not only the offense but the defense and the special teams and just being able to have that camaraderie to where we're playing off of each other, and I think that's what is going to allow us to be where we want to be."

This latest loss makes the Rams just the fifth outright preseason Super Bowl favorite in the past 50 seasons to have a losing record through six games. None of the previous four made it to the Super Bowl. Before even reigniting any talk of hoisting a Lombardi Trophy, however, Los Angeles needs to get in a more consistent rhythm on both sides of the ball to dig itself out of the hole it's dug.

#141. Who's to blame for Dodgers' shocking NLCS loss vs. Brewers? Five places to point fingers

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Milwaukee Brewers are going to the World Series for the second time in franchise history and the first time as a National League team (the Brewers were still in the American League when they went to the World Series in 1982). This also means the Los Angeles Dodgers have been eliminated, and their shot at becoming baseball's first threepeat champion since the 1998-2000 New York Yankees ended on Thursday night. The Brewers have swept the Dodgers in four games in the NLCS, doing so one year after the Dodgers swept them in the 2025 NLCS.

Who is to blame for the Dodgers going four-and-out in the NLCS? There's plenty of blame to go around, so let's assign it, shall we?

We have to start here. The Dodgers got swept in the NLCS because the Brewers outplayed them in every phase of the game. The Brewers got better starting pitching. Their bullpen was better. Their defense and baserunning were better. Their offense was better at both stringing together hits to build a rally and launching the ball out of the park. Pat Murphy out-managed Dave Roberts as well. You name it, and the Brewers did it better than the Dodgers this series.

"It's a pretty simple answer," Dodgers infielder Max Muncy said after Game 3. "We're playing like shit. They're playing great."

As much as we want to (and will) blame various Dodgers for the sweep, the single biggest reason they got swept is that the Brewers were simply the better team. They were the better team in the regular season based on their records (103-59 vs. 100-62) and run differentials (+214 vs. +201), and they certainly played like the better team in the NLCS. The better team doesn't always win a postseason series. In the NLCS though, the better team has played like the better team, period.

The biggest star on baseball's most star-laden team was not himself the last two months of the season. Shohei Ohtani played through knee and biceps injuries and had been so unproductive than Roberts said there would at least be a "conversation" about sitting Ohtani in Game 3. That didn't come to pass, and hey, Ohtani went 1 for 2 with a walk and a hit-by-pitch in Game 3, and hit a home run in Game 4. The homer put the Dodgers up 4-0 on Thursday. The Dodgers didn't score again. The bottom line is Ohtani was a non-factor until it was too late. It's hard to win when your best player is this diminished.

Whenever a team loses in the postseason, the best player gets a disproportionate amount of the blame, and that applies to Ohtani this series. He's clearly not healthy, yet he insists on remaining in the lineup, and he's had multiple chances in the first three games to swing things in his team's favor, but couldn't do it. When the best player underperforms, he wears most of the blame. It has been the way of the world since the dawn of team sports.

Freddie Freeman, not Ohtani, was the worst player in the NLCS by both win probability added and championship probability added. He went 1 for 14 in the series and the one hit came in the first inning of Game 1. Freeman went 0 for 13 after his first NLCS at-bat and that 0 for 13 includes:

That's an awful lot of empty at-bats in clutch situations for one of the best clutch hitters of this generation. Freeman had as many double plays as total bases (one each) in the NLCS, and his only RBI came on a sacrifice fly. You won't beat a team as good as the Brewers with sac flies. You need bigger swings from your best players and Freeman didn't provide them.

Max Muncy went 2 for 12 with six strikeouts in the NLCS. Teoscar Hernández went 3 for 14. Andy Pages went 3 for 12. Tommy Edman went 1 for 7. Will Smith went 2 for 15 in the NLCS. Postseason legend Enrique Hernández went 0 for 8 with a ghasty strikeout in Game 3. The Dodgers had runners at second and third with one out in sixth, and Hernández took two pitches in the zone for strikes, then flailed at slider out of the zone. It was maybe the single worst at-bat of this NLCS.

Freeman was terrible, Ohtani was terrible, and the thing that has so often set the Dodgers apart these last few years -- an elite supporting cast -- was terrible as well. Edman, Muncy, Smith, and the Hernándezes are a combined 11 for 58 (.189) in the four games. Betts (3 for 15 with three walks) and Kyle Tucker (4 for 12 with three walks) were the only Dodgers hitters who escaped scrutiny. They were their most productive hitters and consistently had strong at-bats. Everyone else? 😴😴😴

The manager can not swing the bat or throw the ball for his players, but he can put his team in the best position to succeed, and Roberts did not do that in the NLCS. Game 3, especially, was a managerial mess. Roberts burned the precocious Josue De Paula in the sixth inning when he sent him up to pinch-hit for Miguel Rojas with runners on second and third and one out, then immediately pinch-hit Enrique Hernández for De Paula when the Brewers brought in a lefty reliever.

De Paula is a rookie, I get that, but he has a track record of hitting lefties well in the minors. More accurately, he has a strong track record of making contact against lefties, which is what the Dodgers needed in that spot. A ball in play to get a run home. Instead, Roberts defaulted to the veteran Hernández, who struck out feebly. For all his career postseason success, Hernández went 1 for 14 this postseason, and a .190/.235/.317 hitter in his last 19 postseason games. Roberts never adjusted his priors.

The NLCS was a flashback to pre-2024 Roberts, when he too often showed too much faith in his veterans and had an unfortunate knack for sticking with starters too long. In 2024 and 2025, it all worked out, and Roberts looked like a genius. Those same mistakes, the ones he got away with the last two years, reared their ugly heads. The NLCS sweep is on the players, first and foremost. Roberts didn't play his cards well either. He's made things worse.

#143. NBA's five biggest starting lineup questions: Three guards for Spurs? Morant-Lillard backcourt in Portland?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The games played on NBA Opening Night represent just one of 82 for each team. And in pretty much every case, the roster a team starts a season with won't be the one it takes into the playoffs. If nothing else, there are usually at least some injuries. In some cases, there will be trades or free agent additions that wind up mattering in April and May. It's only one game. The players in a team's starting lineup don't need to define its season.

Yet opening night represents something of a declaration of intent. The players who start your first game represent who you want your team to be at its best. When conditions are optimal, when everyone is hopefully healthy and you've had a whole offseason to prepare, who are the players you plan to lean on? You'll have 81 more opportunities to change your mind, but who a team wants to be can often tell us quite a bit about who that team winds up becoming.

So, with opening night less than a week away, let's look at some of the biggest starting lineup questions around the league. Which teams are still making up their minds, and what are the decisions they're weighing with the 2026-27 season now at hand?

Before their preseason debut, the Spurs revealed that Dylan Harper would start alongside Stephon Castle and De'Aaron Fox. Soon after, Fox became a late scratch due to hip and leg tightness. Fox missed the next handful of preseason games, but on Wednesday against the Suns, the Spurs finally got to try it. The results were successful on balance: they went plus-10 in 25 possessions together in a victory. That success is an outlier compared to its performance a season ago.

The Spurs used the trio together for only 54 regular-season and 83 postseason possessions. In those tiny samples, San Antonio got killed. There are diminishing returns on ball-handling. There aren't with shooting. Fox, Harper and Castle are all strong individual creators and relatively weak 3-point shooters. Forcing them to play together cramps the floor for each of them as drivers. San Antonio's season took off last year when it moved Julian Champagnie into the starting lineup. The formula of two ball-handlers, two shooters and one unicorn just took the Spurs to the finals.

Eventually, Harper will start. He's too good not to. Fox, starting a four-year max extension, might be too expensive to bench. Some degree of experimentation with the three guards together was inevitable. The reality here is that Harper and Castle are long-term fixtures and Fox might be untradeable. The Spurs have to at least find out if they're viable together, but last year's success and common sense suggested that they would toy with the trio in small doses. That brief preseason glimmer hints that the Spurs might be willing to push a bit further. We should still probably expect Harper to come off the bench to open the season, but San Antonio made a big change midway through last year, so don't be surprised if Harper's play forces the issue by the spring.

We know Luka Dončić, Austin Reaves and Walker Kessler will start for the Lakers. As for the other two slots? All JJ Redick has told us is that "the other two spots will not be two White guys." Quentin Grimes has started all three preseason games and seems like an obvious favorite for one of the slots. He's the cleanest 3-and-D fit on the roster, and the Lakers need someone to guard opposing point guards. His spot should be pretty straightforward.

The final slot is a bit harder to parse. If it's another 3-and-D wing, which is probably the easiest niche to fit in with all of this ball-handling, then Ziaire Williams would seem to have the advantage. He and Matisse Thybulle both signed for the minimum this offseason, but Thybulle's health history suggests he's best used in a smaller bench role to preserve his body. The Lakers invested more money in Sandro Mamukelashvili, but they might need him as their backup center. And even if they don't, his skill set tilts the starters a bit too heavily toward offense. Jake LaRavia has the incumbency advantage. He started 43 games a season ago, mostly due to injuries elsewhere, and the coaching staff already knows him.

The final answer might play out over a bigger regular-season sample. If someone stands out across 10 or 15 games, or if the lineup data suggests a change is warranted, none of those contenders for the fifth slot have the sort of stature that would make it hard to bench them. The early guess here is that Williams starts on opening night, but the Lakers will mix and match to find who fits best, particularly with Dončić and Reaves.

Rookie coach Micah Nori is essentially on a year-to-year contract with the Trail Blazers. One of his bosses, whether it was head of basketball operations Joe Cronin or owner Tom Dundon, spearheaded the acquisition of Ja Morant, presumably with the expectation that he would be able to bounce back into All-Star form. That probably isn't happening if Morant is coming off the bench, and yet Nori himself has said that pairing him with presumed starters Damian Lillard and Deni Avdija doesn't make sense. That's too much ball-handling and not enough shooting and defense.

In a perfect world, Portland would start a defensive-minded guard between Lillard and Avdija. Jrue Holiday certainly fits the bill, and so does emerging fourth-year guard Scoot Henderson. There are several notable contractual factors to consider. Henderson is headed for restricted free agency. Avdija can be renegotiated and extended next offseason, but only if Portland clears the cap space to do so. Morant bristled against Grizzlies coach Tuomas Iisalo's unconventional rotation strategy a year ago. That doesn't exactly scream "eager to come off the bench for the first time in his career." How any of them will handle iffy lineup choices or a reduced role is a major question.

This is one of the more interesting cases of palace intrigue in the NBA right now. When you're coaching for your job from Day 1, do you aim to appease your bosses, or do you act in what you believe is the best interest of your team, hoping to prove yourself right? The likeliest outcome here is that Portland sacrifices some early games by starting Morant but makes a change if and when it doesn't work.

The Pelicans made a widely-panned trade to nab Derik Queen in the 2025 NBA Draft lottery. He simply is not defensively viable playing next to Zion Williamson. You'd think the solution here would be straightforward: trade Williamson. It frankly should have happened half a dozen times by now. Alas, the Pelicans went out of their way to message that Williamson was staying at the trade deadline last season.

For now, they're stuck together -- at least on the roster. On the court, it seems as though Yves Missi will be one of the starting bigs. It makes sense defensively. He's a burgeoning rim protector with great athletic tools who needs more minutes. But this organization has invested too much in Queen to minimize him with a bench role. And while Williamson's long-term destiny might be the bench, that would have to come on a better team than this. When he's healthy, Williamson is still the best player on this team.

So the options here are to play two ill-fitting players together or split them up in an unproductive way. The eventual Williamson trade can't get here quickly enough, but for now, New Orleans has to navigate these messy dynamics.

The Raptors are probably this season's most notable example of a team that should be judged on the lineup it closes games with, not the one it starts games with. Collin Murray-Boyles is a better, more versatile player than Jakob Poeltl at this point. He played more than Poeltl in the playoffs. But Poeltl started over him at center in the playoffs last season and will likely do so again this year. As a way to minimize the physical toll of putting the 6-foot-7, 245-pound Murray-Boyles against opposing starting centers given how undersized he is, that's sensible. When it counts, though, he'll be the player on the floor.

The more interesting question here relates to resume vs. fit. RJ Barrett has only ever been a starter. He's a beloved Canadian national who made an iconic game-winning shot in the playoffs last season. He's also on a roster that needs his individual shot creation far less than it ever has. Toronto needs shooting and defense next to Kawhi Leonard and Scottie Barnes. Ja'Kobe Walter brings more of both than Barrett. Given his expiring salary and Walter's ascent, Barrett is an obvious mid-season trade candidate.

The question here isn't about opening night. Poeltl and Barrett almost certainly start alongside Leonard, Barnes and Immanuel Quickley. The question here is how long the Raptors put off starting their best lineup. Will they go all-in on Walter and Murray-Boyles after seeing the roster for a bit? Will it happen in the playoffs? They'll likely close games before they start them, but those two are too good to stay on the bench all season. It's a matter of "if" more than "when" for them.

#145. Brentford contact police after rugby ball kicked into stadium from high-rise flat during Liverpool match

Brentford have made contact with the police after a video went viral of a rugby ball being kicked into the Gtech Community Stadium from a high-rise flat during their 2-1 defeat to Liverpool.

The club have commented after footage of the incident was spread around on social media, condemning the actions as "dangerous and potentially very harmful".

The ball appeared to initially hit the roof of the Gtech's East Stand but footage later emerged of a coach inside the ground removing it from inside the ground, indicating that it had bounced down to the pitch.

"Brentford Football Club is aware of an incident involving an item being kicked from a height towards the field of play during Saturday's match against Liverpool," the club said in a statement. "Such behaviour is dangerous and potentially very harmful.

"The matter has been referred to the police and the club is supporting the relevant authorities in their investigation to help identify those responsible and take appropriate action, which may result in criminal prosecution.

"The matchday safety of fans, staff, players and officials is of utmost importance, and the club will support all efforts to ensure action is taken."

The Gtech, which has hosted the Bees since they moved from Griffin Park in August 2020, is part of a wider development project for the Brentford East district and is therefore surrounded by blocks of flats and other commercial buildings.

Alexander Isak struck a late winner as Liverpool came from behind to beat nine-man Brentford, eight minutes after a wonderful Victor Munoz goal cancelled out Keane Lewis-Potter's opener for the hosts.

The victory carried Liverpool above Brentford into fifth, with the Bees one place back in the Premier League table.

#148. Open Thread: Spurs 2022 draft picks all waived before start of 2026 season

Back in 2022, the San Antonio Spurs drafted three players in the first round — Jeremy Sochan (9th), Malaki Branham (20th), and Blake Wesley (25th). The pick that brought Branham was acquired from the Toronto Raptors and the Wesley pick from the Boston Celtics.

All three joined the Silver & Black and began developing. Sochan in particular was shuffled through various roles as the team developed, but never locked into a position. As the Spurs continued to grow, Branham and Wesley found themselves with diminishing roles as the team built around Victor Wembanyama. The emergence of Stephon Castle and a monster trade for De'Aaron Fox left the 2022 drafted duo in the dark.

On July 9, 2025, Branham and Blake Wesley were traded to the Washington Wizards in exchange for Kelly Olynyk. Last February, the Spurs waived Sochan. He went to the Knicks and picked up an NBA championship.

The NBA season starts Tuesday. On October 17, all three of the Spurs 2022 draft picks were waived by their respective teams.

After picking up his championship ring, Sochan signed with the Portland Trail Blazers but was waived after four preseason games. Branham, who'd been with the Washington Wizards since being traded in 2025, he signed with the Orlando Magic in September. Wesley, who landed in Portland after initially being traded to the Wizards, signed with the Los Angeles Clippers on a one-year contract.

All three were waived within 24-hours of one another on Saturday.

#149. Jake Bauers named NLCS MVP as Brewers advance to World Series after sweeping Dodgers

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Milwaukee Brewers have won the 2026 National League pennant. They swept the two-time defending champion Los Angeles Dodgers with a 6-4 win in Game 4 Thursday night in Game 4. The NLCS MVP is Jake Bauers and it's one heck of a story. We'll get to that.

Bauers went 4 for 14 in the series, but he made his hits count. He doubled in two runs to cut the Dodgers' lead in half in Game 4 and had the big blow in Game 3 with a go-ahead, two-run home run in the seventh inning. He had six RBI in the four-game series and that doesn't even include the impact he had in Game 2 with a 12-pitch walk in the third inning that helped chase 2025 World Series MVP Yoshinobu Yamamoto from the game.

"There was never a doubt in that dugout what was going to happen," Bauers said after the game. "We knew we were going to win."

An interesting twist here is that this is the first LCS MVP for the Brewers franchise. They won the American League pennant in 1982, but the MVP in that ALCS went to a player from the losing Angels: Fred Lynn, who went a ridiculous 11 for 18 (.611) with two doubles, a home run and five RBI in the five-game series. He was easily the best player in the series, but it still sounds weird to have a player from the losing team to be named the most valuable player in the series.

There was no such worry in this series. The Brewers thoroughly dominated the Dodgers in every facet of the game. They had more than a handful of the most valuable players in the series. Arguments could have been made for William Contreras and Aaron Ashby. Robert Gasser was outstanding in his five scoreless innings in Game 3. JoJo Romero and DL Hall were great. Jackson Chourio hit a huge homer. Garrett Mitchell hit two. David Hamilton was 4 for 7 with a home run. Christian Yelich was good.

As for Bauers, he's floated through seven different organizations and nearly retired after the 2023 season, but continued his career because his then-pregnant wife needed health insurance. He spent time in the minors and majors in 2025. This season, he had a breakout, hitting .266/.389/.484 (140 OPS+) with 22 doubles, 26 homers, 86 RBI, 93 runs and 3.3 WAR.

#150. Alexander Ovechkin announces this will be his last NHL season: 'Let's have fun'

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Alex Ovechkin's 22nd NHL season will be his last, the Washington Capitals superstar announced on Monday."This is gonna be my last year," Ovechkin told his teammates in a video the Capitals posted to social media. "It's sad, but it is what it is. We have an unbelievable team this year. There are 82 games left. Let's make the playoffs, and let's have fun."

Ovechkin has already established himself as the greatest goal-scorer in hockey history with 929 tallies, and he still has 82 games to add to that total before he hangs up his skates.

The No. 1 overall pick in the 2004 NHL Draft, Ovechkin immediately established himself as a prolific scorer by notching 52 goals en route to winning the Calder Trophy as a rookie.

Since then, Ovechkin has won the Rocket Richard Trophy as the NHL's leading goal-scorer a record nine times. The Capitals legend's resume also features an Art Ross Trophy and three Hart Trophy wins.

The crowning achievement in Ovechkin's illustrious career is leading Washington to its first Stanley Cup in 2017-18. After coming up short in a number of postseasons prior to that, Ovechkin led all playoff performers with 15 goals and won the Conn Smythe Trophy as a result.

Following the 2025-26 season, there was speculation that Ovechkin could retire, but he signed an incentive-laden one-year deal with the Caps.Sensing that this could be Ovechkin's final season, the Capitals loaded up to give their franchise icon one more shot at the Stanley Cup. Washington signed former Buffalo Sabres winger Alex Tuch in free agency and acquired winger Jordan Kyrou from the St. Louis Blues via trade.

No team is as loaded on the wings as the Capitals, and they have one of the best rosters in the Metro Division. Washington has the ingredients to challenge the defending Cup champion Carolina Hurricanes and get Ovechkin one more ring before he rides off into the sunset.

#152. NBA Western Conference tiers: Spurs, Thunder in a group of their own ... what about new-look Lakers?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Western Conference has been the NBA's superior half for a while, but that might be shifting. The West has two elite teams at the top who are among the favorites to challenge for a championship, but after that, there's a grab bag of playoff and play-in teams that could shake out in any number of ways.

On Thursday, we revealed our preseason Eastern Conference tiers. And with the season set to begin next week, here's our first installment of Western Conference tiers.

This is how it figures to shape up for at least the next half-decade. Maybe Oklahoma City isn't scared, but having to battle the Spurs and Victor Wembanyama until further notice just to get out of the West can't be what anyone was hoping for. After the Thunder won the title two years ago, the Spurs skipped the line and defeated the Thunder in last year's Western Conference Finals, sending the then-defending champs home. Jalen Williams was unavailable for much of the regular and postseason, but he's ostensibly healthy now. Chet Holmgren didn't acquit himself well against Wembanyama in the postseason (then again, few did), but he still made All-NBA and finished second in the Defensive Player of the Year race. And Shai Gilgeous-Alexander is the reigning two-time MVP. The top-tier talent in OKC is significant, and it's bolstered by the NBA's deepest supporting cast. Three useful rotation pieces in Lu Dort, Isaiah Joe and Aaron Wiggins are gone, and no one in OKC will blink. Cason Wallace, Ajay Mitchell and Jared McCain, last season's trade deadline reclamation project, are more than capable of filling those gaps. As always, coach Mark Daigneault is spoiled for options. The Thunder can match up with any team in the league and beat you in more ways.

The Spurs are way ahead of schedule after reaching the NBA Finals for the first time in nine years. Coughing up several massive leads, including a 29-point meltdown in Game 4, on their way to losing in five games to the Knicks is probably not how they wanted it to go. And yet the present and future are bright in San Antonio. At 20, Dylan Harper is already one of the most impressive two-way guards in the league, and, on the merits, he ought to be in the starting lineup. Just ask him. (In fairness, he tried to walk that back this preseason.)

Harper outplayed De'Aaron Fox in the Finals, but Fox's new four-year, $221 million deal likely keeps him among the starting five. Either way, Harper should get plenty of minutes from coach Mitch Johnson. Stephon Castle, 21, was an All-Defensive caliber player last season and upped his shooting efficiency from deep and at the line in the playoffs. The Spurs also signed Tobias Harris in free agency, which might move Julian Champagnie back to the bench. Either way, the reserves figure to be deeper this season. But ultimately, everything revolves around Wembanyama, who, at 23 years old, is already arguably the best player in the world. Wembanyama became the youngest person in history to be named first-team All-NBA and reach the NBA Finals. For good measure, he was also the first unanimous Defensive Player of the Year in league history. All of that should terrify the rest of the league.

In the West, it's the Spurs and Thunder, a big gap, and then everyone else.

Nikola Jokic raises the Nuggets' level significantly. The three-time MVP has shown time and time again that he makes everyone around him better. And he's finally playing alongside someone who's earned serious accolades after Jamal Murray made his first All-Star and All-NBA teams, becoming Joker's first teammate to be named to the latter. Christian Braun, Cameron Johnson and Aaron Gordon all missed significant time last season due to injury. Having them back and healthy will go a long way toward buoying Denver's chances. (The Nuggets starters had a robust plus-13.5 net rating last season.) The problems arise for the Nuggets once David Adelman is forced to go to a bench that once again looks thin (with apologies to newly added DeMar DeRozan). The Nuggets are also the only team in the second apron, which has a lot to do with why Peyton Watson, coming off a breakout season, was shipped to Cleveland. Denver will miss him at both ends of the floor.

Everything went sideways for the Rockets at various points last season. They lost Fred VanVleet to an ACL injury and decided to empower Amen Thompson as the fill-in point guard. It didn't always go great. Thompson is a heady passer and an otherworldly athlete and defender, but running the show was outside of his comfort zone. Not having an outside shot (or any shot) didn't help him on that front. The Rockets tried to go ultra big, which worked for a while until Steven Adams got hurt. In the end, especially in the disappointing first-round exit to an undermanned Lakers squad, Houston's offense looked completely lost. Alperen Sengun is only 24, but his shooting inefficiency has so far prevented him from leveling up from a good big man to great. Too often, the Rockets relied on Kevin Durant to bail them out and take on added responsibility, particularly in crunch time. KD is one of the great players in NBA history, but there's only so much he can do. A fully healthy Rockets roster should provide more options for coach Ime Udoka, but the questions about what this offense can actually achieve linger.

The Wolves decided to roll the dice in the offseason. Tim Connelly, one of the best front office execs in the NBA, evidently made the calculation that last year's roster wasn't good enough to get out of the West. That's a fair assessment. The Wolves added Ayo Dosunmu at the deadline, then scrambled in the postseason when they were hit by injuries, including Donte DiVincenzo popping his Achilles. Not great. In response, the Wolves dumped Julius Randle on the Nets and then moved former Sixth Man of the Year and fan favorite Naz Reid, an unprotected first-round pick, pick swaps and a handful of second-rounders to Charlotte for LaMelo Ball. As the spin goes, it will be the first time Anthony Edwards has played with a passer of Ball's caliber, and the Wolves are taking a chance on a talented but flawed player who might just figure out how to play team basketball in Minnesota. That was the thinking. I hate it. But even with Ball's maddening me-first freelancing, the Wolves should still be comfortably in the playoffs. How long they stick around is another matter.

That makes five teams. Six make the playoffs proper. That probably leaves the Lakers by default. After bidding farewell to LeBron James, the Lakers signed Austin Reaves to a four-year deal worth $184 million. Then they overhauled a huge chunk of their roster. The Lakers acquired Walker Kessler from Utah for two unprotected first-rounders and two pick swaps, then signed him to a four-year, $140 million deal. In theory, Kessler, an excellent rebounder and a top-notch rim protector, should slot in perfectly as the center the Lakers have longed to put alongside Luka Doncic. Provided Kessler is available. He played just five games last season. It's a monster bet by the Lakers in every way. They also brought in Quentin Grimes, Sandro Mamukelashvili and Collin Sexton. Add them to Jarred Vanderbilt, Jake LaRavia, Kevon Looney, Bronny James, Matisse Thybulle and first-round pick Cameron Carr, and coach JJ Redick suddenly feels like he has pieces that fit for the first time in his three-year tenure. That might be optimistic, but hey, it's still October.

"Probably the first time in my 3 years here that I feel like the pieces actually fit together.”— JJ Redick(h/t @ohnohedidnt24) pic.twitter.com/m0XlBfRqLB

All four of these teams would probably like to make the playoffs proper, but wishing doesn't make it a reality. As it stands, two of them won't make it out of the play-in. And the two that do are likely headed straight into the Spurs-Thunder wood chipper.

The Blazers were plucky last season and even took a game off the Spurs in the first round. Since then, owner Tom Dundon has invited an avalanche of negative press, including going to war with the city of Portland over arena demands. The Blazers hired Micah Nori as the new coach on a cut-rate deal. And they traded for Ja Morant, who the Grizzlies couldn't give away at the deadline and were happy to have Portland take off their hands. For his part, Nori seems to understand the obvious: Morant and Damian Lillard should not start together. That's different from making sure the team still runs through Deni Avdija, but you have to start somewhere.

The Warriors were thrilled to ink Steph Curry to a discount deal worth $115 million over two years, thereby keeping him in Golden State through his age-41 season. Whether general manager Mike Dunleavy can use those savings to boost an aging and injured roster and make the Warriors contenders again (or something more closely resembling it) seems harder to pull off. Curry played just 43 games last year. Jimmy Butler is still recovering from an ACL injury. Moses Moody is on the shelf to start the season as well. Kristaps Porzingis has suffered a rash of injuries and his health concerns once again have everyone wondering about his status going forward. Al Horford is 40. Draymond Green is 36 and signed a new one-year deal. That last bit is what passes for some of the better non-Curry-related news in Golden State these days.

The Jazz took a big swing at the trade deadline and acquired Jaren Jackson Jr. from the Grizzlies. Even with Utah trading Kessler to Los Angeles, the front court of Jackson, Lauri Markkanen and Jusuf Nurkic (assuming they're all healthy) should be among the better units in the league. Keyonte George took a big leap a year ago. He'll be joined in the backcourt by No. 2 pick Darryn Peterson, whose potential has Jazz fans salivating. After years of tanking and waiting, Utah is ready to win now. Or at least try. At a minimum, they should be League Pass appointment viewing.

Two seasons ago, the Suns won 36 games with Kevin Durant and missed the play-in. Last season, they won 45 games without KD after moving him to Houston, worked their way out of the play-in as the No. 8 seed and got throttled by the Thunder in a first-round sweep. That represents … progress? Yeah, we'll go with that. Devin Booker, Jalen Green, Dillon Brooks, Miles Bridges and another season with a giant question mark at center probably doesn't get the Suns very far. The upside in Phoenix is limited as long as Mat Ishbia is the owner and the mandate is to trade every draft asset not nailed down.

This is where the West falls off a Roadrunner and Coyote-sized cliff. Cooper Flagg had no backcourt to save him and was thrown into the deep end to start last season, only to do swimmingly and emerge as the Rookie of the Year. He looks as good (if not better) than promised and is already a two-way force that Dallas will happily build around. Kyrie Irving is back after missing all of last season with an ACL injury. The Mavs selected Morez Johnson Jr. from Michigan in the first round and hired his college coach, Dusty May, to replace Jason Kidd after new president of business basketball operations Masai Ujiri decided to chart a new course for a franchise in desperate need of it. With Flagg, the future is encouraging, but for the Mavs as a team, that's still a long way off.

The Grizzlies had been barrelling toward a hard reset since trading Desmond Bane to the Magic for four first-round picks last offseason. Then they shipped Jaren Jackson Jr. to Utah and got the Blazers to take Morant off their hands. Now Cameron Boozer, the No. 3 pick, instantly becomes the face of the franchise as a rookie. Ty Jerome, an estimated plus-minus darling whose health has limited the number of minutes and games he's been available to play, should love having Boozer around, as well as big man Zach Edey, who returns after missing much of last season. It's one slow step at a time in Memphis.

Joe Dumars seemed confused about the changes he made to the Pelicans front office. The Clippers were hit with the harshest penalty in league history following the investigation into the Kawhi Leonard no-show cap circumvention scandal. And the Kings are still the Kings. At least Sacramento has Darius Acuff Jr and Ben Simmons' new shot to look forward to.

#153. RI's State Championship Super Bowl has a new home | Exclusive

The ride home for whoever wins the 2026 Rhode Island high school football state championship just got a little longer.

Cranston Stadium wasn't big enough to hold the crowd at last year's Rhode Island Interscholastic League State Championship game between Hendricken and La Salle, but the RIIL has found a solution to ensure that doesn't happen again.

Per a source, plans have been finalized for this year's RIIL State Championship game at Bryant University's Beirne Stadium, with the game being held on Friday, Nov. 20.

The move comes as no surprise to anyone who was at last year's state championship game. Cranston Stadium was packed to the gills, with every seat in the bleachers filled and overflow crowds looking for anywhere to stand to watch a game Hendricken won, 13-3.

That many people in a small space also created a parking nightmare in the surrounding neighborhood.

The stadium lists a capacity of 5,000, but last year's paid attendance was around 4,100 with estimates of 4,300 people on site with absolutely no room for any more bodies. Crowd control became an issue and the RIIL had 11 police officers on site in case things got hectic. An incredibly boring football game may have helped prevent any incidents.

Cranston Stadium became the permanent host for the RIIL Super Bowls in 2008 and served admirably. In recent years, there have been questions about why the 90-year old stadium continued to be the home of Rhode Island's most important games while surrounding states play at larger and more modern facilities.

The addition of Pawtucket's Centerville Bank Stadium added gas to the fire. While the soccer stadium – which is the home for the University of Rhode Island football team while its campus facility is being built – seemed like an obvious choice to become the state's next host for high school championships, there were several issues preventing that from happening immediately.

Cranston Stadium was convenient for the state. It worked geographically and while it dealt with large crowds for the occasional Division I Super Bowl and a Thanksgiving Day game every so often, it didn't come to a head until last fall. Attendance has grown and Cranston Stadium hasn't been able to keep up.

Bryant should, in theory, solve those problems.

Beirne Stadium underwent a facelift – provided by Rhode Island FC, which used the stadium as a temporary home while Centerville Bank Stadium was being built – and re-opened in 2024 with 1,000 additional seats, bringing seating capacity to 4,400. Throw on an additional room for 600 people in standing room areas – designed purposefully – and you're looking at 5,000 people that could safely fit inside Beirne.

The stadium has hosted several high school football games in the last few years. Beirne has become the home field for Davies Tech football the last two seasons and Smithfield High School played there while its new turf facility was being built.

With a La Salle-Hendricken rematch looming and excitement surrounding high school football as big as it's been since the early 2000s, the RIIL needed to play at a stadium that could handle a large crowd and provide the necessary amenities that make the game work. Beirne Stadium's facilities are certainly that.

Bryant last hosted high school Super Bowls in 2007. While the stadium has been regarded by many as an ideal home for Super Bowls – good location, good parking, good facility – there was no way the RIIL could keep people from just walking in.

The new addition limited entrance points, which gives the RIIL a chance to control the crowd from a ticketing standpoint.

It's also a massive win for Bryant football, which has fallen well behind the University of Rhode Island in terms of recruiting the state. The game gives the school a chance to show off its facilities to the two best high school teams in Rhode Island and at least a handful of players will have the potential to play at the Division I FCS level.

The 2026 RIIL State Championship Super Bowl is the only game that will be played at Beirne Stadium. Division II, III and IV will play their games at Cranston Stadium.

While it may seem unfair, teams in those divisions had the opportunity to play for a state championship but elected to stay down in their respective divisions and play for division titles instead.

Further, crowds for Division II, III and IV Super Bowls have been rather lackluster. None of the games have come close to selling out Cranston Stadium, so there was no need to move the games from the site.

The current plan is to have the Division II, III and IV Super Bowls at Cranston Stadium on Saturday, Nov. 21.

Right now the move to Bryant is a temporary fix. The State Championship Super Bowl outgrew the stadium, so it had to be moved.

In a perfect world, all the games would take place at the same facility. There have been rumblings in the past about Beirne Stadium, Centerville Bank and even the University of Rhode Island, once their stadium is complete.

Previously, the RIIL was in a position of weakness when choosing a site. People weren't coming to games and with low ticket sales, cost-effectiveness needed to be a part of the equation.

Now the RIIL is in a position of strength. With football popularity skyrocketing, Super Bowl weekend turns into advertising for whoever the host is. Becoming the host would give Bryant or URI a chance to put their facilities and campus on display for players, students and parents, which would help enrollment.

We won't have answers for a while, but a good showing at Beirne Stadium could lead to a permanent change for the RIIL Super Bowls. We'll know more well after the season is over.

This article originally appeared on The Providence Journal: RI's State Championship Super Bowl has a new home | Exclusive

#154. Cover 32: C.J. Stroud has flipped the script, is set to cash in; plus game balls, biggest gaffes from Week 6

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The NFL is a "What have you done for me lately?" kind of league.

It's that mantra that held back C.J. Stroud from inking what many once thought would be a no-doubter market-setting contract extension last offseason when he first became eligible. However, confidence had been badly shaken with Stroud, particularly after a disastrous playoff run a year ago, and he entered 2026 at a true crossroads in his career. Would he keep trending downward and possibly play himself out of being the long-term option under center? Would he revive himself by looking something closer to the guy he was during his Offensive Rookie of the Year season in 2023? It turns out, the answer is neither.

By some metrics, Stroud is playing the best football of his professional career and has repositioned himself for what could be the largest contract extension in NFL history next offseason.

Don't let Houston's 2-4 record distract you from Stroud being all the way back. The former first-round pick is coming off a largely sensational Week 6 win over the Jacksonville Jaguars in London. Outside of an interception as the lone blemish of his day, Stroud was surgical, completing 24 of 34 passes for 312 yards and three touchdowns. It was his second career game with at least 300 passing yards and three passing touchdowns, and the first since his rookie season.

Foster had to double it!📺: @nflnetwork pic.twitter.com/srjLPbSesF

Through six games, Stroud's EPA per dropback, success rate, and passer rating are all on pace to be career highs. Meanwhile, maybe the most important metric of Stroud's resurgence has been his ability to protect the football. His 0.9% turnover-worthy throw rate is on pace to be the lowest of his career by a wide margin. For reference, Stroud's turnover-worthy throw rate was 2.8% over the last two seasons and 2.2% as a rookie.

There's also been a noticeable uptick in explosiveness out of Stroud, which is a callback to what he did when he burst onto the scene as a rookie. Back in 2023, Stroud's explosives per dropback rate sat at 11.9%, and then fell to 6.8% in 2024 and then 8.3% in 2025. So far this season, Stroud's explosives per dropback rate is back to double digits at 10.5%. His 9.3 air yards per attempt is also on pace to be another career high.

WHAT A CATCH FROM NICO COLLINS HOUvsJAX on NFL NetworkStream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/FSlix6VI5c

So, Stroud is suddenly protecting the football better than ever, while simultaneously being just as, if not even more, explosive.

That sets Houston up nicely to possibly overcome a sluggish start once again and push for a playoff spot. From a big-picture view, it also reestablishes Stroud as a quarterback not only worth investing in, but also possibly making him the highest-paid player in league history at signing.

Provided Stroud maintains this play throughout the rest of the season, he'll be one of the many quarterbacks due for an extension that could reshape the market, joining Caleb Williams, Jayden Daniels, Drake Maye, Lamar Jackson, and others. Those signal-callers will be looking to join Patrick Mahomes and Dak Prescott, who are currently the only two QBs making at least $60 million annually. Mahomes is currently the highest-paid quarterback in the NFL with an AAV of about $63.09 million.

That'll almost certainly be bested next offseason, and Stroud's play has not only revived the confidence in him as the franchise cornerstone for Houston but has put him firmly back in the conversation to be the highest-paid player in the league.

How Game Balls work: Six are awarded to standout players from the slate of teams that won their contests, and only one player on a team can get a game ball.

The Cleveland Browns are in first place in the AFC North thanks, in part, to their reigning Defensive Rookie of the Year, Carson Schwesinger. The linebacker led the team with 13 tackles and forced what proved to be a game-changing fumble in the fourth quarter. Trailing 10-3, Schwesinger was able to rip the ball out of Derrick Henry's hands. The Browns recovered, and that sparked a game-tying touchdown drive.

DROY Carson Schwesinger forces the fumble on Derrick Henry!BALvsCLE on FOX/FOX OneStream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/TY9niNw746

The Tennessee Titans notched their first win of the season by upsetting the Colts in Indy, 26-20. Simmons was a key cog in the victory, creating an important turnover to start the second half. Trailing 13-0 at the start of the third quarter, Simmons forced the fumble on Jonathan Taylor, which helped spark Tennessee to its first points of the day. He also finished with two sacks.

Big Jeff doing it all on that turnover📺: @NFLonFOX pic.twitter.com/k62Fe0nPYK

Hubbard was leaned on quite a bit in Week 6, logging a season-high 28 carries in the win over the Eagles in Philly. He turned those carries into 120 yards on the ground and a touchdown. This is the first time in Hubbard's career that he's logged back-to-back games with at least 120 yards. He's also just one of five Panthers backs to have back-to-back games with at least 120 yards rushing and a rushing touchdown, and the first since Jonathan Stewart in 2009.

Hubbard takes the handoff and picks up 6 CARvsPHI on CBS/Paramount+Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/bHvQ1dKVuD

Bernard continued his breakout in Week 6 as the rookie helped Pittsburgh pull off an overtime win over the Bucs in Tampa. The second-round pick caught 11 of his 12 targets for 87 yards and a touchdown. That score proved to be the game-winner as Rodgers found him on a 6-yard pass during the first possession in overtime. Bernard is the first rookie in NFL history with at least 10 receptions and an overtime touchdown in a game.

Steelers take the lead in OT 🔥PITvsTB on CBS/Paramount+Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/As1KkSab2G

Week 6 stats: 6-of-6 field goals, 18 points scored, long of 43 yards

The biggest upset of Week 6 came in Inglewood, where the Cardinals went into SoFi Stadium and beat the Rams. Kicker Chad Ryland accounted for all 18 of Arizona's points on the day, connecting on all six of his field goal attempts. That included the 43-yard game-winner as time expired. Ryland's six made field goals are tied for the second most in franchise history.

CHAD RYLAND WINS IT FOR THE CARDINALS pic.twitter.com/QfTHlvwVcr

Kenneth Walker remains one of the best -- if not the best -- offseason additions in the NFL. After being on the bye in Week 5, the Chiefs back picked up right where he left off, bludgeoning the Chargers with 6.7 yards per carry for his fourth 100-yard rushing game of the season. Walker's 665 rushing yards are the fifth-most by any player through five games of a season since 1970.

KENNETH WALKER III DOES IT AGAINLACvsKC on CBS/Paramount+Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/bo0Vpy9A29

Travis Hunter had one of his most productive games as a pro on Sunday, but it wasn't perfect for the dual-threat athlete. On the opening possession of the third quarter, the Jaguars had forced Houston into a three-and-out. However, Hunter was unable to get off the field in time, and the play was flagged for too many men on the field. Given that it was fourth-and-1, the five-yard penalty gave the Texans a fresh set of downs. They parlayed that break with an eventual touchdown between C.J. Stroud and Jaylin Noel.

Travis Hunter Was Jogging Off The Field During The Punt And Thought He Had More Time. He Did Not.A Flag Was Thrown And The Texans Now Have A First Down Off It.Costly Mistake. 😬 pic.twitter.com/R6KxUQPaom

In a game decided by a field goal, the penalty was extremely costly.

It was a day to forget for the Falcons rookie third-round pick. Branch fumbled twice in Atlanta's 31-23 loss to Chicago. With less than two minutes left in the first half, Branch muffed a punt, which gave the Bears possession at the Falcons' 10-yard line. It only took them three plays to reach the end zone after that turnover to build up a 21-7 lead at the break.

Bears recover the muffed punt!CHIvsATL on FOX/FOX OneStream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/Bp13sT3Yo5

To make things worse, Branch had another special teams fumble on a kickoff in the closing minutes of the third quarter. The Bears took advantage of that turnover with an eventual field goal, so Branch was responsible for 10 points in what proved to be an eight-point loss.

Second special teams fumble recovery for the Bears today 👀CHIvsATL on FOX/FOX OneStream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/MifNCLxaeA

As you might imagine, Branch was visibly upset on the sideline and could even be seen slamming his helmet to the turf.

Bijan Robinson comforting Branch after his fumble 📺: FOX/FOX One pic.twitter.com/oVJuU0l6Mt

The Bills defensive back was ejected just before halftime of Buffalo's Week 6 matchup with the Raiders after he was seen spitting at tight end Brock Bowers. The penalty also helped set up a field goal for the Raiders before the break.

C.J. Gardner-Johnson has been ejected for unsportsmanlike conduct pic.twitter.com/S2ME5wNiRT

This is the second ejection of Gardner-Johnson's career, with the first coming back in 2024 when he was called for two personal foul penalties in the same game.

It was a night to forget for the Cowboys' offense. Not only did they muster just 13 points in a loss to Green Bay, but they had a comedy of errors in the process. In the first half, with the game still well within reach, Prescott threw interceptions on back-to-back drives while targeting CeeDee Lamb. The second came when the Dallas receiver slipped and fell on his route, which left Brandon Cisse with the easy pick.

Two first half INTs for the @Packers 🧀DALvsGB on NBC/PeacockStream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/CrdFEn7GTC

At the time of the interception, the Cowboys faced just a 10-0 deficit, but the Green Bay turned that pick into a nine-play, 77-yard touchdown drive that extended the lead to three scores. This was also Prescott's first career game throwing two interceptions when targeting Lamb.
