#155. 10 Bears Takes: Caleb’s Comeback, Kyler’s Big Day, an Averted Collapse

The seven-day break between their 31-7 beatdown loss in Green Bay and a second-straight game away from home in Atlanta was enough to make even the most level-headed of Bears fans lose it. In three hours, the Chicago Bears went from a great story that had started three quarterbacks in four weeks to a team that might not be very good. As usual, the narratives fly any time those two teams play, which can make it hard for anyone to turn the page. Luckily for head coach Ben Johnson and his team, they did just that. It helped that they got their starting quarterback back in the mix, but for the better part of four quarters, they looked like the same dominant team we've seen in four of their six games so far in 2026. Before quickly turning the page on this one for a Thursday night showdown with the New England Patriots, let's take a deeper dive into Sunday and where they go next in Week 6's edition of 10 Bears Takes.

1. Caleb Williams' return on Sunday was much-needed, even after a weird media session earlier in the week– why fans should feel optimistic about his play after a three-game absence.

Williams ended last week's Friday practice session as a limited participant, before doing plenty of work in Green Bay before the start of last weekend's game. Speculation all along has been that he would be close to ready for Atlanta, and despite a Wednesday walk-through, it was clear they felt they had given Williams' hamstring injury enough time and were ready to ramp him up.

Then came Thursday, when his first media day in three weeks featured a long opening speech, some pointed statements, and a somewhat contentious set of answers. As always, people rarely take things at face value. Instead, everyone runs with their reactions, and it blows up into something bigger than it was.

In the end, Williams came out on Sunday with some clear motivation to prove his critics wrong and did exactly that. His 83.3% completion rate was a career-high, and he eclipsed 300 passing yards for just the sixth time in his career. Taking out the anomaly that was the Vikings game in Week 2, so far we've seen a new version of Williams where he's not wildly missing throws. Even more impressive, he's continued to take what the defense is giving him. Even if those checkdowns aren't turning into explosives, they are keeping opposing defenses honest, which is allowing for more shots downfield.

To dive a little deeper into his six incompletions: four were throwaways, one was Colston Loveland overrunning a route in the end zone, and the last was a pass where his arm was hit mid-throw. Simply put, he didn't come close to putting the ball into danger, and there were no egregious misses as we saw so often last season.

Even though the offense scored 31 points, it's easy to see how much was once again left out on the field. Between the penalties and missed opportunities in Atlanta territory, there's plenty of meat left on the bone for this offense to continue to get better. That should give fans plenty of faith that they'll keep improving as a unit, and ultimately, 40-point games are far from out of the question moving forward.

No matter how you slice it, it was a great return for the Bears' franchise quarterback. More importantly, the best is yet to come for this offense, assuming their core pieces stay healthy through the last 11 regular-season games.

2. Speaking of returns, Kyler Gordon's first game of 2026 was a stark reminder that when he's healthy, he's one of their best defenders.

Much has been made about his recent injury history and lack of ability. Frankly, it's been justified considering these issues started after he signed his lucrative extension to make him the highest-paid nickel in the league. Despite his lack of availability going back to the start of last season, it's impossible to debate that when he's in the game, he's one of, if not the best defensive players the team has.

Gordon was activated off PUP earlier this week, which made Sunday his first game of the 2026 season. Despite only playing 16 defensive snaps, his three sacks and two forced fumbles were the most that have been tracked from a defensive back dating all the way back to 1982. Even if Gordon isn't the most dynamic coverage guy in the league, his versatility is a huge value to any defense. Defensive coordinator Dennis Allen has always been known for getting the most out of his nickelbacks, and when Gordon has been on the field, the results have been no different.

With the team's secondary in flux due to injuries and their mix-and-match style, fans can expect Gordon's snap count to rise each game until he's settled into a full-time role. That likely means Tyrique Stevenson will go back to the bench, but considering how much both he and Jaylon Johnson have struggled down the field, I'm not sure that's a bad thing. Fourth-round rookie Malik Muhammad should continue to see snaps on the boundary, and if that's the end goal for him beyond this season, it makes sense to continue to play him there.

We'll see how things look once everyone is healthy (if that ever happens), but the offseason plan is starting to show. Once Coby Bryant comes back (hopefully this season), this could be a very different-looking group than the one we saw to open up Week 1.

3. With a short week upcoming, it will be hard for this team not to look too far ahead to their 10-day mini-bye.

It might only be six games into the regular season, but these last few weeks have taken a toll on this team's health. It started with Braxton Jones a few weeks ago, and has since led to Dayo Odeyingbo going on Injured Reserve, while other players like T.J. Edwards, Stevenson, and even Kyle Monangai are on the "week-to-week" timeline. At first glance, the only notable injury the team sustained on Sunday was right guard Jonah Jackson leaving with a hip injury. I guess that we won't get a better idea of what that injury looks like until closer to their game on Thursday, but combine that with Montez Sweat's suspension, and this team is missing a lot of starting talent heading into their Thursday night showdown with a very good Patriots club.

The Bears are in the midst of a tough three-game stretch that started with a road game in Atlanta, followed by a short turnaround with the Patriots, and then a Monday night showdown with the defending Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks in Week 8. Before their win in Atlanta, going 2-1 felt like the "goal". It would leave them at 5-3 overall, and ideally, it would give them tie-breakers over Carolina, Philadelphia, Atlanta, and Seattle, plus a 4-2 conference record heading into a stretch where they'll see a 1-5 Buccaneers team, a Week 9 bye, followed by another favorable matchup against a 2-4 Saints team.

That said, Week 9's bye feels like a long time away, which means the early focus will be on getting through Thursday night and hoping for improved health during their 10-game break before heading to Seattle to face the Seahawks. No one would blame the Bears for looking ahead, and ultimately, if they can get some other important pieces back, it's a win.

The goal now should be to get as many wins as possible before heading into the bye week. For instance, going into their bye week at 6-3 would put them in a prime position to push for the division, or at least a playoff spot, heading into the second half of the season. The regular season is in full swing, and the Bears, like every other team in the league, must find a way to weather the storm and come out better on the other side. A small reprieve is just days away, but first, there's a big game on a national stage waiting for them at Soldier Field on Thursday night.

4. Following an ugly 31-7 loss at Lambeau Field, it would have been easy for the Bears to lay down and go into Thursday night at 3-3. Instead, they came out and dominated for 3 ½ quarters.

We've seen this story play out before. Of course, that was before Ben Johnson and company, but the lengthy history of crumbling after a bad loss is well documented. So, in some ways, the reactions to last Sunday's loss against the Packers were understandable.

Going into Atlanta, it felt like a toss-up game that would come down to how successful the Bears' offense could be. Ultimately, they dominated most of the game, and if not for taking their foot off the gas early in the fourth quarter, coupled with a Roschon Johnson fumble on the next drive, the score would have reflected how dominant Chicago was for most of the game.

No matter the final score, make no mistake: Sunday was a statement game for the Bears, and it was good to see them rebound after such an embarrassing and emotional loss the week before. In reality, this has just been the DNA of Johnson-led teams since he took over in Chicago last season. After losses, the Bears are now 5-2 following a loss in the Ben Johnson era. To take it a step further, the Bears have yet to lose more than two in a row since last season. That should give fans confidence that no matter how bad things look and/or feel in the moment, there's a good chance that they'll find a way to rebound the next week, and usually in convincing fashion. It's a good trait for any team to have, but something to keep in mind following any loss.

5. Williams' return and 31-point effort was a prime example of what this offense is capable of, even with all the meat left on the bone from penalties and prematurely ended drives.

Although it seems clear that this offense isn't going to set the records that Johnson had sought during the preseason, there's still a lot of meat on the bone for a team that is averaging 25 points per game, while starting backup quarterbacks for half of those games. Their red zone woes have been well documented, but to their credit, they were 4-of-5 on Sunday.

The biggest key is trading field goals for touchdowns and not getting bogged down in opponent territory. One remedy is cutting down on penalties, and after a few good weeks in that department, they took a big step back on Sunday with 12 accepted penalties that accounted for 133 yards.

Missing Monangai has hurt their red zone offense, especially inside the 10. That said, the more Williams can get back into the swing of things, the more they can dial in their red zone and goal line offense. They have the weapons and versatile personnel to improve in that department and could also stand to get a bit better on third downs.

All in all, these are situations most Bears fans have dreamed of being in before the arrival of Johnson and company. Their quarterback is playing at a high level, and in his three starts, the offense is averaging 31 points per game with Williams under center. Improvements will always be a focus for an improving contender, but the fact they are having this type of success with so much still to clean up is a very encouraging sign. The best is yet to come for this offense, and as long as Williams stays healthy, improvements should continue in the coming weeks.

6. Injuries have continued to mount. Couple that with Montez Sweat's two-game suspension, and the focus on improving the defense through the trade deadline needs to be a priority.

Those who didn't watch the game will see Atlanta's 23 points and assume the Bears struggled to stop the Falcons' offense. The reality was quite different, especially in the first three quarters. In total, they had five sacks, six quarterback hits, and seven tackles for loss, in addition to keeping quarterback Michael Penix under 100 yards passing until the second-to-last drive of the game for Atlanta.

All in all, Allen and his defense did an outstanding job keeping steady pressure on Penix, getting off the field on third down, and holding the Falcons to 0-for-3 on fourth-down attempts. With that in mind, they'll face a completely different animal on Thursday against the Patriots. With Penix, the book is out: if you pressure him, he's a bottom-10 quarterback throwing the ball. Keep the ball out of Bijan Robinson's hands, and you have a good chance of stopping their offense. With the Patriots, Drake Maye is a top-tier quarterback, and they have plenty of weapons on all levels of their offense.

Overall, Allen has done a nice job of getting the most out of this defense, but injuries have continued to mount for this group, especially on the defensive line. Odeyingbo going on IR was a tough blow, especially after how well he played as an interior pass rusher. Sweat's two-game suspension hurts, if even from a name-value standpoint. Edwards had been playing well this year, and Stevenson's continued hamstring injury hurts their depth at cornerback.

Simply put, the Bears don't have enough horses to win the race. The versatility at defensive back has been compromised due to injury and performance, but ultimately, they need another quality pass-rusher up front. Even when Odeyingbo returns from IR and Sweat from suspension, they don't have enough difference-makers. The trade deadline won't be a "be-all-and-end-all" fix to their problems, but it might be enough to keep them around league average. More importantly, it might help them stay more consistent week to week.

We'll see what shakes out in the coming weeks, and although I don't expect a big move that sends any high-round picks away, players like Khalil Mack and maybe even Zach Sieler could make sense as lower-cost targets. At most, I wouldn't expect either player to go for more than an early Day 3 pick. Don't rule out another addition at cornerback, especially on the boundary. An old friend in Nahshon Wright could provide quality depth for a low price, especially if they aren't happy with what they have right now.

7. These next two games won't be easy, but at 4-2, the Bears have allowed themselves some breathing room if they can simply split them– More on how big of a win Sunday might turn out to be.

Before Sunday, Pro Football Focus' playoff odds had the Bears heading in two different directions depending on how the results panned out.

With a win, their playoff probability went to 64.3%.

With a loss, their chances would have dropped to 36.7%.

Now, it's worth keeping in mind that the season is still very young. Injuries and general inconsistencies will help cloud, and eventually clarify, the playoff picture in both conferences over the next two-plus months. That said, the difference between 4-2 and 3-3 was big. Now, with two big games against both Super Bowl contestants from a year ago, a split in those games would yield a 5-3 record heading into a pair of winnable games with a bye week sandwiched in between.

More than anything, seeing Williams back in action under center was a big confidence boost, not only for fans, but for this team to know what they are capable of. The next two games won't be easy, and they have another tough stretch starting around Thanksgiving, but they've given themselves some breathing room, at least for the time being, with a chance to build on their early-season success. It might be easy to forget, but this same team went on a 9-1 run in the middle of last season's schedule. If this team gets hot, watch out, because it won't matter who they play; they'll have more than a puncher's chance in each one.

8. Last Sunday's loss to Green Bay and the overall reaction to it was a great lesson in not making one game more than it is- one game.

I've said it before, and I'll say it again: The Chicago Bears are a good football team. Sure, they have their flaws, but every team in the league does. No team opens the season and runs away and hides from everyone over the first four to six games of the season. It simply doesn't happen.

Was last Sunday's blowout loss disappointing on almost every level? Absolutely. The Bears talked a big game, had bragging rights for nine months, and despite not having their starting quarterback, they were still favorites on the road at Lambeau. By all accounts, it was an extremely deflating and borderline embarrassing loss to their most-hated rival.

With that in mind, it was still just one game. In total, the Bears went 2-1 while starting backup quarterbacks. It just so happened that their one loss with a backup under center came against the Packers. Sure, their continued struggles in the division are a concern. Sure, you always want to beat the Packers, but I'm not sure losing by an interception in the end zone, or a 31-7 blowout, makes it any better or worse. The reality is, they got punched in the mouth, and now they have to live with that until they see Green Bay again on Christmas night. It is what it is.

What surprised me was how many hot takes flew around about this team as a whole and their head coach. I'll be the first to say that Week 5 might have been Johnson's worst-coached game of his career, and that includes their Week 2 loss to Detroit last season. Context matters, and he has a great handle on this team now, compared with his second career game as a head coach.

That said, the Bears are where they are largely because of their head coach. He's instilled a new culture. A winning culture. He's taken on the "bad guy" persona and has challenged his team to embrace not only the Packers rivalry, but daring to be great by blowing out opponents. Again, Johnson's ego (to an extent) was on full display last weekend, but he's proven time and time again that he can take something like that and learn from it. There was no reason for some of the columns to be written that everyone saw. There was no reason to question his viability as the team's head coach or question his job status. That was all complete nonsense and emotional talk after one loss.

Maybe this team never wins a Super Bowl under Johnson. Maybe they do. The one thing that is clear just a year and a half into Johnson's tenure is that he's the best head coach they've had in two decades and the sky is the limit for this group over the long haul. It's easy to overreact to any one game, but in the end, it's one game. That's an important lesson to remember moving forward, because over the course of a 17-game season, losses will happen. How they respond has been the bigger tell, and so far, the team is 5-2 coming off a loss in the Johnson era.

9. NFC North Lookaround: The Vikings and Lions enjoy early bye weeks, while the Packers hosted the Cowboys on a Sunday Night Football showdown.

This week, both the undefeated Vikings and three-win Lions enjoyed an early bye week. For a team like Minnesota, maybe it wasn't as welcome as it was for a banged-up group like Detroit.

The Vikings are riding high, and if history repeats itself, they are well on their way to finding themselves back in the playoffs after a disappointing 2025. According to Alec Lewis of The Athletic, the Vikings are expected to be active at the trade deadline, although it's worth wondering what they will target. The defense has been elite, but the offense has been about as uneven as it gets. Starting in Week 8, the Vikings will face one of the league's toughest schedules for the remainder of the season. While they've started hot, that will be challenged in the coming weeks.

The Lions face much less certainty. Getting into the bye week above .500 felt like an accomplishment, considering their injuries and poor defensive performances. With a 4th-place finish, they'll face a lighter schedule for the rest of the division, but their inconsistency has been concerning to a certain extent. The offense is still top-tier, but without a better defense, it's worth wondering what their ceiling can be. They come out of the bye with back-to-back home games against division rivals, the Packers and Vikings. We'll see how they fare in those games, but overall, their schedule is the most favorable thing working for them, outside of the high-scoring offense.

Finally, we get to the Packers, who came into Sunday night riding high on a two-game winning streak, and an offense that is finally figuring things out. Despite expectations, it was not a high-scoring game as the Cowboys struggled to get their offense going all night. The Packers are now on a three-game winning streak and have looked markedly better than they did at the start of the season. Their defense is playing much better, and the offensive line has stabilized significantly. Starting next week, their schedule tightens up, but with the way they are playing, each game is winnable.

10. Week 7 Look Ahead: Hosting the red-hot New England Patriots on Thursday Night Football.

After a slow start, the Patriots have figured things out. Not only have they won three games in a row, but they also have a +38-point differential in those three contests. Quarterback Drake Maye had a miserable start to the season, causing many to wonder if something was "broken". The good news for Patriots fans is that his last three games have looked much closer to his MVP-caliber self than the first three games, when they went 1-2. Over his last three games, Maye has a 10:1 touchdown-to-interception ratio, while averaging 292.6 passing yards per game during that stretch.

So far, New England's defense has more good than bad, and as usual, they are starting to get after the quarterback more as of late. As a whole, they have looked like a completely different team during this three-game winning streak, but it's worth noting that they are just 1-2 on the road so far this year.

For the Bears, this matchup challenges them in multiple areas. We'll have to see what Jonah Jackson's injury status is. Still, assuming he misses the game on a short week, the Patriots have a decided advantage on the interior with the likes of Milton Williams and Christian Barmore. New England has been borderline Top 5 against the run and has allowed less than 200 yards per game through the air. Offensively, they'll have star receiver A.J. Brown back, and even if Romeo Doubs can't go, they can stress opposing defenses in multiple different ways between the pass game and rushing attack. One potential saving grace for the Bears is the health of New England's offensive line. They lost three starters on Sunday and are already without their starting center. With a short week ahead, the Patriots could play Thursday night with multiple reserves in the starting five.

All in all, this looks like a quality matchup on paper, but as we've learned, Thursday night games have produced unpredictable results. This is far from a "must-win" game for either team, but the difference between 5-2 and 4-3 is massive, especially with both groups chasing first place from behind the curve. Buckle in; we should have a good game on our hands.

#156. Andy Dalton tells Eagles "no thanks," will sign with another team soon

With starting quarterback Jalen Hurts out indefinitely, the Eagles have had to scramble to fill out the depth chart.

Tanner McKee started on Sunday against the Panthers. They also have rookie Cole Payton, and they added Joe Milton from the Cowboys’ practice squad.

They had 16-year veteran Andy Dalton, but the Eagles cut him nine days ago. They wanted to bring him back, but Dalton has politely declined, we’re told.

Dalton, who has played for the Bengals, Cowboys, Bears, Saints, Panthers, and Eagles, will be signing with a team other than the Eagles as soon as tomorrow. And his arrival in a new city likely will trigger a current member of the quarterback room making his exit.

Which would then, frankly, make that player a potential option for the Eagles.

#157. NBA power rankings: Are experts underestimating the 2026-27 Celtics?

NBA power rankings: Are experts underestimating the 2026-27 Celtics? originally appeared on NBC Sports Boston

The Boston Celtics' 2026-27 season officially begins Tuesday afternoon as they'll take on the Detroit Pistons at Little Caesars Arena.

These C's will take some getting used to. That's because Jaylen Brown, a franchise cornerstone since 2016, was shipped to the rival Philadelphia 76ers in a shocking offseason trade. Boston acquired Paul George in the deal, hoping the veteran will fit seamlessly in the starting lineup alongside superstar Jayson Tatum.

The Celtics also upgraded their frontcourt by signing ex-New York Knicks big man Mitchell Robinson. In addition, they inked widely respected veteran guard Mike Conley to a one-year contract.

Will that be enough for them to maintain their reputation as a threat to win the Eastern Conference? Better yet, should they still be considered NBA championship contenders?

Here's how the Celtics stack up against their competition heading into the new campaign, according to NBA experts' power rankings:

"The Celtics made a carefully considered decision to trade All-Star forward (Jaylen) Brown to the 76ers, but the potential for that to backfire is still enormous. Just imagine the anger and outrage in Boston if the 2024 Finals MVP helps the 76ers win their first championship since 1983.

"While that worst-case scenario became more plausible when LeBron James joined Philadelphia on a veterans minimum contract, Boston should remain one of the East's top contenders after adding Paul George and Mitchell Robinson this summer. Jayson Tatum should be back to his All-NBA level form now that he's 18 months removed from his Achilles tear, and coach Joe Mazzulla has established a winning, high-effort culture that has delivered at least 56 wins in each of his four seasons."

"This ranking feels a little low for a Boston team that is going to win a lot of regular season games, but this first ranking is focused on title contention, and I don't believe these Celtics, as constructed, are as serious a postseason threat (I am higher on the potential of the Pacers and Rockets).

"That said, just having Jayson Tatum back on the court will be welcome, he is a joy to watch. Plus, this team will defend, has depth and athleticism, and will be disciplined under reigning Coach of the Year Joe Mazzulla."

"This offseason was about the shocking Jaylen Brown trade. But now that real games are about to be underway, the focus needs to be on who is here, and that's Jayson Tatum, who Boston decided was the star worth keeping. Joe Mazzulla showed that he is going to get his team to win in the regular season. Everyone focuses on the high volume of 3s, but the focus should be on how Boston dominates the possession battle and makes things hard on opposing offenses consistently. This can be a special season for Tatum individually, and Boston should assume its customary spot near the top of the East standings even if Paul George takes another step further from his prime.

"The question for Boston is what it will do when the jump shots go cold in the playoffs. But even in a tough conference, the Celtics shouldn't be doubted when it comes to hosting a game on the opening weekend of the playoffs."

"The Celtics shocked the world by trading Jaylen Brown during the offseason. They shouldn't experience much of a decline. Jayson Tatum's return should fill the void left by Brown. Paul George is a perfect fit in Joe Mazzulla's system, where he can capably switch on defense and shoot a high percentage from 3 on offense. Mitchell Robinson might be the most underrated addition of the offseason, both weakening the Knicks and adding to an already-elite offensive rebounding team."

"Microscopic sample size be damned, Jayson Tatum and new pick-and-roll partner Mitchell Robinson formed a lethal pairing in the preseason that opposition defenses can't decipher. Robinson's rim-rolling repertoire will create countless corner threes for the trigger-happy Celtics."

#159. Is the Dodgers' dynasty over? Three reasons why Los Angeles' dominance could be nearing an end

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

First, yes, the premise is true: The Los Angeles Dodgers are every bit a modern baseball dynasty. They've won three of the last six World Series. They've won 13 of the last 14 National League West titles and they've made the playoffs for 14 straight years. Over the last decade, they've amassed six 100-win seasons, and that total almost certainly would be seven if 2020 had been a standard 162-game campaign (their 43-17 record that year was a 116-win pace).

The Dodgers across those last 10 seasons have outscored their opponents by a cumulative total of 2,102 runs, which is frankly ridiculous. In second place are the Houston Astros with a run differential of +1,376 since the start of the 2017 season. There's topping all comers, and then there's overwhelming them. This is the latter. So, yes, the Dodgers are a dynasty.

Now, though, that dynasty is in peril. The Milwaukee Brewers swept the Dodgers in four games in the National League Championship Series, ending Los Angeles' hunt for the elusive World Series three-peat. Neither will they win the World Series for the 10th time in franchise history, at least not this year.

On Thursday, the Dodgers suffered their first loss in an elimination contest since Game 3 of the 2023 NLDS. This time, however, feels different, more substantial and with greater forward-looking implications for baseball's flagship franchise.

Because of that, it's time to ponder whether the Dodgers' dynasty is in its waning days. It's impossible to say for certain, of course, but there are three general reasons the Dodgers' current run of dominance may – may! – be coming to an end. Let's explore those reasons now.

The Dodgers this season had the oldest crop of position players in all of MLB, with an average age of 30.9 years. Moreover, a number of core contributors are reaching the age at which deep decline becomes a real possibility. In 2027, Freddie Freeman will be in his age-37 campaign. Max Muncy will be in his age-36 season. Mookie Betts recently turned 34. Teoscar Hernández turned 34 on Thursday. Will Smith turns 32 in March, and we know all about the accelerated aging curves of catchers. Shohei Ohtani is only 32 -- not necessarily a concerning age for a future Hall of Famer -- but no one has been worked harder and has more wear, tear, and fatigue layered upon him over the past several years than the two-way superstar.

This is just the eventual cost of doing business when you build aggressively through free agency and trades paired with long-term extensions as the Dodgers have. To be sure, it's been worth it beyond anyone's hopes, but eventually the bill comes due in the form of high-salary stars on the downsides of their careers.

On the pitching front, they're not quite as long in the tooth, but of the established starting pitchers, only Yoshinobu Yamamoto will be on the right side of age 30 next season. That same rotation is shot through with persistent injury concerns, and the Dodgers, for all their organizational merits, aren't famous for keeping pitchers healthy. There's also no guarantee that they'll be able to retain the services of trade deadline acquisition Tarik Skubal this coming offseason.

To be sure, all is not bleak, as the Dodgers have a strong farm system and an impressive base of young talent. Andy Pages and Dalton Rushing to some extent, but most especially Josue De Paula figures to lift both floor and ceiling, and there's more on the way. However, those in-place and incoming young players may indeed have a hard time replicating the past dynastic excellence of the Dodgers' current core, and it may be some time before they're even ready to try. Not all of them, of course, will work out. In the meantime, the Dodgers must hope that decline isn't linear for those veteran names above. That's especially key since the upcoming free-agent class will provide starkly little frontline help beyond Skubal.

Negotiations are ongoing for the next Collective Bargaining Agreement, and whatever comes out of that complicated wash will very likely affect the Dodgers and their spending capacity in a major way.

The MLBPA -- the union representing the players in these talks -- will probably never agree to a cap-and-floor system that team owners are demanding, but such an outcome is at least possible. The entire rhetorical push for a cap from the league side is centered on the Dodgers, and whatever structural changes emerge will target the top-end spenders. Speaking of which, there's already meaningful common ground between players and owners when it comes to making sweeping changes to how MLB shares local revenues, especially local broadcast revenues.

Commissioner Rob Manfred and the owners who tell him what to do want to bundle all these various and sundry local broadcast rights as one, similar to what the NFL does, and peddle them to the highest bidder (or bidders) once the national broadcast rights are up for renegotiation in 2028. With regard to the Dodgers, this writer recently went a-writin' about this very matter. Here's the relevant excerpt:

This is keenly relevant to the Dodgers. Under former owner/saboteur Frank McCourt, the Dodgers were in bankruptcy proceedings when McCourt sold them to the current owners, the Guggenheim Group. As a consequence of those court proceedings and a resulting settlement with the league, the Dodgers, after signing an $8.35 billion deal with Time-Warner, were obligated to share a much smaller percentage of their local broadcast revenues than other teams were. The Dodgers on average take in $334 million per year in local broadcast revenues, and that figure grows a bit each year since the contract is backloaded (by the end of it, their annual take will be more than $500 million). By contrast, the Marlins in recent years made less than $50 million each year in local broadcast monies, and even the flagship Yankees take in less than half of what the Dodgers do on an average annual basis, at least in terms of local broadcast revenues. Call it the "Dodgers Exception" if you like. It's not only giving the Dodgers much greater financial latitude, but it's also keeping money out of the revenue-sharing pool. That Dodgers broadcast contract runs through 2038, by the way, with a higher payout each year.

Nationalizing such broadcasts would eliminate that competitive advantage because it would require MLB to buy out the Dodgers' contract and or purchase the Dodgers' regional sports network.

While the MLBPA is not yet on board with such a drastic overhaul of the current revenue-sharing system -- they want some incentives to remain for small-market owners to actually invest in the product, which most of them barely do -- there is some meaningful shared territory here. Indeed, in their opening proposal to the league back in May, the union called for steeply increased sharing of local broadcast revenues. The upshot is that the next CBA will involve a significant transfer of revenues from large-market clubs to small-market clubs on a sustained basis. That means a financial haircut for the Dodgers and less room in the budget to do what they've been doing so well for the past decade or so.

Whatever the specifics, it's a near certainty that the new CBA, which will take effect before the 2027 season begins -- whenever that is -- will make the Dodgers' "dynasty maintenance program" far more difficult.

No, this isn't as dire as Frank McCourt somehow managing to bankrupt the cash-printing Dodgers, but principal owner Mark Walter has serious legal and financial worries right now. Once the standard-bearer for proper ownership in MLB, Walter is being investigated by the feds for potential loan fraud through his holding company, TWG Global. At the same time, he's the subject of multiple lawsuits, one of which is a class action suit alleging mishandling of client retirement funds.

All of this may mean major fines, settlements, or judgments against Walter's interests. Walter has already sold his controlling share of the NBA's Lakers and his minority stake in Chelsea F.C. of the English Premier League. While the Dodgers insist Walter isn't putting the club up for sale, it's hard to trust what parties with vested interests say about such things. Even if Walter doesn't sell the Dodgers, it's entirely possible, maybe even likely, that his appetite for spending on player payroll will be diminished. And that's assuming he'll even be allowed to spend at such levels according to the terms of the next CBA.

Never count an Andrew Friedman team out, of course, and the Dodgers aren't suddenly going to tumble to a win total in the seventies next season. They'll still probably be among the top quartile of MLB teams. However, their fading ability to dominate -- the Brewers had a better record and run differential against a tougher schedule this season -- looks poised to continue fading. That's a jarring reality for the team that's lorded over the sport for the last decade. But a reality it is.

#160. Uefa gives Infantino two-week deadline to release key documents

European governing body Uefa has told Fifa it must release key documents and answer all questions relating to its governance and decision-making by a deadline of 2 November.

At the Fifa Council on Thursday, president Gianni Infantino apologised for his World Cup sell-off plan - but failed to offer a full explanation for how the proposal was devised.

In the letter seen by BBC Sport, Uefa general secretary Theodore Theodoridis said that world football's governing body had failed to address "a number of fundamental questions".

"Others remain unanswered, and the information and documentation requested have not been provided," it read.

The letter included eight pages of questions covering a number of issues, from the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) private investment, to the Fifa Peace Prize and the controversial suspended ban given to USA striker Folarin Balogun at the World Cup.

"The withdrawal of FFE, the acknowledgement of mistakes and the announcement of 'potential governance reforms' do not answer how the relevant decisions were taken or why the Fifa Council was not involved at the appropriate stage," it continued.

"Any refusal to disclose information or documents should be justified individually, with a clear explanation of the specific grounds relied upon.

"These questions require answers now. They cannot be deferred until the next meeting of the Fifa Council - nor can future governance reforms substitute for scrutiny of decisions already taken and accountability for them."

Uefa did not outline what steps it intended to take should Fifa not meet the deadline.

The questions were first put to Infantino at the Fifa Council last week.

Football Association chair Debbie Hewitt - a Fifa vice-president - said afterwards that "if he doesn't answer those questions, he's not fit to be Fifa president".

#161. NBA's most overrated players: James Harden and Paul George make list -- and so do some young All-Stars

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Earlier this week we published our CBS Sports Top 100 NBA player rankings, knowing it's impossible for anyone to agree on these sorts of lists. That's sort of the point of doing them. They're (hopefully civil) conversation starters. One person might have Victor Wembanyama as the No. 1 player heading into the 2026-27 season, another person may have Nikola Jokić or Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, but everyone is going to have those guys near the top of their list.

For the purposes of this article you're about to read, we're looking for the significant discrepancies between where a player ranked on the CBS Sports final list, which was a creation of cumulative staff votes, and where a player ranked on our individual list. Based on these discrepancies, we published our most underrated players on Wednesday (James Harden was one of them), and now we're polling our writers for their most overrated players (James Harden is again one of them).

See, reasonable minds can disagree. Let's get to it.

Top 100 ranking: 22 Why that's too high: Mobley is clearly talented and a phenomenal defender, but I have a hard time buying a guy who is a third option offensively as the 22nd best player in the league. Mobley took a step back as a shooter last year and given he's also not a dominant interior player, there are just a few too many limitations to his offensive game for me to place him as high as some of my colleagues. The defense is fantastic, and he's a productive offensive player, but I am in the "need to see it to believe it" camp with regards to another leap coming from him that puts him into that top-20 conversation. -- Robby Kalland

Top 100 ranking: No. 34 Why that's too high: In an alternate universe, Duren might land on the underrated list. He bet on himself last year and made his first All-Star and All-NBA teams. Then he went out and faceplanted in the postseason, getting badly outplayed by Wendell Carter Jr. for much of the first round against the Magic and then mostly being a no-show against the Cavs in the second round. When Cade Cunningham desperately needed support, Duren's points per game plummeted from 19.5 in the regular season to 10.2 in the playoffs. That decidedly poor performance led to a contentious and protracted contract negotiation between Duren and the Pistons this offseason. Duren eventually signed a new five-year deal worth $200 million, a handsome sum to be sure. But it was also a far cry from the $287 million max contract for which he was eligible. When your own team is playing hardball with you at the bargaining table and there are reports you might rather play for the Kings because you feel "disrespected," maybe something has gone sideways -- sort of like us ranking him ahead of better bigs such as JJJ, Joel Embiid and Anthony Davis. -- John Gonzalez

Top 100 ranking: No. 47 Why that's too high: This is not a career-achievement ranking. When we put this list together, nobody factored in Harden's MVP almost a decade ago or his pre-pandemic scoring title, or at least they shouldn't have. This is a 2026-27 projection. As Brad Pitt said to the dude playing David Justice in Moneyball, "I'm not paying you for the player you used to be, I'm paying you for the player you are right now." And right now Harden is merely a good regular-season player durability and ball-dominant numbers have deceived the Cavs into thinking he's worth $100 million over the next three years (well, that and they traded Darius Garland, who's 10 years younger and generally the same player, to get him).

But I'll tell you what: If we do want to make this a career-based evaluation, how about those 48 career playoff games that Harden has had more turnovers than shots made? Forty-eight! He had seven of them in last year's postseason, when he averaged 19 points and five assists on 29% 3-point shooting. Do you have any idea how many NBA players could average pretty damn close to those numbers if their team gave them the ball as often as Harden? A lot. Those are not even close to good enough numbers from a guy who has to be extraordinarily good offensively to cover for his continued pathetic defense.

At the end of the day, Harden is an innings eater. He's going to get you through the 82-game slog, but you do not want him on the mound in the playoffs. I'm just going to go down the list of guys ranked behind him in our Top 100 and name the guys I am very confident most coaches/GMs would prefer to have on their team over Harden through the lens of winning playoff basketball: Jaden McDaniels, Trey Murphy III, Mikal Bridges, Desmond Bane, Damian Lillard, Josh Hart, Aaron Gordon, Alex Caruso, Payton Pritchard, Jrue Holiday, RJ Barrett, Devin Vassell, Ajay Mitchell, and I'm leaving guys like Cason Wallace and Isaiah Hartenstein and Draymond Green off because I know people who only know how to look at box scores are going to laugh at that. But trust me, if a GM would rather have Harden running their team than Draymond, even at this point in his career, playing his role going into a playoff game, they either don't know ball or secretly want to get fired.

I know the argument against some of these guys I just named is that they can't be the focal point of an offense, but listen, if you're a real playoff team, you already have that guy, and he's much better than Harden. For the Cavs, that's Donovan Mitchell. Winning playoff games becomes about having as many winning support players around the star(s) as possible. The Cavs would be a bigger threat in the playoffs with any one of the guys I just listed than Harden. They just don't have the name value. -- Brad Botkin

Top 100 ranking: No. 67 Why that's too high: Even though the trade happened over three months ago, I'm still trying to wrap my head around the Celtics willingly trading their second-best player (Jaylen Brown), who is also a consensus top-20 player around the league, for … Paul George? It would've been a great trade maybe seven years ago, when George was coming off an MVP-finalist season with Oklahoma City, but not only has George declined as a player, but he also has one of the worst contracts in the league.

The Celtics are one of the smartest organizations in sports, so I still can't wrap my head around the trade. But going back to George's ranking, I think it's about 20 spots too high. George is still a good player, but I would comfortably take 15-20 players over him in our top 100 right now. Maybe he proves me wrong and has a great season with Boston, but I was surprised to see names like Cason Wallace, Domantas Sabonis, Ivica Zubac, RJ Barrett, Ajay Mitchell and even Ja Morant ranked behind him. -- Cameron Salerno

Top 100 ranking: No. 76 Why that's too high: I've never been able to get over Brandon Ingram's 3-point volume miraculously rising during contract years and then regressing back to the norm after he's signed. Maybe it's a coincidence, but it feels as though Ingram struggles to find the balance between the shot diet the NBA likely wants for him and the mid-range heavy approach he seems to prefer. There are elements of this dilemma throughout Ingram's game. At points, he's shown basically every skill you'd want a high-end wing to have. He defended really well at the end of his Lakers tenure, and it didn't follow him to New Orleans. He'll have stretches as a legitimate playmaking plus and then they'll disappear thereafter. All of it folds together into a player that can frustratingly feel like less than the sum of his parts. We don't know when exactly he suffered that partially torn Achilles and how much it affected him in the playoffs... but it feels notable that Toronto was substantially more competitive against Cleveland without its second All-Star than with him last spring. Scoring was a chore without Ingram in that series ... but it was a chore with him as well, and the younger Raptors gave Cleveland a series by mucking up the game and defending extremely well. The skill has always been here for Ingram. It just never adds up into the sort of impact on winning that you'd hope for. -- Sam Quinn

#162. The Morning After: Jalen Ramsey is the glue to the Steelers’ defense

Last week, Dave Dameshek asked me who was the one piece on defense the Steelers couldn't afford to lose. I said that we may find out it was Joey Porter, as the Browns were able to have their way with the Steelers' secondary and the cornerback room was wearing very thin.

It turns out the glue to the defense wasn't Porter, though – it's Jalen Ramsey.

The future Hall of Fame defensive back had one of the best games of his career on Sunday, totaling 10 tackles, four tackles for loss, and two sacks, including the game-sealing sack on 4th-and-8 in overtime to clinch a 26-19 win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.

Lest we forget that Ramsey is doing all of this with a broken wrist that he suffered in Week 1. Yet despite that injury, he hasn't missed a game, and his versatility has been exactly what the Steelers had hoped it would be when Patrick Graham said he would play the STAR role. Per Sumer Sports, Ramsey has eight run stops – that is tied for the league lead among all cornerbacks with Cooper DeJean of the Philadelphia Eagles. His two sacks are tied for second among corners, as Kyler Gordon made his return to the Chicago Bears' lineup in Week 6 and had three in one game. His reliability in this role, combined with his tackling ability (only two missed tackles on the season) has made him irreplaceable. Players like Ramsey evolve as they get to the final holes of their career, and he has done just that. While he may no longer be the outside bump-and-run man-to-man lockdown cornerback he was in the late 2010s, his pure talent as a football player has seen him grow into being dominant as this Joker in the deck for the Steelers' defense. Some guys lead with words, Ramsey leads by example – playing hurt, not making excuses, and showing that he is still more than capable of directly impacting the outcome of games.

It's the morning after game day, and the Steelers are tied for the lead in the AFC North.

The Steelers signed Jamel Dean away from Tampa in the offseason with the hopes of forming a tremendous one-two punch at corner with he and Joey Porter. Obviously, Porter is now gone and Dean has become the top dog at the position, and he answered the bell against his former team with a tremendous performance.

Dean broke up six passes, which is a single-game record for the Steelers. Additionally, he allowed just three receptions on 11 targets, which is the second-lowest number of catches allowed when targeted 10 times this season. Who is first? His teammate, Asante Samuel Jr, who allowed two catches on 10 targets last week against the Indianapolis Colts.

And not to pat myself on the back, but when I made the Steelers' mock schedule and predictions in the offseason, I said Jamel Dean would have a game-sealing interception.

Dean has been tremendous, and is a big reason why the Steelers currently rank top 10 in EPA against the pass and success rate.

The coach the Steelers miss the most was standing on the other sideline on Sunday. Danny Smith's special teams unit was always a reliable one for the Steelers – the same cannot be said about this current group. Kaden Wetjen had a terrific 59-yard kickoff return negated by a Cole Holcomb penalty, which took the Steelers from starting at Tampa Bay's 41 to starting at their own 20. There was another special team penalty on a punt, this one on Doneiko Slaughter. The Steelers were set to start at the Bucs' 44 yard-line but instead had to start at their own 46. Throw in yet another Chris Boswell missed field goal, and you have a unit that has done a 180 over the course of just six games.

Nick Herbig was awesome, recording his first two sacks of the season. Need to see more of that going forward.

We talked about it across our other post-game pieces, but what a performance from both DK Metcalf and Germie Bernard. Both stepped up in massive ways, combining for 22 receptions.

If the Steelers are going to be aggressive before the trade deadline, safety and linebacker are far bigger needs than receiver. Dare I say call the Chargers about Derwin James.

Congrats to Yahya Black for his first career sack and Daylen Everette for his first career interception. Big plays from young building blocks.

Let us know what you think in the comments. Be sure to bookmark Behind the Steel Curtain for all the latest news, breakdowns, and more!

#163. Steelers pull out 26-19 win over Bucs in overtime

Nothing was going right for the Steelers on Sunday. They trailed the Buccaneers 16-3 in the fourth quarter.

The Steelers dominated the fourth quarter, gaining 230 yards and forcing two Jalon Daniels interceptions. Their fourth-quarter scoring drives were 68, 24, 37 and 2 yards.

Chris Boswell’s 58-yard field goal tied the game 16-16 with 1:55 left. Two plays later, former Bucs cornerback Jamel Dean intercepted Daniels. Dean went 40 yards with the return of the errant pass before Daniels pushed him out of bounds at the Tampa Bay 3.

The Steelers couldn’t get it into the end zone, but Boswell’s 20-yard kick with 1:21 left gave the Steelers their first lead.

They left too much time for the Bucs, though, as Tampa Bay needed only a field goal to send the game to overtime.

With eight seconds left, Chase McLaughlin kicked a 53-yard field goal to tie it 19-19. It was McLaughlin’s fourth field goal of the day, with the others from 43, 47 and 52 yards.

The Steelers got the overtime kickoff, and Aaron Rodgers got his seventh overtime win with a 12-play, 70-yard drive that burned 6:45 of the 10-minute period. He threw a 6-yard touchdown pass to Germie Bernard for the game-winner.

The Bucs drove across midfield, but on fourth-and-8 with 1:06 remaining, Jalen Ramsey sacked Daniels to end it. Ramsey had two sacks as did Nate Herbig.

The Bucs sacked Rodgers five times and frustrated him for most of the game. But he finished 33-of-49 for 253 yards with two touchdowns and an interception. DK Metcalf caught 11 passes for 93 yards, and Bernard had 11 catches for 87 yards and a touchdown.

The Steelers outgained the Bucs 300 to 224.

Daniels was 22-of-43 for 164 yards with a touchdown and two interceptions.

#164. New-look Lakers set to prove they are NBA title contenders

He is unwavering in his belief that the newly constructed Lakers can compete for an NBA championship this season and that is the conviction coach JJ Redick has instilled into his group.

It is why the Lakers play the game, Redick mused, and it is the standard this organization has set.

The Lakers have won 17 NBA championships — the second most in the league — with the last coming in 2020.

So, as the Lakers prepared to open the regular season Wednesday night against the Golden State Warriors at Crypto.com Arena, Redick explained why he believes these Lakers are championship contenders.

"Well, I think that every season," he said. "Unless somebody blatantly tells me that we're not trying to win, I think that every year. That's why I say I'm confident. I said the same thing last year and for all of January and February that we were going to figure it out at some point and we did. And then we had some injuries. So, being a championship-level team or being a — I don't like the word 'contender' — but being a team that can make a run and can play in the playoffs and can play different ways in the playoffs, those things take time and it doesn't mean you're going to be in the NBA Finals.

"It's just not the way this works, particularly with the way the playoffs work in terms of just matchups and what you can exploit and what you can't exploit versus certain teams. But I think because of our talent, because of our fit, because of our depth, I really like our team."

Read more: What we learned from the Lakers' preseason games and training camp

Luka Doncic said his first glimpse of what the Lakers could become was when he invited his teammates to his home country of Slovenia for a bonding experience.

As the unquestioned leader of the Lakers now that LeBron James has departed to Philadelphia, Doncic organized the trip. It was basketball, golfing and rowing. It was dinners and get-to-know-you conversations.

It was over these four or five days in August that Doncic also saw a Lakers team with championship potential.

"Since the first day. That simple," Doncic said. "Since the first day everybody came together in Slovenia, I believed that we can win a championship."

Yet this is a team with nine new players and Redick is trying to incorporate them on a Lakers team that is playing in the uber-tough Western Conference that most experts believe the San Antonio Spurs and Oklahoma City Thunder are the creme de la creme of the NBA.

The Lakers acquired Walker Kessler, a 7-foot-2 center they received from Utah in a sign-and-trade deal in which he was paid $130 million over four years and in which L.A. sent two unprotected first-round picks and two first-round swaps to the Jazz.

Lakers center Walker Kessler tries to block a shot by Warriors center Yaxel Lendeborg during a preseason game last week. (Ethan Miller / Getty Images)

The Lakers added depth in Quentin Grimes, Collin Sexton, Matisse Thybulle, Ziaire Williams, Sandro Mamukelashvili and Kevon Looney.

They join Doncic, Austin Reaves, Jake LaRavia, Adou Thiero and others to form the 2026-27 Lakers.

"I think in terms of integrating all the new guys that have been available, which I think is everybody except for Collin in live play, it's been pretty seamless," Redick said. "It's a smart group. … We've been able to probably install more, particularly on the defensive end, than we have in the last couple years.

"Last year we had six total practices in the preseason because of the amount of games and the back-to-backs and the travel and all that. And we played opening night, so that's another day that we didn't get to practice. So I think we end up with 12 [practices] this year. We get double the amount of practice time, so I think that's a blessing when you have new guys."

Doncic, Reaves and Kessler are the sure things, but the other two spots are not certain. Those three started alongside Williams and Thybulle in the final preseason game against the Denver Nuggets on Friday night. Grimes started the first four preseason games.

Lakers guard Luka Doncic, left, bring the ball upcourt under pressure from Nuggets guard Christian Braun their final preseason game on Friday. (Ben Liebenberg / Associated Press)

"I think we have a lot of guys that could start," Reaves said. "Unfortunately there's five guys that are gonna start. Like JJ said a while back, he's pretty sure of three of them. The other two, regardless of who we roll out there, we have high confidence in."

Reaves is the longest-tenured Laker entering his sixth season and he knows the high expectations that come with playing for the iconic franchise.

Last season, he had James to lean on, Marcus Smart was steady and Rui Hachimura was part of the fabric.

But they are all gone and now Reaves, who signed a four-year, $180-million contract extension, is one of the leaders.

"Yeah, I don't know anything else," Reaves said. "This is what I came to, but obviously it's the Lakers, and it's one of the most covered sports organizations in the world. So they're gonna praise you when you're doing good and not when you're not.

"So you just gotta [know] whatever that goes on outside these walls doesn't really matter. It's just what goes on inside these walls. And if anybody has any questions, I'll give them the best knowledge I have. But like I said, they're high character guys that care about the right things. So, I think that'll take care of itself."

Lakers guard Austin Reaves gets past the Warriors defense for a left-handed layup during a preseason game last week. (David Becker / Associated Press)

The Lakers were 53-29 last season, finishing fourth in the West and getting knocked out in the second round by the Thunder.

They have two more days of practice before the journey begins.

"I think you're always trying to get better," Redick said. "And even later in the season, you tweak plays, you tweak the offense and you tweak coverages. It's just constantly evolving. There's no like, 'Oh, we're done. Now we're going to go play.'

Sign up for our weekly newsletter on all things Lakers.

#165. Why Cowboys' star-studded offense has suddenly gone silent under Brian Schottenheimer

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Everyone and their grandmother knew the Dallas Cowboys defense was going to be a weakness once again in 2026, with Jerry Jones still struggling to replace the presence of Micah Parsons.

The Cowboys' offense becoming a significant part of the problem is nothing short of stunning, and that's on Brian Schottenheimer. After losing 24-16 against the previously 0-4 Tampa Bay Buccaneers in Week 5 and a 23-13 non-competitive defeat against the Green Bay Packers in Week 6, it's no longer a fluke. Dallas' "Greatest Offense There Is" (GOTI) has gone dark.

Dallas is out to a 2-4 start to 2026, tied for the Cowboys' worst start to a season this decade.

In Schottenheimer's first year as the head coach and play-caller in 2025, Dallas' offense soared, ranking seventh in the league in scoring (27.7 points per game) and second in the NFL in yards (391.9 yards per game). While harsh, lifeless is a fair descriptor for this season's back-to-back faceplants. The Cowboys have scored fewer than 20 points in consecutive Dak Prescott games for the first time since the Jason Garrett era.

"I mean, defense to me played a good enough game for us to go out there and win this, and we just didn't hold our own on offense," Prescott said last night, via The Dallas Morning News.

* Cowboys: Consecutive Dak Prescott starts with under 20 points scored for the first time since 2019 (Jason Garrett's last season as head coach)

So how can a team with a top-10 quarterback, two top-10 receivers (CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens),three star offensive linemen and a running back coming off ranking top 10 in the NFL in rushing yards in 2025 (Javonte Williams) look this lost?

Schottenheimer's offense has become stale seemingly overnight. Last season, Dallas ranked in the top half of the league in play action rate (28.2%), under-center rate (38.4%) and motion rate (56.6%). This season, the Cowboys now profile as dead last in the NFL in motion rate (36.5%), 28th out of 32 teams in under-center rate (30.4%) and 20th in play action rate. This was always going to be a pass-forward offense with Prescott and All-Pro caliber weapons at receiver like Lamb and Pickens, but between Smith missing the first four weeks of the season with a thumb injury and general inefficacy (76.0 rushing yards per game, second to last in the NFL) in 2026, Dallas is running the football at the lowest rate in the league at a 32.5% clip.

Tempo (average time between snaps in seconds)

A static offense that doesn't require opposing defenses to think too much is an easy one to defend against. Prescott (335 yards and a touchdown on 32 of 45 passing) and Lamb (17 catches for 189 yards receiving and a touchdown) went off in Dallas' 34-30 road win at the Houston Texans in Week 4. Houston is notorious for being one of the more vanilla defenses schematically and relying on their high-end talent up front at all three levels to win the day for them. Houston blitzes just 24.7% of the time in 2026, the sixth-lowest rate in the NFL, because they believe Will Anderson Jr. and Danielle Hunter are enough more often than not. Skill vs. skill, Prescott, Lamb and Pickens can go toe-to-toe with nearly every defense in the league. They won that battle with the Texans' defense.

Over the last two weeks, against the Buccaneers (43.9% blitz rate, the third-highest in the NFL) and the Packers (33.9%, tied for the 10th-highest in the NFL), two defensive play-callers who get creative with their pressure packages on a weekly basis, Dallas hasn't presented many answers. Much of the reason for that is Schottenheimer not having the aforementioned easy buttons -- play action, lining up under center to make defenses wonder if it's run or pass, motion rate and running the ball -- makes Prescott's life against the blitz and more schematically-sophisticated defenses much more difficult.

Forcing Prescott to come up with all the answers himself in real time while processing everything happening on the field is hanging him and his teammates out to dry. The result is him completing just over half his passes (15 for 29) when targeting Lamb and Pickens at Lambeau Field against the Packers in Week 6 for 143 yards and two interceptions. After lighting up the Texans for 17 connections for 189 yards and the game-winning touchdown pass from 12 yards out with 40 seconds left in Week 4, Prescott has completed just 11 of his 23 throws to Lamb for 79 yards and two interceptions across the last two weeks. The inability of the Cowboys' offense to regularly get Lamb and Pickens the ball had Dez Bryant befuddled on his couch Sunday night.

"We have some of the best WRs in the National Football League. The Packers aren't doing anything exotic, so I don't know why we're not attacking the outside more aggressively," Dez Bryant wrote Sunday night. "Hitch routes, hooks, go's and slants are all there."

Until Schottenheimer reincorporates some of the sophistication from 2025 into his 2026 offense, Prescott and the rest of Dallas' highly talented offensive pieces will continue to be stuck grinding their gears. The on-field talent present can be a well-oiled machine, but it's going to take the right formula from Schottenheimer to get the Cowboys' offense humming once again.

#166. Liverpool must learn lesson from Michael Olise mistake

Liverpool generally have a pretty good record in the transfer market.

Over the past decade the Reds have recorded a lot more 'hits' than they have 'misses' when it comes to signing players.

Some of the best value Premier League transfers ever have come in this period, see Andy Robertson and Mo Salah, but the club has still made its mistakes.

Some of those errors have been overpaying for certain players, but others have been not bringing targets in at the right time and then missing out.

One such target is Michael Olise, who joined Bayern Munich from Crystal Palace for just £50 million in 2024.

Two years on from Olise's move to Bavaria the Frenchman is being linked with a staggering £150 million move back to the Premier League or Real Madrid.

Any clubs interested in Olise now will look back and kick themselves knowing that they could've saved themselves £100 million had they acted 24 months earlier.

There is absolutely a lesson to be learned from this for Liverpool, who should now be looking at the talent available across the Premier League and trying to recruit before they move on.

Somone like Kevin Schade is the perfect example. The German has been quality for Brentford since his arrival in the Premier League and looks ready to make the next step.

Liverpool could let him move on to another top team abroad, but they will then likely have to pay a hefty premium if they do ever want to bring him to Merseyside.

Schade isn't the only player that falls into that bracket, there are examples of players at almost every single team in the division who look ready to step up to a top team, and Julian Ward must not make the same mistake again.

#168. 2026-27 NBA GM survey takeaways: Spurs favored to win title with Wemby as MVP, league execs unsure about 76ers

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The NBA released its annual GM survey on Thursday, which polls all 30 general managers across the league to get their takes ahead of the upcoming season. The 25th annual GM survey was heavily represented by the Spurs and superstar big man Victor Wembanyama, as the franchise received the most votes (50%) to win the 2027 NBA title.

San Antonio was voted as the favorite to win the title over the Thunder (43% of the votes), with the Knicks and 76ers also receiving votes. Last season, Oklahoma City was the heavy favorite among NBA general managers (80% of the vote) to win the title.

Wembanyama was also voted as the overwhelming favorite (77% of the votes) to capture his first MVP. Nikola Jokić, Anthony Edwards, Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, and Jayson Tatum also received votes to capture the most coveted individual award in the sport.

Also represented in the survey was Spurs second-year guard Dylan Harper, who is considered the heavy favorite to have a breakout season, ahead of the likes of Cooper Flagg, Collin Murray-Boyles, Amen Thompson, and Cason Wallace. Harper primarily came off the bench during his rookie season but was one of the stars of the playoffs. The Spurs have already experimented with throwing Harper in the starting lineup during the preseason alongside fellow guards De'Aaron Fox and Stephon Castle.

Let's dive into some takeaways of what NBA general managers got right (and wrong).

It should come as no surprise that general managers picked Wembanyama as the MVP. The Spurs superstar is coming off a season in which he averaged 25 points, 11.5 rebounds, 3.1 blocks and 3.1 assists. Wembanyama was voted as the NBA Defensive Player of the Year last season and became the first player in NBA history to win the award unanimously. The next step for Wembanyama is capturing his first MVP award and the cards are set up for him to do so this season.

Wembanyama was a very popular name throughout the ballot. Here are the categories in which Wembanyama finished first or at least received votes from general managers.

The hype around the freshmen class in college basketball turned into one of the biggest storylines of the NBA season because of how many teams tanked to secure a top pick in the draft. In the GM survey, Grizzlies forward Cameron Boozer (50% of the vote) was picked to win Rookie of the Year honors.

Again, for anybody who followed college basketball last season or watched Boozer play in summer league or preseason, that should come as no surprise. Boozer is the most NBA-ready player of his star-studded class because of his elite basketball IQ, passing and rebounding. Boozer was ranked No. 1 in our preseason rookie impact rankings, ahead of AJ Dybantsa and Darryn Peterson -- the top two picks in the 2026 NBA Draft to the Wizards and Jazz, respectively.

In the survey, Dybantsa and Peterson weren't even picked behind Boozer to win the award. That honor went to Caleb Wilson, the No. 4 pick in the draft, who should make an immediate impact as a rookie with the Bulls. Wilson (20%), Dybantsa (17%) and Peterson (13%) all received votes.

Last year, it was Flagg (97%) who was the heavy favorite to win Rookie of the Year. While Flagg ultimately won the award, his former Duke teammate, Kon Knueppel, made it an intense and close race down the stretch. Expect more of the same this season. Another name to keep an eye on who should be getting more Rookie of the Year attention: Darius Acuff Jr. The former Arkansas star will be handed the keys to the offense immediately and will put up big numbers during his first NBA season with the Kings.

After signing LeBron James in free agency and making a big trade for Jaylen Brown, the 76ers were voted by NBA GMs (73% of the votes) as the team that made the best overall moves this offseason. The other notable teams that received votes were the Heat (10%) and Hornets (7%).

The 76ers also made several other moves during the offseason, including signing Kentavious Caldwell-Pope, Anfernee Simons and Dean Wade in free agency and drafting Labaron Philon Jr. with the No. 22 pick. Philon, who had a breakout season at Alabama, was projected to go in the lottery but fell all the way to the 20s.

While Philadelphia was one of two teams from the Eastern Conference -- with the defending champion Knicks being the other -- to receive votes to win the title, NBA general managers are skeptical about what the new-look 76ers will look like. Philadelphia was voted as the team whose level of success this season is the toughest to predict. The 76ers (27% of the votes) ranked ahead of the Timberwolves, Lakers, Jazz, Warriors, Pacers and Trail Blazers.

Unsurprisingly, the 76ers have the second-shortest odds to come out of the East, behind the Knicks.
