#170. Fantasy Football Week 6 Booms & Busts: Caleb Williams makes triumphant return, breathes life into Colston Loveland, Luther Burden III

The main window of Week 6 was not the prettiest selection of football. We dealt with injuries and underperformance, not to mention four pesky bye weeks. But at least we have Caleb Williams back in our fantasy lives. And that means the Chicago offense is back in business.

Williams was much better in real life than fantasy for Sunday's 31-23 win over Atlanta. He completed 30-of-36 passes for 305 yards, getting 8.5 YPA. He didn't run much (three yards) and he was limited to one touchdown pass, which means Williams came in under projection in any league. But he passed the eye test, and he got his playmakers back into the swing.

We can finally take Colston Loveland off the milk carton. Loveland returned a 6-65-1 line on seven targets, and the lone incompletion was on a wide-open opportunity at the left pylon. Loveland won on schemed plays and his touchdown came on a broken play, made possible by a Williams scramble and a confident throw into coverage. Welcome to the season, No. 84.

Luther Burden III also had a perfect day, catching all of his targets en route to an 8-95-0 log. Rome Odunze was limited to four targets, so his 3-39-0 was less than expected. But it was reassuring to see Ben Johnson clicking with the play sheet, dialing up play action and designed QB movement at the right times. So many of the Williams completions came to wide-open receivers; Johnson wins as much as anything.

The running backs scored the other touchdowns and thus returned their fantasy freight: D'Andre Swift (70 total yards) punched in two rushing scores and Roschon Johnson came through as a Hail Mary (15 touches, 85 total yards, TD). Bottom line, this offense can support a bunch of winning fantasy plays almost every week, so long as Williams stays healthy and Johnson keeps his mojo.

The Chicago defense can be a boost as well. Although the Falcons only managed 257 total yards and were never really in Sunday's game, they did collect 16 fourth-quarter points and made the final score respectable, pushing the game over the total. Kyle Pitts Sr. (the prequel to Loveland) had two of the scores on a 5-60-2 day. Drake London (4-62-0) was muted on 10 targets, and Bijan Robinson had the rare quiet day (53 total yards). But most of the time, the Falcons are an easy fantasy handicap.

Both teams get challenged next week — Chicago hosts the Patriots while the Falcons welcome the 49ers. Get your popcorn ready for both.

Speaking of the Patriots, they finally had their offensive skill sheet where they wanted it on Sunday. A.J. Brown (ankle) made his first start since Week 1, and TreVeyon Henderson (ankle) completed his miracle week of rehab by playing as well. Alas, both players turned into fantasy traps. Brown managed just 3-27-0 despite 10 targets, dropping multiple passes, a shockingly messy day. And Henderson was held to 40 yards on eight touches, in addition to a lost fumble.

Drake Maye's distribution this year reminds you of early Tom Brady — where the favorite receiver is the guy with the good matchup. DeMario Douglas (7-86-1), Hunter Henry (4-48-1) and Romeo Doubs (1-42-1) caught Maye's three touchdown passes; sadly, Doubs hurt his shoulder on the scoring play. Brown surely will keep target-hog status on this offense, but good luck deciphering patterns in the rest of this passing game moving forward.

As for Rhamondre Stevenson, he also underwhelmed despite a primo spot. He was limited to 36 yards on 14 carries, and Corey Kiner (11-57-0) helped drain the clock.

Forget what you thought about the Texans two months ago. It turns out the defense isn't so hot, and C.J. Stroud is probably better than you think. Stroud chucked for 312 yards and three scores as the Texans held off the Jaguars 34-31 in London — never an easy thing to do — and he thrived with a wide distribution, targeting 10 different teammates. It's interesting that despite the presence of Nico Collins and the trades for Kayshon Boutte and Marvin Harrison Jr., it's Jaylin Noel having a breakout year. He caught all of his targets en route to 4-107-1, his third straight game of fantasy relevance.

Stroud's efficiency was needed, because Woody Marks was underwhelming — 15 carries, 56 yards. The Texans get the Giants next week, then step into a Week 8 bye.

An extra overtime drive helped Jaylen Warren take a sad song and make it better. Sharing work with Rico Dowdle all day, Warren had a couple of second-level plays in OT and eventually made 78 total yards on his 16 touches. Dowdle had 10 touches for 49 yards and managed a better YPC. This rough 60-40 type of split can be assumed moving forward.

Germie Bernard (11-87-1) was the star of the passing game, winning on a bunch of quickly-defined routes and scoring the final touchdown. This was the rare day where Aaron Rodgers focused on his two main wideouts — Bernard and DK Metcalf (11-93-0) saw 27 of his 44 pass attempts. I don't know the Metcalf matrix — he's been inconsistent all year — but the Steelers should move the ball against New Orleans next week, so we'll keep an open mind. Bernard is quickly pushing into the Rookie of the Year mix.

— Whatever you paid for Chuba Hubbard in August, it was worth it. Hubbard handled a lovely 28 rushes at Philly, rolling up 120 yards and a touchdown. The Panthers only used one other carry on a running back. Carolina's line is getting healthier, and Hubbard often gets more than what's blocked. Hubbard faces a strong challenge against Tampa Bay's front next week, then it's a bunch of fruitful draws — Packers, Broncos, Saints. He's looking like a possible league winner.

— Jameis Winston is the type of quarterback who can get benched on any start, and it happened again in Week 6 against the Saints. And miracle of miracles, J.J. McCarthy (243 yards, 11.6 YPA) actually moved the Giants in catch-up mode. Call it garbage time if you will, but we're just happy the ball kept arriving to Malik Nabers (12-165-0, 15 targets) and Isaiah Likely (6-99-1, 11 targets). The Ravens have to be kicking themselves for not finding a way to keep Likely; they tried, but didn't offer enough. It's hard to watch Mark Andrews play every week.

John Harbaugh has an interesting QB choice for next week against Houston. The Giants rest in Week 8.

— The Ravens and Browns had a rock-fight type of game, with a meager 23 points and 472 total yards of offense. Tyler Huntley is obviously a backup quarterback, and Deshaun Watson should be one, too. At least Zay Flowers (66 yards, 11 targets) can look forward to the eventual return of Lamar Jackson. The Browns have assembled a lovely receiver room, but there's no one to deliver the ball.

— I wanted to keep an open mind with Tanner McKee, but 4.8 YPA against an ordinary Carolina defense doesn't feed the cat. At least McKee kept pumping the ball to the returning DeVonta Smith (7-75-1), who got home on 14 targets (say this for McKee, the touchdown pass was gorgeous). Dallas Goedert was also a reasonable play (6-61-0, eight targets), and at least Dameon Pierce (50 yards) applied some touchdown deodorant. Dallas is a great draw next week, but is McKee ready for the moment?

— Maybe the Rams aren't the Super Team they're made out to be. An 18-16 loss at home to Arizona is embarrassing, and there's nothing fluky about it — the Rams were outgunned and outplayed for three hours. A late rally bumped Puka Nacua up to 6-80-0, but Davante Adams was quiet (3-39-0) and Tyler Higbee didn't see a target (the Rams opted for a different tight end, as Colby Parkinson had five short catches and a late touchdown).

The Rams' backfield was closer to a 50-50 split, with Kyren Williams handling 13 touches (67 yards) while Blake Corum had 11 (60 yards), including a touchdown catch. The Rams have to ask themselves some difficult questions before next week's game against the Raiders.

— While the Giants were able to support their two primary pass catchers, the running back room was the ultimate false promise. Najee Harris was announced as the pre-game starter, but he did nothing — four carries, two yards. Cam Skattebo ran just six snaps and didn't touch the ball at all. Tyrone Tracy Jr. vultured a couple of touchdowns (one a nifty catch-and-run), part of eight touches and 45 yards. Devin Singletary also showed up, five touches and 33 yards.

It's a mess. The Giants clearly aren't in love with Skattebo, but no one else here has major upside. Tracy came out with the touchdowns, but he's always been something of a journeyman. I hope your running back desperation doesn't push you to the Meadowlands this month.

— The Green Bay backfield went nowhere, as expected, against Dallas. Pierre Strong and MarShawn Lloyd are not meant to be NFL starters, and the Green Bay offensive line is one of the worst in football.

I'd be careful with Josh Jacobs expectations moving forward. Obviously Jacobs has been a capable pro and just being tied to an offense that can move the ball — through the air, anyway — offers some fantasy value. But Jacobs is entering his eighth year, he might not be in game shape yet, and his YPC dropped to 4.0 last season. If I rostered Jacobs in any trading league, I'd make sure my opponents knew he was available. At least see what's out there.

#171. Giants put J.J. McCarthy in with Saints up 34-10 in fourth quarter

It’s J.J. McCarthy time for the Giants for the rest of the day.

After the Saints turned Jameis Winston’s second interception of the day into a 34-10 lead, the Giants pulled their starting quarterback and replaced him with McCarthy. McCarthy had been in for one snap to run the zone read in the first half, but this time he’s actually playing quarterback.

McCarthy’s first drive didn’t end any better than Winston’s final two, however. He was picked off by cornerback Martin Emerson, who also had one of the two interceptions off of Winston.

The Giants led Sunday’s game 10-0, but the Saints have steamrolled them in the second half. We’ll find out after the game if there’s any chance of a lasting quarterback change for John Harbaugh’s club.

#172. Reacting to your Celtics Hot Takes

We're 24 hours out. A day away from tangible, real, meaningful Boston Celtics basketball gracing the court and our screens for the first time in 170 days. With that, there's only one thing to do.

I invited Feed followers to exorcise all of their excitement and angst by sharing their "Hot Takes" about the upcoming Celtics season. Let's analyze the spiciest of those takes, judge how likely they are to come true, and get ourselves riled up one last time before we embark on that long journey to Banner 19.

"The Celtics finish top five offensively and top three defensively." Celtics_fan_in_va

Starting us off, we need to address the elephant in the room. It can be difficult to come up with a truly spicy take when your subject is Joe Mazzulla's Boston Celtics. Read through 90% of team sites, forums and local media, and a top-five finish on both ends would be suitably hot. UV protection required.

Dig into the data from Joe's previous iterations of the Celtics and the take starts to feel a little frosty. Check out Boston's finishes in offensive and defensive rating from 2022–23 through 2025–26, Joe's full tenure as head coach.

In each of Mazzulla's four seasons at the helm, Boston has finished comfortably inside the top five offensively, while ranking no lower than fourth defensively. In fact, according to NBA.com, Boston became the first team since turnovers were tracked in 1977 to finish in the top five on both ends in four consecutive seasons.

Nothing is a certainty in the modern NBA, particularly with injuries, but with no true emerging giant joining the ranks of Oklahoma City and San Antonio, I think it's completely reasonable to expect Boston to rank in the top three defensively and top five offensively in 2026–27.

Now that's a take! Across four seasons, Boston is 127–37 (.774) at home. During the championship season in 2023–24, the C's went 37–4 at TD Garden, one of the best home records in NBA history and the best of any team in the 2020s.

Eaglemike predicts that Boston not only surpasses that mark, but that a Jayson Tatum-led Celtics team joins perhaps the greatest team in franchise history, the '86 Celtics, atop the mountain of all-time regular-season home records at 40–1.

The argument for it would be the degree to which this Celtics roster is optimised to maul teams night after night. There are options on the bench, depth throughout the roster, the added three-point volume of Paul George and Mitchell Robinson attacking the glass on both ends. If you view Tatum as essentially a swap for Brown from last year, I think it's clear that the team Joe has access to for the majority of this season is far superior to last year's roster.

This group is also far better equipped to survive cold shooting nights, thanks to its ability to rebound and generate turnovers. That speaks to Boston being a juggernaut both home and away, but I struggle to buy a Celtics team with ammunition still left in the chamber, and a number-one option returning from a serious injury, equalling one of the NBA's most sacred records.

BOSTON, MASSACHUSETTS – OCTOBER 14: Neemias Queta #88 of the Boston Celtics reacts after scoring a basket against the Charlotte Hornets during the second half of the preseason game at the TD Garden on October 14, 2026 in Boston, Massachusetts. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Brian Fluharty/Getty Images) | Getty Images

"Queta wins 6th man of the year." PDCeltics

Here's a cleaned-up version that keeps your tone and structure while smoothing the flow and fixing spelling:

This is the season where Neemias Queta seeks to earn tenure at Big Fella University. Questions around Queta's quality and consistency from last offseason feel as though they were voiced a long time ago. According to DataBallr, Boston was 6.3 points per 100 possessions better defensively last year when Queta took the court, and he played his part offensively too, scoring an efficient 10 points a night while doing all the big-man basics that helped facilitate higher-usage offensive players. Neemy was pivotal to Boston on both sides of the floor last year.

Rewarded with a $56 million extension, Queta is here to stay, but preseason outings against Charlotte and Philadelphia have suggested that he will take up a new role on this year's C's. No coach has employed the "Hack-a-Mitch" ploy more frequently than Mazzulla over the past couple of seasons. To avoid endless trips to the charity stripe in the final two minutes of quarters, it seems Robinson will be the nominal starter for the Celtics this year, opening up an opportunity for Queta to compete for a major accolade.

As it stands, the Portuguese big man can't be found on either the short or long lists of Sixth Man of the Year candidates. Payton Pritchard has short odds at +400, so in fairness to PDCeltics, this is a hot take.

The case for Queta competing for the award would be an analytically driven one. I'd have to expect him to post magnificent on/off or EPM numbers, while also coming up with huge plays in pivotal moments, to truly vie for honors. Queta's game doesn't resemble those of the other bench big men who have walked away with the Sixth Man trophy. Naz Reid and Montrezl Harrell were spark plugs of sorts, with a unique proclivity for juicing an offense. Queta didn't drag Boston's offensive rating down when he was on the floor last year, but he didn't accentuate it either.

The last true-blue big man to win the award for doing big-man things was Roy Tarpley in 1987–88. Queta winning would represent a landmark shift in how the award is judged. For that reason, while I think Queta could be one of the very best bench players in the league this year, his chances of winning 6MOY are rightly astronomical.

"The platoon of Queta and Robinson gives the Celtics the best 48-minute center combination outside of Denver and San Antonio." Geno-Time

Geno-Time would make a great analyst. This is a brilliant level of hot take. It's sufficiently spicy but I believe it bares real scrutiny. The Celtics are looking to imitate the success of their former Finals opponents, the 2024 Dallas Mavericks, with their big-man tandem of Robinson and Queta. Neither Robinson nor Queta possesses the skill set to vie for an All-Star berth, but together they provide an insanely high floor at the five for Boston. I'll list a few other tandems and rotations below that I think are worthy of consideration once you take Denver and San Antonio out of the equation:

Naz Reid, Moussa Diabate and Ryan Kalkbrenner

Isaiah Hartenstein, Chet Holmgren and Aday Mara

In my view, all of the above rotations possess more raw talent than Boston's frontcourt. Injury concerns surrounding Steven Adams and Rob Williams, however, raise real questions about their ability to outplay Neemy and Mitch over the course of a season. The likes of Beringer and Aday Mara are also unproven at the NBA level, so there's certainly an argument that Boston will have a true top-tier rotation at center this season.

The key to Robinson and Queta providing more value than the bigs above lies with Boston's stars. Luka Doncic and Kyrie Irving unlocked Daniel Gafford and Dereck Lively II, two non-All-Star bigs, to great effect, helping them outperform their individual talent level and making the Dallas frontcourt imperious throughout the 2024 season.

I don't think Queta and Robinson will be the third-best big-man rotation in the league this year, but if they are, expect either the best season of Jayson Tatum's career or a major leap from the subject of our next take to be the key to their success.

CLEVELAND, OHIO – OCTOBER 08: Jayson Tatum #0 and Payton Pritchard #11 of the Boston Celtics sit on the bench during the first quarter of a preseason game against the Cleveland Cavaliers at Rocket Arena on October 08, 2026 in Cleveland, Ohio. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Jason Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images

"Payton Pritchard is named to the All-Star team as a coach selection or injury replacement." Larksnado

PPayton winning Sixth Man of the Year isn't a hot enough take to qualify for this list, so we have to skip a few steps and get into real Sean Evans, make-your-head-explode territory. Larksnado's claim that Pritch makes his first All-Star team this year is one I've considered and investigated in seasons prior.

Fans and analysts alike have suggested for years that Pritchard, a game-breaking college guard who has improved in each of his six NBA seasons, could possess the requisite skills to make the jump from high-impact player to perimeter star in the same way Jalen Brunson has since taking up residence in NYC.

To figure out Pritchard's chances of making an All-Star team, we can look at a few different things. Firstly, let's consider his competition for places in the East ahead of the upcoming season. Here's a list of Payton's stiffest competition:

If healthy, Brunson, Cunningham, Mitchell and Maxey are close to guarantees for places on the All-Star roster. I haven't included Haliburton in that group because we can't be 100% certain that he returns to his pre-injury level, but his name can at least be pencilled in.

That leaves Harden and Herro, both former All-Stars who will be in contention, followed by Derrick White, Coby White, Bane and Alexander-Walker, all of whom occupy a similar position to Pritchard, on the outside looking in. Typically, there are a maximum of six guards selected per conference, but with injury replacements we could argue that number might rise to seven next season. Crucially, I believe every player listed above is more likely to start for their respective team. Starting leads to usage, usage leads to points, and points lead to All-Star recognition.

The scenario in which Pritchard makes the All-Star team looks something like this: it becomes clear within the opening ten games that Boston needs Pritch as Tatum's legitimate second option when the two share the floor, as well as the primary option for bench units. That leads to a spike in usage into genuine All-Star territory.

Of the last 14 guards to make their first All-Star appearance, only Fred VanVleet (23.7%) and Tyrese Haliburton (23.8%) posted a usage rate below 27.1%. Pritchard's career-high usage came last year, when he posted a rate of 21.6%, so we would need to see Payton empowered to a degree that he hasn't yet come close to before.

Whilst that makes Pritchard's All-Star case seem a little far fetched his lineup data with JB on the court last year is proof that he can play at an All-Star level:

Payton Pritchard's 2025–26 numbers with and without Jaylen Brown on the floor. Source: DataBallr.

If Pritchard keeps up that form in non-Jayson lineups this year and assumes an Austin Reaves like role alongside Tatum there's a chance that Larksnado is looking awfully smart come February this season.

"Paul George will play more games than LeBron James" Jeff Clark (That's right, the Jeff Clark!)

Jeff was too kind commenting this on the Feed. This could be an article unto itself, and I'm sure it's something we're all rooting for heading into the season.

The numbers don't look good. Over the last five years, LeBron has played 73 more regular-season games than George, with PG13 missing half the season or more in each of his last two seasons.

I believe Jeff's take is rooted in the idea of role difficulty and need. George is entering his seventeenth season, and I believe the last time he had this little on-ball responsibility was his sophomore NBA season, fifteen years ago. George has already done some interesting stuff as a point forward for Boston in the preseason, but first and foremost I expect him to be a plus role player this year.

Hit the role-player shots, switch on defence, occasionally create off the bounce. Games played aren't all the same. George shouldn't be required to take on the most physical assignment on any given night this year. He'll have the widest driving lanes to the rim that he's experienced since the bubble, minimising the contact that can lead to awkward landings or contact injuries. George can be nursed through the season with a view to contributing each night and building towards playoff impact.

LeBron James, on the other hand, is still, even at 42 years old, LeBron James. Contact at the rim is inevitable. On-ball responsibility, touches and physicality are all givens when your talents, even in year twenty-four, still command the ball. I believe Jeff has read James' sciatica quotes, empathised, factored in his usage and come to the conclusion that an injury could be on the horizon for James this year, whereas George might simply avoid that same level of wear and tear.

The theory that James will sit more often because of Philadelphia's star power is also worth considering. With stars in their prime around him, LeBron can afford to skip back-to-backs and manage his schedule, just as his co-star Joel Embiid will. We know Boston will seek to strangle the regular season, and we know Philadelphia will seek to survive it.

"Paul George will be NBA Finals MVP" C's the day (Great username)

Paul George calling "Ball Game" in the biggest game of his career would perhaps be the highlight of my NBA watching life and a worth while ending to my favoutite Basketball GIF of all time. Lets pray for this one.

The man has an eight year old son. Streaming with Speed feels like a before kids activity.

Could this be the end of the stream as we know it?

"KP and Horford retire at the end of the season" Celtics_fan_in_va

"Hugo Gonzales marries Steve Jobs' widow and buys the Celtics." Saint Stephen

Lauren Powell Jobs has three kids and hasn't remarried since Jobs' death in 2011. Powell would also have to sell her 20% stake in the Washington Wizards to make this happen but let's be honest… Who wouldn't for Hugo?

#173. 49ers vs. Commanders how to watch: 'Monday Night Football' time, channel, odds and prediction

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

In the Week 6 edition of "Monday Night Football," the San Francisco 49ers play host to the Washington Commanders.

San Francisco is riding high atop the NFC West with a 5-0 record, having defeated the defending Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks in a barnburner last week. The Niners have battled injuries on both sides of the ball all season, yet have remained unbeaten. They can create a three-game lead in the division with a victory on Monday night.

Washington is coming off an absolute debacle last Sunday against the New York Giants, wherein the Commanders had a chance to kick a field goal to win the game at the end of overtime, but bungled the clock management as badly as any team you'll ever see. The Commies are just 1-3-1 entering this game, and they're looking to avoid falling further into the basement in the NFC East.

Will the Niners continue to roll, or will the Commanders pull off the upset? We'll find out soon enough. Before we break down the matchup, here's a look at how you can watch the game.

Jayden Daniels looked no worse for wear last week in his return from another dislocated elbow. He completed 17 of 25 passes for 199 yards, while also rushing nine times for 103 yards and two touchdowns. Had he and the entire offense not totally brain-farted at the end of overtime, it would have been a wildly encouraging performance for Washington's rest-of-season outlook.

While Daniels has been excellent when taking off to run in his three starts, Washington's running backs have been extremely inefficient on the ground. Jacory Croskey-Merritt (who was ruled out for this game after not practicing all week), Rachaad White, Austin Ekeler and the recently-released Kaytron Allen have combined to average just 3.7 yards per carry. The offensive line has created little push up front, with the backs collectively gaining just 0.95 yards before contact per carry, according to Tru Media, and the backs themselves have broken tackles at the second-lowest rate in all of football.

The 49ers, meanwhile, have allowed just 3.7 yards per rush to enemy running backs, with great tackling being the primary method of limiting yardage. Backs have gained 1.47 yards per carry before contact (an above-average mark), but only 2.22 yards after contact thanks to the lowest broken-tackle rate in the league. As a result, San Francisco has allowed only two explosive runs all season, per Tru Media, the fewest in the NFL.

San Francisco has also been mostly strong against the pass, checking in 10th in opponents' EPA per dropback and 5th in opponents' success rate. The 49ers have allowed quarterbacks to complete only 64.4% of their passes at an average of 6.1 yards per attempt, with just five touchdowns and three interceptions in five games.

It's tough to know what to make of Washington's passing game because it hasn't been at full strength for most of the season. Daniels missed two-and-a-half games. Chig Okonwko missed two. Terry McLaurin and Stefon Diggs each missed one and saw their snaps limited in another. The Daniels-McLaurin-Diggs trio has shared the field for only 57 plays so far this season, according to Tru Media. Daniels is just 15 of 30 for 129 yards on those plays, but he has thrown for three scores and scrambled for 62 yards.

Daniels should, in theory, see at least some clean pockets with the 49ers again playing without Nick Bosa, but Washington's offensive line has yielded pressure on over 38% of dropbacks so far this season, so the Niners could have a chance to get into Daniels' lap and force him into tough throws and mistakes. With the generally sticky coverage the San Francisco corners have played so far this season, it could be tough sledding for Washington in the passing game on Monday night.

San Francisco has been the league's fourth-most efficient offense by EPA per play, according to Tru Media, ranking second with the pass and 14th with the run. Brock Purdy is playing at as high a level as any quarterback in football, completing 69% of his passes at an average of 8.4 yards per attempt with a league-high 13 touchdown passes and just two interceptions. Purdy also has a 57.9% passing success rate, which ranks as the best in the league.

Purdy has done that despite hemorrhaging wide receivers throughout the season. Ricky Pearsall was lost for the year in training camp. Christian Kirk (listed as questionable for this week) has yet to make his 49er debut. De'Zhaun Stribling was injured in Week 1. Demarcus Robinson went down in Week 2. Deebo Samuel and Jacob Cowing were knocked out of last week's win over the Seahawks. Mike Evans has been playing through a painful rib injury. (He's also questionable for Monday night.) George Kittle spent the first two weeks ramping up to a full workload after last season's Achilles tear. And yet, here the 49ers are.

Washington, meanwhile, has been one of the league's friendliest pass defenses. Every team the Commanders have faced has thrown for at least 257 net yards. Four of the five teams have gone more than 300 and two of them exceeded 400. The Commanders have allowed opponents to complete 65.2% of passes at an average of 7.1 yards per attempt, with 14 touchdowns and just three interceptions. The 103.9 passer rating against the Commanders to date is the sixth-worst mark in the league. It's very easy to see San Francisco finding success through the air so long as Evans suits up for the game.

Christian McCaffrey is sharing the workload in the run game far more this season than in years past, with 61 carries for 286 yards againt Kaelon Black's 37 carries for 136 yards. McCaffrey's 4.7 yards-per-carry average is far better than what he posted over the last two years (4.0 and 3.9), and his rushing success rate of 45.9% is seventh-best out of 48 qualifying running backs. That figure is the second-best mark of his career, behind only the 2023 season, during which he led the NFL in rushing yards.

The Commanders have actually been stingy against the run this year, allowing only 3.9 yards per carry, with opposing backs limited to 0.69 yards per attempt before contact by the defensive front. Washington having similar success stopping the run here is important because it could make the 49ers one-dimensional, but the Commanders' pass-funnel defense also plays right into San Francisco's hands because of how efficient the 49ers' passing game has been so far this year. Purdy and Co. should eat, even if McCaffrey doesn't.

I picked against the 49ers last week and regretted it almost immediately after seeing how their offense struggled against the stingy Seattle defense. Needless to say, Washington's defense is not of the same quality. I know the 49ers are still hemorrhaging wide receivers, but as long as Brock Purdy, Mike Evans, George Kittle and Christian McCaffrey are healthy and Kyle Shanahan is calling the plays, they are going to move the ball efficiently. And I don't trust the Commanders to do quite enough to keep up with their explosive offense.

#174. Man Utd risk missing out on ideal Carrick replacement as club ponders immediate managerial change

Manchester United have been heavily linked with Antonio Conte, but Juventus could decide to act first after Sunday's humiliating defeat.

The Red Devils may be pondering a managerial change after a woeful start to the season. They currently find themselves in 13th place in the table, having only gathered seven points in as many Premier League rounds.

Most sources believe that Michael Carrick's position remains safe for now, but another one or two poor results could change the narrative.

(Photo by Francesco Pecoraro/Getty Images)

With Carrick's position under scrutiny, a host of profiles have emerged as potential candidates to succeed the 45-year-old.

The most recent odds suggest Eddie Howe is the favourite, followed by Conte, whose name has been gaining steam in recent weeks.

Conte himself fueled the rumours by announcing his desire to take over a falling giant and restore its status.

Many in England have interpreted it as a message to the Man Utd board. Nevertheless, the Italian media argued that these words echoed a desire to rejoin Juventus, who haven't won a league title in six years.

The Turin-based giants are enduring another poor campaign. On Sunday, they plunged to eighth place in the table after suffering a 0-3 defeat at home to Lazio. Therefore, the pressure is piling on Luciano Spalletti, who is beginning to lose the plot.

According to Juventus insider Romeo Agresti, the Bianconeri are genuinely considering a managerial change, with Conte emerging as the solitary candidate.

(Photo by Gabriele Maltinti/Getty Images)

The last time Man Utd sacked their manager was on the back of a 1-1 draw at Leeds, replacing Ruben Amorim with Carrick. As for Juventus, they brought in Spalletti after pulling the trigger on Igor Tudor's reign in the aftermath of a defeat to Lazio.

Ironically, the two results were replicated on Sunday, but neither club has decided to act, giving additional credit to their incumbent manager.

However, if Conte is ready to return to management, the club that shows more urgency could reap the benefits, while whoever shows more patience would be left to rue their luck.

The 57-year-old is one of the most decorated managers of the past 15 years, with five Serie A titles with three different clubs and a Premier League title with Chelsea.

The Italian tactician also has a track record of taking the most out of his players and implementing a winning mentality.

Therefore, many would argue he's the best available solution for United, who might have to act swiftly and decisively.

#176. Explaining the NBA's mutual option trend: Could it be used to fight back against the dreaded second apron?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

In late June, the Oklahoma City Thunder re-signed Isaiah Hartenstein to a three-year, $75 million contract. On the surface, it was a pretty standard deal for a high-end starting center -- until you looked at the fine print. Included was a mutual option for the 2028-29 season, the final year of the deal. ESPN's Bobby Marks told Jake Fischer that it was the first mutual option he could remember in a contract since the Toronto Raptors gave Jerome Williams one in 2001. In fact, according to Fischer, several teams didn't even know such options were possible.

And yet, as he so often has, Thunder general manager Sam Presti has once again become a roster-building trailblazer. We've seen five mutual options come since Hartenstein's, and they land all across the contractual spectrum:

In the span of a single offseason, we have gone from 25 years without mutual options to mutual options becoming a burgeoning industry standard. So how did that happen? How do these options work? And could they become an antidote to the daunting luxury tax aprons that have so dominated roster-building discourse over the past several years? Let's dig into the NBA's newest contractual trend.

A typical option gives one party the power to decide whether to continue the contract into its final year. A player option allows the player to decide whether to stay with the team at his predetermined salary or become a free agent, while a team option gives that power to the team. Pretty straightforward.

In the case of a mutual option, either party can unilaterally decide whether to continue the contract. If the player feels he cannot get a better deal in free agency, he can elect to stay and the team cannot object. But if the team feels the player is a bargain on his option number, it can elect to keep him at that figure regardless of how the player feels. The player only becomes a free agent if both sides elect to make him one.

There are two pretty clear use cases for mutual options. The first is when a team and a player are simply sick of each other and want a separation that a trade, for whatever reason, cannot offer. Expect such uses of mutual options to be rarer. More often, they will be a tool for collaboration rather than separation. When both sides want to continue their relationship, these options allow them to renegotiate on terms that make sense for both sides, with the security of knowing that if a mutually beneficial arrangement cannot be found, either side can simply elect to keep their existing deal intact.

Most lower-level contracts today include team options simply because teams have the leverage to negotiate more favorable terms with less accomplished players. Teams with enough financial flexibility can also essentially buy team options from players they're negotiating with by offering more money up front. On the other end of the spectrum, many superstar contracts (or... well... Lakers contracts) include player options for the opposite reason. Stars have the leverage to demand player options because they know their teams won't risk upsetting them by denying them. Occasionally, there's also a give-and-take in which a player can buy a player option by leaving a bit of money on the table.

But you could theoretically argue that every middle-class contract would be better served ending in a mutual option rather than a standard, guaranteed season. Why wouldn't both sides want the flexibility to renegotiate while knowing they wouldn't have to do so? The only downside, which is far outweighed by the benefits, would be the risk of damaging your relationship with a player by refusing to renegotiate if and when he wants to. A standard guaranteed season offers plausible deniability to teams in those situations. We'd love to pay you more now, but our hands are tied by the CBA, so we'll have to wait until next year.

Again, the benefits outweigh that specific risk. There's a reason these options are becoming so popular. In fact, they might be the most powerful weapon front offices have yet created to combat the aprons.

NBA contracts are extremely rigid. They're unlike NFL contracts, in which players and teams can renegotiate at nearly any time. If a player has a guaranteed option-free year on his contract, there is nothing he can do to change his salary unless his team has the cap space to renegotiate and extend him. When he wants to extend, there are specific terms in the CBA dictating how much he is allowed to make in that extension. Free agency, if only in name, is the only real path to genuine flexibility for players and teams.

The aprons are similarly rigid. The number is set at the beginning of the league year. If you trigger a hard cap, you are not allowed to exceed it for any reason. Even without a hard cap, finishing the season one dollar above the second apron still freezes a first-round pick just as finishing tens of millions of dollars above the line would. These numbers are fixed. Mutual options make it so a player's cap figure underneath those fixed aprons don't need to be.

Take the Hartenstein example. The Thunder entered this offseason roughly $40 million above the second apron. Hartenstein had a team option, and he used it to lower his 2026-27 salary by around $5.4 million. The Thunder currently are around $6.9 million below the second apron. Essentially, Hartenstein gave the Thunder extra wiggle room, but in exchange, he got two more years of long-term security.

Let's apply this framework to his mutual option two summers from now. By that point, the Thunder will be paying most of their key players market-rate salaries. Cason Wallace and Jared McCain will no longer be on rookie contracts. Either Ajay Mitchell's cheap extension will have ended or he will have signed a new deal through his 2027-28 team option by then. Shai Gilgeous-Alexander's supermax contract will have kicked in, and Chet Holmgren and Jalen Williams will be in the middle of their own 25% max contracts.

Hard decisions are coming for Oklahoma City at that point. Inevitably, players will be moved and the Thunder will almost certainly be above the second apron by then. Yet they still might want to keep Hartenstein, and Hartenstein seems as though he'd prefer to keep playing for the Thunder. Having the mutual option allows both sides to get what they need. The Thunder could lower Hartenstein's immediate cap hit early in order to ease their luxury tax and apron burdens. Hartenstein could give himself more years of long-term security. And if the two sides are far apart on negotiations? Either one could simply decide, "let's stick with what we have and try again in a year."

You can apply this framework to virtually any notable salary cap threshold. A team is $5 million above the second apron, but has a mutual option on a player it wants to keep long-term? Great. Take the $5 million pay cut, get below the second apron and tack a few years onto the back end of the contract. A team needs cap space to sign a marquee free agent? Same idea.

We could even apply this principle in reverse. Say a team knows it has immediate flexibility, but is worried about its future. It could use a mutual option to give a player a raise... but then have his salary decline in future years or carry a team option when one is needed. If a team hopes to keep a budding star or key supporting piece ahead of an impending free agency, a mutual option offers access to contract structures that extensions may not.

Take the Deni Avdija situation in Portland. His cap figure is so low that he's virtually impossible to extend without generating the cap space needed to renegotiate. If he had a mutual option, Portland could simply agree to new terms with him (that would likely be below his fair-market value, but far above what he would otherwise make), and then use the option to make a free agent. With full Bird Rights, they'd effectively be side-stepping the league's strict rules on how much a player is allowed to make in an extension.

Mutual options represent largely risk-free flexibility in both a league that has always minimized flexibility and an era in which maximizing it is paramount. That's why these options are getting more popular. The potential rewards simply outweigh the plausible risks.

As a matter of course, players should always seek player options when they have the flexibility to do so, while teams should do the same under the same circumstances. Every contract negotiation is unique. These options will inevitably be a compromise.

That means that teams should only really use them when they need to compromise. Ironically, the team most questionable in using mutual options this offseason is the only one to give out more than one. The Nets were the first team to follow Oklahoma City's lead by offering mutual options to both Moe Wagner and Keon Ellis. The difference is in their respective cap situations. The Thunder have the NBA's best roster and a cap sheet that reflects it. The Nets entered the offseason with max cap space.

While we can't say anything definitively, the implication of having that space is that they could have simply used it to buy team options. They're paying both Ellis and Wagner $9 million this season. They had the flexibility to go up to, say, $11-12 million in exchange for more favorable second-year terms, but elected not to do so. Considering their cap flexibility, the Nets simply wouldn't have had trouble re-signing either of those players even if they'd signed them to one-year deals. They took on the risk of getting stuck with bad money without an obvious reward.

This is still such a new tool that Brooklyn might become something of a test case for the field. Maybe in a year, those mutual options make sense for reasons we can't currently predict and other cap space teams use them similarly. Maybe they become a cautionary tale. We're in mostly uncharted waters here, and how this first batch of mutual options works out will go a long way toward informing how the rest of the league wields them moving forward.

#177. C.J. Gardner-Johnson faces a potential suspension for spitting

The ejection of Bills safety C.J. Gardner-Johnson for spitting on an opponent raises an interesting question, as it relates to the additional discipline to be imposed by the league office.

Last year, the NFL adopted a new approach to spitting. It now results in a one-game suspension, sort of.

It started when Eagles defensive tackle Jalen Carter spit on Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott before the first play from scrimmage in the regular-season opener. Because Carter’s ejection covered the entire game, his punishment — a fine in the amount of a game check — simulated a suspension.

Later in the season, Bengals receiver Ja’Marr Chase spit on Steelers defensive back Jalen Ramsey. The officials didn’t see it, so Chase wasn’t ejected. Instead, he was suspended for the next game.

For Gardner-Johnson, the ejection caused him to miss half of the Week 6 game against the Raiders. Will he be suspended for another full game? Will the league fashion an NCAA-style targeting punishment that keeps him out for the first half of the Bills’ next game?

Because Buffalo has a Week 7 bye, the clock isn’t ticking as loudly as it ordinarily would be. Still, the league has a decision to make given the new precedent that was set in 2025, when the punishment for spitting morphed from a fine into a suspension. And Gardner-Johnson presents the first example of a player who missed roughly half of a game after being ejected.

#181. Jalen Hurts blood clot timeline: How Eagles QB went from controversial London start to being out for season

Jalen Hurts blood clot timeline: How Eagles QB went from controversial London start to being out for season originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

The Eagles are under fire for their handling of Jalen Hurts' latest diagnosis — one that is far more severe than typically seen in the sports world.

On Monday, Philadelphia announced that its star quarterback was diagnosed with deep vein thrombosis. Scans discovered that the blood clot issue that affected Hurts in the lead-up to last week's game against the Rams had moved to his lungs.

Hurts is expected to miss the remainder of the season as a result of his diagnosis. Many are wondering how he and the Eagles got to this point. Concerns over Philadelphia's management of Hurts' ailment — including the decision to let him fly after discovering that he had a blood clot in his left calf — are scrawled across social media and message boards at present.

With that, The Sporting News takes a look at the full timeline of Hurts' blood clot issue.

What to know about Jalen Hurts' recovery timeline

Revisiting the blood clot issue that forced Chris Bosh to retire at 31

Philly's ongoing timeline of sports misery

Here's an exhaustive look at the timeline of Hurts' blood clot diagnosis, from its initial screening in his calf to the latest reports that clotting has been found in his lungs.

Hurts requested treatment on his calf after practice, explaining to Eagles staff that he was cleated in the calf during the Eagles prior game against the Rams. He was a full participant in practice in the lead-up to Philadelphia's matchup with the Jaguars in London.

Hurts takes part in Eagles' final practice prior to the team's departure to London. He and his teammates board a flight to the English capital, arriving late Friday night.

Hurts undergoes screening in London for calf issue. Specialists return with an initial diagnosis of left calf superficial vein thrombosis, per Hurts' agent, Nicole Lynn. Per NFL Network's Ian Rapoport, Hurts was in the hospital until 4 a.m. BST Sunday morning. As part of the hospital's screening process, he was advised not to sleep, per Rapoport. Hurts stays awake roughly 36 hours before taking the field against Jacksonville, per The Ringer's Tom Pelissero.

The Eagles' medical staff and independent doctors in London concluded that "activity and mobility were important and that Jalen could safely play", according to a statement released by the organization on Oct. 15.

Hurts throws for 220 yards and one touchdown as Philadelphia falls to the Jaguars, 19-17.

After returning to Philadelphia and participating fully in Wednesday's practice session, Hurts undergoes a second ultrasound. Doctors find that Hurts' blood clot had traveled up his bloodstream. He is advised to sit out the Eagles' Week 6 fixture against the Panthers.

Hours before undergoing his scan, Hurts called his calf injury a "unique experience" while speaking with media.

"I don't want to get into the details of leading up to the [Jacksonville] game and whatnot," Hurts said. "Got nicked up in the Rams game."

Philadelphia announces that Hurts will miss the Eagles' Week 6 clash with the Panthers, citing the results of the follow-up ultrasound as the reason for his absence.

"His health and safety are our highest priority," the organization declares.

The Eagles announce plans to place Hurts on injured reserve, per ESPN's Adam Schefter and NFL Network's Ian Rapoport. The decision comes amid "consultations with numerous doctors and experts" that spanned in Saturday, per Schefter. He is ruled out indefinitely with his malady.

Philadelphia announces that Hurts was diagnosed with deep vein thrombosis and bilateral pulmonary emboli. Per multiple reports, Hurts' blood clots moved to his longs. He'll miss the remainder of the year with the ailment, according to Rapoport.

"He is clinically stable and has no significant functional limitations," the Eagles said in a statement.

The organization laid out Hurts' purported treatment plan, stating that their star quarterback will be placed on blood thinners.

"Jalen's prognosis is very good, and we expect a full recovery," Philadelphia said in a statement. "We anticipate that he will have the opportunity to resume contact football activities when off the blood thinners. ... We anticipate that he will have no long-term effects."

#182. Giants have a QB controversy: J.J. McCarthy makes case to replace Jameis Winston

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The New York Giants have a quarterback question to address. Jameis Winston is 2-1-1 in his four starts under center in place of the injured Jaxson Dart, but the team also traded for J.J. McCarthy last month, who received his first extensive action as a Giant during Sunday's 34-27 loss to the New Orleans Saints.

After Winston threw his second interception of the game and set up the Saints with an opportunity to extend their lead to 24 points, John Harbaugh made the decision to replace him with McCarthy. The former No. 10 overall pick of the Minnesota Vikings came in and led three straight scoring drives, and had the Giants in position to send the game to overtime. McCarthy completed 11 of 21 passes for 243 yards, one touchdown and one interception, and may have stolen the starting job from Winston.

The Giants sit atop the NFC East with a 3-2-1 record. With the Dallas Cowboys' tragic defense and Jalen Hurts sidelined indefinitely with a blood clot, New York has an inside track to a playoff berth. This is not just a lost season because Dart went down in Week 2. So, should Harbaugh start McCarthy in Week 7 when the Giants travel to Houston to take on the Texans? Or, should he stick with Winston? Let's take a look at some pros and cons of promoting McCarthy to starter.

If you watched the Giants game on Sunday, you know how frustrating it was. New York jumped out to a 10-0 lead -- only to allow the Saints to score 34 unanswered points. With the game tied at halftime, the Saints scored 17 points in the third quarter, while the Giants went three-and-out and then turned the ball over. After another three-and-out followed by another interception, Harbaugh knew something had to be done. That's when McCarthy went in.

McCarthy threw an interception on his fourth passing attempt, but then led a six-play, 52-yard drive that was capped by a Tyrone Tracy Jr. touchdown and a successful Isaiah Likely two-point conversion to trim the deficit to 16 points. Following a Saints three-and-out, McCarthy took the Giants offense 73 yards down the field on just three plays, and hit Likely for a 24-yard touchdown to make it a 10-point game.

McCarthy was given the opportunity to lead a game-tying drive with 57 seconds remaining in the fourth quarter with zero timeouts. It came down to a fourth-and-1 from the Saints' 14-yard line, where McCarthy couldn't connect with Likely in the end zone.

McCarthy's 243 passing yards were the most in a game in the last 35 years by a quarterback with zero passing yards through three quarters, per CBS Sports Research. He came in and turned a 34-10 game into a 34-27 game. That's tough to ignore.

This game has already established that there is a quarterback controversy. Why not ride the hot hand?

JJ McCarthy SHINED in his Giants debut:- 243 Passing Yards- 26 Rushing Yards- 1 TD, 1 INTAll in just one quarter. pic.twitter.com/QGjADfd7eI

It's understood why the Vikings moved on from McCarthy. He completed 57.6% of his passes for 1,632 yards, 11 touchdowns and 12 interceptions last season, and was holding back a team that boasted a top-three defense and a talented supporting cast headlined by Justin Jefferson. McCarthy became the only first-round pick at quarterback since 1970 to finish last in completion percentage and TD-INT ratio in their debut season.

McCarthy is a 23-year-old kid who just got to the Giants three weeks ago. I want to know how he's coming along in learning Matt Nagy's offense. Does he have enough of a handle on it to start, run the operation effectively and handle whatever wrinkles Nagy may want to throw in? McCarthy looked pretty good on Sunday, but that situation was entirely different. The Giants were down double digits in the fourth quarter of a game. McCarthy came in with zero pressure and just tried to make plays downfield. Playground football. It's not like you can claim McCarthy came in and "ran the offense." I'm curious how comfortable he is with this brand-new playbook, and how much Nagy would have to change the game plan if Harbaugh made the call to change quarterbacks.

This may be the best argument for starting McCarthy right now. He entered the game in the fourth quarter and ended up leading the Giants in rushing yards. On the first play of what could have been the game-tying drive, McCarthy scrambled up the middle for 28 yards -- getting the ball from the Giants' 29-yard line into enemy territory quickly. Winston can't do that.

McCarthy isn't Lamar Jackson by any means, but he will tuck and run if you give him that opportunity. He's more capable of moving the chains with his legs and keeping defenses honest than Winston.

The Texans may be 2-4, but they are certainly finding their rhythm. Houston has strung together two straight victories after DeMeco Ryans took back play-calling duties on defense, including a 34-31 upset of the Jacksonville Jaguars across the pond. The Texans no longer statistically have one of the league's top defenses, but this is still an aggressive unit capable of pressuring the quarterback.

Danielle Hunter and Will Anderson Jr. make up the best pass-rushing duo in the NFL, and the Giants could potentially be down their top two tackles. Right tackle Jermaine Eluemunor missed this week with a calf injury, while left tackle Andrew Thomas left Sunday's game early to be evaluated for a concussion. A road matchup against a surging Texans team is not exactly a conducive situation for a young quarterback learning a new offense to make his first start.

The Giants have a Week 7 date with the Texans in Houston, and then will enjoy their bye in Week 8. Week 9 against a Jalen Hurts-less Philadelphia Eagles team could be the ideal time to promote McCarthy. You give him the bye and a full week of practice before he takes over your team. That makes sense, and gives Winston one more chance to save his job.

#183. Todd Monken wants to enjoy the win over the Ravens while he can

In Week 1, the Browns were embarrassed by the Jaguars. Former Steelers coach Mike Tomlin, quoting JuJu Smith-Schuster, declared on NBC, “The Browns is the Browns.”

The biggest win of the season came on Sunday, when the new Browns beat the old Browns to create a three-way tie atop the AFC North. Because the Browns have beaten both the Ravens and the Steelers, both of whom are 4-2, Cleveland is in first place.

And first-year head coach Todd Monken intends to relish it. Until tomorrow.

“I’m going to enjoy tonight,” Monken told reporters after the 13-10 win. “And that’s what you have to do in the NFL. These are the nights that you don’t ever want to end, because tomorrow it’s on to the next game. And so, I sit there, I know it sounds really goofy, but you sit there in bed and you don’t want the night to end. It’s 10:30 and you’re tired as hell and you want to be up another 15, 20, 30 minutes to enjoy it, because, shit, tomorrow I’ve got to look at the offensive tape and then you’ve got to move on to the next game.”

The next game could push the Browns to 5-2; they head to Tennessee to play the Titans. And the Browns are road favorites.

The best news is that the Browns are relevant. They’ll likely be jockeying for a playoff berth after Thanksgiving.

In a league littered with teams that claim they want to win the Super Bowl, the truth is that they hope to still be in the mix after the fourth Thursday in November. Because that’s when the NFL season truly starts.

This year, the Browns will likely be one of the teams that is hoping to finish strong enough to earn a spot in the AFC playoff field, and to win as many games as they can once the single-elimination phase commences.

#184. Dallas Mavericks 2026-27 coach preview: Can Dusty May make the jump?

Dusty May might be the most fascinating person in the Mavericks organization this season.

Dallas hired him straight out of Michigan after he won the 2026 national championship, and the hire immediately became one of the offseason's biggest swings. May had already built a reputation as one of college basketball's brightest coaches after taking Florida Atlantic to a Final Four, then turning Michigan from an 8-24 team into a 37-3 national champion in two years. He also became the first college coach to jump directly to an NBA head coaching job since John Beilein left Michigan for Cleveland in 2019.

That history matters because this transition usually goes poorly.

Brad Stevens worked. Billy Donovan worked. A lot of others did not. John Calipari lasted just over two seasons in New Jersey, Rick Pitino struggled in Boston, and Beilein's Cleveland experiment ended after only 54 games. The NBA asks coaches to manage adults, egos, travel, and a schedule with significantly less practice time than college basketball allows. May knows all of that.

He also believes the modern college game has prepared him better than some of those coaches. At his introductory press conference, May pointed to NIL and the transfer portal as experiences that forced college coaches to deal with agents, paid players, roster churn, and many of the same relationship-management issues NBA coaches face.

Now he has to prove that theory in Dallas.

Does Dusty May's system actually translate to this Mavericks roster?

In theory, I love a lot of what he wants to do. May's offenses have been built around pace, spacing, ball movement, and shot quality. He wants rim attempts, free throws, and catch-and-shoot threes. He does not want an offense that settles for bad midrange shots or spends 15 seconds watching one player dribble. His Michigan team had one of the most efficient offenses in college basketball last season, and his overall approach is much closer to the modern NBA than most college coaches run.

That sounds great until you look at the Mavericks. Kyrie Irving is basically the only proven high-level ball-handler on the roster, and he's also one of the best midrange scorers ever. Cooper Flagg can create, but Dallas should not want him initiating every possession. Zaccharie Risacher is still figuring out what he is. The rest of the roster has plenty of wings, forwards, and bigs who attack better than they create.

May's teams also tend to play with a lot of freedom, and that can lead to turnovers. That is what I worry about with this group right now. Dallas does not have a bunch of elite decision-makers who can constantly make live reads without mistakes.

May becomes one of the rare college coaches whose style actually looks even better in the NBA. That is the dream. Dallas plays fast. Flagg becomes a monster in transition. Kyrie still gets freedom to use the midrange when it is there, while the rest of the team becomes much more disciplined about generating threes, layups, and free throws. Risacher finds an actual role. Morez Johnson Jr. develops quickly because he already understands what May wants.

May has also always been a relationship coach. Michigan's culture was built heavily around unselfishness, development, and player buy-in, and that matters as much as any X's and O's. If he can get NBA veterans to buy in the same way his college players did, Dallas could establish an identity much faster than most young teams.

The defensive side is interesting too. May has shown he is willing to adapt to his personnel rather than forcing one system. At Michigan, he leaned into size and versatility and built the nation's top-ranked defense instead of simply copying what worked at FAU. That adaptability is probably why I rate him so highly.

The NBA isn't college basketball, and May will find out quickly that a good system isn't the same as having players who can run it.

The turnovers pile up. Dallas struggles to create offense whenever Kyrie sits. May wants to use versatile centers as passing and decision-making hubs, but Dereck Lively II is already dealing with injuries, and the rest of the center rotation may not be built for that kind of responsibility. The offense becomes too theoretical and not practical enough for the roster he actually has.

May's calm demeanor and collaborative approach should help. However, professional players still respond differently than college players. Beilein's failure in Cleveland is a pretty obvious reminder that even an elite college coach can lose an NBA locker room quickly.

If May cannot adjust quickly, Dallas could spend the season trying to run a system designed for players it doesn't have.

Establish an identity. I do not think this season should be judged entirely by wins and losses. Dallas needs to know what a Dusty May basketball team looks like by April. Does Flagg look more comfortable? Does the offense create easier shots? Do players understand their roles? Can May develop young players while still holding veterans accountable? Can Dallas play with the pace and movement he wants without turning the ball over constantly? That matters more than whether the Mavericks win 39 or 44 games.

I am high on Dusty May. Part of that is probably because he came from Indiana (Go Hoosiers) and I loved what he did at Michigan, but there are real basketball reasons to believe in him too. His style is modern. His offenses make sense mathematically. He has shown he can adapt to different personnel. Players seem to buy into him, and his college teams already looked more like NBA teams than most.

But this is still a massive gamble. The history of college coaches jumping directly to the NBA is ugly, and Dallas' roster isn't built perfectly for what May wants to do. He could be the next Brad Stevens. He could also find out very quickly why almost nobody makes this jump successfully.
