#185. NBA over/under predictions for every Eastern Conference team: Knicks, 76ers overvalued? Raptors ready to rise?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

We're less than a week out from the start of the 2026-27 NBA season, and it stands to be a wild one after a summer of major movement, particularly in the Eastern Conference with LeBron James and Jaylen Brown to the 76ers, Kawhi Leonard to the Raptors, Giannis Antetokounmpo to the Heat, Jayson Tatum back for the Celtics, Tyrese Haliburton back for the Pacers and LaMelo Ball gone from the Hornets.

In 2007-08, all eight playoff teams in the Western Conference won at least 50 games. That is crazy. I don't think it will happen again, but it could in this East. There are that many good teams. Ultimately, I think there will be enough cannibalism to keep most of these really good teams in the 47 to 53-win range. I think the Pistons decline while the Raptors and Pacers rise. But by how much?

That's what we're here for. To predict the over/under win totals for each Eastern Conference team based on lines currently set at FanDuel. This was a tough exercise, but the receipt is printed. There's no going back now.

The Hawks are following the modern blueprint of wings galore, adding Lu Dort and Aaron Wiggins to an already deep stable of Jalen Johnson, Nickeil Alexander-Walker and Dyson Daniels that helped lead them to 46 wins last season and a brief 2-1 lead over the Knicks in the first round of the playoffs.

But the East is better and deeper this year, and the new lottery odds may hit Atlanta particularly hard. Last year, the Hawks went 20-6 after the All-Star break, with 10 of those wins coming against actively tanking teams. The incentive to bottom out isn't there anymore, and with more teams actually playing to win down the stretch, teams like the Hawks will have to earn those late-season victories that fueled them a year ago. Atlanta is a better team than it was a year ago, but the win total won't reflect that.

Boston won 56 games a year ago and stands to be a better team this season, at least through the first 82 (we'll see if Paul George can actually stay healthy for the playoffs and how much Jaylen Brown's individual offense will be missed in postseason play).

Look at it like this: Jayson Tatum, who basically didn't play last season, replacing Brown from last year's team is one upgrade. George replacing Anfernee Simons is two upgrades. Mitchell Robinson replacing Nikola Vucevic is three upgrades. Payton Pritchard has already made his leap, but he is waiting to pop out of the void left by Brown in the No. 2 hole.

Now add in another year for all the youngsters (Boston's wing depth is unending) and the sneakily better fit that George represents over Brown (he's not the better player in a vacuum, obviously) as an elite shooter, especially off the catch, with a lower usage and turnover rate that slides seamlessly into Boston's drive-and-kick game. I worry about the lack of athleticism and rim pressure, but Joe Mazzulla's system is a regular-season cheat code. Continuity. Offensive rebounding. Derrick freaking White. I'm all over this Celtics team, in the regular season at least.

Brooklyn won 20 games last year while having no interest in winning. They went out and got Julius Randle, whose ability to initiate offense will be a major crutch for Brooklyn's bottom-barrel backcourt. Randle and Michael Porter Jr. give the Nets some punch and there's some sneaky depth here. The Egor Demin leap is coming.

It's true, Brooklyn won virtually all its games last season against fellow tankers, and nobody will be trying to bottom out this season. But Jordi Fernandez can really coach and the incentive to lose is gone as the Nets don't own their 2027 pick (Houston has swap rights). If they trade Porter Jr. during the season, everything changes. But as it stands, I actually like Brooklyn to approach 30 wins.

Big picture, the LaMelo Ball trade was a good move. The Hornets are headed in a good direction with Kon Knueppel and Brandon Miller as the franchise faces, and the veterans they added in the form of Naz Reid, Grayson Allen and Royce O'Neale bring stability and plenty of shooting. This is a pretty good team.

And yet, I just can't get past the lack of creation without Ball (Coby White is more of a scorer). Last year, Charlotte's offense plunged by almost 12 points per 100 possessions when Ball sat, per Cleaning the Glass, from the 97th percentile to the 36th. It's true, the numbers also looked great with White in Ball's place, but in small samples.

Again, the zoomed-out direction of this team is sound, but zooming in on this season, with how much better the East has gotten, the adjustment to playing without Ball, and the injuries Miller, Knueppel and White are dealing with to start the season, I think this year is going to be the one step back in Charlotte's two-steps-forward plan.

Josh Giddey has become a guy who almost guarantees a competitive team most nights, but Chicago doesn't have enough to consistently win. Caleb Wilson will do the "flashes greatness but isn't consistent" rookie thing. Matas Buzelis has all the gifts and I think he could be in the race for Most Improved Player with more offensive license, but like Wilson, he will be contributing more to the bucket of impressive performances than leading to consistent winning.

Norman Powell and Nicolas Claxton are winning players, but Powell, with the second year of his deal being a team option, is ripe to be traded at the deadline. There's a lot of size in Chicago with a stable of guys going 6-foot-7 and up, but the shooting, defense and depth are all going to be bottom-third material. Chicago getting to 30 wins in this Eastern Conference, with no more easy ones over tankers, is a stretch.

On paper, there's too much core talent here to feel safe going under 49 wins. The Cavs have averaged just under 54 wins per season over the last four years. They've won 106 regular-season games over the last two. With guaranteed offensive production from multiple sources, two big-time bigs and a bench sniper in Sam Merrill, this team, with all its continuity, is built for the regular season.

But at some point, James Harden isn't going to be a guaranteed 50-win guy. Cleveland lost a lot of its depth (Dean Wade, now in Philadelphia, was a big part of many of their best lineups). Peyton Watson probably isn't going to log the usage he did for his big stretch in Denver last season when key players were out, so that might not be quite the pickup you think unless he gets back to defending at an elite level. To be honest, this is one I would stay away from, but if I had to bet, I would lean toward the under. I just think this team is losing steam.

We all saw Jalen Duren's struggles in the postseason. We know Detroit is lacking a second independent scorer (Tobias Harris was the closest thing they had to this and he's gone). We know spacing is a real issue with Duren and Ausar Thompson on the floor.

The counter is that this team won 60 games last season, which would require a historic plunge to fall below 48 in the following season with largely the same roster. They were also the best team in the league against the best teams (17-7 with a plus-5.6 point differential vs. the top 10 teams, per Cleaning the Glass).

The Harris subtraction is significant. The absence of his individual shot-making, particularly late in possessions, is going to put even more on Cade Cunningham to create every shred of offense for this team. Cunningham is the closest thing to Luka Doncic in terms of one-man shows, but even he has limits. We saw it in the postseason, when turnovers piled up and a historic run of scoring performances was required just to dig out of a 3-1 hole and escape the eighth-seeded Magic in the first round.

If it sounds like I'm making a case for both sides of this line, it's because I am. This is one of the toughest calls, in my opinion. Ultimately, the defense will be there every night. Isaiah Joe will bring some needed shooting alongside Duncan Robinson. John Collins is a sneaky good add with his ability to be a corner 3 spacer and athletic two-man partner with Cunningham, who, for my money, is just too good to oversee a historic falloff.

So I'll go over. Slightly. The Pistons are definitely going to regress, but a 13-game regression is too much.

This one is easy for me. Indiana returns the same team that was one win from an NBA championship in 2025. We've seen enough guys immediately rediscover their stardom following Achilles tears to trust Tyrese Haliburton to pick up where he left off. Everything is designed to flow through him, and Pascal Siakam was an All-NBA caliber guy.

The depth is concerning to some, but I'm a big Andrew Nembhard believer. There are still wings everywhere you look. Rick Carlisle is still the coach. The big change from that Finals team, of course, is Ivica Zubac subbing in for Myles Turner. It will look different without Turner's stretch shooting, but Zubac is superior at every other facet of the game and gives the Pacers true offensive diversity.

Once they figure out the different schematics, Zubac raises the ceiling with his defense, passing and post play. Indiana is a better team than the one that nearly won it all. The time it may take to rediscover their rhythm with Haliburton notwithstanding, this win total is way too low.

Half-court cramping is a concern with Bam Adebayo and Giannis Antetokounmpo on the floor together, but let's not overcomplicate this. The Heat are working with one of the best players in the world in Antetokounmpo, one of the best defenders in the world in Adebayo, and one of the best coaches in the world in Erik Spoelstra.

Miami has the makings of a top-five defense. Antetokounmpo's paint gravity will generate plenty of open 3s, and quietly the Heat have a number of guys -- Andrew Wiggins (41%), Klay Thompson (38%), Bobby Portis (46%), Tim Hardaway Jr. (41%), Davion MItchell (40%), Simone Fontecchio (38%) -- who can feast on these looks in an up-tempo drive-and-kick setting. Pelle Larsson is tailor-made for a breakout season.

I'll admit, I was pretty worried at first about the offensive fit of a Giannis/Bam/Mitchell starting lineup, and it still presents some problems. But the more I think about this Heat team and all the little battles that it is going to consistently win, the more comfortable I feel in taking this over.

There's some sneaky talent on this team, but the core of the best players -- Tyler Herro and Myles Turner, and Kyle Kuzma -- are pretty ripe to be traded if the Bucks can find a taker.

Milwaukee doesn't own its 2027 draft pick, so in one sense, there's no incentive to lose. But it also means the new lottery structure, which penalizes the three worst teams, doesn't apply to them either.

So the Bucks are basically free to play around with their young guys, particularly No. 10 overall pick Brayden Burries, with no fear of it costing them lottery odds. In the end, somebody has to lose games in the East, and I think the new lottery structure is going to impact the bottom dwellers' win totals more than the contenders. Milwaukee falls short.

This line feels low given the sweet taste we all still have in our mouths of Knicks basketball. They looked like a juggernaut as they won their first championship since 1973. How could they not win 52 games with the only real loss being Mitchell Robinson?

For starters, they only won 53 last year, so we're not talking about a regular-season behemoth. This team is built for the playoffs and who knows how motivated they're going to be to play their best in November and December? I won't call it a championship hangover, but maybe more of a slight relaxation.

Mike Brown is likely going to be even more cautious with starter workload than he was last season, when he dialed back the Tom Thibodeau 82-game boot camp. The Karl-Anthony Towns contract stuff is a potential distraction. Josh Hart and Miles McBride are playing for new deals. The East is way better, which should, theoretically, reduce every team's win total from the previous season if they're returning the same roster.

It's not to say the Knicks can't or won't win 55-plus games. The continuity and confidence are at a high. Jalen Brunson will swing close games. The talent and chemistry are obviously elite. But there's just too much parity among too many East teams, and I think the Knicks somewhat slow-play the first three months, knowing their health and energy come playoff time is way more important than their seed.

Full disclosure: I would stay as far away from this bet as humanly possible. Orlando's season could go 10 different ways. But I'm a sucker for the talent, just as I was last season when I believed a top-four or even top-three seed was in the cards. Injuries prevented that from happening, but it wasn't just that.

The Paolo Banchero experiment is frustrating. Can he coexist with Franz Wagner? The needle moves closer to no every season, it seems. But I'm not ready to give up yet. When Banchero is on, anything seems possible for this team. The defensive infrastructure is there. New coach Sean Sweeney is probably a real offensive upgrade from Jamahl Mosley, but the coaching change is another unknown.

Bottom line, the Magic were a mess last season. Banchero shot even worse than normal, Wagner and Jalen Suggs combined to miss 73 games, and they still stumbled into 45 wins. They did a lot of that work against tanking teams, yes, but Desmond Bane was as advertised and we saw how tough they can be in the playoffs when everything is clicking. Assuming they finally get a fair shake health-wise, I can see this team approaching 48-50 wins. I can also see them falling into the 30s. Again, I would stay away. But it's October, and hope springs eternal, so I'm going glass-half-full with the over.

If ever a team was more focused on preserving energy and health for the postseason than emptying the regular-season tank for a bit better seed, it's the 76ers.

The starting lineup is loaded. Dean Wade will tie together many secondary lineups and could even become a closing option. Depth is good, but losing Ariel Hukporti for the season is a blow.

Nobody in their right mind can predict Joel Embiid to play more than 50 games. Hell, he hasn't played more than 39 in any of the past three seasons. LeBron James will turn 42 in December. There's a perfect world where all these high-usage stars identify, and embrace, their most favorable roles -- James orchestrating, Tyrese Maxey playing more off ball, Jaylen Brown scaling back the isos and maxing out his defensive focus and energy, Embiid balancing what will be a frequent and forceful transition attack with his back to the basket and mid-post face-ups -- but that will come (if it does at all) at the end of a season-long experiment with plenty of losses along the way.

The scoring talent, particularly late in games, is so deep here that Philly is going to win its share of games. But these kinds of superteams with redundant skill sets tend to start relatively slowly and spend long stretches as works in progress. In my mind, there's also no way this line wasn't inflated to start with, given the hype around this team. It started above 50 wins and is coming down because people are seeing the light. I still think it should be two ticks lower.

If Kawhi Leonard plays in 60-plus games, the Raptors are going to fly past this number. That's admittedly a big if, but Leonard played 65 games last year and was one of the league's best players.

The fit here is already worked out. Leonard does a lot of the same things as Brandon Ingram, he just does them way better. Scottie Barnes may be a superstar one day, but for right now, he's more suited to the second-star role Leonard allows him to play.

This team is going to defend and run like crazy. RJ Barrett is the third option and he scored 20 points per game last year; he's either a luxury third guy and long defender or a trade chip on an expiring contract. Collin Murray-Boyles is set to explode. Immanuel Quickley averaged 16 and 6 last year on 38% 3-point shooting.

Barnes and Leonard take a lot of the same shots from the same spots, but Leonard's 3-point range spaces this offense out. Barnes is a budding playmaker. I don't love Jakob Poeltl as the starting center or the depth behind him, but everything else about this team looks awesome. I think they cruise past 50 wins.

The Wizards could double their win total from last year and still fall short of this number. If you're excited about this team because of Trae Young and Anthony Davis, you're looking at it wrong.

Young is a one-way ticket to mediocrity even with a good team around him, and this is not a good team relative to its Eastern Conference competition. Davis is more likely to be injured or traded than the centerpiece of a playoff roster.

We'll all be watching AJ Dybantsa with great interest. Tre Johnson. Alex Sarr. Bub Carrington. Kyshawn George. Bilal Coulibaly. This is where the hope for the future lies, but it won't be enough to win 35 games.

#187. Phillies plan to keep Trea Turner at shortstop, hire ex-Mets manager as infield coach

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

When the 2027 MLB season begins, Trea Turner will again be at shortstop for the Philadelphia Phillies. On Thursday, president of baseball operations Dave Dombrowski said Turner will open next season at shortstop, but will need to play well to remain at that position. Dombrowski also said Bryce Harper will move back to first base next year.

"He did not have a good year. He needs to fix things with his swing. He knows he has to be better at shortstop. I told him that is mandatory. I told him he cannot play shortstop like he did in 2026 going into 2027," Dombrowski said about Turner (via NBC Sports Philadelphia). "... He's played (outfield) before. He prefers playing the infield but we'll wait and see if he can improve there, and if not we can discuss moving him out there."

Turner, 33, had the worst season of his career in all phases in 2026. He hit .242/.297/.378 in exactly 700 plate appearances, numbers that are comfortably below league average, and his shortstop defense was poor. That was according to both the eye test and the numbers: 21 errors, minus-17 defensive runs saved, and minus-8 outs above average.

You needn't look back far to see the last time Turner was a comfortably above-average hitter and defender. He finished fifth in the NL MVP voting in 2025 and was great on both sides of the ball. This past season was the first time in Turner's career that performance was an issue. He had been one of the game's most consistently excellent players since arriving for good in 2016.

This is a bad offseason to need a shortstop. The best free agent shortstop is likely Mauricio Dubón, who is more of a super utility guy than an everyday player. There are some appealing trade candidates, namely Zach Neto (Los Angeles Angels) and possibly Jeremy Peña (Houston Astros), though the Phillies may not have the prospects to win a bidding war.

Infielder and top prospect Aidan Miller missed almost the entire 2026 regular season with a back injury and has eight career games of Triple-A experience. He could be a midseason replacement for Turner in 2027, assuming his back cooperates. Bryan Rincon is not as touted a prospect as Miller, but he's a no-doubt shortstop defensively. He could be a midseason option as well.

The best shortstop solution may be second baseman Bryson Stott, who has shortstop defensive chops and shifted to third base as part of Philadelphia's defensive realignment following the Luis Arraez trade. Re-siging Arraez, moving Stott to short, and shifting Turner to the outfield might be the team's best arrangement, defensively. For now, the Phillies will stick with Turner at short.

In addition to the Turner (and Harper) news, Dombrowski also announced Thursday that the Phillies have re-signed reliable lefty reliever Tim Mayza to a one-year contract, and named former New York Mets manager Carlos Mendoza their new third base and infield coach. The Mets fired Mendoza in June.

The Phillies went 88-74 this year and clinched a wild-card berth of the final day of the regular season. They lost the Wild Card Series to the NL East rival Atlanta Braves in three games. Philadelphia named interim manager Don Mattingly their full-time manager earlier this week.

Next season will be Year 5 of Turner's 11-year, $300 million contract. He is signed through 2033.

#188. Flyers Recall Camp Standouts Ahead of Monday Matchup With the Avalanche

The Philadelphia Flyers have made some roster moves ahead of their Monday matchup with the Colorado Avalanche.

On Sunday, the Flyers placed defenseman Cam York on injured reserve with an upper-body injury retroactive to October 8th, while also loaning forward Jack Studnicka and defenseman Helge Grans back to the Lehigh Valley Phantoms.

Grans registered no points in his one NHL game this season. Studnicka has played in 3 games this season for the Flyers as the 4C. He also did not register a point during his time with the Flyers.

That opened up three roster spots for the Flyers. Following the moves on Sunday, the team only filled one of those spots, recalling defenseman Hunter McDonald to the team. McDonald has played in one career NHL game, the season finale last season against the Montreal Canadiens, where he registered an assist.

McDonald is a big, physical blueliner who had a pretty strong training camp. However, it was really down to Simon Benoit, David Jiricek, and Oliver Bonk, and McDonald never really had a chance despite his strong camp.

That still left the Flyers with two roster spots open. They filled those on Monday morning.

With the status of Owen Tippett, Tyson Foerster, and Sean Couturier still in question, the Flyers have recalled forwards Alex Bump and Cole Knuble from the Phantoms.

Bump made the team out of training camp, but was sent down after the very slow start. But Bump has been on a tear in Lehigh Valley, scoring 7 goals in 5 games while also adding an assist.

Filling the final spot is Cole Knuble, son of former Flyer Mike Knuble. Knuble had an excellent camp, practically putting him on roster watch, and was, in all fairness, deserving of a roster spot. However, he started his year in the AHL, where he has scored a goal and 3 assists in 6 games.

Now, Knuble has got his much-deserved call-up to the NHL. If he is in the lineup on Monday, Knuble will be making his Flyers and NHL debut.

The Flyers take on the Avalanche on Monday at 7:00 PM ET at Xfinity Mobile Arena.

#191. Jameis Winston: I'd love to put myself in a better position to execute

Giants quarterback Jameis Winston spent the fourth quarter of Sunday’s game watching J.J. McCarthy try to pull off an improbable comeback and the day ended without any certainty that he’d be back on the field in Week 7.

Head coach John Harbaugh said the immediate aftermath of a 34-27 loss to the Saints was not the time to make an announcement about a starter moving forward. Winston threw a touchdown as the Giants moved to a 10-0 lead in the first quarter, but he was pulled after 34 straight Saints points and a pair of second-half interceptions.

McCarthy led the Giants to 17 points and had a shot to tie the game on the final drive, which made his argument for getting the start next week pretty straightforward. Winston was asked what he’d say to Harbaugh about his case.

“That’s him. You know, that’s the decision that he’ll have to make,” Winston said, via a transcript from the team. “What I would love is to just put myself in a better position to execute. And that just starts with me. Things that I can control, going out there every single play, doing my very best.”

McCarthy has only been with the Giants for a few weeks, but they traded for him so that they had an option other than Winston as they played out the season in the wake of Jaxson Dart’s knee injury. That option looked like a viable one on Sunday and his time as a starter is likely coming even if he isn’t on the field for the first snap in Houston next Sunday.

#192. Clippers rebuild includes developing young core alongside veterans

The Clippers will have their hands full when the season opens trying to contend in the always tough Western Conference after being slapped with the harshest penalties in league history for violating salary cap circumvention rules.

With Kawhi Leonard, James Harden and Ivica Zubac gone from last season's team, they'll focus on developing a new core of stars, including rookie Keaton Wagler, when they open play Wednesday by hosing the Sacramento Kings at Intuit Dome.

Another positive for the team: Tyronn Lue is a proven asset as coach and he'll be tasked with developing and blending in the younger players. Wagler spent the summer building up his body and has potential to be a strong defender.

The league's year-long investigation is over and the Clippers have a clear path, albeit rocky, to move on and again become competitive in the West. They finished ninth in the conference last season and were eliminated by the Warriors in a play-in game.

Now fully recovered from a foot injury, two-time All-Star guard Darius Garland will be counted on to provide floor leadership. Also returning are former All-Star guard Bradley Beal, guard Kris Dunn, forward Derrick Jones Jr. and center Brook Lopez.

"I think we can surprise a lot of people," Garland said.

Garland is fully recovered from toe and foot ligament injuries. In 19 games last season, he averaged 19.9 points with 6.4 assists. With a full offseason and training camp, Garland is expected to be one of the team's top players.

Other young players to watch are guard Kobe Sanders, who had a productive rookie season when averaging 7.3 points and nearly 20 minutes a game as part of the rotation, and center Yanic Konan Niederhauser, who had his rookie season end early because of a foot injury but he showed promise over 41 games.

Forward Brandon Ingram, driving against Clippers forward Derrick Jones Jr. last season, is now a teammate after the Kawhi Leonard trade was completed following the salary cap circumvention investigation. (Ronald Martinez / Getty Images)

Additions include All-Star forward Brandon Ingram and guard Gradey Dick, who were part of the Leonard trade to Toronto, wing Max Strus, guard Jalen Pickett, forward Baba Miller, forward Isaiah Jackson and forward Nick Martinelli.

"I know [there are] little to no expectations for us this year," said Ingram, who will miss the start of the season while recovering from May surgery for a partially torn Achilles. "We have enough in the building to compete. This is what we love to do. So, we'll go out and compete every single night, learn, go on to the next game and get better and better."

Strus also will be out for a while after injuring his right foot during training camp.

Departed from the team are forward John Collins, guard Bogdan Bogdanovic, forward Nicolas Batum and wing Bennedict Mathurin.

Also noteworthy: owner Steve Ballmer won't be sitting courtside after being banned by the NBA for a year as part of the team's steep punishment for circumventing salary-cap rules. Top basketball executive Lawrence Frank has been banned for six months. The penalties included the loss of five first-round draft picks.

"I give our players a lot of credit … the leadership is great [and] the morale is great, even in these tough situations," Lue said at the start of training camp. "That's good to see, when you have your players coming in every day, giving everything they have; a lot of teams don't have that."

#193. Deone Walker wrecked NFL’s highest-paid center in Bills win over Raiders

Deone Walker is probably going to be the antagonist in Tyler Linderbaum's nightmares for a while.

The Raiders made Linderbaum the NFL's highest-paid center this offseason, inking him to a three-year, $81 million deal with $60M guaranteed at signing, and the Bills disruptive nose tackle demolished him for a large portion of Buffalo's 33-30 win over Las Vegas in Week 6.

Now, Walker was only credited with one pressure on 30 pass-rush snaps, but he "won" his one-on-one reps with Linderbaum far more frequently than that, and he wreaked havoc against the Raiders run game, a ground attack that only averaged 3.3 yards per rush.

With this film session, let's start there, and I'll begin with the most emphatic display of Walker's dominance in this game:

What's the appropriate response to that rep? Linderbaum had become an elite-level center during his time in Baltimore, before he signed the monster free-agent deal in Las Vegas. He routinely won with a tremendous combination of balance, agility, and power.

Remember too, Linderbaum was an All-State wrestler in high school who famously pinned Tristan Wirfs back in a 2017 match between the future NFL offensive linemen.

Walker tossed the 6'2", 305-pound Linderbaum aside like he was a practice-squad long-snapper on that rep then wrapped up Mike Washington for a short gain. All-Pro level highlight there.

At Iowa and early in his career with the Ravens, Linderbaum was a menace in the run game because of how rapidly he erupted out of his stance when either climbing the second level or getting to reach blocks across a gap. He regularly carried out those duties with ease. The movement element to his game is why Linderbaum was a first-round pick and a big reason why he signed such a lucrative deal in March.

Linderbaum's speciality was irrelevant here against Walker:

And that is the exact type of block on which the smaller but more explosive Linderbaum should get the better of Walker. The clear win for Buffalo's second-year defensive tackle wasn't a fluke.

He had managed an even cleaner victory later in the game on a similar blocking concept that amounted to a tackle for loss:

I'm telling you — 6'6" and 345 should not be physically capable of shooting a gap like that on Linderbaum.No way, no how. But Walker did.

The majority of his pass-rushing opportunities featured double teams. Yet when Walker was given a chance to rush man-on-man, he either freed himself from the block or caved the pocket in front of Kirk Cousins.

This was the Raiders first offensive play of the game. Walker initially bull rushed Linderbaum, but take note of how he countered off it late it get a hand up near the throwing motion of Cousins:

That's a reasonably high-caliber rep for a defensive tackle who probably wasn't credited with a pressure on the play. He has regularly still impacted the pocket even when he's been technically blocked.

And check this rep from Walker going full Swim Diesel on Linderbaum to force a hurried throw and incompletion from the Raiders veteran quarterback:

Through six games — before Monday Night Football — there are only three defensive tackles with more pressures than Walker's 22. He's been a stalwart against the run too.

At 22 years old, while playing 70.9% of Buffalo's defensive snaps, Walker is playing like one of the best interior defensive linemen in football.

His performance against the league's highest-paid center should remind everyone of that.

#194. NBA Eastern Conference tiers: Knicks on top, but new-look contenders emerge after eventful offseason

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Eastern Conference has long been viewed as the inferior half of the NBA. Seven of the last 15 championships have been won by the East, but the West has been the deeper of the two conferences with more teams capable of hosting a parade in the end. Getting through the West was trumpeted as a monumental accomplishment. Winning the East was something that some team had to do eventually, but few of them got much credit for it by comparison.

That perspective has shifted. The East is stacked. With at least 10 teams having designs on the eight playoff spots, it appears we're headed for one of the most competitive races the conference has produced in quite some time. With the NBA tipping off in less than a week, here are our first Eastern Conference tiers heading into the season.

The Knicks have earned a tier all to themselves after winning their first championship in more than half a century. New York entered the playoffs as the No. 3 seed, then laid waste to the competition. The Hawks somehow took two games off them in the first round. Incredibly, that was the best performance by any of the opposition. The Knicks swept the 76ers and Cavaliers before mounting remarkable comeback after comeback against the Spurs to win the Finals in five games. It was an epic, all-time performance.

New York should be feeling pretty good about its title defense despite the history stacked against it (and the attendant pressure of the organization deciding to press pause on contract negotiations). For starters, there are the starters. The Knicks' first five is intact from last season, and we've already seen what Jalen Brunson, Karl-Anthony Towns, Mikal Bridges, OG Anunoby and Josh Hart can accomplish when they're all healthy and locked in. They're the best starting lineup in the league.

After that, coach Mike Brown will have more work cut out for himself this season. Backup center Mitchell Robinson left New York for Boston. In his place, the Knicks signed Andre Drummond, a capable enough rotation player but not nearly the rim protector or defensive presence that Robinson provided. Landry Shamet and Jose Alvarado stuck around and were rewarded with new contracts. We'll see how much run is earned by Jordan Clarkson, Miles McBride (whose production and playing time fell off in the postseason) and the rest of the bench.

Defending their title won't be easy, but then doing so never is. The Warriors were the last back-to-back champs in 2017 and 2018. Since then, we've had a new winner in each of the last eight seasons. But until someone knocks them off, the Knicks are the title holders. Grabbing the Larry O'Brien Trophy means going through New York.

Whoa boy. Did we mention the East is stacked? Each of these teams can make a case for being the biggest challenger to New York's throne, but all of them come complete with questions and concerns when it comes to claiming the crown for themselves.

We'll take each of these in alphabetical order (rather than the betting odds) to avoid angering one of the fanbases and inviting them to storm the CBS Sports Bastille.

The Cavaliers reached their first conference finals without LeBron James last season. It was also the first time Donovan Mitchell advanced that far in his playoff career. Then they got embarrassed by the Knicks -- and embarrassed themselves in the process with coach Kenny Atkinson saying something inadvisable about the whole thing and James Harden somehow going one step further. In addition to keeping their core four together of Mitchell, Harden, Evan Mobley and Jarrett Allen, the Cavs managed to bring breakout wing Peyton Watson to Cleveland in a sign-and-trade with the Nuggets. That starting five is as good as any in the league. The bench is more troublesome following the losses of Dean Wade, Keon Ellis and Dennis Schroder. Atkinson is looking at a lot of Jaylon Tyson and Sam Merrill minutes. And years after the rest of the league sold all of its Mario Hezonja stock, the Cavs suddenly bought some. We'll see what kind of returns they get on that investment, if any.

The Celtics had what could charitably be called a volatile offseason. After getting upset by the Sixers in the first round of the playoffs, they dangled Jaylen Brown, a former Finals MVP coming off the best season of his career, in a failed trade attempt for Giannis Antetokounmpo. Then they shipped Brown to Philly, of all places, for Paul George and picks. To say the Boston faithful was not initially thrilled about that is an understatement. PG is seven years Brown's senior and has had injury issues at times, but if he's available, he's at minimum a 3-and-D presence who should slot nicely into the starting lineup. The Celtics addressed their starting center concerns by snagging Robinson from the Knicks, but how many minutes and games they can count on from him is one of Boston's biggest variables. Derrick White remains one of the best defenders in the NBA, but he's coming off the most inefficient shooting season of his career. How Joe Mazzulla, ever the galaxy brain tinkerer, might meddle with the nightly rotation is anyone's guess. The Celtics are still one of the deepest and best-run teams in the NBA, but there are more variables in Boston this season than there have been in years.

Detroit spent much of last season atop the Eastern Conference standings -- only to barely squeak past the Magic in seven games in the first round and then lose to the Cavs in seven in the second. Cade Cunningham made All-NBA for the second straight season, but the rest of the Pistons were far from consistent when coming to his aid. Jalen Duren made his first All-NBA team, flamed out in the playoffs and then proceeded to get into a nasty and protracted contract negotiation with the front office in the offseason. A five-year deal worth $200 million should help heal the hurt feelings, but how long might any bitterness linger, even with Duren saying all the right things about mending the relationship? Ausar Thompson was a Defensive Player of the Year finalist, but his offensive game was (and might still be) lacking in the extreme. Tobias Harris is gone, replaced by John Collins, who should be an upgrade. Isaiah Stewart was traded to Memphis, leaving Paul Reed as the backup big. Duncan Robinson and newly acquired Isaiah Joe are quality shooters, if not much else. Daniss Jenkins will fill the backup point guard minutes. After Cunningham, the Pistons are once again headed into the season without a reliable second option.

Kawhi Leonard is back in Toronto. He's an obvious upgrade in the starting lineup over Brandon Ingram, who was alternately ineffective and unavailable during his time with the Raptors. Leonard is coming off one of his best statistical seasons, and pairing him with Scottie Barnes makes an already good Raptors defense something closer to terrifying. Barnes and Leonard instantly become one of the best two-way combos in the league, and they should give opposing teams fits on a nightly basis. The basketball concern in Toronto is making sure Leonard is around for the postseason. He played 65 games a year ago, but over the last decade, he's cleared that threshold just three times.

And then there are the new-look Sixers. On paper, Tyrese Maxey, VJ Edgecombe, Jaylen Brown, LeBron James and Joel Embiid are among the most formidable starting units in the league. The upside here is huge -- as is the potential for the franchise to pull its latest faceplant. How will Maxey, coming off his first All-NBA nod, be utilized with three superstar veterans starting alongside him? For that matter, how will Edgecombe, who had a brilliant rookie season, fit in? How will Brown be deployed with his new team when last season, with his old one, he wasn't asked to defer to anyone? Will Embiid be healthy enough to contribute after missing 150 games over the last three seasons? And what about LeBron? He's arguably the greatest player of all-time, and he decided to go to Philly on a vet minimum to play for a franchise that hasn't gotten out of the second round in more than a quarter century.

That's a lot of talent, a lot of egos, and even more unknowns about how this thing plays out. Whatever you do, just don't ask whose team this is.

Heat fans are likely apoplectic about being relegated to Tier 3. (Please direct all concerns to @SamQuinnCBS.) Miami won the Giannis Antetokounmpo sweepstakes, but doing so required a bushel of draft capital as well as Tyler Herro, Jaime Jaquez Jr. and Kel'El Ware, all of whom are useful rotation players if not something north of that. The projected starting lineup of Giannis, Bam Adebayo, Andrew Wiggins, Klay Thompson and Davion Mitchell should be fearsome on defense. The concern here, even with Thompson in town, is spacing and shooting. The Heat could use more playmaking and shot creation, too.

The Pacers made the NBA Finals just two seasons ago and came within one win (and possibly one ruptured Tyrese Haliburton Achilles) of holding a championship parade. After taking a gap year last season, Haliburton is back. Waiting for him is new center Ivica Zubac, acquired at the deadline from the Clippers. Much of the roster that reached the Finals remains in place, as does Rick Carlisle, who is on everyone's short list as one of the best coaches in the NBA. If Haliburton takes time to knock off the rust, it could be slow going for the Pacers. If he looks anything like the version of himself that turned in one of the great individual postseason performances before getting hurt, Indiana will quickly graduate into the contenders tier, much to the chagrin of the rest of that already overloaded category.

The Hawks! The Hawks were the only team to beat the Knicks more than once during the postseason. Jalen Johnson is a triple-double machine. Nickeil Alexander-Walker went from a quality sixth man in Minnesota to a valuable starter in Atlanta. Dyson Daniels is a defensive dervish and Onyeka Okongwu is an underrated big. Lu Dort and Aaron Wiggins have come over from OKC to bolster the rotation. The Hawks should be good. Good enough to break into the contender tier is another matter, though.

After years of underachieving, the Magic dumped coach Jamahl Mosley in favor of Sean Sweeney. We'll see if he can make Paolo Banchero and Franz Wagner work together. So far, no one has been able to crack that code. Desmond Bane was a useful defender and the Magic's best (only?) reliable shooter from distance last season. As always, Jalen Suggs is entering another season with everyone waiting for him to make the leap or at least make it through the majority of the campaign without missing significant time due to injury.

It feels rude to include the Hornets -- last year's feel-good, fun-watch team -- in this tier. Charlotte made the right call by moving on from LaMelo Ball. But even with addition by subtraction, getting out of the play-in looks like it will be even harder for the Hornets this season, considering the field in front of them.

The Bulls should be excited about Caleb Wilson and the new front office led by Bryson Graham. The Bucks and Nets are rebuilding and we can probably forget about them until further notice. As for the Wizards, they've indicated that they want to compete this season by giving Trae Young a fat four-year, $212 million deal that no other team seemed willing to offer or even come close to dangling.

They also decided to hold onto Anthony Davis, who has played a grand total of 29 games since the Lakers traded him. The Wizards lucked into the first pick and selected AJ Dybantsa. Alex Sarr had a good season last year. Why Washington isn't investing heavily in its young players instead of choosing this ill-advised two-timeline path is hard to fathom. Maybe because the Wizards can't stop being the Wizards.

#195. Simone Biles rocks all-white with 'football material' at Colts game

Simone Biles rocked an all-white look to support her husband, Indianapolis Colts safety Jonathan Owens.

The gold medalist, 29, was spotted at Lucas Oil Stadium in a short-sleeved top and matching shorts at the Colts game against the Tennessee Titans on Sunday, Oct. 18.

Similar to previous outfits, Biles added her beau's number, "38," in the middle of her shirt and "Owens" on the back of her bottoms.

"We did the 38 and owens out of the football material & I'm obsessed," she wrote in her Instagram Stories.

Biles also provided a closer look at her fall-coded ensemble. She wore a brown trench coat and leather boots with a mini Chanel purse.

Simone Biles: Gold medalist promotes 'Skin to Believe In' so others won't feel embarrassed

The customizations are reminiscent of her outfit at the Colts-Washington Commanders game in London earlier this month.

Biles made a statement on the field with a stone-colored off-the-shoulder trench coat paired with a matching floor-length pencil skirt from PrettyLittleThing. She also added "38" and "Owens" to the look with shiny gems.

In an interview with Us Magazine in September, Simone Biles spoke about being referred to as a WAG, a common term for the wife or girlfriend of a professional athlete.

"It just doesn't bother me because I know who I am and what I've accomplished outside of it," Biles told the outlet. She continued, "It doesn't matter when somebody's like, 'Oh, Simone's one of the WAGs.' Don't care. I know I've done great things on an Olympic level and for the mental health community, foster (care) community, all of this stuff. To me, it doesn't seem derogatory because I know exactly who I am."

Taylor Ardrey is a news reporter for USA TODAY. You can reach her at tardrey@usatodayco.com.

#196. Falcons signing Andy Dalton, cutting Cooper Rush

The Falcons are making a change in their quarterback room.

Andy Dalton is signing with Atlanta, and he’ll take up the roster spot the Falcons will open up by cutting Cooper Rush, according to multiple reports.

As PFT reported Sunday, Dalton was offered a contract by the Eagles, but he turned them down to sign elsewhere today. Now we know that elsewhere is Atlanta.

The 38-year-old Dalton was traded from Carolina to Philadelphia in March and played in one game for the Eagles, throwing an interception while Jalen Hurts was being checked with a concussion. The Eagles cut him shortly after that, but when Hurts had to go on injured reserve with a blood clot, they wanted Dalton back. Dalton had other offers.

The best offer came from the Falcons, who have already played four quarterbacks this year: Rush, Michael Penix, Jack Strand and Tua Tagovailoa. If Penix stays healthy, Dalton will stay on the sideline, but that’s a pretty big “if,” and Dalton may just become the fifth quarterback to play for the Falcons this season.

#197. Dave Roberts sparked MLB's only 3-0 playoff comeback, and he'll try to do it again with Dodgers

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The two-time defending World Series champion Dodgers are one loss away from elimination. The Dodgers again fell to the MLB-best Brewers in Game 3 of the NLCS on Wednesday night (MIL 6, LA 2), giving Milwaukee a comfortable 3-0 lead in the best-of-seven series. Los Angeles is trying to become baseball's first threepeat champion since the 1998-2000 Yankees.

"I think they have more experience. They're really taking great at-bats. They're taking better at-bats than they did last year," Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said after Game 3 when asked about the difference between this year's Brewers and the Brewers that the Dodgers swept in the NLCS last year. "Their ball-in-play averages, gosh dang, it's got to be .400. When they put the ball in play, it's a hit. They're also slugging, which they didn't do last year. Those are good combos.

"Defensively they're everywhere and making plays, and it's hard for us to certainly create, build innings, and score. Where I thought last year we did a better job of slugging and having those guys play from behind."

Historically, teams that have taken a 3-0 lead in a best-of-seven have won 41 of 42 series, with 32 sweeps. The one comeback was, of course, the Red Sox over the Yankees in the 2004 ALCS. New York bludgeoned the Red Sox 19-8 in their Game 3 win, then Boston did not lose again the rest of the postseason en route to its first World Series title since 1918.

If the Dodgers are going to become the second team to mount a 3-0 series comeback, they can look into their own dugout for inspiration. Almost 22 years ago to the day, Roberts stole a key base against Mariano Rivera in the ninth inning of Game 4, then scored the game-tying run. Boston won Game 4 in 12 innings.

"It's certainly possible. I've lived it," Roberts said Wednesday when asked about the possibility of coming back from 3-0. "I think the thing is that our guys have been battle-tested, as was that team I was a part of. I think the mindset has to be -- teams have been down before 0-2, 0-3 -- it's just you've got to win tomorrow. It's an elimination game. We've played in a lot of elimination games. We've just got to get a win. We've got to find a way to build some momentum, and it takes all of us."

Here is Roberts' steal and Boston's ninth-inning comeback in Game 4:

"Even with Mo on the mound, and as bleak as things looked, we felt as if we were still in the game," Roberts told MLB.com in 2020.

For the Dodgers to mount a 3-0 comeback (or even just force a Game 5), they have to hit, first and foremost. Los Angeles has yet to hit a home run in the NLCS, and the team has scored seven runs in the three games. The Dodgers are slugging -- slugging -- .187 as a team. They're 2 for 16 with runners in scoring position. The 16 is the telling number there. They're not even creating opportunities.

A comeback will take scoring runs (duh) and likely a signature moment, like Roberts' steal. It doesn't have to be a stolen base. Maybe it's a pitcher escaping a jam with a key strikeout, or a big hit, or a big defensive play. There are lots of ways to have a signature moment in this sport. In 2004, Roberts did it with his legs. Will the Dodgers find a way to do it in Game 4 on Thursday?

"I think they've seen the documentary," Roberts said after the Game 3 loss. "They know it can happen."

#199. NFL Week 6 overreactions: Time for Colts to clean house? A.J. Brown trade a mistake for Patriots?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The battle between two of the NFL's most woebegone franchises lived up to its lack of hype Sunday. In fact, in terms of excitement, it more than lived up to it. But the on-field product was a special sort of fun-bad.

Titans 26, Colts 20. It's the first win of the year for Tennessee, and a stunning one at that. The Titans trailed 13-0 at halftime and looked completely lifeless. Bench Cam Ward? Throw in the towel? It seemed on the brink.

And then the Colts, being the generous team they are, quite literally gave it away over the next four possessions:

From up 13-0 to down 20-13 in about 18 minutes of game time. Horrifying stuff. The Colts actually tied the game on a Taylor touchdown, only for the defense to commit an awful pass interference to set up a Titans field goal. Tennessee tacked on another field goal late.

A collapse in all three stages? Against a winless team? For an organization already skating on thin ice? Check, check, check. Which leads me to say ...

Since 2020, there have been 16 in-season coaching changes. Shane Steichen will either be the next or, at the very least, join that list.

This was an unacceptable collapse. The Titans are completely inept offensively. The only way they could do anything was if the Colts blew it, and the Colts blew it over and over again. I've generally been a proponent of Steichen as a good offensive mind, but as a head coach, you have to be more than that. You are responsible for everything, and in that matter, Indianapolis isn't close to good enough.

Steichen can't play the game, though, so we turn to the players ... and the person who chose them. Chris Ballard is in his 10th season as Colts GM. The team has one playoff win over that span, and it was back in 2018, his second year. He has been completely unable to find a quarterback, and his latest attempt is turning out as bad as the others.

Remember, at the start of Ballard's tenure, he had Andrew Luck. Andrew Luck retired ahead of the 2019 season. It's been that long. Inexcusable. He has tried half-measures with veterans. He tried drafting one (Anthony Richardson). He has failed in every measure. The defense remains iffy at best, even after the blockbuster (and, in retrospect, misjudged) Sauce Gardner trade.

But really, it all comes back to Jones: He was 22-for-42 for 269 yards, a touchdown and two interceptions. He took six sacks. He's tied for the NFL lead in turnovers. Sunday, he simply did not put an NFL-caliber product on the field.

INT by Flott‼️📺: @NFLonFOX pic.twitter.com/XuoBtoPyIe

Remember, the Colts signed him to a two-year, $88 million deal over the offseason, even though they were bidding with ... no one. There is an out after this year that would carry $35 million in dead cap, but continuing with him would be even more punitive for a franchise long overdue for a reset.

Colts owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon is known for standing on the sideline and keeping notes. Her only notes needed from Sunday? It's time to clean house.

This is simply a non-playoff team right now. Here are the stunning numbers from the Rams' stunning 18-16 loss to the Cardinals:

Sean McVay summed it up aptly: "There's nothing positive that I can say about today."

The offense has very little juice, outside an occasional excellent play by Puka Nacua or Davante Adams. It just feels really stagnant; Stafford used play action on 37% of his dropbacks last year and averaged 8.4 yards per pass on those throws. This year, it's down to 25% and 7.2, respectively. And when a team doesn't have juice, it has little room for error. But the Rams keep making errors: penalties, turnovers, missed assignments, etc.

Meanwhile, the defense just isn't causing much havoc. And the special teams issues remain. New kicker Blake Grupe got hurt in the first quarter, forcing the Rams to adjust on the fly.

Even if the Rams had won, it's not close to good enough. Sean McVay said as much. If they lose in Week 7, it's officially panic time.

JOSH ALLEN DOING JOSH ALLEN THINGS!!!!📺: CBS pic.twitter.com/F0GGilwmd6

Well, well, well, if it isn't a three-way tie atop the AFC North through six weeks?! The Browns, Steelers and Ravens are all 4-2, and the Bengals (on bye this weekend) aren't far behind at 3-2.

Cleveland technically leads the division thanks to Sunday's 13-10 win over Lamar Jackson-less Baltimore, and Pittsburgh is second because it has a better in-division record.

Sorry, Browns and Steelers fans, but neither one of you is winning the division. Cleveland's largest win this season is by four points. It lost to the Jets just last week. Deshaun Watson looked awful Sunday. The Steelers looked similarly awful, needing a late comeback to force overtime against the Baker Mayfield-less Buccaneers. As it turns out, playing against backup quarterbacks is very helpful.

Both teams rank in the bottom half of most major offensive stats. The quarterback play simply isn't good enough and won't be good enough, especially when put up against Lamar Jackson and Joe Burrow rather than Tyler Huntley and Jalon Daniels.

A.J. Brown's grand return from IR was ... not so grand. Three catches for 27 yards on 10 targets. Officially, he's been charged with two drops. Unofficially, given his high standards, it was probably more. He even bobbled away a Jets onside kick, but lucky for him, a teammate recovered to clinch the Patriots' 26-19 win.

It's worth being concerned about the debut, but to say the trade is a bust or a mistake would be a drastic overreaction. Yes, it's been a tough start with the injury and the underwhelming return. But let's not write it off. He won on the routes New England brought him in to win: quick in-breakers and deep balls. Drake Maye missed him on one of each, and Brown failed to finish other opportunities he did have. It sounds like a silly thing to say, but if you cut the tape right before the ball arrives, Brown's film would look encouraging.

Of course, he has to make the plays that are there. Getting open doesn't gain yards, score points or win games. Brown will bounce back, and he can still be a huge boost. He came back from his high ankle sprain earlier than expected. Let's give him a week's worth of grace.

Another week, another outstanding performance for C.J. Stroud. The fourth-year pro threw for 312 yards, three touchdowns and an interception and led the game-winning drive in the Texans' 34-31 win over the Jaguars.

The numbers are one thing, but the film is just as good, if not better. This is one of the best throws you will see all season.

WHAT A THROW FROM CJ STROUD.HOUvsJAX on NFL NetworkStream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/Z8LUxZceAl

Foster had to double it!📺: @nflnetwork pic.twitter.com/srjLPbSesF

This is Stroud at his best: laser-accurate, huge arm, can access every part of the field. It's been missed the past few years, and the Texans should be very glad it's back. Not only that, but he is improving at mitigating negative plays. His interception Sunday was really bad, but it was his first all year. He's also taking fewer devastating sacks than he did last season. And he's doing it all while still not having much of a run game.

The Texans and Stroud didn't reach an extension in the offseason. He had been awful in the playoffs, and while both sides said the right things, no agreement happened.

He is very much on the way to earning that massive extension this offseason, though. This offseason is setting up to be a huge one for quarterback deals — Caleb Williams, Jayden Daniels, Drake Maye and Bo Nix from the 2024 class, Bryce Young from Stroud's 2023 class and Lamar Jackson are all looking for a new deal. Stroud's deal will put him among the top five highest-paid quarterbacks, and it will be well-deserved.

The Panthers topped the injury-battered Eagles 25-14 in straightforward fashion. Bryce Young threw a pair of touchdown passes, and Chuba Hubbard ran for 120 yards and a score. Philadelphia was without Jalen Hurts, its top three running backs and a bunch of other players. It's not a super notable result by any measure.

But Philadelphia still has a really good defense, and Brad Idzik flashed excellent play calling, including on both touchdowns to Tommy Tremble.

Tremble tuddy 🔥#CARvsPHI📺: CBS pic.twitter.com/lTK7jniQy1

No. 2 on the day for Tommy Tremble!CARvsPHI on CBS/Paramount+Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/k2atMk31qb

I was also super impressed by Young's work on RPO throws, something Idzik and Young have worked into this offense really well.

Idzik took over calling plays from Dave Canales this offseason. It has been a perfect promotion. Carolina has one of the most aggressive offenses in the NFL in terms of passing rates. It's a really well-designed offense that empowers Young and accentuates his strengths. In an NFL that loves young, innovative play callers, Idzik is part of the next wave of hotshots.

#200. Onsi Saleh’s tax comments reinforce the Hawks’ patient approach

Onsi Saleh has consistently emphasized financial flexibility, but his latest comments offer an important clarification: Atlanta has the authority to enter the luxury tax when the right opportunity comes.

During an appearance on SiriusXM, the Hawks' president of basketball operations discussed navigating the NBA's apron restrictions and making responsible roster decisions.

"Even with us, we could go in the tax and we have full authority on the tax," Saleh said.

That statement matters because maintaining flexibility can sometimes leave fans wondering whether an organization is willing to spend. Saleh's explanation suggests Atlanta's approach centers on choosing the right investment and understanding the consequences that follow.

The luxury tax and the aprons are separate thresholds. Paying the tax carries a financial cost, while crossing the apron levels brings additional roster-building restrictions. At the second apron, teams lose tools such as the midlevel exception and the ability to combine outgoing player salaries to acquire a more expensive player. Those limitations can make improving an already expensive roster considerably harder.

For Atlanta, keeping options available can create opportunities when other teams need to reduce spending. Saleh discussed that advantage, and the Hawks' offseason already provides an example of how it can work.

Oklahoma City traded Lu Dort, Aaron Wiggins and Isaiah Joe in moves that helped bring the Thunder below the second apron. Atlanta acquired Dort and Wiggins, adding championship experience and perimeter depth while Oklahoma City addressed its financial commitments.

The Thunder were not prohibited from keeping those players. However, the costs and restrictions associated with an expensive roster helped create circumstances Atlanta could exploit. That distinction illustrates why financial discipline can have basketball value beyond the money saved.

Saleh's challenge is recognizing when preserving flexibility becomes less valuable than using it. Keeping room to maneuver helps Atlanta pursue upgrades, but that flexibility ultimately needs to translate into a stronger team around Jalen Johnson.

His comments do not establish a spending timetable or identify a particular move. They do, however, indicate that entering the tax is an available option rather than a boundary the front office has been instructed never to cross.

That leaves the central decision with Saleh and his staff: determining which opportunity justifies the commitment. Spending on a roster that still needs substantial work could leave Atlanta paying more while making its next improvement harder. Spending when the right pieces are in place could help sustain a team capable of competing deeper into the postseason.

For now, Saleh's message remains consistent. The Hawks want to make smart decisions, benefit from opportunities elsewhere and preserve the ability to act decisively. His willingness to discuss entering the tax adds substance to that approach. When Atlanta believes the moment has arrived, Saleh says the authority to spend is there.

#201. Fantasy Football Stock Report: C.J. Stroud finding form, Patrick Mahomes no longer sure-fire start after Week 6

As I write this on Sunday night, 13 of 14 Week 6 games are in the books (with Monday night remaining) and the season is continuing to round into shape. Sort of. There were promising improvements. Concerning trends. Performances that changed our early outlook on players and teams. As always, some of these shifting perspectives will have permanent ramifications in fantasy football.

With that in mind, I've compiled another full fantasy stock report. These are the most notable risers and fallers heading into Week 7.

I don't want to overreact here, but it appears C.J. Stroud might finally be rediscovering the trajectory he had at the end of his Rookie of the Year season back in 2023. It looked at the time like Stroud might be one of the best young quarterbacks and a future face of the league, then he seemed to lose confidence and precision over the next couple years. But watching him perform in London on Sunday, he looks back.

He completed 24 of 34 passes for 312 yards and three touchdowns (and one INT) and expertly maneuvered the Texans offense to a last-second win. He's now had 20+ fantasy points in three straight games, with multiple offensive touchdowns in all three and 307 passing yards per game. It certainly doesn't hurt that Nico Collins is healthy, Jaylin Noel is breaking out, Marvin Harrison Jr. looked better as a Texan and Tank Dell could return soon.

Stroud needs to maintain this pace for more than three weeks before we anoint him as a rest-of-season QB1, but the arrow is clearly pointing upward.

Germie Bernard was one of the top waiver-wire pickups of the week and he rewarded fantasy managers immediately to the tune of 11 catches on 12 targets for 87 yards and a touchdown. He ran 44 routes — two fewer than DK Metcalf — and the passing offense essentially ran through the two of them all day. With Roman Wilson out and Aaron Rodgers continuing to put up meaningful numbers, the second-round rookie out of Alabama is very quickly ascending into weekly FLEX consideration, if not higher.

Only 13 players have had 11+ receptions in a game across 32 teams and six weeks and Bernard is one of them ... among company like Jaxon Smith-Njigba, Puka Nacua, CeeDee Lamb, etc. That kind of production doesn't often fade into a supporting role and the Steelers offense needs impact players. It's particularly worth noting that Metcalf has not been as good or as involved as he was on Sunday in most of the weeks prior, so in his down weeks, Bernard might even be Pittsburgh's WR1. For fantasy, that makes him a must-roster player with must-start upside down the road.

Colston Loveland and Luther Burden III were two of the most highly touted and anticipated players in fantasy entering the season ... and both had been disappointments through the first five weeks. Burden was the WR26 entering Week 6, with just one game in double-digit fantasy points and zero games over 65 receiving yards. Meanwhile, Loveland had been an unmitigated disaster, with a season-high of 8.7 fantasy points and no touchdowns through five games. Both showed up in Week 6 with Caleb Williams back at the helm, finally offering some hope for the stardom we were promised. Burden caught all eight of his targets for 95 yards (all team highs), while Loveland caught six of seven targets for 65 yards and his first touchdown of 2026.

The easy interpretation would be that Williams' return made all the difference, but it's worth remembering that Loveland did absolutely nothing in Williams' first couple of games this season, so we're going to have to monitor this a little further. Rome Odunze was also quiet in Week 6, and it's not only possible, but probable, that there will be a bit of a rotation between these three throughout the year. Still, it was great to see that both players do, in fact, have the upside to dominate through the air, and managers can breathe at least a small sigh of relief amid previously growing "bust" concerns.

Join or create a Yahoo Fantasy Basketball league for the 2026-27 NBA season

After a massive dud in Week 5 — one catch for six yards on five targets — we were forced to question whether Carnell Tate's breakout Week 4 was an aberration. Sunday's performance against the Colts (sort of) answered that question. The fourth overall pick snagged six of seven targets for 70 yards and his first NFL touchdown, topping 16 fantasy points for the second time in three weeks. He accounted for 54.5% of the team's catches and 68.6% of their receiving yards, and scored the team's only offensive touchdown.

On the one hand, it's concerning that this offense is still so anemic on the whole. It undoubtedly lowers Tate's overall ceiling and will likely make it difficult for the rookie to finish as a high-end WR2 very often. On the other hand, the fact that he's such a focal point for Cam Ward and Co. is certainly promising and should translate into fewer duds moving forward, as Tate continues to develop and grow into the league. Rookie wide receivers typically get much better for fantasy late in the fall and into winter, so these early signs are encouraging. It certainly doesn't hurt that Tate has, on paper, a very green schedule for wide receivers over the next couple of months. He's probably worth acquiring if you can get him on the cheap.

Cam Skattebo was one of my favorite plays heading into the weekend, considering the glorious matchup with the Saints ... and instead John Harbaugh decided to punish him for recent fumbling issues with zero touches on the entire day. It would have been more reasonable if the Giants' running backs who did see touches didn't total 34 yards on 14 carries, resulting in a 34-27 loss in which J.J. McCarthy was their leading rusher ... in one quarter.

The optimistic perspective here would be that this was a one-week lesson for Skattebo, and that the rest of the depth chart was so ineffective that he'll work his way right back into the RB1 role moving forward. But after literally zero touches (on just six snaps), the optimistic perspective seems more like wishful thinking. It's not like Skattebo had been incredibly efficient or productive outside the fumbles — with just 3.6 yards per carry on the year — so there's no guarantee he reassumes 15-touch-a-game volume. And it's clear the Giants' running game is a problem in general.

Skattebo's certainly not in the RB2 conversation right now, and it's not impossible he loses all fantasy relevance in the coming weeks. Check back in next week to see what Harbaugh does with this backfield.

Patrick Mahomes is currently the quintessential case of "NFL success doesn't always equal fantasy success." The Chiefs are 5-0 and Mahomes had thrown multiple touchdown passes in each of his first four games, but after totaling more than 50 fantasy points in Weeks 1 and 2, he's averaged just 15.14 per game since Week 3 and scored a season-low 11.48 in Week 6. The primary issue, exhibited on Sunday, is that he doesn't need to carry this offense anymore — he has Kenneth Walker III for that job.

He threw one interception and zero touchdowns against the Chargers, but the Chiefs still won 22-6 as Walker racked up 128 yards and another two touchdowns on the ground. It doesn't mean Mahomes won't be a QB1 — he was the QB7 in points per game through his Week 5 bye — but outings like this showcase why he likely won't be the every-week star he has been in years past. You can still start him most weeks, particularly in contests that project to be high-scoring and close for Kansas City. But on that note, he has the Seahawks, Broncos and Jets on the horizon. If you have him, you might want to consider a streaming alternative for the near future, or trade him on name value.

If he's on another team, mark your calendar for Week 10 and think about trading for him then if possible.

Ashton Jeanty has become a regular in this section of the column and somehow he keeps trending down. And if you're glancing at his box score and wondering why, take a look at his carries and yards. The second-year running back managed just 22 yards on 10 carries this week after hitting just 27 on 10 carries last week. And this was a Buffalo defense that had been among the softest against running backs all season. Jeanty's averaged fewer than 4.0 yards per carry in every single game since Week 2 and fewer than 3.0 in four of his last five games. Meanwhile, Mike Washington Jr. played 33% of the snaps on Sunday but logged nine carries (to Jeanty's 10) and totaled a much more attractive 43 rushing yards (4.3 per carry).

Now, of course, Jeanty did score a goal-line rushing touchdown and caught four passes for 36 yards, so his 13.8 fantasy points ended up decent enough. The problem is that his value is dwindling down to just that: receiving work and touchdowns. And while the receiving work has been consistent, this was Jeanty's first rushing touchdown of the year. He's just the RB18 in points per game since Week 2 and has flashed very little upside over that span. You're essentially beholden to starting Jeanty every week, but he's likely to remain a low-end RB2 (at best) most of the weeks.

Jaylen Warren had been a fantasy superstar in Rico Dowdle's absence, and his brilliant production in Pittsburgh's offense had given many (me included) hope that he'd remain the bell-cow back upon Dowdle's return.

He did still double Dowdle's carries (14 to seven) but that was his lowest carry mark since Week 2, as were his 50 rushing yards. Additionally, Dowdle matched Warren's four targets, which is particularly discouraging given how good Warren had been as a receiver the past few weeks. In three games with Dowdle, Warren has scored 7.8, 8.7 and now 8.8 fantasy points. Incredibly consistent ... and incredibly mid.

In the three games without Dowdle, Warren had scored 19.1, 14.1 and 33.8.

The drop-off is precipitous and disappointing. Worst of all, Dowdle was very good in his change-of-pace role, averaging 5.7 yards per carry, and it makes real-football sense for Pittsburgh to mix-and-match the two, as painful as it is for fantasy.

Warren is still a viable FLEX option moving forward, and will likely have a few more RB2 weeks down the stretch, but it's now much tougher to envision him as an RB2 on the season.

It's starting to look like the "Marvin Harrison Jr. was a great Arizona decoy" theory might hold some water. In two games without Harrison, Michael Wilson has had incredibly similar stat lines: four catches on seven targets for 30 yards and four catches on seven targets for 32 yards. After snagging 18 of 30 targets for 184 yards and a touchdown the two weeks prior, this has been a stark and concerning left turn.

Kendrick Bourne has picked up much of the slack and Trey McBride has continued his voluminous ways, so the era of double-digit targets for Wilson might have come to a rapid close. Now, with that being said, he did still see seven targets on Sunday, his sixth straight game hitting that mark, so Wilson's still undeniably involved. The problem is that with Jacoby Brissett at quarterback and the general inconsistency of the Cards' offense, seven targets isn't always enough for fantasy relevance in Arizona — see Wilson's four games with single-digit fantasy points for reference.

He's still valuable, but is dropping from WR2 range to FLEX range after consecutive disappointments.

#203. Brian Schottenheimer: Cowboys' effort and fight is right, but mistakes are killing us

Cowboys head coach Brian Schottenheimer defended his team’s effort but not the results after Sunday night’s loss to the Packers.

On a night when Dak Prescott threw two interceptions, Schottenheimer pointed the finger at turnovers.

“The effort is right, the fight is right, but mistakes are killing us,” Schottenheimer said. “We’ve got to protect the football.”

At 2-4, the Cowboys are not a good team right now, but there are no good teams in the NFC East and the Cowboys are actually the betting favorites to win the division. Schottenheimer thinks there’s still a future for his team.

“We’re in a hole. We’ve put ourselves there. There’s one way out of it. I told our guys we’ve got to work, we’ve got to find solutions, we can’t repeat mistakes. And they understand that,” Schottenheimer said.

Although Schottenheimer defended Prescott’s effort, he made clear that he wasn’t happy about the interceptions.

“The ball matters more than anything in the National Football League,” Schottenheimer said. “It’s the ball. Second, it’s the line of scrimmage. And we haven’t been very good in the last two games, so that’s what we’re responsible and accountable for, and I stand up here and accept that.”

#204. Warriors' Kristaps Porziņģis breaks silence on mysterious health issues, remains out indefinitely

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Golden State Warriors will begin the season without one of their expected key contributors as Kristaps Porzingis will remain sidelined indefinitely due to an unspecified health issue.

Porziņģis, who signed a two-year, $40 million deal in the offseason, missed the entirety of training camp and all of their preseason games to this point, but returned to the Warriors facility for the first time this fall on Tuesday. Porziņģis and the Warriors each released statements on Wednesday offering a vague update on his status going forward.

Porziņģis, 31, posted to social media that he's been working with doctors and is "getting better and better," but is still not ready to return to the court and must remain patient.

"Hello people, I'm working with doctors and experts to figure out how to be fully back to good health asap. Honestly, I'm getting better and better. I just have to stay patient, and I believe I'll be feeling great again soon," Porziņģis wrote. "It has definitely been frustrating dealing with some health stuff that you can't exactly pinpoint, on top of injuries throughout my career, so it has added up for sure, but we will get through it. Health is wealth. Thank you for all the support."

He followed that up by speaking directly to the "internet doctors" who have been trying to diagnose him and tried to quiet some of the rumors about his condition.

I appreciate all the internet doctors trying to diagnose and help, but I'm in the best hands. So everyone can relax now 😄🙏🏼 and I don’t have hiv or aids.

The Warriors said that Porziņģis met with general manager Mike Dunleavy and vice president of player health and performance Dr. Rick Celebrini upon his return to the team practice facility on Tuesday. The team did not provide a timeline for Porziņģis' potential return and said the "specific contents of that meeting will remain private."

"Porziņģis will remain out indefinitely due to the same health-related matter but will be around the team," the Warriors said. "An update on his status, including the potential resumption of practice, playing status or timeline, will be provided when available and appropriate."

The Warriors added Porziņģis in a deal with the Atlanta Hawks ahead of last year's trade deadline. He played in 15 games for Golden State, averaging 16.1 points, 5.3 rebounds and 2.3 assists. The No. 4 pick in the 2015 NBA Draft, Porziņģis has dealt with health and injury issues throughout his career. While knee injuries were a common problem earlier in his career, various mysterious health issues have persisted in recent seasons. During his time with the Boston Celtics, Porziņģis was sidelined while experiencing fatigue and was later diagnosed with postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS), which can cause rapid changes in heart rate, exhaustion and dizziness.

Porziņģis was expected to take on a major role this season for the Warriors and being around the team seems like a step in the right direction. Still, until he's able to return, the Warriors' frontcourt rotation will be a bit thinner than initially planned. Al Horford and Charles Bassey are the other center options on the roster beyond Draymond Green, and the Warriors figure to play some small-ball lineups that could incorporate rookie Yaxel Lendeborg, who has impressed in the preseason, at the four spot.
