#205. Dodgers on the brink: Facing NLCS sweep vs. Brewers, a baseball dynasty could go out with a whimper

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

LOS ANGELES -- The quiet blared in the Dodgers clubhouse like a siren. A deafening absence of noise. The kind of desperation that screams through whispers.

The quiet lingered over Max Muncy as he sat at his locker, scrolling through his iPhone. Cut-sleeve dark gray shirt with his white Dodgers pants still on, he dodged the disappointment with his thumbs. Instead of getting dressed, he marinated in the 3-0 NLCS deficit against the Brewers a little longer.

The quiet muffled the voice of Blake Snell, who spoke so softly that even in the hushed home clubhouse one could barely make out his words. The bill of his black-and-camouflage Los Angeles cap hovered over his face, but it still couldn't hide his disappointment.  The silence taunted Kiké Hernández at his locker, his face pointed toward the floor as he rummaged through his closely cropped, bleached-blond hair, searching for answers.

This home clubhouse has known the raucous rage of victory better than any other recently. The two-time defending World Series champs have filled this space and others with champagne and euphoria, three times in the previous six seasons. They made a noise that history could hear.

But Wednesday night, this place, with its wooden walls and royal blue chairs, sounded more like a mausoleum than a mosh pit. Muted by Milwaukee.

The Brewers have simply been better. Smarter. Tougher. Hungrier.

The Brewers have a 3-0 lead in the NLCS. One more victory and they'll capture the National League pennant for the first time in team history. They can finish a sweep of the Dodgers, who have been the World Series favorites all year long, on Thursday night.

"It's a pretty simple answer," Muncy said. "We're playing like shit. They're playing great."

They're close to being consumed by the quiet. A 3-0 hole in this NLCS, following a 6-2 beatdown in Game 3 at Dodger Stadium, feels insurmountable even for a club that's repeatedly proven its resolve. Because across from them, a young, exuberant bunch is not only fearless against the $433 million juggernaut. They can sense the mortality of the legends they're facing. The Dodgers are being forced to wrestle with the end of their dominance.

In some ways, this is playing out predictably. Dynasties often end with epic thuds. Their demise, when it comes, is sudden -- or so it feels. Their excellence trains the expectations. Especially these Dodgers, who've rallied from the improbable, who've authored moments of magic, whose endless well of talent always produces a hero. So when the dominance dies, or meets a greater great, it feels like it came out of nowhere.

So it has been with the Dodgers. Their inevitability morphed into impotence. Their supremacy's screeching to a halt. Withering away is their chance to become the first three-peat champs since the Y2K Yankees.

The ends of eras don't come with announcements. Or reprieves. And the only antidote for their unraveling is the hope of more magic. Los Angeles heads into Game 4 under a cloud of quiet, searching internally for answers that once came so easily. Once unstoppable, the Dodgers appear to be coming undone.

"We've done it before," said Hernández, whose personal October magic is running on fumes, "but we've never been in this big of a hole."

Even as Snell dealt, yielding just one run on a first-pitch homer by Jackson Chourio to open the game, the angst never left Dodger Stadium. Even when Will Smith delivered a bases-loaded, two-run double off Abner Uribe, one of the Brewers' top arms in arguably baseball's deepest bullpen, the nervous tension never loosened its grip.

This is what the Brewers do. They take the air out of teams, out of their offense and out of their audience. They make it hard for opponents to breathe. Their three Game 3 home runs punctured the lungs of the Los Angeles faithful.

The Brewers waited out Snell. They didn't have a choice. Snell, a starter not known for his command, could suddenly pelt a bee in the butt with his four-seamer. His fastball played in the zone, drawing a 46% swing-and-miss rate. He punched out nine batters across six frames.

The goal is to coax Snell's stuff up in the zone. But with the slider and changeup working, and the curveball altering batters' eye level, the Brewers struggled to pick their poison.

"Snell was unbelievable," Brewers manager Pat Murphy said. "Like, he was absolutely on it. Like, this guy was sensational."

Yet the seismic shift rocked the Dodgers in the seventh when Andrew Vaughn drew a walk on a curveball that Snell got underneath, leaving it up and out of the zone.

Then Jake Bauers battled Snell through an 11-pitch at-bat, forcing the left-handed pitcher to shy away from his fastball. On that 11th pitch, with the count full, Snell had no choice but to go back to it.

His no-doubter traveled 412 feet before landing in the right-field bleachers for a two-run homer. Milwaukee led 3-2. The next batter, Garrett Mitchell, followed with another blast to right.

"I just left a fastball over the middle to Bauers," Snell said. "Hats off to him. What an at-bat. I threw him everything I had."

That's the reality of the end. At some point, everything the champion has is no longer enough. Whether fatigue or regression or leveled-up competition, the best they can do becomes insufficient.

The Dodgers sent out Tarik Skubal, the two-time Cy Young Award winner acquired at the deadline, in Game 1. They lost.

They sent out Yoshinobu Yamamoto in Game 2, easily one of the best postseason starters of this generation. They lost.

Then, in Game 3, they turned to Snell, another two-time Cy Young Award winner, at home. They lost.

For much of this year, the Dodgers were certain Shohei Ohtani would be OK. That the war of attrition, the force of his stubbornness, would somehow heal the injuries to his right bicep and his left knee. Los Angeles would eventually infuse his once-in-a-lifetime skill set into this series.

Yet Ohtani hasn't looked right. He hasn't homered in nearly two months. Last postseason, he hit eight.

The wear and tear of his folkloric physique, it seems, has begun to take its toll. His left leg drags, barely lifting off the grass as he walks to the plate.

He's 32 with a lot of baseball miles on his body. His knee can no longer withstand the torque and power that only he can generate. He has virtually become a singles hitter in these playoffs.

And after the game, Ohtani's locker remained vacant. Engulfed by the quiet.

Ditto for Mookie Betts. His empty locker surrendered to the quiet. His game turned down a few volumes. Despite putting together quality at-bats in this series, the 34-year-old is no longer the star he used to be.

Betts is trying to become the only active player to have four World Series rings. And the Dodgers are trying to become the first NL team to threepeat. But the chance to make history is fading from their grasp. It might already be over.

"I don't know the mindset of being down 0-3," Muncy said. I've never been down 0-3. So I can't tell you."

Little time. Few words. No answers. In the world of the Dodgers, the quiet is getting louder.

#207. NFL news, live updates: Eagles QB Jalen Hurts reportedly out for season as he undergoes treatment for DVT, blood clots in lungs; Colts fire Chris Ballard

Week 6 of the NFL season is very nearly a wrap, with the Washington Commanders and San Francisco 49ers on "Monday Night Football" to close out the slate.

But before that, Monday morning brought some unexpected news, as the Colts announced they fired GM Chris Ballard, who's been in the role since 2017. Indianapolis fell to the Titans on Sunday.

Also on Monday morning, the Philadelphia Eagles and NFL agent Nicole Lynn released a joint statement on the status of Jalen Hurts, clarifying his diagnosis and treatment plan. He will reportedly be out for the season as he undergoes treatment with blood thinners after a diagnosis of a deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and blood clots in his lungs, per ESPN's Adam Schefter.

The Kansas City Chiefs, meanwhile, remain one of three undefeated teams after beating the Los Angeles Chargers on Sunday. LA is now the lone team in the league sitting at 0-6 as the seats of Jim Harbaugh and Mike McDaniel heat up.

The Miami Dolphins didn't have a chance to rack up a win while on a bye this week, but the Tennessee Titans sure did, walking away with the team's first win under head coach Robert Saleh on Sunday with a 26-20 victory over the Indianapolis Colts.

What other NFL news stories will emerge coming out of Week 6? Follow along with Yahoo Sports for the latest, including injury updates and more.

After the Philadelphia Eagles officially placed Jalen Hurts on injured reserve over the weekend, the team and his agent released a joint statement on his condition Monday, saying the quarterback is dealing with deep vein thrombosis as well as bilateral pulmonary emboli.

As a result of that diagnosis, Hurts will be placed on blood thinners, and is unable to play football until he is fully recovered. Hurts' prognosis is "very good," per the joint statement.

"Over the past few days, Jalen Hurts has received comprehensive medical evaluations by physician experts. In the interest of transparency, we are providing additional information on the diagnosis and treatment plan related to his condition.

"Jalen was initially diagnosed by specialists in London with a left calf superficial vein thrombosis. After further testing and monitoring, the current diagnosis is deep vein thrombosis, as well as bilateral pulmonary emboli. He is clinically stable and has no significant functional limitations. His treatment should only involve anticoagulation [I.E. "blood thinners"]. During this time, he will not be allowed to participate in any contact activities, including football.

"Jalen's progress is very good, and we expect a full recovery. We anticipate that he will have the opportunity to resume contact football activities when off the blood thinners. In the meantime, he will remain active around the team and continue to condition. More importantly, we anticipate that he will have no long-term effects.

"We are thinking of Jalen and looking forward to a strong recovery."

Hurts will be out for the remainder of the 2026 season as he undergoes treatment, per ESPN's Adam Schefter.

The Indianapolis Colts are moving on from general manager Chris Ballard. The team announced Monday that Ballard was relieved from his duties.

In a statement, team owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon said the she felt the change was necessary in order for the team to compete for a championship.

Daniel Jones isn't at risk of losing his starting job just yet. Indianapolis head coach Shane Steichen, after the Colts' 26-20 loss to the previously winless Tennessee Titans, confirmed that Jones will remain his starting quarterback moving forward despite his struggles this season.

"I think he knows he's got to play better," Steichen said. "I've gotta coach better. There's a lot of things, it's not on one guy. But we've got to do a lot of things better."

Jones, who made it back in time to start this fall after his Achilles injury late last season, has not played well in recent weeks. He went just 22-of-42 passing for 269 yards with a touchdown and threw two interceptions in Sunday's loss. Despite the Colts dominating the first half offensively — the unit racked up 232 yards while Indianapolis' defense held Tennessee to just 64 yards in the first two quarters — they had to settle for field goals twice despite being in prime position to find the end zone.

Calls for Mike McDaniel's job are only getting louder.

This time, however, Jim Harbaugh wasn't as strong in his defense of his offensive coordinator.

Harbaugh, after the Los Angeles Chargers fell 22-6 to the Kansas City Chiefs on Sunday, said that they are going to "have to address everything, and especially, offensively." The loss knocked them to 0-6 on the season, marking their worst start since 2000. Coincidentally, Harbaugh was on that Chargers roster as a quarterback that finished 1-15 that season — including five starts, where he threw for 1,330 yards, 8 touchdowns and 8 interceptions.

When asked about McDaniel directly and if he was going to keep calling plays, Harbaugh said they were "going to look at everything."

"The job I'm doing, it starts with me. We'll watch this and get with our offensive coaches," Harbaugh said, via ESPN. "I see the effort, I see the work being put in in the meetings, on the practice field, and to get that to translate to the field is what's necessary. Feel bad for our players, our team, our coaches, our fans. And [offense] needs to be addressed."

The Los Angeles Rams lost wide receiver Davante Adams during the final stretch of their loss to the Arizona Cardinals on Sunday.

Adams, on the Rams' final drive of the contest, suddenly pulled up and started hopping in the back of the end zone. He reached for his left knee as play went the other way, and he eventually limped off the field to the sideline.

Adams did not return to the game. Further specifics of his injury are not yet known.

#208. Davante Adams suffered non-contact leg injury late in Sunday's loss to Cardinals

The slumping Rams may be scrambling to find help at receiver.

Veteran Davante Adams suffered a non-contact injury to his left leg late in the game. He pulled up when running into the end zone on a pass route, reached for his left knee, and hobbled off the field for attention.

The Rams had only one more offensive play, a go-ahead touchdown that did not last.

Coach Sean McVay wasn’t asked about Adams’s apparent injury during the post-game press conference.

Last year, Adams missed the final three games of the regular season with a hamstring injury (and still led the NFL in touchdown catches).

For the season, Adams has 30 catches for 480 yards and four touchdowns. The bulk of the production came in Week 2 vs. the Giants (195 yards) and Week 3 at the Broncos (137). In the other four games combined, he has 148 total receiving yards.

Still, they need him. Puka Nacua, who missed the two games (hip/groin/pre-hernia) in which Adams went off, is their top target in the passing game. On Sunday, Nacua had six catches for 80 yards, including three for 62 on the Rams’ final drive of the game.

Beyond Nacua and Adams, the Rams have Konata Mumpfield, Jordan Whittington, Tutu Atwell, C.J. Daniels, and Alex Bachman at receiver. They may need to find someone else, depending on whether and to what extent Adams will miss time.

The question becomes whether they’re willing to eff them picks in an effort to acquire a receiver via trade before the deadline arrives in 22 days. And the situation will invite even more scrutiny of the decision to invest their bonus first-round pick from last year’s trade with the Falcons on a quarterback and not a receiver — especially since it was obvious that they don’t have much depth behind Nacua and Adams.

#209. 2026-27 NHL season predictions: Expert picks for Stanley Cup playoffs, champion and major awards this season

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Following a brief offseason and an expedited preseason, the 2026-27 NHL season has arrived. Before the puck drops on opening night, we have some predictions to make.

If this season feel like it's staring earlier than usual, that's because it is. The NHL is adopting an 84-game regular season, which just means more hockey for the rest of us. That also means a long and arduous journey to the Stanley Cup is ever so slightly more difficult.

So, what will that journey look like? The Carolina Hurricanes are looking to defend their title as Cup champions, but they'll have to contend with a deep Eastern Conference and some real juggernauts in the Western Conference. With that in mind, we logged our expert predictions for the playoff field in each conference -- and there were a few surprises -- before making our Stanley Cup Final selections.

We also called our shot on the winners of each major individual award. Connor McDavid is looking for his fourth Hart Trophy, but he's got some competition from an up-and-coming superstar in his own division. Races for the Norris Trophy and Vezina Trophy should be pretty wide open, and unexpected candidates always emerge throughout the season.

It should be a fun season in the NHL, so follow along with all our coverage at CBS Sports. Let's get things kicked off with the season preview and predictions, which will of course be 100% accurate.

Baumgartner: I don't see many new faces entering the conversation when it comes to the Eastern Conference playoff race. A healthy Florida Panthers side will slot themselves right back towards the top of the Atlantic, and a revamped Washington Capitals side should be able to make some noise in the Metropolitan. Besides that, I have six 2026 playoff teams returning to the dance in 2027.

Nivison: As much as I hate to go with chalk in preseason predictions -- because it rarely happens that way -- there's no denying the top dogs in the West. The Avalanche and Stars are the class of the Central Division, and the Golden Knights should pound a pitiful Pacific Division into a pulp. Things get more interesting behind those clear Cup contenders, and I'm projecting another significant leap forward from the Mammoth. I also think Macklin Celebrini will be successful in dragging the Sharks to the playoffs in his third NHL season.

Nivison -- Columbus Blue Jackets: The Blue Jackets have been agonizingly close to the playoffs in each of the last two seasons, and I think they get over the hump in 2026-27. There are still questions in Columbus. Can Adam Fantilli be a franchise player at center? Is the forward group as a whole good enough to keep pace in a competitive Eastern Conference? Still, I am sure the Blue Jackets have a really strong blue line, led by Norris Trophy winner Zach Werenski, and goaltender Jet Greaves is on track to become a Vezina Trophy candidate. Internal improvements from the young core will then get Columbus above the cut line.

Baumgartner -- San Jose Sharks: The Sharks narrowly missed out on the 2026 Stanley Cup Playoffs, finishing just four points short of the second wild card. San Jose added a good group of veterans over the summer, but the most important offseason move was selecting Ivar Stenberg with the No. 2 pick in the Draft. Stenberg joins the youth movement in San Jose, which is spearheaded by new captain Macklin Celebrini, who broke the Sharks single-season points record with 115 last season. The Sharks are a better team than they were last year, and with Celebrini entering his third season as a legit Hart Trophy contender, this team won't be fun to play against.

Nivison: Yes, the Mammoth have a brutal path coming out of the Central Divison, but just close your eyes and imagine this scenario with me. Logan Cooley becomes a superstar center. Dylan Guenther hits 50 goals. Dmitry Simashev asserts himself as a budding top-four defenseman. Anders Lee and Vincent Trocheck provide necessary veteran depth. Now open your eyes. Utah is your Western Conference champion.

Unfortunately for the Mammoth, they will run into a refreshed Panthers team that now has double-barreled Tkachuks. Last season, we found out that all it takes to stop Florida is to hope all of its key players miss significant time with injury. The long offseason was probably a blessing in disguise as it allowed the Panthers to get healthy, and that's bad news for everyone else. The structure in front of the crease will limit some of the volatility we saw from Jacob Markstrom in New Jersey, and Florida wins its third Stanley Cup in four years.

Baumgartner: Before last season, the Carolina Hurricanes' kryptonite was the Eastern Conference Final. The Hurricanes were able to overcome their demons and win the East before ultimately taking home the franchise's first Stanley Cup since 2006. In the West, the Dallas Stars have been running into the same problem. After three straight seasons ending in the Western Conference Final, the Stars regressed last postseason, flaming out in the first-round to the Minnesota Wild. The Central Division will once again be a gauntlet, but I'm ready for Dallas to take the next step and reach the Stanley Cup Final.

While Dallas has continued to fall short in recent years, the Panthers have done the opposite. The Panthers made three consecutive Stanley Cup Final appearances, winning back-to-back Cups in 2023-24 and 2024-25. Last season, Florida's three-peat attempt came to a halt on day one of training after captain Aleksander Barkov went down with a non-contact injury, tearing both the ACL and MCL in his right knee. An offseason of healing for Barkov, and the rest of the banged up Panthers, has the team refreshed entering September for the first time in years. With nearly the entire 2025 Stanley Cup winning core still on the team and Brady Tkachuk added to the fold, Florida looks ready to win its third Stanley Cup in four seasons.

Nivison: Celebrini should have won the Hart Trophy last season, but for some incomprehensible reason, he wasn't even a finalist. This year, Celebrini replicates that performance and gets San Jose to the postseason to take home his first MVP award at age 20. Hughes posts a career year in his first full season with the Wild, and Spencer Carberry gets his flowers for winning the Metro Division after missing the playoffs last year.

Baumgartner: McDavid's ability to take over a game was evident nearly every time he touched the ice last season. His 24 points (11 goals,13 assists) in the final 14 games of the regular season -- without Leon Draisaitl in the lineup -- was one of the many reasons I put him No. 1 on my Hart Trophy ballot. With just two years left on his current contract, desperation may start to kick in to get the job in Edmonton, which would lead to another MVP-caliber season. Barkov is healthy and the frontrunner to win his fourth Selke, and Dahlin will have another strong season to take home his first career Norris Trophy.

#210. Meltdown in LA: What went wrong for Rams as Cardinals earn largest upset of the season

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

As Chad Ryland's 43-yard field goal went through the uprights as time expired, the Cardinals capped a wild finish and opened up a whole new set of questions for Los Angeles. The kick, which gave the Cardinals an 18-16 win over the Rams, marked the largest upset of the season. Arizona, which entered as 13.5-point underdogs, also tied for the largest upset of any game in the past five years. It was the largest upset loss of Matthew Stafford's career thus far.

The Cardinals, who did not score a single touchdown, led 15-12 with under three minutes left. Stafford led a quick touchdown drive, fueled by big completions to Puka Nacua and capped by a 5-yard touchdown pass to Colby Parkinson with 47 seconds left. Punter Ethan Evans made the extra point after new kicker Blake Grupe got hurt making a tackle earlier in the game.

The Rams then kicked off into the end zone — sending the ball to the Cardinals' 35-yard line — and Jacoby Brissett found Jalen Brooks for a 21-yard play on the first play of the drive. Add in a 15-yard unnecessary roughness penalty on Josh Wallace, and that was all it took to set up Ryland's game-winner.

BRISSETT TO BROOKS PAST MIDFIELDAZvsLAR on FOX/FOX OneStream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/YcxBytI37I

Give tons of credit to the Cardinals, who earned their first win since the season opener. The maligned defense had a major bounce back after allowing 45 points last week to the Lions, and the offense rolled up 338 yards and scored on six of its 10 drives. Yes, all the scores were field goals, but Arizona's ability to stay on track — Brissett didn't take a single sack and didn't turn it over after the first possession — was key. Arizona had nearly 10 minutes more of possession time than Los Angeles did.

But this is really on the Rams, who are 2-4 after entering the season as the Super Bowl favorite. In fact, it's the same record as the Cardinals.

The offense was disjointed, the defense failed to make the big plays, and special teams issues loomed large again.

Before the madness at the end of the game, it looked like this would be the defining play of the game: fourth-and-8, and the Rams do this.

Pass is incomplete and the Cardinals force a turnover on downs 👀AZvsLAR on FOX/FOX OneStream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/u0bfxJgdFJ

A running back screen — and a failed one at that — in that situation sums up the Rams offense's woeful day. Stafford finished 25-for-33 for 222 yards, two touchdowns and no interceptions, but before that, it was an absolute slog: 18-for-26 for just 137 yards. Add in three sacks, and Stafford had a putrid 4.2 yards per attempt.

Stafford was getting rid of the ball in 2.50 seconds. He had thrown two deep passes. He was averaging 4.6 yards downfield per throw; for reference, Bo Nix is at 4.9 yards, and that's the lowest number through six games in the past 20 years.

In other words, basically nothing in the explosive department. The Rams had only two plays of 20+ yards, and both came on the last drive. Keep in mind this is a defense that allowed five plays of 20+ yards in three quarters against the Lions in Week 5.

There were a few opportunities for big plays — Stafford missed an open Nacua on one notable one — but largely, the quick-passing game appeared planned, and the Cardinals dominated it.

If big plays aren't on the menu, there's no margin for error elsewhere. The Rams had plenty of mistakes, though. Arguably, the biggest was a Tyler Higbee fumble.

SIMON + BURKE ON THE FUMBLE AND RECOVERY 😮‍💨#AZvsLAR | 📺 FOX pic.twitter.com/QyCLr3X7wZ

The play before that, Stafford stumbled and fumbled — untouched — when trying to wheel out of the pocket. He recovered the ball, but it set the Rams way behind the sticks on another unforced error. And in another key moment, Los Angeles failed on a fourth-and-1 on a run by backup tight end Davis Allen, a curious play call at best.

The Rams also committed four penalties, three crucial:

The Rams are tied for the 12th-most offensive penalties and tied for the fourth-most defensive penalties this season.

After a Brissett interception on the first drive, the Rams did not have another takeaway. They also recorded zero sacks against a quarterback who's among the more statuesque in the game and an offense down its top offensive lineman (Paris Johnson Jr.) and its top running back (Jeremiyah Love).

The Rams have eight sacks all year. Entering "Sunday Night Football" that is tied for the third-fewest in the NFL. And four of those eight came in one game, against the offensively hapless Eagles. Myles Garrett's absence is a major issue, but several other talented pass rushers aren't getting it done.

Grupe nailed his first field goal attempt, a 44-yarder, in the first quarter. Good news! But the Rams gave up a 40-yard return to Devin Duvernay on the ensuing kickoff, and Grupe hurt his knee making the tackle.

New Rams kicker Blake Grupe is doubtful to return after making this tackle pic.twitter.com/EgxKFTFSsq

The Rams have now lost games by two, three and four points, and special teams problems have featured heavily in all three. The Grupe injury is out of their control, but it came after they allowed yet another huge kickoff return.

Simply put, the Rams have huge problems in all three phases, a truly stunning sentence to type. A team all-in on a Super Bowl just lost to a team that's been counted out for months. Sean McVay's nightmare start continues to get worse.

#211. NBA's most underrated players: An improving LaMelo Ball, a picked-on James Harden ... and a rookie?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Every year, major media outlets (including us!) release a list of the best players in the NBA. And every year, that list is remembered for maybe a dozen or so slights. Social media typically rallies a handful of fanbases to outrage against how unfairly the outlet in question is treating their favorite player, and among those aggrieved cities, a few turn out to be completely correct when the season actually arrives, thereby invalidating the entire exercise in their eyes.In defense of those outlets (again… ours included!), the voting body is not a monolith. Just because one list is lower on your favorite player than you think it should be doesn't mean every individual voter was.And so, with our list of the top 100 players in the NBA now released, we've decided to give our voters the chance to join those social media hordes and explain where we believe our colleagues erred. Each of our voters selected one player, based on their own top 100 rankings and the final list we published as a group, to name as the league's most underrated player. Maybe we were too low on your favorite player as a whole, but maybe you'll cut us a bit of slack when you find out that he had at least one staunch defender in our ranks.

Top 100 ranking: No. 30Why he should be higher: The Hawks' young star wing upped his production, improved his shooting efficiency and was the No. 1 option on a playoff team to earn his first All-Star and All-NBA selection in 2025. I think that's deserving of a bit more than the No. 30 spot in our rankings. Yes, Johnson showed some growing pains in the playoffs, but was also dealing with a hellacious Knicks wing defense that went on to win a title. It's not hard to see this guy continuing to climb the NBA ladder into superstardom this season, and at 25 he's got plenty of runway to continue improving. He will continue to get more comfortable with being in a leading role, and his playmaking ability at 6-foot-8 is what every front office dreams of.  -- Robby Kalland

Top 100 ranking: No. 41Why he should be higher: If you're a skeptic because of his defense, his durability, even his maturity, fine, I can acknowledge those are real issues. I don't think people grasp just what an incredible shot-creator LaMelo Ball was last year. From Dec. 6 on, the Hornets had the NBA's best offense last season. In that span, the Charlotte offense declined by 13.2 points per 100 possessions during the minutes played without Ball... just below the amount the Nuggets declined without Nikola Jokić (13.4) in that same window. Charlotte's starters had the highest offensive rating of any five-man lineup to play 200 minutes last year at a bonkers 134.9 points per 100 possessions.

Well... let's look at how those starters fared without LaMelo last season. Brandon Miller's true shooting was four percentage points higher with Ball on the court than without him. The other three starters (Kon Knueppel, Miles Bridges and Moussa Diabaté) all saw their true shooting decline by at least eight percentage points without him. Last season saw Ball post his lowest individual scoring and assist numbers since his rookie year... yet it was far and away the best NBA season he's ever played. His presence is transformative for everyone else on the floor offensively, and keep in mind, he's mostly wasted that effect on bad teams. Now he gets to amplify Anthony Edwards, and I'm betting that will trigger an overdue wave of appreciation for one of the game's best young creators. -- Sam Quinn

Top 100 ranking: No. 47Why he should be higher: What are we doing here? Donovan Mitchell recently went too far when he tried to make the case that "the only reason" Harden isn't venerated like LeBron James and Kevin Durant is "because of championship convos." That particular caveat groans from the hilarious weight it carries. Mitchell went out on a limb, and it immediately snapped. But here we are at the other end of the spectrum with guys like Franz Wagner and Paolo Banchero ranked ahead of Harden. Harden is an 11-time All-Star with eight All-NBA nods to his credit. He's a former MVP. He's a three-time scoring champ. He was named to the NBA's 75th Anniversary team. Wagner and Banchero are ... not those things. Harden hasn't exactly covered himself in glory in the postseason, particularly where his defense and judgment have been suspect. Still, it ought to be possible to hold more than one thought at a time. He's surely flawed — just as he's better than we give him credit for in our rankings. -- John Gonzalez

Top 100 ranking: No. 68Why he should be higher: Sabonis missed nearly the entire 2025-26 season due to a knee injury. When he's healthy, Sabonis is one of the best floor-raisers in the NBA because of his rebounding, screening and passing. When the Kings had the best offense in the NBA during the 2022-23 season, it was because of Sabonis. He operated as the hub of the offense and created shots for others within the flow of the system. Sacramento's current system — and the lack of the right personnel around him — has led people to forget how good he can be. Sabonis, when healthy, is a top-40 player in the league. -- Cam Salerno

Top 100 ranking: No. 94Why he should be higher: It's strange to say a rookie is underrated before he's even played a regular-season game, and you can never read too much into preseason. But from what we've seen from Boozer so far, in addition to his college tape, it's hard to not be super excited. He already has NBA-level size and strength and is extremely polished on both ends of the floor. Just look at some of the stuff he's doing already as a 6-foot-10 forward.

cameron boozer off the dribble rim finishing pic.twitter.com/jhkryMfGZu

Plus, in Memphis, he'll be starting from opening night and given every opportunity to produce. All told, it's easy to understand why he's the favorite for Rookie of the Year in a loaded class. Whether he wins that award or not, there won't be 94 players better than Boozer this season. -- Jack Maloney

#212. Sabres Could Trade for 6-Foot-8 Old Friend Amid Dahlin Injury

The Buffalo Sabres have already had a bumpy season as far as injuries to defensemen are concerned.

They're currently missing Rasmus Dahlin due to an injury sustained a week ago. That comes after Mattias Samuelsson and Olen Zellweger both dealt with injuries late in the preseason that put their regular season availability in doubt.

It's the kind of bad injury luck that makes a team well aware of whether it could use some more depth. And while the Sabres aren't terribly positioned defensively, a few injuries could certainly make things a lot shakier in short order.

They could find potential help, though, in an old friend.

Sabres fans obviously won't have forgotten Tyler Myers. It's tough to forget a 6-foot-8 defenseman that suited up in Buffalo for years.

Myers currently plays for the Dallas Stars, who acquired him before last season's trade deadline from the Vancouver Canucks.

He's not much of an offensive difference maker anymore, but Myers is still an NHL-level defenseman.

Recently, he was named by The Athletic as a logical "under-the-radar" trade candidate for the Stars.

"Six-foot-8 defensemen don't grow on trees, though, and Myers — acquired at last season's deadline — could be appealing to a contender looking for depth on the right side," The Athletic's Mark Lazerus wrote.

There was no initial connection to the Sabres made in that article, but it's a fit that certainly makes some sense on paper.

Of course, Dahlin is a left-shot defenseman and Myers is a right-shot, so generally speaking, Myers wouldn't solve Dahlin's injury absence all by himself.

The Sabres will also be hoping Dahlin is back sooner rather than later, so this deal would ideally not be about Dahlin in the first place.

Instead, it'd be about adding veteran experience to the right side of defense in a way that could help over the course of a long season.

The Sabres have youngsters like Zach Metsa and Louis Crevier occupying spots on the right side, and this isn't to say Myers should take their spot. But he could serve as a great mentor, and injuries have been popping up fast and furious around the NHL this season, so Myers would also provide a great depth addition.

Lazerus does suggest in The Athletic's article that the Stars are more likely to be buyers than sellers, so maybe it'd take a very specific scenario for Buffalo, or any team, to pry Myers from Dallas.

But if he truly becomes available, it's not hard to imagine Myers in a Sabres uniform. He's already worn one many times.

#215. Bears DB Kyler Gordon: Return to lineup was "everything I wanted"

Bears defensive back Kyler Gordon’s lack of availability over the last two years has been a source of frustration for the Bears and his return to the lineup on Sunday illustrated why the team has missed him so much.

Gordon had three sacks and two forced fumbles, including a strip-sack of Falcons quarterback Michael Penix late in the fourth quarter that allowed the Bears to run out the clock on a 31-23 victory. He’s the second Bears defensive back to record three sacks in a game and the second defensive back for any team with at least three sacks and two forced fumbles in the same game.

Gordon missed the first five games of the season and all of the summer while working his way back from a calf injury that limited him to five appearances in 2025. After the game, he called the return “everything I wanted.”

“I wanted to be on the field and contribute, add to this team and help the direction we’re going to go, and that’s what I did,” Gordon said, via the team’s website.

No one will be expecting weekly repeats of Sunday’s exploits, but the Bears will be banking on Gordon staying in the lineup and working to make their defense better as they try to build on their 4-2 start to the season.

#216. State of the Ravens’ roster entering Week 7

The Baltimore Ravens have been battered around in the first six weeks of the season. They've lost starters and depth players to both short-term and long-term injuries with several already on season-ending IR. With the Browns game now over, let's check in on the current make up of the Ravens' roster and practice squad.

Active: Lamar Jackson, Tyler Huntley, Joe Fagnano

Lamar Jackson is expected back soon, potentially for next week's game against the Cincinnati Bengals. He's been phenomenal when healthy, and a 1-1 result in his two absences is not bad. Tyler Huntley did what a backup quarterback does: put together a solid game and then showed why he's a backup and not a starter. Undrafted rookie Joe Fagnano remains on the roster as the third-string quarterback, though Jackson's injury has elevated him to the No. 2 role for the last few weeks.

Active: Derrick Henry, Justice Hill, Rasheen Ali

Many expected the Ravens to carry four running backs rookie Adam Randall mysteriously landed on IR during 53-man roster cuts. There have been zero updates on his health since then, and no word on when his 21-day practice window before activation will start. The run game has slowed down in recent weeks with the offensive line shuffling and the injury to Lamar Jackson, but Derrick Henry still has seven touchdowns in six games. Hill has been explosive in his role as the third-down back, throwing blocks, catching balls, and mixing in the occasional 20-yard carry. He's averaging 7.4 yards per carry this season, albeit on a limited sample size. Ali hasn't seen snaps on offense and was putting together a solid contract year on special teams before multiple gaffes on Sunday in Cleveland.

Active: Mark Andrews, Matt Hibner, Josh Cuevas, Nick Vannett

Practice squad: Ty Pezza, Lucas Scott (FB)

The Ravens lost tight end Durham Smythe for the season to an Achilles injury in Week 4 against the Titans. In response, they signed veteran Nick Vannett off their practice squad to replace Smythe's inline blocking. Matt Hibner also suffered a hand injury in Week 5 against the Falcons that has him out against the Browns and maybe longer, but head coach Jesse Minter said it won't be an IR situation. Outside of that, the biggest problem in the room is Mark Andrew's inability to transition from the YAC monster he once was to the possession tight end he is now. If he can transition into simply attacking the ball at the catch point and going down instead of trying to hit the button for the YAC option at the catch point, this room will be in better in great shape once Hibner and Josh Cuevas get involved as the explosive options. The latter had four catches for 44 yards and a touchdown in Cleveland.

Active: Zay Flowers, Rashod Bateman, Tez Walker, Ja'Kobi Lane, LaJohntay Wester, Elijah Sarratt

Practice squad: Chris Moore, Gage Larvadain

This might be the best wide receiver room in franchise history. Zay Flowers has been undeniably a top-5 pass-catcher this year and leads the league in several metrics. If you're looking at a graph on social media, he is probably in the upper-right (very good) corner of it. Rashod Bateman looks very comfortable in his role, shining when Flowers was absent in Week 2 and led the team in yards in Week 5's win. Tez Walker is still fighting for more playing time, but his ability as a deep threat is apparent in how often he can be seen flying by defensive backs on film. And now, Ja'Kobi Lane has returned to add a contested-catch element everyone has been excited for since he started balling in OTAs. In his first game back he had four catches for 40 yards as part of a clear effor to get him involved. Sarratt is best known for a costly holding penalty for now, but he was always going to face an uphill battle for snaps. This group can be truly special once Jackson returns at quarterback and the pass game takes over as the driving force for the offense.

Active: Ronnie Stanley, John Simpson, Vega Ioane, Andrew Vorhees, Roger Rosengarten, Carson Vinson, Emery Jones Jr., Cam Jurgens

Injured reserve: Danny Pinter (out for season), Jovaughn Gwyn, Ethan Pocic

Practice squad: Chuma Edoga, Kyle Hergel, Gerad Lictenhan, Andre James, A.J. Arcuri

This unit has been decimated. All three preseason starting center options are out long-term. Danny Pinter was declared out for the season in training camp; then both Jovaughn Gwyn and Ethan Pocic were lost in Week 3 with IR placements shortly after. Their eventual return hasn't been ruled out, but the Cam Jurgens trade seems to be signaling that the Ravens don't expect those guys to contribute again this year. Rookie guard Vega Ioane has been admirably playing center in the meantime, with Andrew Vorhees and Emery Jones each starting one game at right guard. Ioane will slide back to his natural position once Jurgens clears concussion protocol and enters the starting lineup.

The Ravens activated Kyle Hergel and Chuma Edoga this week against the Browns as depth with both Vorhees and Jones questionable. Hergel is out of elevations and could be added to the 53-man roster as the backup center moving forward.

Active: Nnamdi Madubuike, Travis Jones, Calais Campbell, John Jenkins, Broderick Washington, Aeneas Peebles

Practice squad: Rayshaun Benny, David Olajiga

This group has been led by the resurgence of Nnamdi Madubuike, who has picked up where he left off pre-injury as a dominant 3-tech, and Calais Campbell's continued excellence in his 19th NFL season. Travis Jones hasn't been bad, but he has not lived up to post-extension expectations. He missed a large portion of camp with a pec injury, so hopefully he'll continue to round into form. John Jenkins and Broderick Washington have disappeared at times as the unit's designated run-stoppers, and I personally continue to question their activation over Aeneas Peebles – especially Washington. Speaking of which, Peebles has been a healthy scratch since Madubuike's return, despite the pass-rush win rates he stacked in the early weeks beforehand. Washington was sidelined in Week 6, but Peebles only got a handful of snaps. His penetration ability may only come into play in specific game scripts.

Active: Trey Hendrickson, Mike Green, Tavius Robinson, Zion Young, Ethan Burke

Practice squad: Adisa Isaac, Kaimon Rucker

Trey Hendrickson's return to the lineup could take this group to new heights. He was fantastic in his first couple of games while playing with a broken finger. He may lack elite counting stats, but his pressure and win rates match his film of a disruptive, productive rusher. In Hendrickson's absence in Weeks 4 and 5, Mike Green stepped up massively with eight pressures and a pass rush win rate over 20%. However, he and his All-Pro teammate cannot seem to get going when they are both on the field. Tavius Robinson's pass rush metrics haven't been great, but he leads the team in sacks and continues to be a menace against the run. He consistently makees plays and could be pricing himself out of Baltimore this coming offseason. Zion Young has a solidified role on run downs, and his play strength consistently shows up on tape, even if his pass rush impact has been up and down. UDFA Ethan Burke nabbed his first sack against the Titans, but his role on defense will likely be minimized with Hendrickson's return.

Active: Roquan Smith, Trenton Simpson, Teddye Buchanan, Jay Higgins, Carl Jones

This group has been excellent, specifically Smith and Simpson. Smith is bouncing back from two down years following Mike Macdonald's departure. Simpson has been a weapon, flying around the field with unmatched physicality. Outside of Kyle Hamilton, he has arguably been the best player on the Ravens' defense in the first six weeks. The decision that will surround keeping Simpson and Smith's cuttable contract next year will be fascinating to see this offseason. Teddye Buchanan will likely factor into that decision as his playing time continues to grow following the knee injury he suffered last year. He made plays last week in his highest snap-count game as the Ravens kept all three of those linebackers on the field more often to bottle up Bijan Robinson. Jay Higgins and Carl Jones mostly factor in as a special teams contributors; the latter has picked up extra snaps with Ja'Kobi Lane replacing Chris Moore on the active roster.

Active: Marlon Humphrey, Nate Wiggins, Chidobe Awuzie, Chandler Rivers, Keyon Martin

Practice squad: Amani Oruwariye, Lardarius Webb Jr.

This group has been up and down to start this year. They lost T.J. Tampa early in the season after expecting him to take on a significant rotational role. Humphrey and Wiggins have seen the majority of snaps outside, while Minter has occasionally rotated in Chidobe Awuzie. Both have made plays throughout this season, but multiple wide receivers have had big games against the Ravens. Keyon Martin started the season as the slot corner in dime packages, but rookie Chandler Rivers took over in Week 2. Rivers' play has been a rollercoaster, especially in coverage, which led to Martin getting his job back in Week 6. There's been little update on when Tampa or Bihlal Kone, who was placed on IR before the initial 53-man roster, could return. Either one of them would be welcomed depth and fit Minter's scheme well.

Active: Kyle Hamilton, Malaki Starks, Jaylinn Hawkins, Keondre Jackson, K'Von Wallace

Outside of Kyle Hamilton, this room has been a massive disappointment for most of the season. Hamilton is, of course, playing at his usual All-Pro level. But Malaki Starks and Jaylinn Hawkins have had rough starts to the season. Both are playing with hesitation and simply looked uncomfortable in the first quarter of the season with tackling issues that hurt the whole defense. Starks has looked better across the last few weeks, especially during last week's homecoming in Atlanta. The Georgia native played at 100 miles per hour and aggressively drove downhill against Bijan Robinson and the Falcons' other skill players. In that game, Hawkins' snap count took a big hit due to the Ravens playing three-linebacker looks, but he was back to a regular workload in Cleveland. The call for Hamilton to move back into coverage in tandem with Starks to help the secondary's pass defense has been loud, but that would limit his impact around the line of scrimmage. Keondre Jackson continues to be the special teams demon he was last year and could be ready for a defensive role if injuries pop up. K'Von Wallace hasn't seen defensive time and primarily offers depth on special teams.

Active: K Tyler Loop, P Ryan Eckley, LS Nick Moore

After tons of doubt about Loop's position on this roster, the second-year kicker proved himself to start the regular season. He hit a massive game-winner against Dallas and converted his first five attempts over 50 yards, something he struggled as a rookie. He even set an M&T Bank Stadium record with a 64-yard field goal in Week 4. Loop did have his worst miss of this season against the Browns, mishitting a 49-yard attempt that proved to be massive in the loss, but on the flip side, the Ravens might be 2-4 without him right now. Ryan Eckley has been perfectly average as a rookie punter without any major mistakes, which is all you can ask for. (Remember Jordan Stout's rookie year?) Nick Moore continues to be the engine of the unit and has even gotten involved on a few tackles.

The vision for this roster is finally aking shape after early-season struggles. If Lamar Jackson and Cam Jurgens are ready to play next week, the Ravens will field their best game day squad this season. While the loss against the Browns was brutal, there's a clear path for this team to be very good if Jackson stays healthy and Jurgens raises the floor and ceiling of the offensive line. Younger contributors like T.J. Tampa, Adam Randall, and Bilhal Kone are all available to come off IR as well, which could cause some more roster shifting. Players on the fringes of the roster like Carl Jones and K'Von Wallace would likely be the first to if space is needed, but as always, injuries can make these moves clearer.

#218. NFL Week 6 winners and losers: Giants face QB, RB turmoil while Browns take control of AFC North

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

A little over a month ago, Jameis Winston watching a New York Giants game from the sideline would have been a non-story. In Week 6, it was a defining reality of the team's disheartening 34-27 loss to the New Orleans Saints. That is how far the Giants have fallen since their exciting season-opening win. Everything is still in front of them, and they might just have found their starting quarterback for the rest of the year in J.J. McCarthy, but there is no other way to define Sunday's defeat as a step backward.

Meanwhile, another team that has spent the majority of this decade at the bottom of its division is on the rise. The Cleveland Browns won their fourth game of the year this week and now hold tiebreakers over two of their rivals as they stand atop the AFC North. Preseason expectations? Forget about them. Deshaun Watson has the Browns cooking.

The dichotomy between winners and losers is always stark in the NFL, and Week 6 in particular displayed just how wide the chasm can be. Below are those who came out on top and those who were not nearly as fortunate during Sunday's action.

The situation in the Meadowlands is not a complete disaster, given that the Giants still lead the NFC East, but Sunday's loss hurts. There is no such thing as a "must-win" game in Week 6, but what the Giants just experienced was a defeat in a contest that held a lot of hope for New York. The opportunity to pull further ahead in a downtrodden division while playing a Saints team on a three-game losing streak escaped them. That result could haunt them down the line.

Not only had New Orleans gone a month between victories, but it also trotted out a quarterback in Tyler Shough who has broken bones in his non-throwing hand. The New York defense watched the injured signal-caller throw for three touchdowns and rack up 34 points. And on the other side of the ball, perhaps John Harbaugh should not have relegated Cam Skattebo to the sideline, because giving him only six snaps and holding him without a touch did not help the Giants' offense. He struggled with fumbles in Weeks 1-5, yes, but he remains one of the team's top weapons and was noticeably absent while the unit around him floundered.

It was a pleasant surprise to see McCarthy enter the game for the Giants and amass 243 passing yards and a touchdown in the fourth quarter alone, but now New York faces questions about whether to trust McCarthy as a starter moving forward or whether to continue with the "Jameis Winston experience." In other words, Harbaugh is stuck between a rock and a hard place.

The last time the Browns held at least a share of first place in the AFC North this deep into a season was more than a decade ago in 2014. A team that entered the year projected to be in the mix for the No. 1 overall draft pick leads its division a month and a half into the campaign. First-year coach Todd Monken deserves heaps of credit for orchestrating a 4-2 start and putting his squad at the forefront of the most competitive divisional race in the NFL.

Cleveland has the same record as the Steelers and Ravens, but it now holds the tiebreaker over both rivals thanks to the Week 6 triumph over Baltimore. Its defense was excellent from the second quarter onward, holding the Ravens off the board after a 10-point first period and opening the door for its offense to squeak out a win. Watson's shockingly clutch performances just keep on coming, and this time, he set up a game-winning 37-yard field goal off the foot of Andre Szmyt as time expired.

The Los Angeles Rams, by way of tiebreakers, are the last-place team in the NFC West through Week 6. That is a sentence so difficult to fathom, considering their offseason successes, that it almost does not feel real. Anyone who has watched them play over the season's first month and a half understands why they hold a 2-4 record: They have looked nothing like the superstar-laden squad they are on paper. But that does not make it any easier to digest just how stunning a failure these first six weeks have been.

The bewildering 18-16 loss the Rams sustained at home against the Arizona Cardinals was the biggest upset of the season to date. Cardinals kicker Chad Ryland walked it off with a 43-yard field goal to push the NFL's most disappointing team to the bottom of their division.

Maybe Myles Garrett will fix this team when he recovers from his knee surgery, but the Rams feel more than one player away. Matthew Stafford has not been anywhere near as sharp as he was in his MVP season last year. Puka Nacua's absence hurt the offense in the first two games, the defense continues to allow far more points than anticipated and three different players have attempted a field goal or extra point in the last two games. This is a mess.

Tom Brady has company in the history books — there is now a tie for the fastest quarterback to reach 100 career wins. It took Patrick Mahomes only 131 games to cross the century mark, which matches the volume of contests Brady required to reach that threshold. Joe Montana was the third-fastest at 139 games.

Mahomes secured win No. 100 against the Los Angeles Chargers and did so in convincing fashion. His defense did the heavy lifting as the Kansas City Chiefs stifled Justin Herbert and the opposing offense in a 22-6 smothering, but he held up his end of the bargain, too, with an efficient effort through the air: 23-for-30 for 272 yards. Kenneth Walker III aided Mahomes with another remarkable performance in the ground game with 128 rushing yards and a pair of touchdowns.

It might be tanking season in Philadelphia. Jalen Hurts is on injured reserve as he recovers from a blood clot in his leg. The offensive line is in shambles. The running back unit is a shell of its former self due to a plethora of injuries. Nolan Smith suffered a concussion on Sunday. The Eagles slipped to 2-4 on the year with a 25-14 loss to the Carolina Panthers. There is hardly anything for fans to cling to as a source of optimism that this season will turn around.

The Panthers sacked Tanner McKee on the first play from scrimmage, and that set the tone for a game that was always just out of the Eagles' reach. McKee was serviceable in his third career start, but hardly anything more than that. He will need to be more efficient if Philadelphia is to stay above water during Hurts' absence, but that might not be the point anymore. The arguments for this franchise to tear everything down and look to the future are as strong as ever.

A couple of things went poorly for the Texans during their trip to London, but neither cost them the game. They overcame an untimely C.J. Stroud interception and another head-scratchingly porous showing from their defense to notch a 34-31 win over the Jaguars in Jacksonville's home away from home. Ka'imi Fairbairn booted a game-sealing field goal at the horn to give Houston its second-consecutive win and move the squad one step closer to becoming just the second team in NFL history to reach the playoffs on the heels of an 0-4 start.

Stroud was fantastic outside of that fourth-quarter turnover. He continues to show immense growth after falling under the microscope for a disappointing 2025 season, and he completed 24 of 34 passes for 312 yards and a season-high three touchdowns on the Jaguars. The interception was only his first of the year, and he did not take a sack. This is as comfortable as Stroud has looked running the Houston offense since he won the NFC Offensive Rookie of the Year award three seasons ago.

The biggest winner on the Texans' side in Week 6, however, might have been Marvin Harrison Jr. It would have been understandable if he was silent less than a week after being traded from the Arizona Cardinals, because learning a playbook on such short notice and doing so while traveling overseas is a significant task. Instead, he caught three passes on four targets for his best game of the campaign. The numbers were still modest, but this is a solid starting point for him as he works to rekindle his career in a new situation. His chemistry with Stroud, which dates back to their Ohio State days, was clear. As it regrows, it could help Harrison turn into the star he was expected to be.

The greatest players in football have a special gift: They often show fans something they have never seen before. Josh Allen tends to do that on a regular basis. He did it again in the Buffalo Bills' 33-30 win over the Las Vegas Raiders. On the same throw in which he tied Jim Kelly for the most touchdown passes in Bills history, Allen recorded one of the most eye-popping highlights of the year.

Josh Allen just threw a BACKHAND TOUCHDOWN PASS to Keon Coleman 🤯 pic.twitter.com/nYIaD8HM0L

The scramble and underhanded flick to Keon Coleman gave the Bills a 10-point buffer, which came in handy since the Raiders rattled off 17 points in the fourth quarter. Allen finished the day with 255 passing yards and two touchdowns.

To be clear, the Steelers won and are right where they want to be in a tie atop the AFC North, so Mike McCarthy has done plenty well in his first year as Pittsburgh's coach. True at the same time, however, is that Sunday was one he would largely like to forget. And it would have been even worse if not for the team pulling off its biggest fourth-quarter comeback in 34 years.

The Steelers might have won the game in regulation if McCarthy had held onto his second timeout. Tampa Bay was rushing its special teams unit onto the field in the closing seconds, needing to convert a 53-yard field goal to force overtime. The kick would have come in a battle against the clock — with the game ball in play rather than a kicking ball — had McCarthy not asked for a stoppage. His timeout allowed the Buccaneers to set everything up, and they converted to force the extra period. There is no guarantee they would have missed if the Steelers had let the clock play out, but it would have been a much tougher attempt.

McCarthy also had the unpleasant experience of spending the entire halftime break in the sideline medical tent. He said after the game that he had his foot stepped on, which explains the limp he displayed as he walked into the tent at the end of the second quarter.

Mike McCarthy (ankle) QUESTIONABLE #Steelers #NFL pic.twitter.com/EijrUvY7R8

A win is a win, but it was an adventure for McCarthy to get there.

There is an extremely short list of NFL players since the 1970 merger to record a touchdown and an interception in the same game. Travis Hunter now resides on that list. He shined on offense and defense in the Jaguars' international defeat to the Texans, so even though it came in a losing effort, this is precisely what was promised when he arrived in the league as a unicorn two-way talent.

Prior to the season, the Jaguars committed to deploying Hunter primarily at cornerback with a limited number of snaps at wide receiver, and they have executed that plan. His offensive opportunities have been — and likely will continue to be — few and far between. But Sunday's three-tackle, four-catch game resembled the unfathomable production he posted in college and exemplified what is possible if coach Liam Coen expands his snap count.

Win No. 1 is in the books; the Tennessee Titans will not go 0-17. They built their first second-half lead since Week 2 and, unlike last time, actually closed it out for a 26-20 victory over the Indianapolis Colts. Two touchdowns and two field goals in the fourth quarter helped them erase what was a 13-0 halftime deficit, and no play was bigger than the punt block Oluwafemi Oladejo returned to the end zone for a go-ahead touchdown. Joey Slye's field goals in the final two minutes and three seconds were the difference.

Maybe this is the win that breaks the seal and helps Robert Saleh salvage Year 1 of his tenure. The offense is still subpar, and Cam Ward had another clunker of a game, so it is still more realistic that Tennessee scuffles its way to the finish line. But confidence goes a long way.

Rule No. 1 as a punt and kick returner is to hold onto the ball. Zachariah Branch failed to follow that rule in the Atlanta Falcons' 31-23 loss to the Chicago Bears. The rookie muffed a punt and fumbled during a kickoff return, and the Bears recovered both loose balls to help them build an overwhelming 31-7 lead.

Bijan Robinson comforting Branch after his fumble 📺: FOX/FOX One pic.twitter.com/oVJuU0l6Mt

Atlanta nearly bailed Branch out with a ferocious comeback effort. The Bears pulled their starters early in the fourth quarter, which opened the door for Atlanta to score a pair of touchdowns and threaten to tie the game. It still came up a touchdown and 2-point conversion short, though.

#219. Lakers coach JJ Redick on Bronny James: 'I don't think he's played well' in preseason games

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Through the Lakers' first four preseason games, guard Bronny James hasn't been able to find a rhythm. James, who is entering Year 3 of his NBA career and playing his first season without his father, LeBron James, on the same team, has 11 points and 12 turnovers combined in the preseason.

In the Lakers' 101-89 loss to the Warriors on Wednesday in Las Vegas, James went scoreless in 11 minutes of action. James attempted just two shots and finished with one rebound, one steal and four turnovers.

After the game, Lakers coach JJ Redick said James hasn't "played well" in the Lakers' preseason games but has had good practices leading up to the preseason.

"I thought he had a really nice September and a good summer with us, but I don't think he's played well in the four preseason games, but he's had good practices," Redick said. "Again, some of it is just rhythm, some of it is who he's playing with. He's played a lot of minutes, especially in the second half of games with our two-way guys. Tonight he played with Rafael (Castro), who has been with us for three days. Some of it is like the group he's with. I think that is not necessarily setting him up for success."

The Lakers guaranteed James' deal for the 2026-27 season at $2.29 million earlier this summer as part of the four-year, $7.89 million contract he signed after being selected with the No. 55 overall pick in the 2024 NBA Draft. Heading into this summer, only $1.25 million of the $2.29 million salary was guaranteed.

The Lakers currently have 16 players on their active roster and will have to trim it down at least one spot ahead of cutdown day on Monday. Los Angeles has one final preseason game against the Nuggets on Friday before opening the regular season at home against the Warriors on Oct. 21.

After playing 27 regular-season games in 2024-25, James appeared in 42 last season. The younger James also split time with the South Bay Lakers (now the Coachella Valley Lakers), the team's G League affiliate. James shot 38.6% from the 3-point line (on 1.4 attempts per game) and earned playoff minutes throughout the first round against the Rockets.

However, heading into Year 3, it's unclear what his role looks like. Lakers star Luka Dončić didn't play against the Warriors on Wednesday, but Redick still played 16 different players, with James logging 11 minutes off the bench.

#220. Dodgers manager Dave Roberts explains leaving Blake Snell in before costly back-to-back home runs in Game 3

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

After six innings of work in Wednesday's Game 3 of the NLCS, Los Angeles Dodgers lefty Blake Snell had more than done his job. After allowing a first-pitch home run to the first batter of the game, Snell settled in and rode a crackling fastball in front of his abundant secondaries to a nine-strikeout, one-walk performance in which he allowed only that one run. Manager Dave Roberts, though, decided to let Snell come out for the seventh inning, and that proved a crucial decision in the eventual 6-2 loss to the Milwaukee Brewers that pushed the Dodgers to the brink of elimination.

Snell entered the seventh inning having faced 21 batters, which put him well into the perilous third time through the opposing order. The Brewers' four-five-six batters were due up, and a right-handed batter, Andrew Vaughn, was due up first. Snell walked him on seven pitches. Then Jake Bauers stepped in, and Roberts left Snell in to face the lefty. On the 11th and final pitch of the marathon at-bat, Bauers turned the game on its ear:

Snell's night still wasn't over, even after being worked for 18 pitches by the previous two batters. Another lefty, Garrett Mitchell, ignored the platoon disadvantage and made it back-to-back homers off a laboring Snell:

That was the first time in Snell's career that he'd allowed consecutive home runs to left-handed batters. Given the punchless Dodgers offensive attack, those two homers all but ended the game and the series. That put Roberts' decision to push his luck with Snell under the microscope.

"I just saw that through the sixth inning, and then once we got to the seventh inning, I think he retired 13 or 14 in a row and his stuff was really good," Roberts said postgame of his decision to stick with Snell. "I don't think they were seeing him well. I was trying to get him three more hitters. We had Evan (Phillips) for that fourth hitter. He had his way with those two lefties and took care of Vaughn.

"Obviously the leadoff walk hurt. Hasn't given up a homer all year, but it just -- it's baseball. For me, I felt good with where Blake's stuff was at. You've got to give Bauers credit. He put together another good at-bat, which he did at their place and spurred that rally, and then right there saw eight, nine pitches and ended up hitting a homer."

And of the decision to stay with Snell even after the Bauers home run, Roberts said:

"The Bauers at-bat, it's the middle of the at-bat, so he's going to finish that at-bat. Then he gives up a homer, you're down a run. For me, I just don't think it made sense, given where he was throwing the baseball, pitch count, all that stuff, to allow him to get through Mitchell, where I thought he took -- he was throwing well against him, yeah."

Snell indeed had not allowed a home run all season up until Game 3. That season, though, has been far from a full one thanks to shoulder and elbow issues.

He also didn't allow a home run in his NLDS start against the Braves. That, however, was never going to last, especially with a pitcher like Snell, who doesn't have any ground-ball tendencies of note. Regression on that home runs allowed front was always coming for him, and it came in Game 3 at just the wrong time. Making it all possible was Roberts' decision to let Snell pitch longer than he should have.

#221. Kawhi Leonard: a hero’s complicated return to the Toronto Raptors

When Kawhi Leonard became a Toronto Raptor for the first time in the summer of 2018, he looked shellshocked. "There's just more questions you have to ask me in order for me to tell you about myself," he said, introducing himself to an organization and city he reportedly had no interest in joining.

Leonard had fallen out with his former team, the San Antonio Spurs – one of the most respected franchises in professional sports – due to differences in opinion about an injury that had limited him to just nine games in the 2017-18 season. The Los Angeles native had hoped to end up in southern California, but instead the Raptors risked it all by swapping franchise cornerstone DeMar DeRozan for one year of an injured, malcontent Leonard. It worked: Leonard led the Raptors to their maiden championship on the back of a historic playoff run, averaging 30.5 points, 9.1 rebounds, 3.9 assists and 1.7 steals en route. Leonard won his second finals MVP to go alongside the one he had claimed with the Spurs when he helped them to the title in 2014.

Related: LeBron James is everything Philadelphia wants. And everything it can't stand | Bryan Armen Graham

"The narrative of not wanting to come to this city is gone," the team's president, Masai Ujiri, said at that 2018 press conference, speaking to insecure Raptors fans who had watched American players like Vince Carter, Tracy McGrady, and Chris Bosh leave Toronto since the franchise opened its doors in 1995. "We should move past that. Believe in this city. Believe in yourselves … We are proud of who we are."

But even a historic season wasn't enough to convince Leonard to stay north of the border. After a long and contentious free-agency period managed by his uncle, Dennis Robertson, Leonard spurned the reigning champions in favor of his hometown Los Angeles Clippers. "There wasn't as much anger in 2019 as there was with Vince Carter or some of the other guys who left," says Bruce Arthur, who has covered Leonard since 2018 for the Toronto Star. "I think he was given a little bit of special dispensation because he was going home, because he had delivered a title, and because I never felt like there was ever a connection outside of Kawhi the basketball player, with Toronto."

Raptors fans' anger was instead directed towards the Clippers, who not only showed up to almost every Raptors game during the championship season, but who also, we now know, went under the table to ensure Leonard signed lucrative endorsement deals totaling over $50m – violating the NBA's salary cap rules.

Robertson was suspended for five years and Clippers owner Steve Ballmer was handed the harshest punishment in NBA history, including the loss of five first-round draft picks and a year-long suspension. However, thanks to a side-deal between the NBA and its Players Association executed to avoid arbitration, Leonard was given a relatively light $700,000 fine (he has earned $375m in salary so far in his career).

"Kawhi's … gotten away really clean from what is obviously out-of-bounds behavior," says Arthur, who reported that Leonard – as much as he pleads ignorance to all this – was in the room when Robertson asked the Raptors for an ownership stake in the Toronto Maple Leafs and at least $10m per year in no-show sponsorship deals in 2019. "So, perfect heist-type stuff from Kawhi."

Despite being one of the greatest players of his generation, the 35-year-old has burned bridges on his way out of every franchise he's played for. Spurs fans are still upset by the way his injury was handled in 2017-18, while Clippers fans are distraught about being left holding the bag without even a genuine apology from Leonard. But Raptors fans have much more complicated feelings towards the seven-time All-Star – arguably the best player in franchise history.

On the one hand, "There was a sense of defiance, especially the first year after Kawhi left [when the Raptors lost to the Boston Celtics in Game 7 of the Eastern Conference semi-finals] ... and there was a great deal of pride that went into that," says William Lou, the host and creator of the Hello and Welcome podcast. But as time went on, "The Clippers were humbled in a basketball sense. They never could get that version of Kawhi … that Toronto got in their one year, and so it's hard to be too mad."

Arthur says Raptors fans will always associate Leonard with the championship win. "I think the bottom line isn't necessarily about a lack of moral reckoning by Raptors fans as much as: this guy's so good that you forgive him, right?" says Arthur. "The [championship] was the greatest moment in franchise history by galaxies. Two and a half million people on the streets of Toronto for the parade. That was one of the best days Toronto's ever had."

The sentiment was seemingly shared by the organization. Despite being frustrated by the way his previous free agency unfolded, the Raptors front office couldn't pass up the opportunity to grab the lifeline Leonard represented – even in his mid 30s. The Raptors have failed to win a playoff series since 2020, a stretch that includes three grim seasons of 30 wins or fewer. Last season, the franchise pulled itself out of the dregs of the league thanks to a star leap from 25-year-old Scottie Barnes and a handful of smart trades and draft picks, but the Raptors looked like a relatively expensive, middle-of-the-pack team with a difficult path towards contention until Leonard not only became available, but pushed his way towards Toronto.

"This city took a liking to my family, and I took a liking to this city," Leonard said in the team-owned documentary series Open Gym after the Raptors traded Brandon Ingram, Gradey Dick, two first-round picks, two second-round picks and a pick-swap for him in mid-September. "Hopefully they embrace me back and [I] give them my all again, and we can make something special happen once again."

Although there were extenuating circumstances leading to Leonard's return – he and the Clippers are under investigation by the Justice Department – it is meaningful that he chose the Raptors over big-market championship contenders like Miami, Minnesota, and Detroit. It's also important that he proclaimed his desire to retire a Raptor before signing a two-year, $115m extension with the franchise. "He deserves to have his jersey retired somewhere," says Lou. "But due to the circumstances of his career, he kind of was a player without a home."

Leonard now has a chance to rewrite his complicated legacy with a familiar franchise. Leading the Raptors back to anywhere near the promised land would ensure him a jersey retirement ceremony, a first-ballot Hall of Fame induction, and Canadian sports immortality.

The Raptors, meanwhile, aren't just getting an upgrade at the wing position; they are getting an all-time great coming off one of the best seasons of his career – an American superstar who experienced all the small cultural discomforts of playing in Toronto and still had such positive memories of the fans, organization, and city that he chose to return to.

"It's a little surreal having this guy who leaves after a championship, and you think the story's done there, and then he becomes the biggest scandal in the NBA, and then somehow forces his way to the Raptors," says diehard Raptors fan Imman Adan. "But I definitely think him coming back cements Toronto's legacy."

It's complicated, of course. It always will be so long as the Raptors are the lone NBA franchise outside of the United States. But no matter how Leonard's second tenure in Toronto plays out, his return is a stamp of approval – one that many Raptors fans have been waiting for since the franchise began.

F1 fans celebrate after the Formula 1 United States Grand Prix sprint race at Circuit of the Americas on Saturday, Oct. 18, 2025 in Austin. (Aaron E. Martinez/Austin American-Statesman)

#223. Kyren Williams: Offensive inconsistency "probably because I'm not out there"

Sunday’s 18-16 home loss to the Cardinals dropped the Rams to 2-4 and continued a start that has many people scratching their heads given how high the hopes were for the team heading into the season.

Everyone associated with the team is fielding questions about why things have gone so poorly, including running back Kyren Williams. Williams was asked about why he thinks the offense has been inconsistent from drive to drive over the first six weeks and he pointed to his role in his answer.

“I can’t tell you, bro,” Williams said, via Adam Grosbard of the Orange County Register. “Probably because I’m not out there.”

Williams played 70 percent of the snaps in the first five games and he outsnapped Blake Corum 42-16 on Sunday while fielding 13 touches to 11 for Corum. Williams’ workload is in line with last season, but down from its peak in 2024 and he’s seeing fewer carries than at any point since he became a starter. He was asked if he’d like to see that change in the coming weeks.

“I can’t really call that. It’s not on me,” Williams said. “But I just think no matter what, we gotta continue to have the energy. You gotta continue to, when plays are made, be excited, be happy so we uplift not only the offense but the defense and the special teams and just being able to have that camaraderie to where we’re playing off of each other and I think that’s what is going to allow us to be where we want to be.”

Musing about playing time and soul-searching about how to get into a groove weren’t the kinds of things people expected from the Rams this season, but that’s what happens when losses start to pile up and the Rams need to get right in a hurry if they want to avoid those things becoming the most consistent part of their season.
