#224. The Packers overcame disastrous first down results in win over Cowboys

The Green Bay Packers had plenty of bright spots in their victory over the Dallas Cowboys on Sunday Night Football, but the team's first down offense was not among them. The Packers consistently shot themselves in the foot at the start of offensive series throughout their 23-13 victory, regularly losing yardage and requiring Jordan Love to go into hero mode on second- and third-and-long situations.

Fortunately, Love did just that, as he threw for 276 yards and a touchdown while adding a second score on the ground, all while being pressured on nearly 50 percent of his dropbacks. With the Cowboys' defense consistently seeing big numbers on the yards to go category on the scoreboard, they were able to tee off on Love, hitting him several times and recording three sacks.

The fact that the Packers were able to score 23 points — a number that probably should have been more like 30, had their receivers caught the football in the end zone consistently — is truly remarkable given the disaster that the Packers put up on first down. Of the Packers' 27 plays run on first down (not including one defensive penalty), the team failed to gain yardage on 13 of them, either via incomplete pass, no gain or loss of yardage on the ground, or an offensive penalty. That's roughly half of the time that the team still has double-digit yards to gain after a first down play.

In those 27 snaps, the Packers managed to have a "success" (defined as picking up at least 40% of the required yards to gain) on just 5 of them. That's a hilariously bad 18.5% success rate on first down, and consistently setting themselves up in long distance situations required Love and the Packers to have a 65% success rate on 3rd and 4th downs to make up for it.

Indeed, Love was 2/7 passing for just nine yards on first downs; on all other downs, he was 22/34 for 269 yards and a touchdown. (His rushing touchdown, a quarterback sneak, did come on first down).

The run game was no better than the passing game, either. MarShawn Lloyd, Pierre Strong, and Kaleb Johnson combined for 15 carries on first downs, gaining a net of just 25 yards. Because of the long distances, I counted only six true running plays on other downs. Furthermore, the run game had as many plays go for no gain or negative yardage on first downs as they had gains of four yards or more (four each).

And then the Packers also had three first-down penalties and a sack, only adding to the ugliness.

Here's a look at the play-by-play results on first downs on Sunday night. As a warning, you may want to find an eyewash station after looking at this.

Love pass incomplete; PENALTY – ineligible man downfield

Again, it's shocking that the Packers were able to put together a successful offense with such dramatic ineptitude on first down. Credit Jordan Love for being fearless and accurate in the pocket for this team being able to put together five scoring drives to reach the 20-point mark, and for putting still more balls in places where his receivers should have made plays and pushed the team closer to 30.

If the Packers can clean up their execution and start getting positive yardage on first downs with more regularity, this offense could very easily take a big step forward.

#227. 2026 NHL free agent tracker: Patrick Kane returns to Blackhawks on two-year contract

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

NHL free agency has slowed down in late July, but some notable names are still coming off the board. Most notably, Patrick Kane is returning to the Chicago Blackhawks on a two-year contract worth $16 million, the team announced on Thursday.

Already a Chicago legend and future Hall of Famer, Kane won three Stanley Cups and a slew of individual awards with the franchise that selected him with the No. 1 overall pick in 2007. Kane's first stint with the Blackhawks lasted 16 seasons, and he piled up 446 goals and 779 assists in 1,161 games. Kane ranks inside the top five of just about every statistical category in franchise history, and he will get the chance to keep climbing those lists over the next two years.

The Blackhawks sent Kane to the New York Rangers at the 2023 NHL trade deadline, and he played just 19 regular season games there before hitting free agency the next summer. Hip surgery delayed Kane's decision until November of that year, but he ultimately landed with the Detroit Red Wings, where he's spent the last three seasons.

Last season was Kane's best with Detroit, and it proved that he still had some gas left in the tank, at least offensively. Kane posted 16 goals and 41 assists in 67 games -- with 19 of those points coming on the power play.

In his second stint with the Blackhawks, Kane will add another level of playmaking to the power play, and he should strengthen a top six forward group that's bereft of proven talent. Kane will also be an excellent mentor and sounding board for fellow No. 1 overall pick, Connor Bedard, who is set to miss the first month of the season after undergoing shoulder surgery.

Kane isn't the player he once was, but he'll give Chicago a bit more pop at the top of the lineup, and his first game back in a Blackhawks jersey will be a huge night for the city.

#228. NBA rookie impact rankings: 10 first-year players who will make presence felt immediately

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Entering the 2025-26 college basketball season, the hype around the incoming freshmen class was palpable. Led by the likes of Darryn Peterson, AJ Dybantsa, Cameron Boozer and Caleb Wilson, that group departed college basketball as one of the best freshmen classes of this generation.

Now, as those players enter their rookie seasons in the NBA, there is even more hype surrounding what could be one of the best rookie classes this century. Peterson and Dybantsa are joining unique situations: the Jazz and Wizards both missed the playoffs, but there is infrastructure in place for those teams to make a huge jump this season. Peterson and Dybantsa won't have to shoulder the load of being the guy from Day 1.

Because of how deep this class is, other players throughout the lottery are set for a significant role immediately. One name to watch is Kings guard Darius Acuff Jr., who will be handed the keys to Sacramento's offense immediately. Acuff was an All-American during his one-and-done season at Arkansas and was the best true point guard in the sport.

Outside of the top 10 picks, Warriors forward Yaxel Lendeborg — the oldest player drafted in the first round — should get an opportunity to start from Day 1. With Kristaps Porziņģis' status in limbo to begin the season, Lendeborg's number will be called on even more than anticipated.

With the season on the horizon, here are the 10 rookies who could make a significant impact for their respective teams. All rookie of the year odds are via FanDuel Sportsbook.

Boozer was comfortably the best player in college basketball last season. He went No. 3 to the Grizzlies anyway because Peterson and Dybantsa were in the same draft class. Boozer probably goes No. 1 in most years, but not in 2026.

What makes Boozer so good? It's a combination of his elite basketball IQ, passing and rebounding. Boozer is a bruiser down low who uses pump fakes to draw contact to get to the line. Boozer attempted 280 free throws at Duke last season, which ranked No. 4 among all Division I players. I'm comfortable with saying that Boozer will be the best rookie in the league this season because of his floor and projected role. He can be a 20/8 player as a rookie.

After 3 preseason games, here are Cam Boozer’s per 30 minute averages:21.3 points 8.6 rebounds 5.2 assists 57% fgs pic.twitter.com/CK4m679C2s

Peterson had a roller coaster of a freshman season at Kansas. After entering last fall as the projected No. 1 pick in the 2026 Draft, Peterson was sidelined for nearly a dozen games due to cramping issues. When Peterson was on the floor, he showed why he was one of the best guard prospects of this era.

Peterson's shotmaking ability is second-to-none in this class. What should be interesting to see this year is how Peterson plays on the ball in an experienced Utah lineup. In high school, Peterson's on-ball usage rate was high. At Kansas, however, it was less apparent. Peterson should thrive as a shooter in his rookie season and has a chance to make a real impact. My semi-hot take entering the year is that Utah finishes top six in the West, with Peterson playing a huge part in that leap.

Darryn Peterson's game is translating to the league immediately ⭐ pic.twitter.com/2J3UsQj5iG

The No. 1 overall pick in the 2026 NBA Draft is joining a Washington team that has had an interesting last 10 months. The Wizards bought low on Trae Young and Anthony Davis to pair with their young core and now, after winning the lottery and landing Dybantsa, finishing in the top 10 of the loaded Eastern Conference shouldn't be out of the question.

As mentioned earlier, Boozer ranked No. 4 among all Division I players in free-throw attempts. Dybantsa ranked first in that category while playing in three fewer games. Dybantsa is exceptional at getting to the free-throw line. He is able to draw contact with his bendy frame, which allows him to find space against defenders on drives to the hoop. He is also an incredible mid-range shooter. If his 3-point shot improves, it will be a game-changer.

AJ Dybantsa is playing hungry 😤 pic.twitter.com/mH4H7ZI6NQ

Wilson's freshman season at North Carolina was cut short after two separate hand injuries. If he doesn't get hurt, he is probably a first-team All-American. That's how good he was. Wilson was one of the best dunkers in college basketball last season and ranked near the top of the country in that category.

Wilson's swing skill in the NBA will be 3-point shooting. At UNC, he attempted just 27 3-pointers and made only seven. However, during summer league and throughout the preseason, Wilson has been taking more shots from beyond the arc. If the shooting is real, it completely changes his ceiling. Wilson should be an interesting ROTY candidate because his usage rate could be higher than that of many on this list.

Caleb Wilson put his skillset on display in tonight's preseason action!17 PTS (6-10 FGM)4 REB5 AST pic.twitter.com/jgEuyDoEzd

In our way-too-early Rookie of the Year predictions, I went with Acuff. If someone picked outside of the top four has the most realistic chance of winning the award, it's him for a few reasons. The most obvious one is that his usage rate on a given night will be higher than almost anybody in this class.

The Kings are handing Acuff the keys to the offense, and he should benefit tremendously from playing next to Domantas Sabonis, who is one of the best screeners in the NBA. That duo was on full display during Sacramento's preseason opener against the Lakers, when Sabonis set hard screens for Acuff and allowed the former Arkansas star to find open space to create. #230. Brief Steph Curry injury scare exposes the fragility of the Warriors this season

Brief Steph Curry injury scare exposes the fragility of the Warriors this season originally appeared on NBC Sports Bay Area

SAN FRANCISCO – The worst of all fears for the Warriors and their fans flashed before their eyes Sunday afternoon during an open practice at Chase Center.

The sight of Stephen Curry limping off the court and into the locker room.

Everything seemed normal as Curry was dribbling up the court, darting from the left wing to the right wing. But when he stopped to pivot, he suddenly froze, took two more dribbles and tossed the ball behind him as he left the court favoring his right leg. The immediate concern was that this could be a reoccurrence of the runner's knee diagnosis that sidelined him for nine weeks last season.

That is not the case, according to the Warriors, who say Curry tweaked his right ankle.

"He said he's fine," coach Steve Kerr said, unusually tersely, nearly an hour later.

How sad is it, though, that Curry tweaking an ankle allows the Warriors and their fans to breathe easier? That it could have been worse?

"Always, always," Kerr said when asked if his heart skipped a beat when Curry limped into the locker room.

"But he's fine. I went and talked to him after he went downstairs, and I went in the training room. He's doing fine."

If Curry is indeed "fine," the Warriors and their fans can restore their most optimistic hopes for successful start to the regular season that begins Wednesday night against the Lakers in Los Angeles.

Yet the momentary scare on Sunday is an overt reminder of Golden State's fragility as it prepares for the next 82 games. Neither Jimmy Butler III nor Moses Moody is expected to be available before 2027. The availability of Kristaps Porziņģis, who missed training camp and all six preseason games, is an ongoing mystery. Butler and Porziņģis represent 40 percent of the projected starting lineup, and Moody started 49 of the 60 games he played last season.

Age is an obvious issue for these Warriors, but it's only one factor within the overall health that can dictate how high they can fly. Most NBA observers see their roster and immediately dismiss them as non-contender.

"We don't really pay attention on that much on this," Gui Santos said. "It doesn't matter a lot what the big noise or what they say about us because at the end of the day, what really matters is what we show on the court. if we have, like they say, 'the old guys,' but it's Steph . . .  Steph can go there and drop 30 every night. And Dray (Draymond Green) is one of the best passers and the best defender of the league.

When everyone is healthy, the Warriors have a roster that can beat any team in the league. On paper, general manager Mike Dunleavy has done a commendable job of integrating accomplished veterans with intriguing youngsters. In reality, Golden State will enter the season with the most injury-weakened starting lineup in the league.

The plan is for the available veterans like Green (36), Al Horford (40), Gary Payton II (33) and Georges Niang (33) and – hopefully Curry (38) — to stay upright and prop up youngsters like Santos (24), Brandin Podziemski (23) and rookie Yaxel Lendeborg (24).

No one is more essential than Curry to ensuring Golden State will have a fighting chance against all opponents. His presence still scares the rest of the NBA.

On Sunday, seeing him come to a halt and limp off the court put a scare into the Warriors and their fans, who understand how they'd look without him.

#232. The Ravens found a loophole in the NFL rulebook, and ran the most creative trick play of the season

The Ravens had a rotten offensive day on Sunday, largely because the team is a mess without Lamar Jackson — but one play caught everyone's attention. In the first quarter we saw a 29-yard pass to tight end Josh Cuevas, who was lined up in the left guard spot, more or less tearing apart everything we know about offensive football.

The anecdotal response to this play is fairly universal: How is this legal? It just feels wrong to see a player move out of the left guard spot, catch a pass, and take it for a huge gain. However, this is legal in the rules — it just skirts around two elements of the rulebook to allow it to happen.

Firstly there's "Position of Players at the Snap," which states:

"Eligible receivers must be on both ends of the line, and all of the players on the line between them must be ineligible receivers."

The Ravens still had receivers split wide as eligible, satisfying the first element of the rule — and on this play Cuevas was off the line of scrimmage, meaning that everyone between the two players on the line was ineligible. Furthermore, Cuevas' position ensured he would not be an ineligible receiver as defined by the rules, because:

"Players who are not on either end of their line or at least one yard behind it when the ball is snapped"

Again, Cuevas was off the line — making him a legal, eligible receiver.

In terms of whether or not this will catch on, probably not. It was a really cute football play, but Baltimore OC Declan Doyle probably only gets one or two shots at this a season. Putting a tight end in the spot of a left guard off the line of scrimmage is just asking for a pass-rushing DT to absolutely blow up the tight end as a blocker, with the play relying entirely on the trickery of the defense not knowing who was eligible at the snap.

Moreover, teams will study this film and have their defense pay closer attention to both the positioning of players along the offensive line — as well as which players report as receivers pre-snap. Believe it or not, this play has been run before in the NFL. It's not as if Declan Doyle invented the play, it's just not used because, again, it turns out having five specialized blocking linemen in the NFL is kind of important, unless you want your quarterback flattened into a pancake.

Still fun to look at and realize how many elements of the NFL rulebook can still be bent.

#233. Last time the Chargers were 0-6, their QBs were Ryan Leaf, Moses Moreno and Jim Harbaugh

The Chargers are 0-6 for the first time since 2000. Chargers head coach Jim Harbaugh remembers that well.

That’s because Harbaugh was one of the quarterbacks on the terrible 2000 Chargers, who were 0-6 through six weeks like this year’s Chargers. That 2000 Chargers team ended the season 1-15.

The Chargers began the 2000 season with Ryan Leaf as their starting quarterback. Leaf had been the No. 2 overall pick in 1998, was awful as a rookie and missed all of his second season with a shoulder injury. The 2000 season was Leaf’s last chance in San Diego, and it did not go well. Through the first two weeks, the Chargers were 0-2 and Leaf had one touchdown pass and five interceptions, so they benched him for Moses Moreno in Week 3.

Unfortunately, Moreno was also terrible, and he suffered a shoulder injury in that Week 3 game, so Leaf started again in Week 4. But after Leaf again struggled in Week 4, he was benched again, this time for Harbaugh.

Harbaugh started Week 5, and he completely transformed the Chargers’ offense: Through the first five games, Moreno and Leaf had combined to average 131 passing yards, and totaled one touchdown pass and seven interceptions. In Week 5, Harbaugh threw for 348 yards, with two touchdowns and one interception, against the defending Super Bowl champion Rams. Unfortunately for the Chargers, their defense couldn’t stop the Greatest Show on Turf, and the Rams won 57-31.

Harbaugh kept the starting job for four more games, but he didn’t play as well, and by the time the Chargers were 0-10 they went back to Leaf to close out the season.

Leaf won one game as the starter, but the Chargers’ 1-15 record was the worst in franchise history. At least, the worst so far. Harbaugh’s 2026 Chargers have a chance to break the 2000 team’s franchise record for the most losses in a season.

#234. Aaron Rodgers calls for NFL to examine Buccaneers' field over player-safety concerns

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

After throwing darts during the final stages of the Steelers' come-from-behind win over the Buccaneers, Aaron Rodgers took a shot at Raymond James Stadium's playing surface. Rodgers didn't hold back when asked about the playing surface during his postgame press conference.

"It's got to be one of the worst playing surfaces in the league. When we're talking about player safety, that's a real concern," Rodgers said. "I'm thankful I didn't get hurt today, but I've been injured twice on this field before, and in my opinion, the turf was a factor both times. I know USF plays here, but that surface just doesn't feel very safe. From my perspective, it's a field that needs to be looked at because player safety should always come first."

Rodgers' first injury in Tampa occurred in 2008, his first season as the Packers' starting quarterback. He injured his right (throwing) shoulder during a 30-21 loss. The injury did not lead to any missed time for Rodgers, who started in each of Green Bay's 16 games that season.

In Week 16 of the 2014 season, Rodgers injured a calf muscle during a 20-3 win over the Buccaneers. Like in 2008, the injury did not sideline Rodgers, who won his second of four league MVPs that season.

Last year, Rodgers called the Steelers' home field "borderline unplayable" following a win over the Browns in which kicker Chris Boswell lost his footing on an attempted field goal. The Steelers replaced the playing surface before their next game (which had been planned before Rodgers' comments).

Raymond James Stadium uses natural grass and shares its field with a local college team.

NFLPA president JC Tretter has lobbied for playing surfaces since 2020. In 2022, he called for an immediate ban on specific slit-film turf surfaces. Several teams opted to remove that turf from their stadiums in subsequent fields.

Rodgers, who threw the game-winning touchdown pass in Sunday's overtime win, is in the middle of his 22nd and final NFL season. Rodgers and the Steelers will now begin preparations for next Sunday's international game in Paris against the Saints.

#235. Avalanche sign star Cale Makar to largest contract in NHL history at $163.2 million

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

This has been the summer of spending in the NHL, and the Colorado Avalanche just broke the bank for star defenseman Cale Makar. On Friday, the team announced that Makar signed an eight-year extension worth $163.2 million.

The contract is the richest in league history -- both in total value and annual value at $20.4 million per year. Makar is the first player in NHL history to cross the $20 million salary threshold.

At 27-years old, Makar is arguably the best defensemen in the NHL, and he will remain in that conversation for quite a while. Makar has already won the Norris Trophy twice, and he was a key factor in Colorado's Stanley Cup run, which ended with him winning the Conn Smythe Trophy.

This past season, Makar posted monster numbers from the blue line yet again as he tallied 20 goals and 59 assists in 75 games. Since entering the NHL in 2019, Makar leads all defensemen in goals (20) and points (507).

"I am so excited and humbled to continue to wear the Avalanche sweater and represent this incredible organization and community," Makar said in a statement. "I would like to thank the Kroenke family, Joe Sakic and the entire Avalanche organization for their commitment, trust and belief in me. I would also like to thank my wife and family for their constant support, as well as Scott, Brian and Steve Bartlett for their guidance and assistance.

"To the Avalanche fans, thank you for your continued support and for welcoming us to Colorado years ago. Colorado has truly become a second home to us, and we are so grateful to be here. I look forward to getting back on the ice with my teammates and continuing to work toward our goal of bringing the Stanley Cup back to the Mile High City."

Over the last three seasons, Makar's impact has been immense in all three zones. He's posted a five-on-five expected goals share of 54.5%, per Natural Stat Trick. With Makar on the ice in those situations, Colorado has outscored its opponents 220-157. In two of the last three seasons, Makar has hit the 90-point mark, and he has 100-point potential at his best.

Makar's $11.4 million raise kicks in in at the start of the 2026-27 season, and it will make things significantly tighter for the Avalanche as they navigate the salary cap. The bright side for Colorado -- and the key in getting this deal done -- is that the team now has each of its core players signed through at least 2031.

There may be some sticker shock upon seeing the $20.4 million average annual value, but that's the new reality in the NHL as the cap rises exponentially. The previous record for highest salary in NHL history was just set earlier this offseason when the Anaheim Ducks signed center Leo Carlsson to a contract worth $18 million per year, and the Chicago Blackhawks announced a $75 million extension for Connor Bedard.

The next domino to fall will be an extension for Minnesota Wild defenseman Quinn Hughes, who is neck-and-neck with Makar as the best defensemen in the world. Waiting until after the Makar deal was announced to sign Hughes could prove to be a mistake for Wild general manager Bill Guerin.

#240. The Welshman seeking NBA title with Timberwolves

With eight different teams the winners over the past eight seasons, it is hard to predict who takes home the NBA's Larry O'Brien Trophy in June.

If there is to be a ninth different name in as many seasons, you might look to San Antonio Spurs, with Victor Wembanyama leading the team to the Finals last season before coming unstuck against the New York Knicks.

Maybe the Philadelphia 76ers off-season moves to acquire Jaylen Brown and sign the NBA's all-time leading scorer LeBron James is an attractive pick, or perhaps the Cleveland Cavaliers.

As the season tips off, the first British-born coach in the NBA, Tim Lewis will be hoping he can assist Anthony Edwards and the Minnesota Timberwolves to their first NBA title.

Lewis has been something of a journeyman in basketball.

Born in Saint Asaph, Wales, he went on to represent the country in the 1990s, before forging a coaching career that spans almost the entire globe.

He has coached the Thailand and Qatar national teams and had spells in Germany, Belgium, Canada, the United States of America and Panama. He most recently worked in Japan as head coach of Eneos Sunflowers who he helped to the Empress Cup in January.

That is not including more than 15 years of coaching England and Great Britain age groups, where he was an assistant to now Minnesota Timberwolves head coach Chris Finch at the London 2012 Olympics.

Lewis was one of the Team GB assistant coaches, alongside Philadelphia 76ers head coach, Nick Nurse.

But Lewis and American Finch's friendship began way before that.

"We played against each other when I was back at [Crystal] Palace and Chris was at Sheffield [Sharks], he said.

"I've had stops with Chris when he was in Belgium and then before the Olympics, I spent six months at Houston with him.

"We've become close, it's almost like brothers. We've known each other 25 years and it's a strong bond."

After a previous brief spell with Minnesota, Lewis left to continue to be a head coach in Japan for three years, but Finch was persistent.

"For the last year and a half, Chris has knocked on the door and said, 'come back, come back'.

"Eventually I gave in this summer again and gone back for a more influential role, with more of an input and impact on things with stuff that's going on and I'm excited."

Minnesota Timberwolves head coach Chris Finch lead Team GB at the London 2012 Olympics where Lewis was an assistant coach [Getty Images]

Lewis had a spell as a replacement coach with Minnesota's G League team, the Iowa Wolves during Covid, before joining the staff the following season with a responsibility for post-game analysis.

"I would just go through all our game plans," he told BBC Sport Wales.

"I had a little bit of player development, but it was time consuming, nobody had done it before.

"Teams do the analysis pre-game of what we're going to do and how we're going to do it with plans, but not post-game.

"I'm not sure how many of the other staff appreciated me critiquing what was going on, but that was my role, and it stayed in place."

As Lewis returns to Minnesota, his role has expanded.

"Pablo [Prigioni] is going to take the lead on the offence and my role will be to help create some of these game plans offensively," he said.

"It's a full assistant's role with responsibility for offensive game planning.

"I look at what the other team are doing defensively and what can we do to maximise our ability to beat them offensively.

"On top of that, some player development with a couple of the young bigs."

Anthony Edwards and LaMelo Ball were the 1st and 3rd picks in the 2020 NBA draft [Getty Images]

In July, Minnesota acquired Josh Green and LaMelo Ball as part of a four-team trade.

Ball scored with 272 three-point shots in the 2025-26 season, the second most of any player in the NBA.

His partnership with Anthony Edwards in the backcourt appears to be an offensive coach's dream.

"Anthony and LaMelo and those guys are going to be exciting to watch," said Lewis.

"With LaMelo, you've got somebody that can now throw the lob and Rudy becomes a bit more of a rim threat, which we haven't necessarily had.

"Teams will find it harder to double-team him when you've got people like LaMelo on the floor with him."

"I don't know whether or not Anthony wants the burden of being the next face of the NBA, who knows?

"He is an immense talent, very responsive, a great kid overall and he's a great person, very coachable and wants to get better."

Minnesota's NBA title hopes were ended 4-2 by San Antonio in the Western Conference semi-finals in 2026 [Getty Images]

It will be a daunting start for the Timberwolves this season, with Giannis Antentokounmpo and Miami Heat first up but Lewis says the team are ready for the challenge.

"We come out of the gate hard, Miami, Orlando, and then Toronto," he said.

"They've all got three bruising power forwards, which is one area where we're a bit light.

"Everybody's worried we don't have size at the four, but Chris [Finch] will figure out how that looks.

"One of the things Minnesota's going to be lucky to do is be able to play different ways and the team's going to be exciting to watch."

The ambition is clear for Minnesota and Lewis, the NBA title is the ultimate goal for 2027.

"We want to make the play-offs and get to the championship games, everybody wants to win a championship, but you've got 29 other teams that are trying to do the same thing," said Lewis.

"Fifty-plus wins a season is what you want, that puts you in a great position to make the play-offs and to be a contender for that first seed.

"You don't ever want to jinx it but everybody's saying this team has an opportunity to go a long way this year, but you never know, we've been close every year.

"Teams are going to have to adjust to the way Minnesota plays and the personnel we have."

In terms of his own predictions for the season, Lewis offered a few suggestions for potential Larry O'Brien trophy winners.

"It's one of the things about the NBA at the moment, it's somewhat unpredictable," he said.

"Teams that maybe surge in the regular season but aren't built to compete in the playoffs.

"San Antonio could be that team, Minnesota could be that team.

"We've had Denver's number now for a number of years, other than the year they won it [2023].

"Who knows what Philly's going to do with the additions they've made."

Lewis says an NBA title would mean "so much" to Minneapolis.

The franchise formed in 1989 as an expansion team, with the supporters patiently waiting to make it to the NBA Finals.

"Minnesota fans are unbelievable," he said.

"It goes way back to Minneapolis Lakers [1947-1960] that are now the Los Angeles Lakers, who did win a championship.

"As an organisation, being able to win in that environment against a bigger market team is always a huge success.

"It's more for the city, it would be an amazing accomplishment."

#242. Why Dodgers can overcome 2-0 NLCS deficit vs. Brewers: MLB champs are down but not out

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The two-time defending champion Los Angeles Dodgers host the Milwaukee Brewers for Game 3 of the NLCS Wednesday evening in Dodger Stadium. The Dodgers are trailing the Brewers 2-0 in the best-of-seven series, meaning the Dodgers need to win four of their next five games or their season is over. The champs are on the ropes, no doubt, as this is an uphill battle. In MLB playoff history, teams falling behind 2-0 are 16-79 in their series.

Given all we've heard so often all season that the Dodgers winning the World Series is so inevitable, it might seem weird to see them with such steep odds. And though I'm sticking with my prediction from the last six weeks (or more) that the Brewers will win the World Series, it would be beyond foolish to count the Dodgers out.

First off, they are going home -- and that's always good. The Brewers were seven games worse on the road in the regular season and went 1-1 in San Diego last round compared to their 4-0 playoff record in American Family Field. Plus, the Dodgers haven't been home since Oct. 4. It'll feel nice to have that familiarity.

Here are four more reasons the Dodgers can come back and win the NLCS.

First things first, it's clear that Ohtani is hurt. He's been dealing with knee and biceps injuries since July and has struggled mightily at the plate since the middle of August. He's now 3 for 20 with seven strikeouts and zero extra-base hits in the playoffs and the Dodgers have thought about benching him -- but he will start as usual in Game 3.

He also continues to be insistent that he isn't hurt that badly and can soon figure things out at the plate. Who are we to doubt Shohei Freaking Ohtani?

If things do all of a sudden click at the plate for the four-time MVP, it changes everything for this Dodgers lineup. Last postseason alone, he had three doubles, a triple, eight home runs, 14 RBI and 13 runs in 17 games with a 1.096 OPS. That's the type of stuff that elevates everyone else in a lineup. He had a three-homer game against the Brewers in Game 4 of the NLCS.

In the playoffs, you're facing better competition, which usually means better pitching and defense and, as such, it becomes much more difficult to string together hits. This means there is increased importance on either small ball -- which is playing for one run a lot of the time -- or home runs. Obviously, though the Brewers gave the Dodgers some runs in the first two games, the pitching-and-defense thing applies to them. They are exceptional at run prevention.

The Dodgers can hit the ball out of the ballpark, though. They were tied for seventh with 204 home runs in the regular season and that's with Ohtani having been compromised for months, not to mention injury affecting Will Smith and a mostly lost season from Kyle Tucker. This is to say that the Dodgers are probably more powerful than their regular-season line indicates.

In their two home games in the playoffs, the Dodgers have five home runs.

So many teams losing two games started by Tarik Skubal and Yoshinobu Yamamoto would be in desperation mode. The Dodgers return home and start two-time Cy Young winner Blake Snell in Game 3. Last time Snell saw the Brewers in October, he was shutting them out for eight innings in NLCS Game 1 last year, striking out 10 and allowing just one hit. Now, he gave up five runs both times he pitched in the World Series and walked five in his previous outing this postseason, so he's not a sure thing, but he does have the ability to go into Ace Mode.

So does Tyler Glasnow, the Dodgers' Game 4 starter. Glasnow only gave up one run in 5 ⅔ innings against the Brewers in the NLCS last year. He has a 1.73 ERA in the playoffs since joining the Dodgers.

And then there's Skubal for Game 5 and Yamamoto for Game 6, should the Dodgers be able to force those games.

The Brewers should be favored to win the series right now, rather heavily, but if things change -- the second the Dodgers start winning, those odds tilt in their favor with this rotation.

Take note again of how the Brewers are worse on the road. Let's say the Dodgers do win three straight in Dodger Stadium before sending this thing back to Milwaukee with a 3-2 NLCS lead.

Now, all of a sudden, all the pressure is on the Brewers. The Dodgers are the two-time defending champs and many of their players have plenty of other experience with deep playoff runs. The Brewers, meanwhile, were swept by the Dodgers in the NLCS last season and the franchise has never won a World Series nor an NL pennant.

If this returns to Milwaukee with a 3-2 Dodgers lead, the nervous energy will be through the roof, even if it's open for Game 6. Even if the Brewers go home with a 3-2 lead, I believe the Dodgers will feel confident they are taking this series.

The Brewers have shown incredible resilience in the first two games of the series, punching back each time the Dodgers land one of their own. They'll need to keep that up in order to combat the Dodgers' championship mentality in order to close things out.

#244. Jets star goalie Connor Hellebuyck requests trade: Where three-time Vezina Trophy winner could land

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

After months of speculation about his future in Winnipeg, Jets goaltender Connor Hellebuyck has confirmed his trade request publicly.

Hellebuyck's name has come up in trade rumors since the 2025-26 season ended, and the rumor mill will only pick back up now that he's gone public with his request. NHL training camps will open soon, and Hellebuyck wanted to provide more clarity on the situation.

"Winnipeg has been home for my entire NHL career, and I will always be grateful for my time there.

"I have never forgotten June 23, 2012. That's the day Winnipeg took a chance on a goalie playing in Odessa, Texas. I gave everything I had from that moment to prove the Jets made the right decision.

"Several months ago, I privately requested a trade. I have tried to handle the situation quietly and respectfully while giving the organization time to explore its options.

"With training camp approaching, I felt it was important to publicly confirm my request. My position has not changed, and I believe moving on is the best path forward for me and my family.

"I appreciate everything Winnipeg Jets fans have meant to me throughout my career and hope a resolution can be reached soon."

In what would become one of the biggest steals in NHL Draft history, the Jets used the No. 130 overall pick to select Hellebucyk in 2012. Just seven years later, Hellebuyck established himself as one of the best goalies in the lea, and he's maintained that level of play for nearly a decade.

A three-time Vezina Trophy winner, Hellebuyck has a legitimate claim as the best goaltender in the world. Over the last three seasons, Hellebucyk has totaled 73.4 goals saved above average, per Natural Stat Trick. That's 20 more than the next closest goaltender -- Andrei Vasilevskiy -- and includes a rather underwhelming 2025-26 campaign.

There have been plenty of years in which Hellebuyck carried mediocre Jets teams, but 2025-26 was not one of them. He actually allowed 0.35 goals above average with a pedestrian 0.895 save percentage. Normally, it would be fair to worry about a 33-year-old goalie with those numbers, but not in Hellebucyk's case.

Hellebuyck backstopped Team USA to its first men's ice hockey gold medal in 46 years at the 2026 Olympics while allowing a total of six goals and boasting a .956 save percentage. He was exceptional in the final against Canada, where he turned away 41 of the 42 shots he faced and made one of the most iconic saves in hockey history.

THAT WAS ONE HELLE-BUYCK OF A STOP. 😳 pic.twitter.com/N3wCimdBGw

The biggest obstacle in a trade might be Hellebucyk's contract. He has five years remaining on his current deal at $8.5 million per season -- and while that may be a lot of term for a goalie his age -- Hellebucyk is worth a lot more than that at his best. The real issue is that he owns a full no-movement clause, which means Hellebuyck controls his fate, and the trade request going public certainly won't improve the team's leverage.

So, where does Hellebucyk land? Without knowing his preferred destinations, it's probably safe to assume that he wants the opportunity to win a Stanley Cup, and the team that acquires him will need the requisite cap space and resources to do so.

With those parameters in mind, here are five teams that could make sense as Hellebuyck trade suitors.

The Sabres were one of two teams frequently connected to Hellebuyck earlier in the offseason, and that makes sense. Buffalo is an ascending team with room to upgrade in the crease. Not to denigrate Alex Lyon and Ukko-Pekka Luukkonen, who were a formidable tandem in 2025-26, but I'm not sure Buffalo can bet on similar performances this upcoming season. Adding Hellebuyck would eliminate that question mark immediately and make the Sabres a favorite to win the Atlantic Division.

In fact, one of Luukkonen or Lyon could go back to Winnipeg to help provide stability in the post-Hellebuyck era. The Sabres also own all their first-round picks for the foreseeable future, and it would probably take at least two of those to pry Hellebuyck from the Jets. Just a year ago, it would be hard to believe that Hellebuyck would waive his no-movement clause to go to Buffalo, but it seems very plausible now.

When the Devils traded Jacob Markstrom to the Florida Panthers in July, I assumed it would only be a matter of time until Hellebuyck was in Newark. To this point, nothing has come to fruition, but New Jersey absolutely needs an NHL-caliber starter. Jake Allen, David Rittich and Nico Daws are on the roster right now, and that won't get the job done.

The Devils were undone by poor goaltending -- and subpar defense -- too much last year. Markstrom allowed 13.7 goals above average, per Natural Stat Trick, and even a diminished version of Hellebuyck would provide a significant upgrade over those numbers. New Jersey has the draft capital to get something done, but it also needs to clear cap space, possibly with a Dougie Hamilton salary dump.

They just won the Stanley Cup with Brandon Bussi in net, so the Hurricanes have proven they don't need elite goaltending to go all the way. Regardless, running it back with Bussi wouldn't be a very safe bet, and adding Hellebuyck would only reinforce Carolina's biggest strength. As we saw in the playoffs, the Hurricanes are already one of the best defensive teams in the league. Put Hellebuyck behind that lineup, and scoring on Carolina becomes a Herculean task.

Thanks to savvy cap management by GM Eric Tulsky, Carolina has the room to add Hellebuyck without jettisoning a current player. Oh, and Carolina has three first-round picks over the next two years. If Tulsky wants to pursue Hellebuyck, he has the resources to do it.

This is more of a longshot, but it would be fun to see the Sharks take a swing if this, assuming Hellebuyck would sign off on a trade to San Jose. Despite the fact that they overpaid for it, the Sharks blue line is better, and there is a wealth of young talent at forward. Another factor here is the current state of the Pacific Division, which is abhorrent. The third playoff spot is up for grabs, and the Sharks could secure it with Hellebuyck in goal.

Superstar Macklin Celebrini is on the final year of his entry-level deal before his $18.8 million salary kicks in next year, so San Jose needs to push the chips in here and figure out the finances next summer. Would the team be willing to trade blue-chip goaltending prospect Yaroslav Askarov to the Jets? San Jose may also need to sweeten a trade package -- or involve a third team -- in order to get Winnipeg to take on Logan Couture's contract.

Yes, Vegas is currently $8.6 million over the salary cap, so there would need to be some impressive maneuvering in order to acquire Hellebuyck. But the Golden Knights have already proven to be cutthroat if a player they covet hits the trade market. Besides, goaltending was optional in Sin City last season. Four goalies combined to allow 23.2 goals above average. Only five teams had a worse save percentage than the Golden Knights.

So, how could the Golden Knights pull off a Hellebuyck blockbuster? Trading an injured Alex Pietrangelo and his contract would help, but that may be costly. Veteran defenseman Brayden McNabb only has a modified no-trade clause, and the same is true for forwards Tomas Hertl, William Karlsson and Ivan Barbashev. Like I said, this would be tough, but the Golden Knights are one team willing to drop the entire egg carton on the floor to make a few omelettes.

#245. Cardinals stun Rams, defeat Los Angeles 18-16

Maybe the Cardinals should only play at SoFi Stadium.

Arizona got its second win of the season on Sunday, stunning the Rams 18-16 for the club’s second victory of the season.

The first came Week 1 at the same venue over the Chargers.

Entering the week at No. 26 in yards allowed and No. 32 in points allowed, Arizona stifled Los Angeles’ offense throughout the contest.

The Rams barely had 100 yards at halftime with three three-and-outs. It didn’t help that the team lost its new kicker, Blake Grupe, to a knee injury early in the game when he made a tackle on a kickoff.

But the Cardinals were able to control the ball and the clock throughout the afternoon, winning time of possession 34:52 to 25:08. And while the club never reached the end zone, Chad Ryland was automatic in Rams territory with his six field goals — including his 43-yard make as time expired to give Arizona the win.

Los Angeles got to the end zone twice — once with Blake Corum’s 15-yard touchdown reception in the second quarter. It then took them until there were 47 seconds left on the clock for Matthew Stafford to find Colby Parkinson for a 6-yard touchdown. With Grupe out, punter Ethan Evans put the Rams ahead with a successful extra point.

But that lead did not hold, as Jacoby Brissett connected with Jalen Brooks for a 21-yard completion to open the ensuing Cardinals possession. An unnecessary roughness penalty tacked on 15 yards, putting Arizona in clear field goal range.

A few plays later, Ryland sent his sixth kick through the uprights for the win.

Brissett ended the day 24-of-35 passing for 218 yards with an interception. Trey McBride led with seven catches for 53 yards.

On the other side, Stafford finished 25-of-33 for 222 yards with two touchdowns. Puka Nacua had six receptions for 80 yards. Davante Adams — who hopped off the field late in the fourth quarter with an apparent leg injury — had three catches for 39 yards.

The Cardinals now have more wins at SoFi Stadium this season — two — than the Rams and Chargers, who have a combined one.

At 2-4, Arizona will be at home to host the Broncos in Week 7.

The 2-4 Rams are reeling and will be in Las Vegas next weekend to play the Raiders.

#247. C.J. Gardner-Johnson faces a potential suspension for spitting

The ejection of Bills safety C.J. Gardner-Johnson for spitting on an opponent raises an interesting question, as it relates to the additional discipline to be imposed by the league office.

Last year, the NFL adopted a new approach to spitting. It now results in a one-game suspension, sort of.

It started when Eagles defensive tackle Jalen Carter spit on Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott before the first play from scrimmage in the regular-season opener. Because Carter's ejection covered the entire game, his punishment — a fine in the amount of a game check — simulated a suspension.

Later in the season, Bengals receiver Ja'Marr Chase spit on Steelers defensive back Jalen Ramsey. The officials didn't see it, so Chase wasn't ejected. Instead, he was suspended for the next game.

For Gardner-Johnson, the ejection caused him to miss half of the Week 6 game against the Raiders. Will he be suspended for another full game? Will the league fashion an NCAA-style targeting punishment that keeps him out for the first half of the Bills' next game?

Because Buffalo has a Week 7 bye, the clock isn't ticking as loudly as it ordinarily would be. Still, the league has a decision to make given the new precedent that was set in 2025, when the punishment for spitting morphed from a fine into a suspension. And Gardner-Johnson presents the first example of a player who missed roughly half of a game after being ejected.

#252. Astros move on from Joe Espada: Is a rebuild next in Houston? Plus more pressing questions

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Houston Astros announced Wednesday that they have not renewed the contract of manager Joe Espada, expanding the leadership void atop the AL West winners and opening up questions about where owner Jim Crane sees this team going.

"We are thankful for Joe's hard work, his passion for the game, and for his commitment to the Houston Astros.  He represented the Astros and the Houston community in the most positive way. We wish he and his family the best moving forward," said Astros owner Jim Crane in a statement.

For the last decade or so, the Astros have been reliable contenders and, for most of those years, a modern baseball dynasty. Since they emerged from their deep rebuild with a postseason berth in 2015, the Astros have hoisted the World Series trophy twice -- albeit with some scandal and controversy appended to one of those trophies -- won more than 100 games in a season on four occasions, and at one point made it at least as far as the ALCS for seven straight years.

Now, though, these bedrock contenders are at a crossroads after seeing many members of that championship core depart over the years, and it may be that their window has finally closed. This can be wondered aloud not only because they were swept in the Wild Card Series by the Chicago White Sox, but also because the Astros in 2026, playoff berth notwithstanding, were a bad team. They finished the season with an 81-81 record despite having played, based on opponents' average winning percentage, the weakest schedule in all of MLB. That made them the only non-winning team in MLB history ever to make the playoffs in a full season. Additionally, the Astros had a -32 run differential during the regular season, which means they had a "deserved" record of 78-84. Again, a bad team.

Now, they enter an uncertain offseason. The ongoing CBA negotiations hang over everything. General manager Dana Brown was let go in August and Crane named himself the temporary head of baseball operations. Espada is now out too. And beyond that, pervasive roster weaknesses mean it may not be advisable for the Astros to try to contend again in 2027.

All of that sets the stage for the three questions that will, in many ways, define the Astros moving forward. Let's explore those now.

This is the most central question of all. On the manager front, the leading "free agents" right now are, in no particular order, former Red Sox manager Alex Cora (the Astros' former bench coach under AJ Hinch), future Hall of Famer Albert Pujols, former Orioles manager Brandon Hyde, former Twins manager Rocco Baldelli, and former Cubs manager David Ross. Maybe current Astros bench coach Omar Lopez, a longtime presence in the organization, gets his shot.

More important -- and much less clear -- is who will become the new general manager and/or president of baseball operations. Idly guessing specific names is a fool's errand when it comes to this kind of vacancy, so we won't do that. The Astros have some capable internal candidates who have been around since the Jeff Luhnow years, and that may be the path of least resistance. Otherwise, select assistant GMs or, in the case of a president of baseball operations search, GMs in other successful organizations will be under consideration.

Is the job an attractive one? On one level, it's one of 30 such jobs in the world, and pretty much every front office employee with their hands in baseball ops aspires to such a role. So yes, it is. More specifically, though, the Astros are not in a good place right now. They're caught in a downward spiral on the field (they've gotten worse every year since winning it all in 2022), and the organization has fallen far behind in terms of player acquisition and development.

Related to all that is the meddling presence of Crane and Astros-legend-turned-right-hand-advisor Jeff Bagwell. Let's explore that latter point more closely while wondering whether leading top-exec candidates might be turned off by the power dynamic in Houston.

Assuming the Astros don't opt to just rearrange their current front office structure -- which probably shouldn't be assumed, truthfully -- the new head of baseball ops needs the freedom to repair and reshape the organization. The problem is there's little reason to think that will be the case. Crane, when it comes to making actual baseball decisions, seems not to know all that he does not know, is far too hands-on, and has given too much power and influence to Bagwell, who's trenchantly anti-analytics at a time when the Astros need much more of that very thing.

Crane, you'll recall, butted heads with James Click, Brown's predecessor, and fired him a week after the Astros won the World Series. Brown hardly distinguished himself, but how much was he truly allowed to implement his own vision for rebuilding the Astros' young talent base? That young talent base remains in a fairly wretched state. If Crane wants the top talent the Astros need in the big chair, then he can't do things like, oh, helm the talks that led to José Abreu's disaster contract or the Rafael Montero extension.

The Astros need a new lead exec in baseball ops, but first, they need an owner who accepts he doesn't know as much as he thinks he knows.

Yes, it's tempting to go for it again in the sad-sack AL West, but the Astros, as repeatedly noted, are not good and, despite the MVP-grade presence of Yordan Alvarez, are almost certainly not going to be good anytime soon. This should lead to a rebuild that sees them pivot to the long-term and begin reconstructing the base of young, controllable talent.

What would this mean? It might mean that whoever's in charge of the Astros -- putatively or in actuality -- opts to trade away select players with at least one year of control or contract remaining, like Josh Hader (assuming he's willing to waive his no-trade clause), Jeremy Peña, Isaac Paredes, Christian Walker, and, yes, maybe even Alvarez and Hunter Brown. No, the Astros don't necessarily need to go scorched earth and trade all of those core contributors, but most of them should be dealt in the name of setting the club up for future success.

Will Crane allow such an approach? And if he does, will he allow his actual baseball people to make those crucial baseball decisions? That's to be determined.

#253. What's next for Connor Bedard, Blackhawks after massive five-year, $75 million contract extension

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Chicago Blackhawks have locked in their franchise cornerstone for the near future. On Saturday, the Blackhawks announced that star center Connor Bedard has signed a five-year contract worth $75 million.

Bedard's $15 million average annual value makes him the third-highest paid player in the NHL for the 2026-27 season. Only Minnesota Wild winger Kirill Kaprizov ($17 million) and the newly-signed Anaheim Ducks center Leo Carlsson ($18 million) are ahead of him.

"Connor has continuously defied our expectations since being drafted, and has quickly established himself as an elite player in the NHL," Blackhawks general manager Kyle Davidson said in a statement. "He utilizes all aspects of his game to not only be a constant threat, but to make the players around him better every time he steps on the ice. Connor's strong work ethic and determination to always improve his game has set an extraordinary standard for our young core, and we're excited for the incredible impact he'll have in this next chapter of Blackhawks hockey."

The No. 1 overall pick in the 2023 NHL Draft, Bedard has already displayed elite offensive upside, even if his overall game still has work to do. Last season, Bedard posted a career high 75 points in 69 games. In 219 NHL games, Bedard has totaled 75 goals and 128 assists.

The biggest issues for Bedard are durability concerns -- he's played fewer than 70 games in two of three seasons and will miss the first month of the upcoming season with a shoulder injury -- and subpar defense. The defense is a common problem for young centers and should improve in the coming years, but Bedard has now suffered multiple shoulder injuries in his career.

With Bedard's long-term contract finalized, both he and the Blackhawks will try to take the next step toward greatness. For the player, that means refining his game in order to become the $15 million man most believe him to be. For the team, that means surrounding Bedard with an adequate supporting cast for the first time in his career.

First and foremost, Bedard needs to get healthy and stay healthy. After missing 13 games with a shoulder injury last year, Bedard suffered another injury that required surgery to fix, and he will miss roughly a dozen games out of the gate in 2026-27. Those issues may delay his jump into the NHL's elite tier of players.

Once back at full strength, Bedard will have to show improvement defensively. He oozes offensive ability, but if Bedard is going to be a true No. 1 franchise center, he has to thrive at both ends of the ice. With Bedard on the ice at five-on-five last season, Chicago surrendered 3.60 xGA/60, per Natural Stat Trick. That was the second-worst number on the team with rookie Anton Frondell bringing up the rear.

That doesn't necessarily mean Bedard was the Blackhawks' worst defensive player, but it does mean he often struggled when going up against the opposing team's best players. Stars -- especially those raking in $15 million per season -- are expected to drive play for their team regardless of circumstance. Bedard didn't do that last season.

Bedard also needs to show more growth in the face-off circle. To his credit, Bedard has already done that, going from 38.9% as a rookie to 47.1% last season. Still, Chicago would probably like to see Bedard closer to 50%, especially with him taking key draws in big moments. Maybe that number keeps rising as Bedard gets strong and adds more tricks in the dot.

If Bedard can round out his game without the puck, $15 million per season will be a very fair deal, especially as salaries explode across the league.

We've already seen what can happen when a restricted free agent has all the leverage in contract negotiations. The Ducks were essentially backed into a $90 million contract after the Philadelphia Flyers signed Carlsson to a massive offer sheet.

That risk was there for Bedard too, which is why Davidson deserves some credit for signing him at a more reasonable cap hit. Bedard still has work to do in order to reach that price point, but his ceiling is worth at least $15 million per season.

The Blackhawks can help their young star by putting more NHL-caliber players around him. Chicago tore it down to the studs in hopes of landing Bedard in the 2023 draft, and while that plan worked, it also created a roster full of holes around the No. 1overall pick. Over the last three seasons, Bedard has had little help.

Chicago already improved its defense this offseason when it acquired Bowen Byram from the Buffalo Sabres. Say what you will about the acquisition cost or his $75 contract extension, but Byram inarguably makes Chicago better on the blue line. That unit still needs work, but it's a step in the right direction.

The real issue is finding Bedard a quality running mate at the top of the lineup. Outside of Bedard, only one other player topped 50 points in 2025-26, and it was 31-year-old Tyler Bertuzzi. Chicago still has $14.1 million in cap space with which to add some firepower, but some upgrades will have to come internally.

It's conceivable that the Blackhawks' lineup will include seven players selected inside the top 50 picks of the last five drafts.

That's an exciting proposition, and fans have reasons to be optimistic about the future. That said, none of those players have really established themselves as future stars, outside of Bedard. Frondell, Nazar and Rinzel seem like the best bets to get there soon, but that's based more on projection than anything tangible.

The first month of the season should be an excellent barometer for the Blackhawks as they assess those players. Bedard will be out of the lineup, and it'll be interesting to see who sinks and who swims until he returns. Once Chicago establishes exactly what it has in its young nucleus, Davidson can then go out and aggressively address needs via trades and free agency.

#256. Why the Celtics are getting a bargain on Payton Pritchard's two-year, $44.2 million contract extension

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Upward mobility in the NBA contractual market is pretty rare. A player's financial destiny is often tied to where he is drafted. Where that player is drafted frequently determines the opportunities he gets early in his career, which in turn determines his rookie extension, what he's eligible for on his next deal and so on. One team-friendly contract tends to beget several, and nowhere is that truer right now than it is for Payton Pritchard.

On Tuesday, he and the Boston Celtics agreed to a two-year, $44.2 million contract extension, according to ESPN. All told, that will guarantee him around $85 million in NBA earnings through the first 10 seasons of his career. That is by no means a bad outcome, on paper, for the No. 26 pick in the 2020 NBA Draft. Just consider it in comparison to the No. 4 pick, Patrick Williams, who has locked in over $130 million in career earnings thus far.

Williams has, at no point, been a better NBA player than Pritchard. He is now a fringe rotation player for the Chicago Bulls, a lottery team. But he was a high draft pick with great physical tools that tend to get players paid. He played for a Chicago team that, through its own poor management, had few other players worth paying, so the Bulls were free to give him a bloated contract, betting on improvement that hasn't really come.

Pritchard has dealt under almost the exact opposite circumstances. He landed on a loaded Celtics team that couldn't find him consistent minutes. Things got bad enough around the 2023 trade deadline that Pritchard reportedly wanted to be dealt. Without much of a resume after three years, the Celtics locked him into a four-year, $30 million rookie extension that guaranteed him life-changing wealth, but still represented a pittance compared to what he was actually worth. He won Sixth Man of the Year and a championship before that extension even kicked in.

Normally, a standard veteran extension can give a player a 40% raise in the final season of their current deal. This is why those early contracts matter. If a team believes in you when you're young, it makes you eligible to extend for more when you get older. Yet Pritchard's deal is so low that he's actually capped at a different figure: 140% of the estimated average player salary in the first year of his extension. He could therefore only extend for around $67 million over three years. He wound up taking the shorter, two-year equivalent of that deal with a mutual option that gives the sides flexibility to tear up the contract and renegotiate something a bit bigger in the 2029 offseason.

That deal, by most analytical measures, is a pretty significant bargain.

Stephen Noh of Sporting News built a tool that determines a player's projected value using the DPM all-in-one metric. It projects Pritchard to be worth around $28 million next year and going forward. This deal keeps him in Boston for an average of $22 million per year.

These projections are based on who Pritchard has already been. It's worth wondering, now that Jaylen Brown has been traded, who Pritchard might soon become. As Yahoo's Tom Haberstroh noted after the Brown trade, Pritchard's usage rate went up nearly nine percentage points when he played without Brown a year ago... and his true shooting improved by four percentage points in those minutes. The Celtics went 32-5 in games in which Pritchard's usage reached or exceeded 22% last season.

Pritchard has never been a full-time starter. There's a chance he will be this season, and if he is, he's suddenly on a roster equipped to give him shots and minutes he's never had before. Some, like Haberstroh, have even suggested he's primed for a Jalen Brunson-esque leap as a small guard finally being given the freedom to spread his wings. While such notions are probably a bit optimistic, it's not unreasonable to believe Pritchard is headed for his most productive NBA season.

And if he is, the Celtics will still have three years of cost control on a severely undervalued player through this extension. If they elect to renegotiate his deal through the mutual option in 2029, they'll have the leverage to yet again do so in a team-friendly manner. After all, mutual options require both parties to opt out. If the Celtics simply want Pritchard to play out the 2029-30 season on this deal, they can make him do so.

Every team in the NBA would rather have high picks than lower ones. The top of the draft is typically where superstars are found, and even if those superstars cost more, they're a prerequisite for championship contention. The Celtics know that. Look at all of the success they had with Brown and Jayson Tatum.

But the Pritchard contract is an example of just how much surplus value nailing a pick later on in the draft can generate. Those are the players who tend to be undervalued on their second contract, which trickles down to their third and fourth deals as well.

In an NBA increasingly obsessed with maximizing every last cent, success stories like Boston's with Pritchard are becoming nearly as essential to genuine championship contention as landing stars always have been.

#258. Jets continue to struggle at the ends of halves under Aaron Glenn

The Jets fell to 5-18 under head coach Aaron Glenn with Sunday’s loss to the Patriots and their play at the end of the first half loomed large in the loss.

New England pushed a 7-3 lead to a 17-3 edge with a field goal and a touchdown sandwiched around a quick three-and-out by the Jets offense. That continued a trend that has been in place since Glenn took over ahead of the 2025 season.

“Yeah, that’s something that—and I think you guys have heard me talk about this before, just the two-minute situation, that we’ve got to get better at that,” Glenn said after the game, via a transcript from the team. “I must say offense and defense, that we have to get better at that. We have to be able to possess the ball more to go ahead and put stress on their defense to try to score points. On defense you’ve got to make sure we stop them when we get that opportunity.”

Per Rich Cimini of ESPN.com, the Jets have been outscored 119-49 in the final two minutes of halves — they traded field goals with New England late in the fourth quarter on Sunday — since Glenn became their coach. That doesn’t include Glenn’s management of the final minute in a Week 2 loss to the Packers as no points were scored while Glenn sat on timeouts rather than push to get the ball back before heading to overtime.

Green Bay would go on to win and the whole package illustrates the situational struggles that have been a hallmark of Glenn’s run with the Jets. His lack of awareness in those moments has angered plenty of Jets fans and they got more fuel for that fire just before the second half got underway on Sunday. In an interview with Aditi Kinkhabwala of CBS, Glenn appeared to believe his team was getting the ball to start the third quarter when it was actually the other way around.

#260. Thunder, Cason Wallace reportedly beat deadline, agree to 5-year, $139M contract extension

Cason Wallace and the Oklahoma City Thunder have agreed to a five-year, $139 million extension to his rookie contract, ESPN's Shams Charania reports.

The two sides beat Monday's deadline for players from the 2023 NBA Draft class to sign rookie scale extensions. Had they not reached a deal before the deadline, Wallace would have played the final year of his rookie contract on a team option, then entered the 2026-27 offseason as a restricted free agent.

With the deal, the Thunder secure a defensive anchor of their core as they seek to win a second NBA championship in three seasons. Wallace, a shooting guard, has developed into one of the best perimeter defenders in the NBA.

Join or create a Yahoo Fantasy Basketball league for the 2026-27 NBA season

The Thunder selected Wallace with the No. 10 overall draft pick in 2023 out of Kentucky. He's expanded his role with the franchise in each of his three NBA seasons.

After starting 13 games as a rookie, Wallace started 43 in 2024-25 and was a key rotation player on Oklahoma City's championship team. He started 58 games last season and is now projected as a full-time starter this upcoming season, when he should expand on his 26.6 minutes per game from 2025-26.

In 77 games last season, Wallace averaged 8.6 points, 3.1 rebounds, 2.6 assists, 1.9 steals and 0.4 blocks while shooting 35.1% on 3.7 3-point attempts per game.

The Thunder traded 3-and-D specialist Luguentz Dort to the Atlanta Hawks in the offseason, signaling their expectation that Wallace would step into a larger role. They've now secured his services for five more seasons and signed their entire starting five to long-term contracts.

With their championship window open, the Thunder will move forward with Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, Jalen Williams, Chet Holmgren, Isaiah Hartenstein and now Wallace, signed through at least the 2028-29 season.

#261. Ducks match Leo Carlsson's $90 million offer sheet: Anaheim star tops list of NHL's highest-paid players

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Anaheim Ducks didn't need the full seven days to decide whether to match the Philadelphia Flyers' record five-year, $90 million offer sheet to Leo Carlsson. Just a few days after Carlsson signed the Flyers' offer, the Ducks announced that they had matched the deal, keeping the Swedish center in Anaheim and making him the highest-paid player in NHL history.

Philadelphia rocked the hockey world last week when they signed Carlsson, and the $18 million AAV was lofty enough that there was uncertainty about whether Anaheim would match the deal. The Ducks could've let Carlsson walk and taken four first-round picks from the Flyers, but they chose to keep their franchise cornerstone instead.

The No. 2 overall pick in the 2023 NHL Draft, Carlsson is still blossoming into a superstar No. 1 center. He took a big step in that direction last season when he posted 29 goals and 38 assists in 70 games. Perhaps more importantly, Carlsson's five-on-five game showed major improvement as the Ducks controlled 53.4% of the expected goals with him on the ice, per Natural Stat Trick.

Carlsson still has work to do in order to become an $18 million player, but he's on the right track. Even if Carlsson doesn't quite get all the way there, he should come close, and the rising salary cap will take away some of the sticker shock over the next several years.

Still, the Ducks were in a legitimate bind, and they still are to a certain degree. After Carlsson signed his offer sheet, Anaheim wanted to avoid a similar situation with 22-year-old defenseman Pavel Mintyukov, so the team locked him in on a five-year, $36 million deal. Mintyukov is a gifted player, but he has very real holes in his game defensively, so that was a desperate gamble on the part of the Ducks.

Now, Anaheim has just over $9 million in salary cap space and another major restricted free agent to sign. Cutter Gauthier, 22, just posted a 41-goal season and needs a new contract. His annual number will almost certainly come in over $10 million, so the Ducks have some maneuvering to do, and that doesn't even take into account the fact that the team doesn't even have six NHL-caliber defensemen on the roster.

Pat Verbeek still has a lot of work ahead of him, but at least he knows his best player is signed through the next five seasons. Now he just needs to figure out what to do with the pieces around Carlsson.

This contract makes Carlsson the highest-paid player in NHL history on an annual basis. He topped Minnesota Wild winger Kirill Kaprizov's record ($17 million), which was set last summer.

That puts a lot of pressure on Carlsson to perform as a true superstar because players making several million dollars less than him already have Hart Trophy wins, Rocket Richard trophies and Stanley Cup rings. Some of that is simply timing. As the salary cap rises, contracts explode, and Carlsson just happens to be latest star player to get a new deal.

When Auston Matthews and Connor McDavid sign new contracts in a couple of years, their annual salaries will rival or surpass that of Carlsson. That said, heavy is the head that wears the crown, and the Ducks are counting on Carlsson to step into an elite tier moving forward.

There are a few players who could join this list in short order. Connor Bedard is still a restricted free agent -- and despite his recent shoulder injury, he should still get a hefty payday from the Chicago Blackhawks. Plus, superstar defensemen Cale Makar and Quinn Hughes are eligible for extensions, and those contracts will reset the market for that position.

#262. Phillies keep Don Mattingly as manager, extend his contract through 2028 season

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Philadelphia Phillies have retained Don Mattingly as their full-time manager. The team made the announcement Wednesday morning and said Mattingly has signed a contract through the 2028 season.

Mattingly entered this past season as the Phillies' bench coach behind manager Rob Thomson. Thomson took over in 2022 after Joe Girardi was fired and took the Phillies to the World Series, not missing the playoffs as manager. But after a 9-19 start in 2026, Thomson was dismissed and Mattingly took over as interim manager. Under Mattingly, the Phillies immediately got hot and crawled back into contention. They went 79-55 under Mattingly and finished with an 88-74 record, avoiding a near collapse in the final week of the regular season to clinch the NL's final playoff spot. The Phillies were then bounced in the Wild Card Series by the Braves in three games.

The Phillies have signed Don Mattingly to a two-year contract for the 2027 and 2028 seasons pic.twitter.com/pvMJoThtFN

Hitting coach Kevin Long and infield coach Bobby Dickerson are not expected to be retained, according to NBC Sports Philadelphia.

Mattingly never dropped the interim tag during the season, but is under contract in 2027 as the team's bench coach. The Phillies were linked to ex-Red Sox manager Alex Cora since he was fired by Boston in April and even offered him the managerial job in April when Thomson was fired. Cora has a strong relationship with club president Dave Dombrowski, but he again turned down the Phillies gig earlier this month.

The Phillies will now keep Mattingly in the dugout, going with a manager familiar with the roster as an uncertain offseason looms with a lockout expected to begin in December.

An interesting note here is that the Phillies general manager is Preston Mattingly, Don's son. It's a difficult thing to track down as great records weren't always kept, but it is believed that this is the first such pairing on an MLB ballclub.

Mattingly, 65, is in his third stint as a big-league manager. He was at the helm of the Dodgers from 2011-15, winning three NL West titles. But he was dismissed after not advancing to the World Series with a 1-3 record in postseason series. He then managed the Marlins from 2016-22, making the playoffs and winning NL Manager of the Year in 2020. His most recent job before joining the Phillies was serving as bench coach for the 2025 Blue Jays, helping win the AL pennant.

As things stand, the Phillies have made the playoffs five straight seasons, though they've gone backward. After the 2022 run to the World Series, they made the NLCS in 2023, the NLDS in 2024 and 2025 before the Wild Card Series this past season.

There is still talent, but the roster is getting older and has a lot less depth. It's a big offseason with a lot of questions for Dave Dombrowski.

At least one item can be crossed off the list.

#264. Kenneth Walker on pace to break NFL records for rushing yards, yards from scrimmage

When the Chiefs signed reigning Super Bowl MVP Kenneth Walker away from the Seahawks in free agency, they knew they were adding a playmaker to their offense. But no one could have known just how many plays Walker would make in his first five games as a Chief.

Walker has 665 rushing yards and 760 yards from scrimmage this season, putting him on pace to break the NFL single-season records in both statistical categories.

If Walker continues at his rushing pace for 17 games, he’d rush for 2,261 yards. That would break Eric Dickerson’s NFL record of 2,105 rushing yards in a season. Dickerson set the record in a 16-game season, and Walker would break the record in his 16th game, at his current pace.

And if Walker continues at his yards from scrimmage pace for 17 games, he’d finish the season with 2,584 yards from scrimmage. The NFL record is 2,509 yards from scrimmage, set by Chris Johnson in a 16-game season in 2009. At his current pace, Walker would break that record in the 17th game of this season.

Walker has quickly become the best running back the Chiefs have had during Patrick Mahomes era and has changed the Chiefs’ offense. Meanwhile, the 3-3 Seahawks are struggling to run the ball and missing him. Walker will be the big story on Sunday night when the Chiefs play the Seahawks in Seattle.
