#266. Why Victor Wembanyama is poised to level up in Year 4 takeover -- and possibly join historic MVP/DPOY company

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

When Victor Wembanyama came into the NBA as the No. 1 pick in 2023, the hype, quite literally, couldn't have been any bigger. Wait, you're telling me there's a 19-year-old kid in France who makes seven-footers look small with the skills of a guard?

You can imagine the "OK, buddy" snickers, because honestly, if you weren't tapping into the EuroLeague circuit, the idea of this guy sounded inconceivable. Some freakish combination of Kevin Durant and Bill Russell? What are you going to tell me next, that in his third NBA season, he's going to become the first unanimous Defensive Player of the Year in league history, finish third in MVP voting and go to the Finals, where his team will hold the lead for more than 70% of the total minutes played, by way of a Game 7 road win over the defending champion Thunder?

Funny you should ask. As it turns out, that's precisely what Wembanyama accomplished last season despite not being old enough to legally buy a beer until the month before the All-Star break. His learning curve looks like the vapor trail of a rocket ship headed straight for the moon.

Not since LeBron James, who averaged an astonishing 31 points, seven rebounds and six assists in his third NBA season, has a player been this dominant this soon. When LeBron carried the 2007 Cavaliers to the Finals, he was 23 days younger than Wemby was when he made his Finals debut on June 3 against New York. LeBron is arguably the greatest player in NBA history, which is probably the only career outcome that could have actually exceeded the teenage expectations with which he was saddled.

It's close to the same for Wembanyama, who is already on a GOAT trajectory. Everyone knows you're supposed to wait until a player has won at least one championship and/or MVP, or hell, at least until he's actually through his rookie contract, before you even start whispering things like that, but Wembanyama is leaving us no choice. He's the best defensive player on the planet to the degree that Stephen Curry is the best shooter on the planet.

Just about everything else in basketball is debatable. Those two things are not. Both Curry and Wembanyama warp the geometry of a court in ways nobody could have imagined before they came along. Curry stretches defenses. Wembanyama shrinks offenses.

NBA.com tracking defines an "open" shot as the nearest defender being at least four feet away, but tell that to all the scared-to-death scorers who have been forced to rewire every spatial instinct they've spent a lifetime calculating, parading into the paint only to come running right back out as if they've seen, well, an alien.

On one half of the court alone, Wembanyama is among the most impactful players in the game. The fact that last season, he became the only player in history to average at least 25 points, 11 rebounds and three blocks on 62% true shooting was enough to claim the No. 1 spot on our CBS Sports Top 100 player rankings.

Quibble with that designation if you must. Call it premature. Maybe it is. There are no fewer than five players with a reasonable claim to that throne, one of whom, Jalen Brunson, just bested Wembanyama in the Finals. This is a projection for what's ahead, however, and the fact of the matter is Wembanyama -- who clocked in at 5-foot-7 in the second grade and hit 6-5 before his 13th birthday -- is growing too fast for anyone to keep up with for much longer.

This is what's most exciting. We get to watch these growth spurts happen in real time, from season to season, month to month, sometimes even game to game. In the first playoff game of his career, Wembanyama hung 35 on the Blazers. When the Timberwolves had the Spurs 2-2 in the second round after Wemby was ejected early in Game 4, he fired back with 27 points, 17 rebounds, five assists and three blocks as San Antonio won the next two games by 59 points.

Then it was OKC in the conference finals, where the dream season was supposed to finally end. Until Wemby went for 41 points and 24 boards in a double-overtime Game 1 win, that is. For me, and I suspect a lot of others, this was the night Wembanyama became the best player in the world. So far, this is the signature shot of his career.

WEMBY, WOW!WHAT A SHOT TO TIE THE GAME AT 108. pic.twitter.com/HELQUpxww7

The nerve to even take that shot as a dead-tired 21-year-old playing in your first conference finals game is one thing. The ability to actually make it as a 7-foot-4 center is out of this world. These are Steph Curry shots, plain and simple. This crossover-into-stepback 3 in a preseason game last week should be impossible for a man of Wembanyama's size.

Shots like this are almost too accessible for Wemby at times. He can get them whenever he wants, and they're a hell of a lot of fun to take, but the reality is that he was only a 34% 3-point shooter last year. He doesn't overdo it (five and a half 3-point attempts a game feels about right for now), and the threat of it alters spatial dynamics in ways traditional shooting percentages can't encapsulate, but on any given night, Wemby can be susceptible to falling a bit too deeply in love with the deep ones.

Indeed, the most obvious next step in Wembanyama's offensive evolution is continuing to drill down on the right shots from the right spots. At the moment, he doesn't have a quote-unquote office. No kill zone like Kevin Durant at the elbow, Carmelo Anthony facing up or SGA stepping back. He may never have such a specific go-to spot or shot given his fluid, freelancing ways, but in general, he can stand to more consistently establish himself closer to the basket.

That's easier said than done. Part of it is just having the intent to do so, but the sheer strength to do it is another matter. Wemby is still maturing physically. Isaiah Hartenstein manhandled him at times in the conference finals -- literally pushing him out of the paint as Wemby was forced to initiate almost all his offense for long stretches from the perimeter, particularly in Games 2 and 3 after he was so dominant in the paint in the series opener.

It was largely the same story early in the Finals, when the Knicks forced him to take 22 of his first 42 shots from outside the paint. But each game, he forced his way a little lower on the court, and by Game 3, you could see the clear markings of his efficiency growing as his average shot distance shrank.

None of this is to suggest that Wembanyama shouldn't look to utilize his jump shooting abilities, but this also isn't rocket science. The closer that a guy who can touch the rim without his feet leaving the ground can operate to the basket, the better. This can happen in a variety of ways. Rim rolls. Short rolls. Post-ups. Lobs. Dunker's spot catches. Face-ups from the Joel Embiid free-throw-extended zones, where he can put the ball on the floor and reach the rim in a single step.

As defenses collectively sink to deter Wemby's point-blank finishes, the soft spots in the short mid-range -- where he took just 20% of his shots last season and made just 42% of them, per Cleaning the Glass -- are seemingly ripe for growth with more frequent exploitation. This preseason look Wemby got against the Suns is a prime example.

Not all jumpers are created equal, and again, 3-pointers, self-created or off the catch, are going to and should be a part of Wemby's arsenal, but on some level, every 3-point shot that Wembanyama takes, especially the crazy off-the-dribble ones, is a win for the defense.

The next step is about launching as many offensive attacks as possible on his terms. Understanding that he is still figuring out what those terms are is going to be like watching a young dinosaur slowly realizing its power to destroy everything in front of him.

Despite his ongoing struggles, Shohei Ohtani will be in the Game 3 starting lineup for the Los Angeles Dodgers on Wednesday in Game 3 of the National League Championship Series against the Milwaukee Brewers, manager Dave Roberts announced Tuesday.

"He's adamant he feels good enough to be in there. He's close to finding something with his swing. I feel great about it," Roberts said Tuesday. "He wants to be in there and help us win a ballgame and win a championship. Great conversation, and I'm excited about having him in there."

Ohtani, who is nursing knee and biceps injuries, is 3 for 20 this postseason and 11 for 70 (.157) with zero home runs in his last 24 games dating back to August 18. He spent 12 days on the injured list in September and has just one hit in eight NLCS plate appearances as the Dodgers have fallen behind 2-0 in the best-of-seven series.

"The results, I take full responsibility," Ohtani said through an interpreter Tuesday. "That's all I can really say, why the results haven't been where I wanted it to be. I think there's different approaches to this, whether that be focusing on reducing the symptoms and getting rid of the pain and/or just making sure that I'm moving well in the swing."

"The symptoms have subdued a lot," Ohtani said. "Especially when I was on the IL, spending that time just being able to reduce the symptoms. As of now with the swing, it's a daily process of trying different things, different feel on a daily basis."

The Dodgers have a very good DH alternative in top prospect Josue De Paula. De Paula, 21, reached base 21 times in 11 regular-season games and has pinch-hit three times in key spots this postseason, and worked two walks. Los Angeles has nine singles and one double in the two NLCS losses to the Brewers. Their offense is lacking.

"We remember vividly at this time last year that he maybe had the best baseball game ever played the day he pitched against us and hit a home run every time up, it seemed like," Brewers manager Pat Murphy said Wednesday when asked about Ohtani's struggles at the plate. "You can't forget that, his capabilities."

Now 32, Ohtani hit .275/.377/.512 with 30 home runs during the regular season, which would be a career year for most players but is a down year for Ohtani. He threw 85 ⅔ innings with a 1.79 ERA before the injuries. Ohtani has not pitched since July 3 and won't return to the mound this postseason.

Teams with a 2-0 lead in a best-of-seven series have historically gone on to win the series 83% of the time. Game 3 is Wednesday night at Dodger Stadium.

#270. Blackhawks' Connor Bedard to miss 4 months after shoulder injury as Chicago's rebuild hits another obstacle

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Chicago Blackhawks couldn't make it through July without getting terrible injury news. After suffering an injury in offseason training, star center Connor Bedard is expected to miss four months after undergoing left shoulder surgery.

Last week, video surfaced of Bedard taking a hard fall in an on-ice training session. He exited the ice in obvious discomfort, and the Blackhawks' worst fears have become reality.

I have video of Connor Bedard leaving practice today with a left shoulder injury, as first reported by @RyanmcgregorCHI. You can hear him in severe pain as he leaves the ice: pic.twitter.com/MySM1UwLht

This is the second shoulder injury Bedard has suffered in a matter of months. In December, Bedard suffered a shoulder injury against the St. Louis Blues, and he was forced to miss 12 games. Bedard has missed at least 13 games in two of his first three NHL seasons, and he will be out for an extended stretch to begin the 2026-27 campaign.

Based on the timeline provided by the team, Bedard should return in early November. In the past, that meant he may only miss two or three weeks, but he'll be out at least double that with the NHL reducing its preseason and expanding to 84 regular-season games. Bedard is now slated to miss over a month, with opening night pushed up to late September.

The No. 1 overall pick in the 2023 NHL Draft, Bedard has flashed superstar potential on many occasions, but injuries and a miserable supporting cast have prevented him from making a permanent jump into the league's elite tier. Bedard's production -- 30 goals and 45 assists in 69 games -- was outstanding last year. However, like the rest of the team, his game still has plenty of warts defensively.

After swinging a polarizing trade for Buffalo Sabres defenseman Bowen Byram, the Blackhawks were hoping their rebuild would finally turn a corner in 2026-27. Bedard is entering his fourth year, other top prospects look ready to assume bigger roles and Spencer Knight has emerged as a budding star in goal.

Now, Bedard's injury has thrown a wrench into those plans, and the Blackhawks will have to weather an early-season storm.

The Blackhawks haven't reached the playoffs once since 2017 -- the 2020 bubble postseason -- and have been rebuilding in earnest since the 2020-21 season. Six seasons later, that rebuild has yielded little progress.

Chicago went 29-39-14 and finished 31st in the league last year. That was an 11-point improvement over the previous season, but it still left them 18 points out of a playoff spot. After digging itself such a deep hole at the start of the rebuild, the franchise still has a long way to go before it re-establishes itself as a Stanley Cup contender.

Even if Bedard had been healthy to start the season, the Blackhawks would've been a long shot to make the playoffs. There are already serious questions about Byram's ability to be a No. 1 defenseman, and there is a big dropoff behind him on the blue line. Up front, a lot of things would need to break Chicago's way in order for the team to contend for the postseason.

The Hawks were -- and still are -- counting on big jumps from Frank Nazar, Anton Frondell and Oliver Moore. Each is a former first-round pick, but they've combined for 194 games and 100 points. It's possible that the trio is quite formidable a few years from now, but in 2026-27? That's a bit of a stretch.

As far as Bedard is concerned, he was poised for another leap forward, but now he'll be behind the curve when he returns in November. It's probably unfair to expect Bedard to be at his best immediately upon his return, especially with a new coach implementing a new scheme, so the first quarter of the season could be gone by the time Bedard is fully comfortable.

That's a tough blow for a player who needs to reach another level for his team to do the same. It could still happen, but Bedard's injury gives the Blackhawks zero room for error. Is the team around Bedard good enough to stay afloat without him for the first 15 games of the season? Is Bedard good enough on his own that he could drag the Blackhawks back into the playoff race when he returns? I just haven't seen enough evidence of either to believe Chicago has more than a slim chance of making the playoffs.

If Chicago is looking for a silver lining, it's that the threat of another team throwing a gargantuan offer sheet at Bedard is much lower now. Opposing teams probably don't want to throw a boatload of money at Bedard without knowing more about the long-term health of his shoulder. That being the case, general manager Kyle Davidson needs to take this chance to hammer out a contract extension with his star in short order.

#273. Ups and downs from Saints vs. Giants

The New Orleans Saints have finally ended their win streak, finding a win over the New York Giants. It didn't start pretty, and it definitely didn't end pretty, but New Orleans survived.

Rookie Barion Brown hasn't been the difference maker on special teams that New Orleans expected when they drafted him to return kicks. But after some highlight plays over the past few weeks, Brown finally had his breakout game against the Giants.

Brown had a 41-yard return that helped open scoring for the Saints on the day, resulting in a field goal for Daniel Carlson. Brown would also have a 23-yard punt return in the game, setting the team up in good position.

Part of the Saints offensive explosion was their valuable field position, plenty of thanks to Brown. The former LSU wide receiver also recorded his first career reception in the win over New York.

The biggest standout on Sunday is no other than cornerback Martin Emerson Jr. The veteran cornerback logged 7 tackles, all solo, a tackle for loss, 4 passes defended, and most importantly, 2 interceptions.

Emerson entered the game after Kool-Aid McKinstry left with what Kellen Moore described as a migraine. Emerson took advantage of the opportunity and became the team's standout player and a game-changer.

With his big game, Emerson has now earned more playtime. It will be interesting to see how the Saints incorporate the veteran cornerback into their defense. Emerson was in a camp battle with Quincy Riley for the CB2 position.

The Saints worked to establish the run, and found success doing so during Sunday's win. New Orleans rushed for 175 yards on 38 carries, averaging 4.6 yards per carry. Kendre Miller led the team with 70 yards.

Three players for the Saints averaged 4.9 yards per carry or better, including quarterback Tyler Shough. Being able to run the ball is all the difference for the Saints offense. Instead of being stuck on third and long, New Orleans faced third and manageable more than not thanks to getting 4 yards on a run on first and second down.

The Saints offense has to prove that they can sustain success in the running game, but a strong showing against the Giants proves it's possible.

Weird, after the third quarter ended, I was expecting to put Moore as a positive after Sunday's game. The Saints were looking pretty with a 34-10 lead after scoring 34 unanswered points. It looked like brilliant resilience by Moore and the Saints offense, who were called out by owner Gayle Benson earlier in the week.

Despite another slow start, with the Saints only finding points within the final two minutes of the first half, the Saints' offensive explosion was brilliant. But of course, Moore has landed as a down for a reason. The Saints absolutely crumbled in the fourth quarter and were one play away from going into overtime despite having a 24-point lead with 10 minutes remaining.

This is all too familiar for the Saints, who found a similar way to lose earlier this season to the Las Vegas Raiders. Moore has proved his teams start slow and also can't finish. It's rare for a team that starts slow and also finishes slow to win a game, but Moore was lucky enough that his team pulled away with the win.

Look, Daniel Carlson finished the day making up for his early mistake, but he hasn't proven to be the consistent veteran kicker the Saints were hoping for when they hired him. Entering Sunday, Carlson has missed a kick in four straight games, including PATs, and added to that on Sunday with a miss from 55.

The veteran kicker quickly made up for it with a 58-yard field goal the very next drive, and another make from 51 yards in the third quarter. Despite his impressive comeback, Carlson needs to prove more to be consistent enough for the Saints' offense to feel comfortable.

#274. Kentavious Caldwell-Pope says 76ers' success will come down to 'us liking each other'

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The last few seasons have seen the decline of the traditional superteam in the NBA, but the loaded Philadelphia 76ers are attempting to buck those trends with a roster stuffed to the brim with veteran talent. LeBron James and Jaylen Brown joined Joel Embiid and Tyrese Maxey on a roster that reached the second round of the postseason a year ago. Recent No. 3 overall pick VJ Edgecombe, mid-level signings Anfernee Simons and Dean Wade and two-time NBA champion Kentavious Caldwell-Pope round out one of the NBA's most talented rosters.

So talented are the 76ers, in fact, that Caldwell-Pope's belief coming into the season is that personal dynamics will ultimately determine the success or failure of the team.

"Our chemistry is gonna be the biggest part for us," Caldwell-Pope said on Monday, via ESPN. "Us liking each other, being able to be around each other and have fun on and off the court."

Caldwell-Pope knows a thing or two about championship chemistry. He won a title alongside James playing for the Los Angeles Lakers, then won another one with Nikola Jokić in Denver. Both of those teams declined, in part, because of personal dynamics after Caldwell-Pope left. The Lakers made an ill-fated trade for Russell Westbrook in 2021 that effectively closed their championship window, while Denver fired both its head coach and general manager late in the 2024-25 season in part over their inability to work together cohesively.

Fellow members of the 76ers have echoed this sentiment. "It's a lot of guys with talent and egos," Brown explained at his introductory press conference. "But to win, you got to be able to sacrifice and have trust and communication." The notion of sacrifice was a theme at James' media day appearance as well. "The luxury of my game is I can do everything," he said. "Literally, I can do everything."

The math makes plain that there will need to be on-court sacrifices. The projected five-man starting lineup of James, Maxey, Brown, Embiid and Edgecombe has a combined 134% career usage rate. Everyone is giving up shots and touches, and that can lead to difficult adjustments on the court and resentments that bubble up off of it. While there are basketball concerns that the team will need to solve over the course of the season, keeping everyone on the same page and engaged while they're working through those bumps will be paramount. You're far more likely to sacrifice for teammates that you actually like, so Caldwell-Pope has a point in that regard.

#275. Phoenix Suns Give Oso Ighodaro A Contract Extension

With the start of the 2026-27 NBA season right around the corner — NBC has a tripleheader on Tuesday! — it's the time of the year where teams start nailing down the details of contract extensions as deadlines to file rapidly approach. That has benefited a former Marquette Golden Eagle, as Oso Ighodaro has agreed to terms on a three year extension with the Phoenix Suns, according to ESPN's Shams Charania.

When Ighodaro was drafted #40 overall in 2024, he signed a deal for three years with a team option for a fourth. The 2026-27 season is the third and final full year of the deal, which the Suns guaranteed for the former Marquette center back in June. Part of the process of agreeing to this extension is Phoenix already picking up the option for the 2027-28 season and thus guaranteeing Ighodaro his nearly $2.5 million salary for that season.

The three year extension then kicks in after that, guaranteeing Ighodaro a paycheck through the end of the 2030-31 season. Spotrac's breakdown of the deal has him making just under $9 million in 2028-29, $9.7 million in Year Two, and then $10.3 million in Year 3. Oso Ighodaro is a $10 million a year player in the NBA, what a time to be alive.

Ighodaro played in 61 games as a rookie for the Suns, starting six times and averaging 4.2 points, 3.6 rebounds, and just over an assist per game in 17 minutes a night. Last season, he played in all 82 games, getting 24 starts for Phoenix. He averaged 6.5 points, 5.1 rebounds, and 2.3 assists in 22 minutes per game overall, but as a starter, that was up to 8.0 points, 6.3 rebounds, and 3.1 assists in nearly 27 minutes per game. Ighodaro started all four games of Phoenix's first round playoff series against the Oklahoma City Thunder last spring, putting up 7.5 points, 7.0 rebounds, and 4.0 assists in more than 32 minutes. That's, uh, not too shabby for a former second round pick, so you can see why the team is enthused about locking him up on a deal that's worth roughly 5% of the salary cap through 2031.

Phoenix opens their season on Wednesday, October 21st, with a road game against the Portland Trail Blazers.

#278. Flyers sign Ducks C Leo Carlsson to record 5-year, $90 million offer sheet

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Philadelphia Flyers have signed Anaheim Ducks center Leo Carlsson to a five-year, $90 million offer sheet, the team announced on Friday. Regardless of what happens from here, Carlsson will become the highest paid player in NHL history at $18 million per year, passing Minnesota Wild winger Kirill Kaprizov.

Carlsson, 21, was a restricted free agent after completing his entry-level contract with the Ducks. Anaheim now has seven days to match Philadelphia's offer, or it will receive four first-round picks from the Flyers in exchange for losing Carlsson.

The No. 2 overall pick in the 2023 NHL Draft, Carlsson is well on his way to becoming a superstar center in the NHL. In just 201 career games, Carlsson has piled up 61 goals and 80 assists while flashing some excellent two-way potential. Last season, Carlsson took a noticeable step forward while leading Anaheim to its first playoff appearance since 2018.

Carlsson fell just shy of becoming a point-per-game player with 67 points in 70 games, and he posted a five-on-five expected goals share of 53.4%, per Natural Stat Trick. Those are sparkling numbers for a center of his age, and he should only continue to improve over the next few seasons.

The Flyers, meanwhile, had a need at center. Last offseason, Philadelphia picked up former Duck Trevor Zegras in a trade with Anaheim, and he was a revelation for the Flyers. Zegras posted a career year with 26 goals and 41 assists while also making great strides defensively under first-year coach Rick Tocchet.

Still, Philadephia is in need of a true No. 1 center at the top of the lineup, and this move would help the team check that box without tanking or relying on draft lottery luck. The Flyers looked to be a team on the rise in 2025-26, and signing Carlsson would only accelerate that ascension.

The big question for Philadelphia -- and now for Anaheim -- is whether Carlsson can become an $18 million player. He's not there yet, but given his age and future salary cap projections, he could get close. Players of Carlsson's caliber are very hard to find, so even Phildelphia did overpay a bit, it might be worth it just to know the team has its franchise center locked down for the forseeable future.

On the other side of the country, the Ducks are in a real bind. They've already lost four members of their blue line in the offseason with Jacob Trouba (free agency), Radko Gudas (free agency), John Carlson (free agency) and Olen Zellweger (trade) going out the door. Losing Carlsson, the biggest prize of the team's six-year rebuild, would turn a tough situation into a disaster for Anaheim.

The path of least resistance, which may be the correct one, might be for the Ducks to match the Flyers' offer and keep Carlsson in the fold. Anaheim has the room to absorb Carlsson's new cap hit, but it would have less money to upgrade the defense. If general manager Pat Verbeek doesn't believe Carlsson is worth that money, he could take the four first-round picks and newfound cap space and go big-game hunting himself. It's just hard to imagine the Ducks find another rising superstar to replace the one they lost.

Until they accrue seven years of NHL service or reach the age of 27 -- whichever comes first -- players become restricted free agents when their contracts expire. When that happens, other teams can submit offer sheets. If that happens, the team that currently holds the player's rights has seven days to match the offer sheet or let the player go, whereupon it would receive compensation in the form of draft capital.

The draft compensation varies depending on how the annual value of the contract. Carlsson's record deal obviously falls into the highest tier, which requires four draft picks over the next five years. Philadelphia currently has five first-round picks over the next four years, so it can pay that price and have one selection left over.

Offer sheets haven't been all that common, but teams are finally starting to use them as valuable roster-building tool. Using them to pluck valuable depth from cap-strapped opponents has been more common, but the Flyers might start a new trend in the NHL.

Let another team draft and develop a young star, then throw a boatload of money at him as soon as he hits the market. There's always the chance the original team matches the offer sheet, but no real harm comes of that, other than maybe some bad blood.

If opponents are going to risk losing their best young players by allowing them to hit restricted free agency, why not make them pay? In this case, Anaheim will either watch its franchise cornerstone go to Philadelphia, or it will be pay an enormous sum of money to keep him.

Let this be a lesson to other teams with budding superstars: Get them extended early or risk a major headache.

#280. Saints may have found a winning formula with rookie OL Jeremiah Wright

We haven't seen the same production from the New Orleans Saints' 2026 NFL Draft class as what buoyed the team to relevance in 2025. Each of their top three picks have missed time with injuries to start the season, and only one of their fourth rounders has consistently gotten into games (wide receiver Bryce Lance, who caught his first touchdown pass on Sunday). That trend could change if their other fourth-round pick stays in the starting lineup. Former Auburn Tigers right guard Jeremiah Wright replaced the injured Cesar Ruiz midway through Week 6's win over the New York Giants, and his physical style of play may have uncovered a winning formula.

Nola.com's Matthew Paras shared the team's run splits with and without Ruiz; the Saints averaged 4.4 yards per carry on nine carriers with him at right guard, improving to 4.7 yards per attempt on 29 tries with Wright in the lineup instead. But that includes a couple of scrambles by Tyler Shough. Focus on the running backs and it's a difference of 3.9 yards per carry (with Ruiz) to 4.5 (with Wright). That's a significant upgrade.

But it may not be as simple as swapping one for another. ESPN's Katherine Terrell highlighted the run bock win rates from TruMedia, which found that Wright had the lowest win rate on the team (60.7%). In comparison, Ruiz won 75% of his blocks, which was better than Wright but still ranked eighth out of ten players. That tracks. Ruiz has been better in pass protection than on rushing plays for most of his career, only really excelling in both phases when Klint Kubiak implemented his outside zone-heavy blocking scheme back in 2024.

Now Ruiz is dealing with a knee injury. He had an MRI in New York and traveled with the team to Paris for this week's game with the Pittsburgh Steelers, but we may have to wait for the first injury report on Wednesday to get an idea of his status. The Saints had the most success against the Giants when they were aggressively leaning on the run game. They shouldn't rush Ruiz back if he's hurt, but they should seriously consider giving the rookie more snaps even if Ruiz is good to go.

Despite being given multiple opportunities to build a consistent contender, the Colts never won an AFC South title under his leadership and currently are in a five-year playoff drought.

That final defeat forced fans to file out early, while leaving a roar of boos to echo throughout Lucas Oil Stadium on Sunday. The constant lack of a pass rush is another stain that can't just be wiped away. Panthers tight end Tommy Tremble punctuated his second touchdown of Sunday’s 25-14 win over the Eagles by turning toward and pointing at defensive back Cooper DeJean.

#286. Michigan football knows what it has in Bryce Underwood. It’s time to move on

Kyle Whittingham said on Monday that Michigan has a plan at quarterback. It's a super-secret plan, by the way: "We're not going to tip our hand" to this week's opponent, No. 6 Indiana, Whittingham said. "But we have a good plan in place."

Curt Cignetti and the Hoosiers must be petrified. That the plan would in some way qualify as good seems to fly in the face of everything we've seen over the first six games of the season.

About the only good idea would be to permanently bench sophomore Bryce Underwood, who tossed a pair of interceptions in Saturday's 21-18 win against Penn State — the only other Big Ten blueblood more miserable than Michigan at this moment — and was replaced by freshman Tommy Carr.

More: Michigan benches Bryce Underwood, but Kyle Whittingham's QB decision isn't over

Seeing his first extended action, Carr accumulated 83 yards of total offense and ran for a touchdown to provide "a spark for the offense," Whittingham said.

The Wolverines know what they have in Underwood. It's not pretty. It's time to pull the plug.

He's made no growth since last season and has played with zero confidence, leaving the former five-star recruit as the only primary Big Ten quarterback with more interceptions than touchdowns. The only starter in the conference with a worse efficiency rating is Maryland's Malik Washington.

Maybe Carr has the skill set to better fit what Whittingham and offensive coordinator Jason Beck need in their scheme. Maybe the spark he brought on Saturday carries over to the second half of the year, and we look back at this reboot under center as a key turning point for the Whittingham era.

At the very least, Carr is an unknown commodity while Underwood is a proven drag on this offense.

Not that who Michigan starts against the Hoosiers will even matter. Indiana is a touchdown favorite in Ann Arbor because of a defense that might be the best in the Big Ten and will be too much for the Wolverines to handle.

The Hoosiers rank fourth in the FBS in scoring at 12.9 points per game, fourth nationally in rush defense at 75.4 yards per game and seventh nationally in allowing 4.3 yards per play. Unless the Wolverines make some sort of magical week-to-week improvement, Indiana's defense will dominate.

But that's an even better reason to put Carr into the starting lineup. This year is cooked: Michigan is not a contender in the Big Ten or nationally, and should be thinking more about what can be done over the second half of the year to get better in 2027.

That will be done by evaluating every piece of the offense, starting at quarterback. Michigan has to improve at the position to challenge the best of the best in the conference. We know Underwood isn't that guy.

Carr might be. Even if he's not, that's valuable information for Whittingham to have heading into a crucial transfer-portal season. Staying the course and hoping for the best is not the answer.

#287. Colts announce firing of general manager Chris Ballard after loss to Titans, DeForest Buckner criticism

The Indianapolis Colts are moving on from general manager Chris Ballard. The team announced Monday that Ballard was relieved from his duties.

In a statement, team owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon said the team's standard "is to compete for championships." She added that she believes "a change in leadership is necessary to meet that standard."

"I am grateful to Chris for his years of service to the Colts and for everything he poured into this organization. He cared deeply about our team and our community, and we wish Chris and his family all the best.

"As I said at the start of the season, the sense of urgency has never been higher. Our standard is to compete for championships, and I believe a change in leadership is necessary to meet that standard.

"Making this change during the season was a deliberate decision. Waiting would only delay the important work that needs to begin now. We will conduct a thorough search for our next general manager and take the time necessary to identify the right leader for the future of this organization.

"I also want to be clear: this decision does not change our goals for this season. We have a lot of football in front of us, and I expect us to compete, improve, and win football games."

The decision comes with the team sitting at 2-4 after six weeks. It also comes after the Colts fell to the previously winless Tennessee Titans in Week 6. After the contest, Colts star DeForest Buckner expressed his frustration with the organization, saying he was "sick and tired of the same song and dance every year."

Ballard has been responsible for that "song and dance" since 2017. While he's experienced some moments of excellence — drafting Shaquille Leonard and Jonathan Taylor and signing Daniel Jones on the cheap in 2025 — he's also experienced some high-profile misses, such as drafting Anthony Richardson, hiring Jeff Saturday, trading a pair of first-round picks for Sauce Gardner and inking Jones to a two-year, $88 million extension ahead of the 2026 season.

Through six games, that extension looks regrettable. Jones has regressed after a promising 2025. This season, he's completed a career-low 59.6 percent of his passes, and has just four touchdowns against six interceptions, two of which came in the team's Week 6 loss.

The trade for Gardner has not only lacked results for Indianapolis on the field — he's yet to record an interception for the Colts and hasn't matched his All-Pro play in New York — it cost the Colts their first-round pick in April and (barring a trade) will mean they won't have a first-round pick in the 2027 draft, either.

The team's next general manager will be tasked with figuring out whether Jones deserves to remain the Colts' starter next season. Even if that answer is yes, finding a long-term quarterback is almost certainly a priority for a team that has been scrambling for stability at the position ever since the surprising retirement of former No. 1 overall pick Andrew Luck in 2019.

#288. Alex Ovechkin re-signs with Capitals: NHL's all-time goals leader back for one year, $4.25 million

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Alex Ovechkin has made a decision about his NHL future. The Washington Capitals legend is back for his 22nd season with the franchise, the team announced on Thursday. Ovechkin has inked a one-year, $4.25 million contract in hopes of getting one more shot at his second Stanley Cup.

While Ovechkin's contract carries a cap hit of $4.25 million for the 2026-27 season, he can earn substantially more due to a $4.75 million bonus that kicks in at 10 games played. If Washington doesn't have the cap space to absorb the entire bonus, whatever remains will be carried over to the 2027-28 campaign.

The greatest scorer in NHL history will return to add to his record total of 929 goals. Even at the age of 40 last season, Ovechkin still notched 32 goals, and he remains a key piece of the Washington power play. With the Capitals retooling their roster, Ovechkin has a realistic shot to chase another championship.

The No. 1 overall pick in the 2004 NHL Draft, Ovechkin immediately asserted himself as one of the NHL's most electrifying players as a rookie in 2005-06. That year, he beat out Sidney Crosby for the Calder Trophy with 52 goals and 106 points. That was just the first chapter in one of the greatest individual rivalries in sports history.

For the last two decades, Ovechkin has made a habit of finding the back of the net. Ovechkin has scored 50-plus goals nine times in his career, and he topped 60 goals in 2007-08. In the process of tormenting opposing goaltenders, Ovechkin has loaded up on Rocket Richard Trophy and Hart Trophy wins, but he's still sitting on one Stanley Cup.

In 2018, Washington finally slayed the Pittsburgh Penguins in the second round and went on to defeat the Vegas Golden Knights in the Stanley Cup Final. Ovechkin won the Conn Smythe Trophy after leading all playoff performers with 15 goals.

Last season, Ovechkin was still an effective offensive threat for the Capitals, notching 32 goals and 32 assists while playing all 82 games. This season, the Washington legend will have to shoulder less of the offensive burden, and that could benefit both him and the team as a whole.

Now 40 years old, Ovechkin is far from the player he was in his prime. That's not breaking news. Whatever defensive game Ovechkin had is completely gone, but that was never his strength anyway. Ovechkin is on the ice to score goals, and he's still quite good at that.

Last year, even in a down year for the NHL's all-time leading goal-scorer, Ovechkin potted 32 goals. That was tied for 33rd in the NHL, and the most impressive part of that total might be the fact that he scored just five power-play goals, which was a career low. Nineteen of Ovechkin's goals came at five-on-five, which put him above Mitch Marner, Kirill Kaprizov, Jack Hughes and Steven Stamkos in that category.

There's also some good news about Ovechkin's dip in power play production. He shot just 5.81% on the man advantage, and he totaled 10.6 expected goals, per Natural Stat Trick. If opponents couldn't figure out how to stop Ovechkin's howitzer of a shot for the first two decades, I doubt they suddenly found a permanent solution last year. If he regresses back toward his career average in that area, Ovechkin should add four or five goals in 2026-27.

The other part of Ovechkin's game that remains stable is his strength -- a core component of his scoring prowess. According to NHL Edge, Ovechkin remains in the 99th percentile when it comes to hardest shot (97.3 mph), number of shots between 90-100 mph (35) and number of shots between 80-90 mph (82).

All the ingredients are there for Ovechkin to score at least 30 goals again next season, so it just comes down to whether the Capitals can offset his defensive shortcomings. Coach Spencer Carbery has already proven he can adjust to that, as evidenced by Ovechkin's complete lack of defensive zone starts in 2025-26. Now that Washington has a deeper lineup, it will only get easier to shelter Ovechkin with favorable deployment.

Washington has been extremely aggressive in building a roster capable of winning now, likely knowing that Ovechkin would return if given the chance to win a Stanley Cup. So, the question is, have the Capitals done enough to make that dream come true and allow Ovechkin to ride off into the sunset with a second Cup ring?

Offensively, Washington is very strong on the wings, especially with Ovechkin back in the fold. The Caps have already acquired Jordan Kyrou and Alex Tuch, a pair of dynamic offensive threats who can put the puck in the net at a high rate. Kyrou is coming off a disappointing season with the St. Louis Blues, but he's proven to be a consistent 30-goal scorer, and the same is true for Tuch. Boone Jenner should also provide some leadership and depth scoring in the bottom six.

In terms of the returning cast, Tom Wilson still has plenty of game after registering a second consecutive 30-goal season, and Aliaksei Protas has developed into a highly effective top-six power forward.

Those players will take some of the attention off Ovechkin, which will only help at this stage of his career. The more attention paid to other weapons, the more opportunities Ovechkin has to get free and load up a powerful shot from a quiet patch of ice.

Another strength of this Washington roster, and one that makes it worthy of consideration as a true contender, is the goaltending. Logan Thompson ranked second in the NHL with 25.9 goals saved above average, and he earned a spot on the Canadian Olympic team. Charlie Lindgren struggled a bit, but he's still a capable backup who gives Washington security in the crease.

Unfortunately for the Capitals, it's tough to win a Cup with just wingers and goaltenders. While Dylan Strome and Pierre-Luc Dubois have been solid at center, the roster is pretty underwhelming down the middle, especially when you stack it up against the best teams in the East. The Florida Panthers, Tampa Bay Lightning and Carolina Hurricanes all have better options at that position.

Defensively, it's a similar story. Washington is good enough to make the playoffs, but does it have enough to lift the Cup? Jakob Chychrun just turned in a stellar season, and the free-agent addition of Vincent Desharnais provides great depth. The issue is that Stanley Cup champions typically have at least one superstar on the blue line, and the Capitals don't check that box.

The Hurricanes just proved that a wealth of star power isn't necessary to win big, but if Washington is going to get another Cup for Ovechkin, it needs to make at least one more upgrade. There's a bigger need at center, but acquiring a true needle-mover on defense could put this roster over the top as well.

#289. David vs. Goliath MLB playoffs won't prove anything about a salary cap -- even if both sides will say they do

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

I'd rather not keep discussing this, but it's impossible to escape salary cap discourse in Major League Baseball in 2026.

The League Championship Series round is upon us, which is the last four teams standing and vying for the piece of metal that is the World Series trophy. The two-time defending World Series champion Dodgers are in the mix, along with three franchises on the opposite end. The Tampa Bay Rays and Milwaukee Brewers are two of the five current MLB franchises with zero World Series titles in their history. The Cleveland Guardians technically have the longest drought, having not won a title since 1948 (when the Brewers and Rays didn't exist).

In terms of history, it is Davids vs. Goliath, and that's where the payroll numbers stand as well.

Figures can vary based on loopholes and clever accounting (such as deferrals and back-loaded contracts). We'll use the competitive balance tax numbers from Major League Baseball. It seems like the number the league is taxing teams on is reasonable. Here are those payrolls, along with their ranking among the 30 MLB teams, for each of the final four in this season's playoffs.

1. Dodgers, $432.8 million19. Brewers, $154.7 million27. Rays, $112.9 million29. Guardians, $93.1 million

We could look at other places, as noted. The year-end 40-man roster salaries, for example, have the Dodgers second behind the Mets (monster deferrals drop the Dodgers way down to $339.6 million on their current 40-man) with the Brewers still 19th, the Rays 28th and the Guardians dead last in 30th with a payroll of less than $75 million.

Regardless, we can see the gap here between the have and the have-nots -- or, more accurately, the big spender and the not-so-big spenders -- and that's one of the main focuses off the field during the league championship series this season, unfortunately.

Before we go any further, and I'm gonna bold this so it doesn't escape anyone:

No, this doesn't prove we don't need a salary cap. And, no, if the Dodgers still win the World Series, it doesn't prove we do need one.

You can't just take results in small-sample playoff baseball, especially in one-year increments, to prove anything of the sort.

I'm not immune to seeing the disparity in the payrolls and realizing it looks absolutely absurd. I just think it's a lot more nuanced than "spending more equals winning automatically" in baseball.

Just look how close the Dodgers were to not winning in 2024 (they fell behind in the NLDS to the Padres) and 2025 (pick absolutely anything in Game 3 or Game 7 of the World Series). They might well win it all this time around, again, but they have an uphill battle to overcome an 0-2 deficit to a 103-win Brewers ballclub.

The owner side in the upcoming CBA discussions would love nothing more than the Dodgers to win it all again so they can say the proof is in the pudding. I have no doubt that some on the MLBPA side would love to see the Brewers topple the Dodgers and point to the low-payroll teams competing in the Fall Classic.

What if the Guardians win? We could look at the 40-man payrolls and say the team with the lowest payroll just won the World Series and WHAT'S UP NOW?!?!?

The MLBPA could easily argue that you can't act like low-payroll teams have no chance of competing with the likes of the Dodgers and Mets if, for example, the Rays and Brewers square off in the World Series after dispatching the Yankees and Dodgers, respectively? And conversely, we can't (or shouldn't) pretend that if the last four teams were, say, the Mets, Dodgers, Yankees and Blue Jays, the ownership side would suddenly become nuanced and say, "hey, this doesn't necessarily mean we need a salary cap." It would all be used as definitive proof.

But it isn't. It's obviously more nuanced than that. One-year results don't necessarily prove anything at all.

At the very least, though, the mix of these four specific teams in the LCS is pretty amusing heading into some inevitably contentious CBA talks.

#290. 5 winners and losers from the Lakers’ preseason

An exciting new era of Lakers basketball kicked off this preseason with lots of excitement and intrigue.

While we only briefly got a look at the new Big 3 that will guide the team into the future, there were plenty of other players fans got a long look at, for better and for worse.

Let's dive into some of the preseason winners and losers for the purple and gold.

Lakers fans didn't have to wait long to find their new fan favorite. As a jack-of-all-trades type of player, Mamu found many ways to make an impression.

Some nights, it was knocking down a barrage of threes. Other nights, it was an unexpected reverse dunk. But most often, it was each of those things and more throughout the game.

Pretty quickly, Mamu established himself as someone who is going to be able to come in and change games with his energy and his versatility, all while getting the fans into the game as well.

A byproduct of the Lakers bringing in multiple new wings this offseason is that Vando became a lot less valuable in that sense. And with head coach JJ Redick already showing his hand in being willing to sit Vando even when there was more of a need for him, it probably shouldn't have been a shock to see how little he was used in the preseason.

Even with the team shuffling through players and lineups because of injuries and rest, it was not an uncommon occurrence for Vando to have to wait until the fourth quarter to get his first minutes.

He can still bring value to the team as a chemistry and locker room guy as everyone on the team seems to like him. But he's very far down the pecking order when it comes to actually getting on the court.

From effectively the first preseason practice on, Williams was mentioned as a standout player. Despite missing time with an injury, Williams seems to be an odds-on favorite for the starting lineup to open the season.

Considering he was waived by the Nets and came to LA on a minimum deal, it's already a strong start to the season. The goal now is to make that a springboard to a better campaign and not the high point.

Coming into training camp, there was supposed to be a battle for the final roster spot and most circled Hardy and Knecht as the guys likely duking it out.

Based on preseason playing time, Knecht seems likely to lose that battle. But Hardy did not paint himself in any sort of glory. The Lakers probably won't cut both of them, but it wouldn't be shocking if they did. President of Basketball Operations Rob Pelinka likes to have an open roster spot going into the season and Hardy certainly didn't do enough to earn a roster spot.

LaRavia's campaign was a roller coaster last year. After a fast start, he hit a funk and struggled for most of the rest of the way. By the postseason, he seemed scared to even look at the basket.

But a revamped jumper and a renewed mindset have him in a much better space this preseason. His shot looks unorthodox, but he's shooting it with confidence and it's going on. It doesn't matter how pretty it looks, just whether he hits it regularly.

If he does, then he's another wing the Lakers can turn to this season.

#291. Rams kicker Blake Grupe ruled out after suffering knee injury minutes into L.A. debut

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Los Angeles Rams' kicking conundrum continues into Week 6, but not in the way you'd expect. After cutting former placekicker Harrison Mevis after Week 5, L.A. seemingly found its solution after signing Blake Grupe to assume the kicking duties. The former Notre Dame kicker made his Rams debut on Sunday and quickly endeared himself to his new squad by netting a 44-yard field goal in the first quarter.

However, things went downhill after that. After initially being listed as doubtful to return, Grupe has been downgraded to out and will not return to Sunday's contest due to a knee injury, the team announced. Grupe suffered the injury while making a tackle on the kickoff following his made field goal. He was seen lowering his shoulder to hit returner Devin Duvernay and came down awkwardly.

New Rams kicker Blake Grupe is doubtful to return after making this tackle pic.twitter.com/EgxKFTFSsq

With Grupe sidelined, the entire kicking operation is reshuffled. Punter Ethan Evans will serve as the kicker, while receiver Jordan Whittington could be the holder, as ESPN notes he was working on holds along the sideline.

So far, however, the Rams have not called Evans' number to kick. After Matthew Stafford connected with Blake Corum for a 15-yard touchdown in the second quarter, they kept the offense on the field for a two-point attempt, which failed. Then, when they were at the Arizona 27-yard line and faced with a fourth-and-1, Los Angeles went for it, but turned the ball over on downs.

Grupe entered the NFL as an undrafted free agent in 2023, initially signing with the Saints. He played for New Orleans until midway through the 2025 season, when he was released. After that, he made stops with the Colts and Jets before finding his way to the Rams. Coming into this game, Grupe had converted 81.9% of his career field goals (86-of-105) and 98% of his extra points (96-of-98).

The kicking game has been an issue throughout the first half of the season for the Rams, and it came to a head during Monday's overtime loss to the Bills. Mevis failed to convert on either of his field goal attempts, including what would've been a game-winner, which was blocked. That forced Los Angeles' hand to make a change in favor of Grupe, but this latest injury keeps them in a kicking nightmare.

#292. Warriors' Kristaps Porziņģis remains away from team as he deals with mystery illness

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

With just nine days until their regular season opener against the Los Angeles Lakers on Oct. 21, the Golden State Warriors remain without big man Kristaps Porziņģis, and it's unclear when that will change. Porziņģis, who signed a two-year, $40 million deal with the Warriors in the offseason, is sidelined with a mysterious illness.

In September, ahead of their training camp in Hawaii, the Warriors announced that Porziņģis would be out indefinitely.

"I'm not marking him down as being out to start the season or anything like that," Warriors general manager Mike Dunleavy said at the time. "He's just not available this week. … Disappointed that he won't be out there tomorrow, but it's early, so don't wantto overreact to anything."

Porziņģis has not been a participant during training camp nor played in any of the team's four preseason games thus far, and when coach Steve Kerr addressed reporters on Oct. 8, he didn't have much of an update.

"[Porziņģis] is not here today. We've obviously been busy in Hawaii and Portland, so we just came in and worked out the vets, had a really good practice. I'll reach out to KP today and check in with him, but nothing new to report," Kerr said. He added that he's texted with Porziņģis, who seems to be "doing OK."

The Warriors traded for Porziņģis at the deadline last season in a deal that sent Jonathan Kuminga and Buddy Hield to the Atlanta Hawks. In 15 games with the Warriors after the move, Porziņģis averaged 16.1 points, 5.3 rebounds, 2.3 assists and 1.1 blocks, while shooting just 43.3% from the field, including 31.1% from 3-point range.

The former No. 4 overall pick, Porziņģis has rarely been able to stay on the floor during his NBA career. Knee issues, including a torn ACL that cost him the entire 2018-19 season, have been the biggest issue. He's reached the 65-game mark just three times in 10 seasons, and in the last three seasons has played 57, 42 and 32 games, respectively for the Boston Celtics, Hawks and Warriors.

Near the end of his final season in Boston in 2025, Porziņģis started dealing with extreme fatigue, and was eventually diagnosed with postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, or POTS, which is characterized by rapid changes in heart rate when a person stands up and can lead to exhaustion and dizziness.

"You know how people say, 'Oh, I'm so fatigued.' I've never used those words. I don't even like to speak in those terms, but I really was like that," Porziņģis said ahead of last season. "At that time, I could just lay on the couch and be a house cat."

Neither the Warriors nor Porziņģis, who hasn't addressed the media since April, have offered any insight into his current illness or whether it's related to POTS.

The Warriors have three notable and well-paid players dealing with issues as the 2026-27 season begins

Despite the obvious concerns about Porziņģis' health, the Warriors opted to re-sign him this summer because of his ceiling when healthy and their limited options to build a competitive team around their aging core of Steph Curry, Draymond Green and Jimmy Butler (who is also sidelined due to a torn ACL). Notably, the second year of Porziņģis' deal only has a partial guarantee of $3 million.

"I think in constructing (the roster), we had to make a decision between talent and availability," Dunleavy said in August. "There was no perfect solution in terms of a combination of the two, and I think we leaned a little bit more towards talent, knowing the team that we have, what we need. And (we) hope that we can get some good luck, but also improve in some areas medically."

So far, the Warriors haven't had much luck with Porziņģis, and between him, Butler and Moses Moody (sidelined due to a torn patellar tendon), they have about $90 million worth of contracts out due to injury.

"Circumstances change every year. You get thrown a lot of curveballs in this business. It's always the same mentality -- next man up, prepare for what's in front of you and support everybody who's not here," Kerr said on Oct. 8. "Whether it's Jimmy or KP or Moses, we're always gonna give our players every bit of support and help them be the best versions of themselves and acknowledge that the train doesn't stop moving. We're having a great camp, really pleased with the progress we're making. Obviously, we'd rather have KP here and part of it, but he's gotta take care of his health and we'll support that and keep moving forward with the team."

#293. The Rams are already looking like big losers in the Myles Garrett trade

Myles Garrett was supposed to be the straw that stirred the Los Angeles Rams' super-team shake. Talk of them as the unquestioned Super Bowl favorites didn't begin until they pulled off a June blockbuster for the two-time defensive player of the year, trading pro-bowl edge rusher Jared Verse and three draft picks to the Cleveland Browns.

Just six weeks into the season, that talk is already dead. The Browns, not the Rams, are shaping up as big winners of the Garrett deal.

Nothing has gone as planned so far for L.A. Garrett was placed on injured reserve after an underwhelming debut, and the Rams have taken on water without him. Through six weeks, they're 2-4 and last place in the NFC West after Sunday's disappointing loss to the Arizona Cardinals. In a division with the 49ers and Seahawks, it's not overdramatic to say they're at risk of missing the playoffs altogether.

Meanwhile, the Browns are 4-2 and first place in the AFC North. And that's without a single sack from Verse, who has been underwhelming in his own right. But he's at least taken the field every game this season, which is more than the Rams can say for Garrett. And he's been solid in the run game, ranking fifth among edge rushers in ESPN's run stop win rate rankings. Cleveland has received immediate returns in the deal.

Even better, if things continue to go as they have, the Browns can win and still get a high draft pick to continue building up the roster. Because they also received the Rams' 2027 first-rounder that's already becoming a much better pick than anyone could have anticipated.

That's the biggest factor tilting this deal in Cleveland's favor right now. Because even if the Browns falter down the stretch of the season, which seems extremely possible in a division where every team is over .500 and the Browns have the worst point differential at minus-16, it's not as likely the Rams' season does a 180.

Even if Garrett comes back as his usual dominant self (which isn't a given for a 30-year-old), he doesn't solve all the Rams' problems. Their offense hasn't been as explosive as we anticipated entering the season, averaging just 22.5 points per game, which ranks in the bottom-half of the league. Matthew Stafford looks every bit of 38 years old. The coaching hasn't been sharp, and the special teams is bad.

When older teams fail, they get blown up. That's what the Rams are facing if they don't pull it together -- and the Browns are holding a few of the pieces that would have helped them in a potential rebuild. It doesn't matter nearly as much if the Browns continue to win games. They're sitting pretty regardless, even after trading their best player.

#294. Falcons sign QB Andy Dalton and release Cooper Rush

The Atlanta Falcons, fresh off a loss against the Chicago Bears, are signing veteran quarterback Andy Dalton. In a corresponding move, they've cut ties with fellow red-headed quarterback Cooper Rush.

To say this is a bit of a curious move would be an understatement, given that Dalton will open up as the third quarterback on the roster. Whether this is the Falcons covering themselves with Michael Penix Jr. getting banged up repeatedly and not wanting to chance Rush getting back into a game in case of a rash of injuries that takes down Penix and backup Tua Tagovailoa, or whether they view Dalton as a possible QB2 over Tua remains to be seen. Either way, Dalton's a slam dunk upgrade on what the team had with Rush, at the very least.

It was recently reported that Dalton had turned down an offer to return to the Eagles, where he was Jalen Hurts' backup until he threw an interception on his lone passing attempt in Week 3 against the Bears; the Eagles released him on October 9. With Hurts going on injured reserve and Tanner McKee, Cole Payton, and Joe Milton as the only quarterbacks in the mix, Philadelphia wanted him back, but he declined to return.

The path to playing time would seem to be much clearer in Philadelphia, which is part of what makes this interesting. One would think for Dalton to sign on he'd have to be given a legitimate chance to compete with Tua to back up Penix, and that's my operating assumption until I hear otherwise.

Dalton has appeared in 180 games in his career with 139 starts, with his last more-or-less full-time role coming back in 2022 for the Saints. Originally a 2011 second round pick for the Bengals, Dalton finished his career second in passing yards and first in touchdowns in Cincinnati's history. He has 254 career touchdown passes and 152 interceptions as his age 39 season rolls on and has typically been a solid backup at worst for the teams he's played for, with a 66% completion percentage and 10 touchdowns against 7 interceptions in his last extended reserve stint with the Panthers from 2023 to 2025. It goes without saying that while his signing adds some intrigue to the backup competition here in Atlanta, my hope is that Penix is both healthy and effective enough that we never see him in 2026.

Give Dalton a warm welcome, and we'll see if he can overtake Tua for backup duties in the weeks ahead.

#295. For revamped Sixers, youth and growth should still matter plenty

For revamped Sixers, youth and growth should still matter plenty originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The surface impression of the 2026-27 Sixers is that they'll lean on experience and star power as they pursue grand ambitions.

LeBron James is the NBA's eldest player, set to turn 42 years old in December and impossibly accomplished. Joel Embiid is a seven-time All-Star, Jaylen Brown a five-time All-Star. Tyrese Maxey is fresh off his first All-NBA team selection. Veteran role players like Dean Wade and Kentavious Caldwell-Pope have made careers largely out of accepting and executing blue-collar work.

That's all well and good. The Sixers won't be naive to the bumps and battles that come with an NBA season. Youth and internal improvement should matter plenty, though.

Time and again, Maxey's teammates have echoed his mantra of "One percent better every day" in press conferences over the past several weeks. It's a solid default to any sort of team-building question and words are words. Still, it makes plenty of sense for this Sixers squad to be focused on steady growth.

While James, Brown and the other pickups from the Sixers' very eventful summer are far from strangers, so much newness always presents major challenges. The awkward turnovers and miscommunications won't stop just because the preseason is over. As James highlighted at media day, patience and day-after-day dedication will be required.

Health permitting, 21-year-old VJ Edgecombe should be a crucial piece of the picture. He was game for anything last season and a well-earned finalist for Rookie of the Year.

"Look at the team I have around me," Edgecombe said with a laugh on Sept. 29. "There's no pressure on me at all. I'm just going to go out there and be myself. Once I'm out there being myself, playing with joy, I think we'll be good."

James certainly does not view Edgecombe as an immature youngster.

"He's just not quiet," the four-time MVP said on Oct. 3 after the Sixers' Blue-White scrimmage. "And I'm saying that in a good way. If there's things that happen on the floor, if there's things that he sees, if there's things that we see, we just automatically figure it out right there. … He's a very cerebral player and he's always looking for ways to get better on the floor, even at his young age.

"It definitely feels like he's much older. It definitely feels like he's not in Year 2. … We have a lot of guys that have been around the block, a lot of guys that have a voice, and a lot of guys that want to get better every day and hold each other accountable. It's great to see."

The Sixers will rely on Edgecombe to keep developing defensively, sink open three-pointers, and trust his instincts as the kid in the starting lineup.

"VJ's gotten better every single day," Maxey said Thursday. "He grows as a player every single day. His mind grows, his athleticism grows. He was dunking last year, but he wasn't dunking like this. You can tell he got a little bit stronger, a little bit more confident. I'm excited to step on the court and compete with him."

Maxey, meanwhile, is 25 years old and exceptional in the self-improvement department.

After averaging career highs last year in points (28.3 per game), assists (6.6), rebounds (4.1) and steals (1.9), what's on his agenda this season?

"I'm at the point now where I've showed what I can do talent-wise, I think," Maxey said following Day 2 of training camp. "Of course I'm going to get to better, but I want to be judged by winning. If we win, that's what I want to be judged by. That's really my main mindset, my whole goal, is finding ways to win.

"And because I've played so many different roles, I'm capable of doing so many different things. I think that's going to be a positive for myself and for this team. I can play on the ball, I can play off the ball, I can play in transition, I can catch and shoot, I can play off pin-downs, I can play in pick-and-roll. I'm going to play however they need me to play."

Shifting to the bench, the notable young names include 23-year-old backup center Adem Bona and rookie guard Labaron Philon Jr.

Philon's role may very well be minor unless another injury or two pops up. The 22nd overall pick won't turn 21 until next month. The starting backcourt of Maxey and Edgecombe tends to log a massive volume of minutes and Anfernee Simons is an established, bucket-getting guard.

However, a world in which Philon eventually seizes a meaningful rotation spot isn't outlandish to imagine. Sixers head coach Nick Nurse said at training camp that he was "super impressed with his vision and his passing and his offensive creation."

Philon played 24.3 minutes per game in his first preseason and averaged 9.3 points and 4.5 assists. He's been curious about all his veteran teammates have to offer, asking questions on topics ranging from Brown's secrets to making tightly contested shots to Edgecombe's process for building a personal routine in the NBA.

Philon has maintained a deep belief in his own game, too.

"I would say I've always been a great passer," he said on Oct. 2. "Having the right guys, the right plays and the right mindset. First, you have to be unselfish. Second, you've got to have guys that want to move on the floor. And then third, it just comes down to making the best decision. For me, the best decision is making the easiest play.

"Right now I don't really need any showtime or any flashy plays. The position that I'm in right now, making the right play every time will be great for me. And I've been doing it. So just seeing that (in training camp) has been good."

The Sixers will happily take right play after right play this season.

The hunch here is that the youngsters will make many of them.

#297. Gattuso says courage helped his players embarrass Juventus

Lazio secured an impressive 3-0 victory over Juventus in Turin, with Gennaro Gattuso praising the courage shown by his players during the Serie A contest. The visitors delivered an effective performance at the Allianz Stadium, taking their opportunities and leaving the home side with plenty to consider after a disappointing defeat.

Juventus had approached the match with confidence following their previous victory against Celta Vigo. However, the Bianconeri struggled to reproduce that form and were unable to make their opportunities count against a Lazio side that proved more effective in front of goal.

Juventus would have expected to compete strongly on home soil, but Lazio had other ideas. The visitors remained determined throughout the match, showing the resilience and conviction needed to secure all three points against a team with considerable quality in its squad.

The Old Lady had opportunities to take control of the contest, but those chances ultimately went unconverted. As the match progressed, Lazio grew into the game and punished their opponents, turning what could have been a difficult evening into a convincing victory.

Juventus also had to cope without Luciano Spalletti on the touchline. His absence did not help the situation, although the players still needed to demonstrate the quality and determination expected of them. Instead, they struggled to respond as Lazio maintained their momentum.

For Lazio, the result represented another encouraging performance in a season in which they have impressed. Juventus might have been expected to provide a stern test, but the visitors showed they were capable of handling the pressure and competing effectively away from home.

Gattuso was pleased with the mentality his players displayed, particularly their willingness to endure difficult periods without losing their composure. Speaking via Tuttojuve, he highlighted the importance of their approach after the final whistle.

"Courage, we didn't get our arm today. We knew how to suffer, I really enjoyed this tonight."

Gattuso's comments reflected his satisfaction with the way Lazio approached the contest. Their ability to withstand pressure and take advantage of their opportunities proved decisive against Juventus.

For the Bianconeri, however, the defeat raises questions about their consistency and their ability to respond when matches become difficult. Spalletti will need his players to show greater determination in the coming weeks, as further disappointing results could increase the pressure on his position as manager.
