#300. NBA pressure rankings: 10 teams and players who will be feeling the most heat this season

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

When you're in the NBA in any capacity -- player, coach, executive, the guys and gals who fire off the T-shirt cannons -- it's a bit of a high-wire act. All eyes are on you to some extent. Of course, not all situations are the same. Some gigs come with added (and sometimes unwanted) attention. With that in mind, here are our pressure rankings as the 2026-27 season approaches.

No one is really expecting anything out of Golden State. Steph Curry and the Warriors only land on the list by their own volition. There's not a ton of pressure here -- except to the extent that they put it on themselves. Curry put to rest any questions about him jumping ship in search of a team better suited to win now when he signed a two-year $115 million extension that will carry him through his age-41 season. In doing so, he noted that part of the reason why he took a discount -- he was eligible for up to $137 million in that new deal -- was to give the Warriors flexibility when trying to improve the roster. Put another way, Mike Dunleavy and the Golden State front office are once more tasked with not wasting what's left of Curry's career.

Maybe the added savings help, but turning these Warriors into contenders for one last run before the core rides off into the sunset won't be easy. Jimmy Butler is still on the mend from an ACL injury. Kristaps Porziņģis has suffered a litany of injuries and health issues. Curry will be 39 in March. The clock has been ticking for a while now, and time is running out on the lot of them. Which is something Curry doesn't necessarily want to hear. When he signed the extension, he declared that "this team should be competitive and go win." OK. Except the West is loaded and making the playoffs proper, rather than just fighting out of the play-in as they attempted and failed to do last season, won't be easy. That's something else Curry doesn't seem keen on.

“That’s how bad it is? To (not) make the playoffs?”* Walks off *“DAMN!”Steph Curry’s reaction after he was asked about people not expecting the Warriors to make the playoffs 😂😂 pic.twitter.com/PBJ5jitSXE

If the next couple of seasons don't produce much in the way of winning and this is a soft launch on the inevitable goodbye, so be it. Curry and the Warriors already made their marks.

Winning the first title in 53 years buys you a lot of leeway. You get to do fun things like stroll past Michael Porter Jr. on your way inside an establishment or even host Saturday Night Live.

Jalen Brunson's monologue! pic.twitter.com/FnPKYkGcu7

The cause for concern at present is the stalled negotiation between Karl Anthony-Towns (as well as Josh Hart) and the front office. That's not nothing, especially with the Knicks announcing via a spokesperson that "we will not be negotiating contract extensions until later in the season." But, hey, to hear Jalen Brunson and Josh Hart tell it: Don't sweat it, Knicks fans.

Beyond that, the Knicks are mainly on this list because they're the defending champs and they'll attempt to do something no one has pulled off in the last eight seasons -- win a second straight title. The last back-to-back champs were the Warriors in 2017 and 2018.

The Knicks face pretty stiff competition to join Golden State in the record books. The East looks as stacked as ever, and whichever team wins the conference will run into whichever behemoth survives from the West. Not easy. If the Knicks pull it off and host another parade, they'll be (even bigger) legends. If not, they'll never have to buy a drink again anyway.

Only slightly more pressure than the Knicks after losing to New York in the Finals, but they're not exactly feeling the heat. The Spurs are way ahead of schedule with an impressive young core that figures to be together and compete for championships for the foreseeable future. Dylan Harper, who outplayed De'Aaron Fox for much of the postseason, including in several critical stretches against the Knicks, is only 20. Stephon Castle, 21, is an All-Defense-caliber player who upped his free-throw and 3-point shooting in the playoffs. And Wembanyama can already do everything. At 23, he was the first unanimous Defensive Player of the Year in league history and the youngest player ever to make first-team All-NBA and reach the NBA Finals in the same season.

Which does not mean that he hasn't had some sleepless nights thinking about what could have been his first championship, only for it to slip away.

"It's been hard to fall asleep sometimes," Wembanyama said. "Hard emotions. But there is a point where you accept that you have to go through it. You have to feel all of it. We don't want to hide from anything."

Wemby on sitting with the emotions of the Finals loss: “It’s been hard to fall asleep sometimes. Hard emotions. But there is a point where you accept that you have to go through it. You have to feel all of it. We don’t want to hide from anything.” pic.twitter.com/Yhh1CJOtCn

An even more motivated Wemby. Woe unto the rest of the league.

This is where things start getting a little trickier. Nikola Jokić is a three-time MVP. He's made eight All-Star and All-NBA teams. Barring another unfortunate flirtation with the absurd 65-game threshold, you can pencil both of those in for nine each. He's also won a title and has a Finals MVP on his résumé. He is unquestionably one of the two or three best players in the world.

And yet, precisely because of his greatness, there's still this sense that the Nuggets should be achieving more. That's not a knock on Joker so much as it's a failure of Denver's various front office leadership over the years to maximize the roster around him. Jamal Murray is coming off the best season of his career, while Aaron Gordon, Christian Braun and Cam Johnson -- who all missed significant time last season -- are ostensibly healthy. On paper, the Nuggets have one of the best starting fives in the NBA. After that, things get dicey as always. The bench is once again thin -- apologies to DeMar DeRozan, Spencer Jones, Cam Whitmore, Julian Strawther and company -- and the flexibility to fix it is minimal. The Nuggets are the most expensive team in the league and the only one in the second apron, which has a lot to do with why last year's breakout wing Peyton Watson is now playing in Cleveland instead of Denver.

Making matters more complicated for the Nuggets: the Thunder and Spurs are deeper and younger, and any chance of Denver adding another title means having to go through them until further notice. One championship is not nothing. There are countless Hall of Famers who don't have that many. But someone as good as Jokić not getting one more chip would feel like a missed opportunity.

Antetokounmpo's long goodbye in Milwaukee is finally over. It took a while for the team and the player to realize it was fun while it lasted and then turn out the lights on that era. Now Giannis is trying to reclaim some of his previous glory. Antetokounmpo is a two-time MVP, Finals MVP and NBA champion. He's made nine All-Star teams and gotten 10 All-NBA honors. He's been selected All-Defense five times. Like Joker, he has nothing left to prove as an individual. Like Joker, winning another title would go a long way to elevating his already Hall of Fame status.

The difference between Giannis and Jokić is that Joker still plays in Denver and still has a good chance of competing with the Nuggets while Antetokounmpo had to decamp for South Florida and is now tasked with revitalizing a team that has lately fallen on hard times. The Heat got extinguished in the play-in last season, and they lost in the first round in each of the two seasons prior. Now here comes Giannis with designs on changing all that.

"I've never been a part of something like this," Giannis said. "I want to leave my mark. I want to know when this chapter is over, if I'm only here for a year, two or whatever it's going to be, I want to leave my mark."

“I’ve never been apart of something like this. — I want to leave my mark. I want to know when this chapter is over, if I’m only here for a year, two or whatever it’s going to be I want to leave my mark”👀- Giannis(Via @5ReasonsSports / @TheHeatCentral) pic.twitter.com/GMx522dk8k

The "never been a part of something like this" component might not sit well with Bucks fans. The only being around for "a year, or two, or whatever it's going to be" might have made Heat fans tilt their heads. Giannis probably didn't need to make life any harder on himself, but he did.

Let's consider the Eastern Conference big picture. The New York Knicks are the defending champs. LeBron James and Jaylen Brown now play in Philly. Kawhi Leonard is in Toronto. Jayson Tatum is primed for a full season in Boston. Where does that leave the rest of what is shaping up to be a stacked conference and a brutal race to reach the finals?

The Pistons have one of the best young guards in the NBA in Cade Cunningham, who made his second All-NBA team last season and finished top-five in the MVP voting. But after perching atop the conference standings for much of the season, they washed out against the Cavaliers in the second round. Meanwhile, the contract negotiation with their ostensible 1A complement to Cunningham, Jalen Duren, did not exactly go well. Duren threatened to sign the qualifying offer until the last possible second before inking his new deal, but what will the relationship between the player and the front office be like moving forward? And while the Pistons are likely thrilled that Duren is staying put, he wasn't nearly as good in the playoffs as he was during the regular season. If he doesn't immediately snap back to form, it will lead people to wonder whether the Pistons have already been left behind in the East.

What about the Cavs? They reached the conference finals for the first time without LeBron, and the first time in Donovan Mitchell's career -- only to get swept without compunction by the Knicks. They added Peyton Watson to the starting lineup, but as good as their first five look, can they reasonably say they're appreciably better this season? Or are they at best in a grab bag of teams that's just hoping to make it through what figures to be an unforgiving slog of a postseason?

Speaking of that grab bag, it's practically bursting. Between the Knicks, Sixers, Celtics, Raptors, Cavs, Pistons, Heat, Pacers (who reached the NBA Finals just two years ago and have Tyrese Haiburton back), Hawks (the only team to beat the Knicks more than once last postseason) and Hornets, you have 10 teams that feel like they should be firmly in the playoffs. Two of them won't even make it out of the play-in. Yikes. Should be fun for the rest of us, if not those teams.

Things didn't exactly end well for Kawhi in Los Angeles. You might have noticed. Leonard's former team was hit with one of the largest penalties in NBA history after the league's investigation found the Clippers guilty of a cap circumvention scheme that funneled tens of millions of dollars to Kawhi in exchange for no-show endorsement deals. As a result, the Clippers were docked five first-round draft picks, while owner Steam Ballmer was suspended from team and league activities for a year. President of business operations Gillian Zucker was suspended without pay for a year, while president of basketball operations Lawrence Frank will be forced to sit out without pay for half a season. Ouch.

Kawhi got off easy by comparison. He had to repay $700,00 in restitution. Now he's back in Toronto, playing for the last team he won a championship with before the Clippers folly unfolded. To bring him back to Canada, the Raptors shipped Brandon Ingram, Gradey Dick, two first-round picks, a first-round pick swap and two seconds to LA. The Clippers were thankful for the draft capital, if not necessarily the players.

The Raptors upgraded big-time with Kawhi over Ingram at both ends of the floor. But Leonard can only help them if he's available. Leonard played 65 games last season, but over the last 10 years, he's cleared the 60-game mark just three times.

Upon returning to Toronto, Leonard inked a new two-year, $115 million extension. Assuming he picks up the player option on the back end, he'll be 37 at the end of that deal. That gives the Raptors a three-season runway to make a deep playoff run and try to win a second title with Kawhi. He and Scottie Barnes will immediately form one of the best two-way wing combinations in the NBA. But they're hardly on the same timeline. Barnes is 11 years younger. What happens if three years come and go and the Raptors are no closer to another title? In that scenario, Toronto won't regret trading Ingram for Leonard, but they might very well miss the cash of picks and swaps they sent to Los Angeles when they're trying to figure out how to (re)build around Barnes -- and prevent him from moving on as Leonard has several times in his career.

At first glance, this might seem high given how unmatched Sam Presti has been at identifying talent while transforming the Thunder into perennial contenders. They have the reigning two-time MVP in Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, an ostensibly healthy two-way superstar in Jalen Williams, and an All-NBA forward in Chet Holmgren who finished second to Wemby in the Defensive Player of the Year race. Beyond that, they have a stacked roster of complementary pieces that can help them at both ends of the floor and give head coach Mark Daigenault endless mix-and-match combinations to crack any given scenario. The Thunder are unquestionably the deepest team in the league.

And yet consider the position they now find themselves in: After winning a championship two seasons ago, they were sent home by the even younger Spurs in the conference finals. SGA is the best player in OKC. He's 28. Wemby is 23. While Holmgren and Williams are 24 and 25, respectively, San Antonio's young guards are even younger. Harper can't even legally drink yet. Eventually, the Spurs age will catch up to them and they'll have to pay all their stars. But, for now, San Antonio is ahead of schedule and its books are relatively clean. (They'd look a lot better if the Spurs can jettison De'Aaron Fox and his four-year, $221 million deal that's set to kick in this season.)

That's not quite the case for OKC. The Thunder aren't so much ahead of schedule as on it. They won a title, but all three of their main men are on mega contracts. Yes, they have a conveyor belt of talent, but you can't pay and keep everyone -- which is why useful rotation pieces such as Lu Dort, Andrew Wiggins and Isaiah Joe will play elsewhere this season. That doesn't mean that Presti won't keep restocking the cupboard, it's just that finding the supplies at the proper price points won't get any easier.

Even if everything goes to plan for OKC, as it did until last season, they'll have the Spurs to spar with for the next half decade -- at least, if not longer -- as well as the rest of the unforgiving Western Conference.

There's some revisionist history happening in the NBA right now, or at least some hoping and coping. A few months ago, when the Celtics traded Jaylen Brown for Paul George, an unprotected first-round pick, a first-round pick or swap depending on where it lands, and two second rounders, news of the deal exploded like a bomb. Brown is  a former NBA Finals MVP coming off the best regular season of his career, while George is seven years his senior and is on what some considered one of the worst contracts in the NBA. Fans, media members and the league were blown away. As one incredulous league executive put it in the aftermath, Brown "got traded for less than Walker Kessler." (On behalf of Kessler and his family: Ouch.)

Brad Stevens did his best to explain his thinking, but breakdowns of salary cap percentages hardly seemed to placate the Celtics faithful who were aghast at swapping Brown for PG, not to mention that they'll now have to watch Brown play against Boston while wearing a Sixers uniform -- one of Boston's most hated foes and the very team that dismissed them from the playoffs in a surprise first-round upset in the spring.

To the extent that there's good news in Boston, Jayson Tatum is back for a full season after returning at the end of the last campaign from an Achilles injury. And the Celtics have long been one of the best-run organizations in the NBA -- not just in recent history, but history full stop. But when you trade one of your best and most popular players to Philly of all places, especially after first dangling Brown for Giannis and creating all sorts of drama when they missed out, it had better work out in your favor or you'll never hear the end of it.

Pretty much everyone in the organization will be feeling the heat this season. Where to even begin?

Brown has already hinted at the Boston-sized chip on his shoulder as he goes about circling games on the upcoming schedule. Joel Embiid is a former MVP who came to camp looking better than ever, but he also missed 150 games the previous three seasons and has never made it out of the second round of the playoffs. Tyrese Maxey took a massive leap last season and made his first All-NBA team, but can he remain in such rarified company when his usage rate might take a hit because of all the other big names now surrounding him? And if Maxey gets pushed down the pecking order, what happens to VJ Edgecombe, who made an immediate splash as a rookie and cemented himself in the starting lineup?

And then there's LeBron, who passed on going back to Cleveland and Miami, or teaming up with Steph in Golden State, or even finally living out that fantasy of his to play in Madison Square Garden, in favor of signing with the Sixers on a veteran minimum contract. James summed up the situation pretty well when he said he didn't leave his family just for the Sixers to keep being the Sixers. I'm paraphrasing, but you get the gist.

Beyond that, head coach Nick Nurse, who is in the final year of his contract, might be on the hottest coaching seat in the league. And while new president of basketball operations Mike Gansey worked several magic tricks to put this all together, several Philly general managers before him made splashy moves that looked good at first before quickly revealing themselves as decidedly less attractive. (Trading for James Harden and giving up Jimmy Butler in favor of retaining Ben Simmons quickly come to mind.)

This is an organization that hasn't made the conference finals since 2001 and hasn't won a championship since 1983. And suddenly the roster is stacked and healthy and among the betting favorites to do those very things. Or they could faceplant once again and put an ugly end to LeBron's storied career. The degree of difficulty here is incredibly high for everyone involved. As Embiid recently put it, "I need to win." He's not the only one.

#301. Ben Simmons’ NBA comeback suffers brutal blow in crushing setback with Kings

Any chance of Ben Simmons making a comeback this season will have to wait until next season.

The Sacramento Kings announced on Sunday that an MRI confirmed Simmons has suffered a torn right Achilles injury during practice.

"Sacramento Kings guard Ben Simmons was injured during a live drill in practice on Sunday, Oct. 18. An MRI revealed a torn right Achilles tendon. Simmons will undergo surgery," the Kings announced in a press release this afternoon.

Ben Simmons to miss the rest of the season due to a right torn Achilles injury. NBAE via Getty Images

Simmons signed a one-year $3.5 million deal with the Kings last month after spending last year as an unsigned free agent. The deal was reportedly a non-guaranteed contract that would've paid him $1 million if he made the opening night roster.

Simmons was once a No.1 overall pick in the NBA Draft in 2016 but spent his career hampered by injuries, including a right foot fracture in 2016-2017, as well as constant knee and leg injuries from 2021-2025.

Simmons was once a No.1 overall pick in the NBA Draft in 2016. AP Photo/Eric Gay

Simmons signed a one-year $3.5 million deal with the Kings last month after spending last year as an unsigned free agent. NBAE via Getty Images

This season, he was expected to be a backup point guard, behind rookie Darius Acuff Jr., who's played in four of the Kings' preseason games.

Simmons has appeared in two preseason games this season and recently had 25 minutes of playing time last Friday when he scored 14 points, with eight rebounds, seven assists, and one steal against the San Antonio Spurs.

The Kings are set to open their season this Wednesday when they travel to Los Angeles to play the Clippers.

#303. Serie A official line-ups and live updates: Monza vs. Cagliari

Dany Mota and Foe Ondoa come into the Monza side, while Cagliari pair M'Bala Nzola with Paul Mendy up front for their trip to the U-Power Stadium.

It kicks off at 18:30 CET [17:30 BST] at the U-Power Stadium in Monza.

Ivan Juric's Monza have just four points from their first six games after their return to Serie A, with one win, one draw and four defeats. They lost 3-1 at Lazio last time out, and have conceded 15 goals, the second-worst defensive record in the division. Gustavo Varela has been the bright spot, scoring four goals in his first five Serie A appearances.

Cagliari are one of the surprise packages of the season, with 13 points from six games, and are unbeaten in four. They held Juventus to a 1-1 draw last time out, but Fabio Pisacane is suspended after his touchline row with Luciano Spalletti, so assistant Giacomo Murelli takes his place on the bench. Daniel Maldini, who has four goals in six games, returns to face his former club.

Juric has a strong record against the Sardinians, losing just one of his last nine Serie A meetings with them, with four wins and four draws.

Monza are without the suspended Lorenzo Lucchesi, so Saba Goglichidze comes into the back three. Matteo Pessina, Idrissa Touré, Jan Ziolkowski, Zeballos and Mayé are all injured. Patrick Ciurria is back in the squad.

Cagliari are missing Mattia Felici and Riyad Idrissi, both with cruciate ligament injuries, as well as Yael Trepy. Murelli pairs M'Bala Nzola with Paul Mendy up front, with Maldini behind them, while Yerry Mina edges captain Alessandro Deiola for a place in defence.

#304. Jameis Winston benched: J.J. McCarthy's thrilling, historic comeback bid comes up short vs. Saints

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

It could be the beginning of a new era in New York, as the Giants benched quarterback Jameis Winston for J.J. McCarthy in the fourth quarter of their eventual 34-27 loss to the New Orleans Saints. While McCarthy threw an interception on his third passing attempt, he rebounded to spark the Giants and made his case to be John Harbaugh's new starter.

In all, McCarthy completed 11 of 21 passes for 243 yards, one touchdown and one interception in his first extensive action with his new team. In 11 minutes of action, he would throw for 243 yards, which made NFL history for the most passing yards in an 11-minute span. He also led the Giants in rushing with 26 yards. Following his interception, McCarthy led a six-play, 52-yard drive that was capped by a Tyrone Tracy Jr. touchdown and a successful Isaiah Likely two-point conversion to trim the deficit to 16 points. After a Saints three-and-out, McCarthy took the Giants offense 73 yards down the field on just three plays, and hit Likely for a 24-yard touchdown to make it a 10-point game.

J.J. finds Isaiah Likely 🙌📺: FOX pic.twitter.com/0fLSL9TMTV

McCarthy was given the opportunity to lead a game-tying or game-winning drive with 57 seconds remaining in the fourth quarter with zero timeouts. On first down, he scrambled up the middle for 28 yards to get the Giants into enemy territory, and then hit Likely for 20 yards to get New York to the Saints' 23-yard line.

The Giants eventually faced a fourth-and-1 14 yards from the end zone with 12 seconds remaining, and McCarthy could not connect with Likely in the end zone. The Giants wanted a flag on this play, but the officials held onto their yellow handkerchiefs.

Saints defense comes up big on 4th and 1 to prevent the TD!NOvsNYG on FOX/FOX OneStream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/mG6S1WoaSs

This was a performance good enough for McCarthy to unseat Winston permanently. Last month, the Giants traded a fifth-round pick to the Minnesota Vikings for McCarthy. The former No. 10 overall pick went 6-4 as the starter for the Vikings in 2025, completing 57.6% of his passes for 1,632 yards, 11 touchdowns and 12 interceptions. He became the only first-round pick at quarterback since 1970 to finish last in completion percentage and TD-INT ratio in their debut season.

JJ McCarthy with an absolutely ridiculous throw to Malik Nabers.The Vikings gave up on him too quickly. pic.twitter.com/WiDBhBEbCB

Harbaugh said after the game he can't answer who his starting quarterback will be moving forward, and that those are not issues decided 10 minutes after a game.

John Harbaugh says Giants QB J.J. McCarthy did a “heck of a job” in end of game. Notes situation was “different” than managing a whole game. Also has “no problem with Jameis.”Harbaugh declined to name starter for next game, emphatic he won’t decide 10 minutes after a game. pic.twitter.com/o1kAyEOJeS

It's called the "Jameis Winston experience" for a reason. Last week in the tie vs. the Washington Commanders, he completed 33 of 54 passes for 326 yards and three touchdowns. Winston actually became the first Giants quarterback to throw three touchdowns in back-to-back games since Eli Manning in 2016. However, his performance on Sunday opened the door for Harbaugh to consider his other quarterback. Winston completed 14 of 26 passes for 152 yards, one touchdown and two interceptions before his benching.

#306. Zach Werenski trade rumors: Six ideal fits for the 2026 Norris Trophy winner, Blue Jackets defenseman

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

According to multiple reports, 2026 Norris Trophy winner Zach Werenski is on the trade block as he's expressed a desire to move on from the Columbus Blue Jackets. Recently crowned the top defenseman in the NHL, Werenski will draw massive interest, but only a handful of landing spots truly make sense.

Werenski is a superstar defenseman at the top of his game, and he will immediately change the outlook of whichever team acquires him. He's now topped 80 points in back-to-back seasons, and the underlying numbers have been spectacular.

Over the last three seasons, the Blue Jackets have had a plus-48 goal differential and a 52.3% expected goals share with Werenski on the ice at five-on-five, per Natural Stat Trick. In 2025-26, Columbus was markedly worse with Werenski on the bench.

With the NHL salary cap rising sharply each year, more teams will have the room to add Werenski's contract, which has two seasons remaining with an average annual value of $9.5 million. With Cale Makar and Quinn Hughes set to get new deals over the next year, Werenski might even look like a bargain.

Werenski is a rare game-changing defender who can drive play from the back end, and these six teams should be in the thick of trade negotiations.

Prior to the 2026 NHL Draft, there were rumors that the Sharks would be willing to part with the No. 9 overall pick to acquire an established defenseman. Maple Leafs defenseman Morgan Rielly was mentioned in connection with San Jose, but frankly, general manager Mike Grier should be thinking bigger. As the newly-crowned Norris Trophy winner and an Olympic gold medalist, Werenski is exactly the type of star the Sharks should be targeting as they ascend to contender status.

Even with a barren blue line and no depth at forward, the Sharks fell just four points shy of a playoff spot last season. Werenski would kill two birds with one stone in that regard. He would give San Jose a bona fide No. 1 defenseman while also giving the offense more firepower -- both at even strength and on the power play. The Sharks have the cap space and the assets to make this happen, and they should be ringing Waddell's phone off the hook.

What if general manager Steve Yzerman was able to convince captain Dylan Larkin to stick around and create perhaps the most dominant defensive pairing in the NHL at the same time? Acquiring Werenski would be the type of boost that puts Detroit's rebuild over the finish line, and the Wings would have two true No. 1 defensemen in Werenski and Moritz Seider. Meanwhile, Larkin may be more inclined to remain with Detroit if his Team USA teammate and fellow Michigander does so.

Would Detroit be interested in giving up Simon Edvinsson, a young defenseman with a lot of upside, in exchange for a finished product? The Red Wings also have the cap space and draft capital to make this deal work. Yzerman needs to be bold this summer. The recipe is there for a huge move.

After letting Darren Raddysh go in a sign-and-trade with the Maple Leafs, the Lightning have a need on the blue line. Julien BriseBois is one of the most aggressive general managers in the league, and he always seems to be poking around the biggest names on the trade market. Besides, Werenski only costs $1 million more per season than Raddysh, and he's a far more complete player.

The salary cap is a slight issue for Tampa with $13.1 million available prior to free agency, according to PuckPedia. The good news for the Bolts is that the vast majority of their roster is already under contract for the 2026-27 season. BriseBois would only need to make tweaks on the fringes of the roster, and he would have roughly $3.6 million to do it. Tampa might have to move a contract out to swing a Werenski trade, but that's doable.

The Ducks need defensive help for two reasons. For one, they were absolutely horrific on their own end last season. Secondly, Anaheim may lose three of its best defensemen with Jacob Trouba, Radko Gudas and John Carlson all set to hit free agency. Werenski would upgrade the Ducks' blue line exponentially, but he would do so in a way that gels with the up-tempo attacking style that Joel Quenneville has implemented on offense.

Leo Carlsson and Cutter Gauthier will both receive gargantuan raises this summer, but the Ducks have $44.6 million in cap space. That will give them plenty of breathing room to acquire Werenski and sign their two young superstars. Anaheim has two first-round picks and two second-round picks in last year's draft, and they have a decent prospect pool to pull from. If the Blue Jackets want established NHL players in exchange for Werenski, that could complicate the deal for Anaheim. The Ducks don't have many players in their prime that they would -- or should -- be willing to trade.

Dallas is one of the strongest teams in the NHL, but it has struggled to find consistency outside of two or three players on the blue line. Werenski would certainly solve that problem, but he wouldn't come cheap. In fact, it would probably cost the Stars a 24-year-old budding star set to make $10.5 million per season through 2033-34. Thomas Harley alone may not be enough to get the deal done, but the cost might be worth the reward for general manager Jim Nill.

If Harley is included in the deal, Werenski would provide superior defense without sacrificing any offense. Plus, as with the Red Wings and Seider, the opportunity to pair Werenski with another Norris Trophy contender in Miro Heiskanen might be too good to pass up. Coming off a disappointing first-round playoff exit, Dallas needs to stay aggressive in order to maximize its championship window.

As an American, I can admit that a small part of this is fan fiction. Reuniting Werenski and Jack Hughes after their "Golden Goal" heroics would be the cherry on top of this deal, but it makes plenty of sense on paper, too.

It's no secret that New Jersey has an interest in acquiring the third and final Hughes brother, Quinn, at some point over the next year. Whether that happens around the 2027 trade deadline or in free agency next summer, it doesn't matter. Both will be too late. Jack Hughes, Nico Hischier and Jesper Bratt are all in their prime, so the Devils can't afford to wait on Quinn to save the day on defense. With Werenski available, New Jersey must strike now to transform itself into a true Cup contender.

In order to pull this off, the Devils would probably also have to move out Dougie Hamilton and his $9 million-per-season contract. Hamilton has a 10-team trade list, which would limit New Jersey's options and create a possible hiccup in negotiations with Columbus. If the Devils can offload Hamilton's contract, however, that would create the flexibility to acquire Werenski and upgrade other parts of the roster.

#307. With Brandin Podziemski's extension, Warriors maintain flexibility for one last title pursuit with Steph Curry

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Golden State Warriors and Brandin Podziemski agreed to a five-year, $110 million contract extension on Saturday, according to multiple reports. That deal will keep the former No. 19 overall pick in the Bay Area for the foreseeable future.

Podziemski, 23, averaged 13.8 points, 5.1 rebounds and 3.7 assists per game last season on 45.5/37.1/79.7 shooting splits, appearing in all 82 games for the Warriors. Podziemski has been a rare hit for the Warriors in recent drafts, and they will reward him with a handsome contract extension that gives both sides some stability going forward.

For Podziemski, he likely looked at the restricted free-agent landscape and saw how declining an extension and hitting the RFA market has gone poorly for many in recent years. With more than $100 million on the table, he gladly signed on the dotted line and will not have to stress over whether he'd have any interest from the larger free agency market next summer.

With their eyes on one last championship pursuit with Stephen Curry, the Warriors have been trying to maintain as much financial flexibility as possible, which is why an extension for Podziemski raised some eyebrows when the news emerged.

Curry, 38, agreed to a less-than-max extension earlier this offseason to help clear additional room for the Warriors next summer to make some needed roster upgrades. For many, the initial reaction to seeing Podziemski's contract number was to wonder how much of that space Curry helped clear that Podziemski's deal would eat up.

However, his cap hold for next summer was set to be $17 million and the first year of his new deal will reportedly start at $18.9 million, meaning they only shaved $1.9 million off their available space. For the Warriors, that's a minimal loss of flexibility, while ensuring the price of Podziemski's next deal wouldn't increase if he had a breakout year in 2026-27.

And because his extension won't kick in until next summer, Podziemski's new deal also won't impact the Warriors' financial situation if they wanted to explore making a move at the trade deadline this season. It does provide a bit of clarity on their backcourt plans for the future with Podziemski alongside Curry, and the most notable thing with the extension is that it would likely preclude Podziemski from being included in any deadline deals.

Golden State can still clear $60 million in cap space next summer if it wants to with Kristaps Porzingis' $20 million deal only guaranteed for $3 million. However, that roster would include only seven players and wouldn't include the cap holds of Jimmy Butler and Draymond Green's. How they handle Green and Butler's impending free agency will determine exactly how much they have to spend next summer, but Podziemski's extension won't have a significant impact on that, other than confirming they can count on him as part of their long-term roster plans.

#308. The Knicks aren’t scared of LeBron James — or a brewing rivalry with superteam 76ers

Josh Hart predicted it. Really, we all did.

"Wherever LeBron [James] went in the East, I figured that'd probably be our opening night [game]," Hart said after Knicks practice Sunday. "That will be good for headlines and box office and those kinds of things."

With training camp and the preseason over, all attention now turns to the opener against the 76ers on Tuesday night at Madison Square Garden.

With it being banner/ring night and the opener, there is already plenty of intrigue and attention. But it is impossible to escape all the extras involved.

The NBA, with LeBron and Jaylen Brown joining the 76ers to create a supposed "superteam" this offseason, is clearly interested in making this a rivalry and season-long storyline. The two teams play each other twice in the opening six games — both on national television. In fact, all four matchups this season are on national television.

Most have labeled the 76ers — with a core of James, Brown, Joel Embiid, Tyrese Maxey and VJ Edgecombe — as the biggest threat to the Knicks' chances of repeating as champions.

Add in the close geographical distance, the recent playoff history between the two teams and the fact LeBron has publicly said he envisioned finishing his career with the Knicks had they not won the title (and is living part-time in New York City), and there are all the ingredients of a renewed rivalry.

LeBron James signed with the 76ers in July. IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

Mike Brown's first head coaching gig was coaching James with the Cavaliers. He knows that when James is involved, everything is just bigger.

"The reality of it, in coach talk, you want to say every game is the same," the Knicks coach said Sunday. "That's what you try to impress upon your guys is, 'Hey, when we step on the floor, no matter who's in front of us, you want to give the same focus, energy and effort to the next possession in front of you.' But because of the talk, because of who he is — he is a large figure not just in life, but in the NBA.

"You also gotta look at the guys they have on the team and the guys they've added and the potential of that team and what we accomplished and what we're trying to accomplish again — all those storylines, with the social media and all that other stuff, it's pressed upon you, pressed upon you, pressed upon you, so it gets larger than life in general."

Jaylen Brown was traded to the 76ers this off-season after spending 10 years with the Celtics. IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

The Knicks would like to treat it like any of the other 82 regular-season games. But the reality is that, one way or the other, it will be used as an early statement in what could become a relentless discourse.

"As a coach, you hope it doesn't, but at times yes, you have to take into account that yes, it can be something that guys think, 'OK, this is a big game,'" Brown said. "It gives you a little bit more juice, a little bit more energy because of all the stuff around it. Is it gonna be a rivalry at the end of the day? I don't know. I don't know where we're gonna be and where they're gonna be. … Because of the storylines and all that other stuff with the social media, could it be right now? Yeah, it's a fun story."

The two teams also represent opposites of sorts.

The Knicks are a bastion of stability, returning nine of their top 10 players in terms of minutes played last year. It's a group that knows each other well and has exceptional chemistry.

The 76ers, by contrast, are a newly assembled unit that must come together quickly with immediate championship expectations.

"Obviously, we have the same team, but sometimes individuals' expectations are different than what they were before," Hart said. "So it's different. Especially a team like that, I'm sure they're gonna have some bumpy times in the beginning of the year because they gotta get used to playing with each other. The media at that point [will say,] 'They should blow it up and trade everybody' and those kinds of things. That's kind of the world we live in."

The world we live in will have a dramatic reaction to Tuesday's result.

#310. Rapid Reaction: Colts announce firing of longtime GM Chris Ballard following brutal Week 6 loss

The Indianapolis Colts (2-4), and specifically team owner and CEO Carlie Irsay-Gordon publicly announced on Monday that longtime general manager Chris Ballard has been relieved of his duties:

Ballard had compiled a 72-82-1 through a little over 10 seasons with the Colts franchise, having arrived in 2017. However, he had just two playoff appearances, 1 playoff win, and 0 division titles during his lengthy GM tenure.

While he initially got off to a hot start following his 2018 NFL Draft Class which included Quenton Nelson, Darius 'Shaq' Leonard, and Braden Smith among others, winning PFWA Executive of the Year for that elite draft class, the quality and returns of his subsequent draft classes largely diminished (aside from arguably 2020, which was a solid haul with both Jonathan Taylor and Michael Pittman Jr. in the 2nd round).

Never one to seriously spend in free agency, Ballard was notoriously frugal, preferring to re-sign his own players and maintain ample salary cap flexibility, despite glaring starting holes on the Colts roster year-after-year, which weren't properly addressed. It was a major point of frustration among the Horseshoe Faithful and local talking heads because it just continued to happen on an annual basis.

That approach changed during the 2025 offseason, when the Colts signed both safety Cam Bynum and cornerback Charvarius Ward to lucrative, multi-year free agency deals, but by that time, it was too little, and too late. It's a fair question of whether either one of those signings have dramatically paid off for Indianapolis either.

Having had two consecutive 8-9 seasons, and stumbling out of the gates to a 2-4 record, with no playoffs in Indianapolis since 2020 (the COVID-19) year, Sunday's brutal home loss to one of the league's worst teams was finally the straw that broke Ballard's maligned tenure with the Colts.

The Tennessee Titans were winless at 0-5 and had an 11-game losing streak in the AFC South, while the Colts were at home and blew a 13-0 lead at halftime—with former franchise legends in the house to honor Adam Vinatieri's induction into the franchise's illustrious Ring of Honor.

Colts fans had been publicly frustrated with Ballard's recent results, and coming off an offseason where Irsay-Gordon publicly proclaimed that, "The Stakes had never been higher" for the franchise, she made good on her word, as Ballard was finally shown the door and exits stage left.

At a certain point, winning results have to matter, and even though Ballard had a strong personal relationship with the Irsay daughters, the on-the-field product and collective talent of the Colts roster both have only continued to diminish. It was time for a change, and quite frankly, it was long overdue.

#311. Stephen Curry 'fine' after leaving practice early following ankle tweak ahead of season opener

Stephen Curry, despite a bit of an injury scare on Sunday afternoon, should be good to go for the Golden State Warriors' season opener this week. Curry went down with a right ankle injury during the team's open practice in San Francisco on Sunday. Warriors head coach Steve Kerr confirmed that Curry's knee wasn't impacted by the incident and that "he's fine."

Curry, after bringing the ball up the floor during the open practice at the Chase Center, suddenly rolled his right ankle while handling the ball near the top of the key. Immediately, Curry stopped and pounded the ball down to the court, clearly frustrated.

He limped off as play stopped and walked over to the bench, briefly doubled over, and then went back to the locker room.

While the timing of the injury scare isn't ideal, Kerr said Curry told him he was fine after the practice ended.

"Always, always," Kerr said when asked if his heart skipped a beat when Curry limped off the floor, via the San Francisco Chronicle's Luca Evans.

"He's fine. I went and talked to him after he went downstairs, and I went into the training room."

Curry averaged 26.6 points and 4.7 assists per game last season, his 17th in the league with the Warriors. Curry only appeared in 43 games, however, and missed a big chunk of the season due to a lingering right knee injury. The Warriors went just 37-45 and missed the playoffs for the second time in three seasons. Curry then signed a two-year, $116 million extension with the Warriors last month.

The Warriors will open the 2026-27 campaign against the Los Angeles Lakers on Wednesday night. Though it looked briefly like it may be at risk, Curry appears to still be on track to start the season as scheduled.

#312. Cam Skattebo demotion: Giants RB logs zero touches, responds to apparent benching

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

In the wake of an array of fumbles this season, Cam Skattebo was completely phased out of the New York Giants offense in Week 6.

Coming into Sunday's action, a report from ESPN noted there would be a change in the New York backfield rotation. Najee Harris was likely to see a large role, while Skattebo was downgraded. The assumption was that even amid a demotion, Skattebo would be in the mix of the Giants' rushing attack. However, that never came to fruition during the club's 34-27 loss to New Orleans.

Skattebo did not log a single carry or a single target on Sunday. This marked the first time in his career that Skattebo was active for a game but did not see any touches. In all, Skattebo played six snaps.

"I didn't expect to have zero," Skattebo said after the game, via The Athletic. "I was expecting to not play as much just like I did. The message was to keep your head down and keep going. They understand the type of player I am, and I just got to continue doing my job and do it to the best of my ability.

Postgame, head coach John Harbaugh said Skattebo's lack of action "wasn't by design" and that he was not benched.

"It was not by design for him not to carry the ball," he said, via Yahoo Sports. "When he was in there, we didn't call any runs. You're not thinking about which back is in the game and how many runs they're getting."

With Skattebo on the outside looking in on the rushing attack, the Giants finished the day with 20 carries for 84 yards (4.2 yards per carry average) and one touchdown. Specifically, Giants backs rushed 14 times for 34 yards and a touchdown. Tyrone Tracy Jr. led the way with six carries, followed by Devin Singletary and Najee Harris, who each finished with four attempts.

On top of the carries, Tracy saw three targets (two catches), while Singletary was targeted once (one catch).

Skattebo's demotion stems from fumbling issues. So far this season, he's fumbled four times, including a back-breaking fumble last week in the overtime tie to the Washington Commanders. That turnover at the Washington 24-yard line eliminated an opportunity for a game-winning kick and instead led to the Giants nearly losing the contest had it not been for Jayden Daniels and the Commanders' offense mismanaging the clock en route to the tie.

"I got punished for what I did (last week)," Skattebo said. "I understand it, so I gotta be ready when coach calls my name, and that wasn't today."

He later added: "It's hard, but I've made mistakes, and I got to own up to them. If that is what they want to do -- keep me on the sidelines because of that -- I totally understand."

New York will be in Houston next Sunday for a Week 7 matchup against the Texans before entering the bye in Week 8.

#313. Trinidad Chambliss says Lane Kiffin wasn't 'truthful' about recruiting struggles at Ole Miss

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Once allies in Oxford, Ole Miss quarterback Trinidad Chambliss and new LSU coach Lane Kiffin are now rivals on the field, and they don't exactly see eye-to-eye on one issue in particular.

Earlier in the offseason, Kiffin claimed that the Rebels' ties to the Old South made it more difficult to recruit black players to Ole Miss. While speaking at the Manning Passing Academy on Friday, Chambliss flatly disagreed with Kiffin's assessment.

"Me, personally, I don't agree," Chambliss said, per the Associated Press. "I don't think that what he said was truthful. ... The Oxford community is nothing but love, and they care about their people no matter what they look like: brown, black, purple, yellow — you know what I mean?"

When Chambliss was exploring his options after transferring out of Ferris State, he and his family visited Kiffin and his staff at Oxford. Chambliss said his family loved the visit and quickly realized it was the right place for him.

"One thing that I can really take away from my visit and the reason why I did commit to Ole Miss is I asked my family what they genuinely thought about the visit, what they thought about the people, if they trusted what they were actually saying, if they're gonna be true to their word," Chambliss added.

"They said, 'I feel like this is the right place.'"

Back in May, Kiffin spoke to Vanity Fair and claimed Oxford's lack of diversity was a challenge on the recruiting trail. Kiffin said that family members of black players have expressed concern about sending their kids and grandkids to Ole Miss, which hasn't happened since he took the job at LSU.

"'Hey, coach, we really like you. But my grandparents aren't letting me move to Oxford, Mississippi,'" Kiffin said. "That doesn't come up when you say Baton Rouge, Louisiana. Parents were sitting here this weekend saying the campus's diversity feels so great: 'It feels like there's no segregation. And we want that for our kid because that's the real world.'"

When Kiffin bolted south from Oxford to Baton Rouge, that instantly ignited a rivalry between Ole Miss and LSU. Kiffin's comments only added fuel to that fire, and his return to LSU on Sept. 19 will be must-see television.

One of the first people to defend Ole Miss in the wake of Kiffin's comments was Archie Manning, a school legend in Oxford. Manning didn't have to address that issue at the Manning Passing Academy on Saturday, but he did speak out about how his grandson Arch was treated by the media last season at Texas.

Entering the 2025 season, Texas was the preseason No. 1 team, and Arch was viewed as the Heisman Trophy favorite. Through the first half of the season, it seemed like that pressure was weighing on Manning, and he struggled to get his feet under him in his first year as a starter.

Archie Manning said unfair expectations were placed on his grandson, who had to work through that pressure before hitting his stride down the stretch.

"I was kinda disappointed in a lot of people," Archie Manning said, via KXAN. "They kind of crowned Arch before he ever played. I didn't think that was fair. It was a little tough start. … I've never been as proud as anyone in my life is the way Arch battled through what he had to go through last year and the way he played over the last eight or nine games."

Eventually, Arch did find a rhythm with the Longhorns, and he led them to wins over No. 3 Texas A&M and No. 18 Michigan. Arch Manning and Texas will face sky-high expectations going into the 2026 season, but this time they're based on an existing track record.

#314. Takeaways from Knicks pausing contract extension talks: Is Josh Hart's time in New York running out?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Only the New York Knicks could crush the vibes of a championship run before even beginning their title defense season. Four notable members of the team, Karl-Anthony Towns, Josh Hart, Miles McBride and Tyler Kolek, are eligible for contract extensions. While keeping the whole team together was always going to be a long shot, the Knicks announced on Friday that they would be tabling all talks until later in the season, forcing all four players to open the season with uncertain financial futures.

But what does this actually mean for the Knicks? Here are three quick takeaways on New York's sudden financial predicament.

For now, the question with Towns remains less about whether he'll get a new deal from the Knicks and more about what that new deal will mean for everyone else. Towns is irreplaceable. There is no other offensive center like him in basketball that has not already won an MVP or will inevitably win one in the near future.

New York let its only other viable starting center option, Mitchell Robinson, leave in free agency, and as we've learned from deals involving players like Ivica Zubac and Walker Kessler, getting a high-end starter at center, even below the superstar level, costs draft capital the Knicks frankly do not have. They'll figure something out with Towns. It's just a matter of when and what.

The Knicks have hoped to get Towns to take a substantial discount, as Jalen Brunson has. While he seems receptive to taking a deal below his $276 million max, the Knicks have seemingly not come close to an actual deal for him. While Friday's news doesn't necessarily preclude a below-market agreement down the line, it does deprive the Knicks of a critical bit of flexibility in how that deal is structured.

Players with multiple years left on their contracts cannot extend during the season. Before the season, however, extensions are fair game. This matters for Towns because he has a $61.6 million player option for the 2027-28 season. If Towns and the Knicks had gotten a deal done before the season, they could have essentially used that option to front-load Towns' new contract and have his salary decline meaningfully from there.

However, should he sign an extension during the season, he would have to decline that option, and his new contract would have to be more balanced. A player's salary cannot increase or decrease by more than 8% annually within a single contract. Major raises and dips must be part of a new contract or extension.

Why is this a potentially preferred contract structure? Because New York's financial cliff isn't coming in the 2027-28 season. It comes a year later in the 2028-29 campaign. That's when Brunson and OG Anunoby will start new deals thanks to their player options. Brunson has already taken a substantial discount once. Don't expect him to do it again. Anunoby is about as irreplaceable as non-All-Stars get. Using that option, the Knicks could have gotten the most expensive year of a new Towns deal out of the way and saved as much flexibility for what comes after as possible.

This format isn't necessarily off the table. Towns could simply pick up his player option in the offseason and try extension talks again at that point. His value could also dip during the season, allowing the Knicks to re-sign him on more favorable terms. But it's always easier to get an extension done early when possible. The last thing the Knicks should want is their back-to-back title bid ruined by contractual sour grapes.

In a perfect world, the Knicks would have preferred to have something done by now. This might not be their preferred structure, as a lower 2027-28 salary would make it easier to duck next year's second apron. But taking the option off the table, if only temporarily, costs the Knicks the flexibility they would probably have preferred.

We should assume that Brunson's next deal will approach 35% of the cap. His discount won the Knicks a championship. Towns won't be quite that high, but it won't be far off either. Anunoby's player option for the 2028-29 season will pay him an estimated 26.2% of the cap, so a new deal probably starts in that range. Mikal Bridges is locked up at around 21% of the estimated cap at that point.

Start doing the math. You're looking at around 110 to 115% of the cap for your top four players once everyone's deals are finalized. You should also assume that those deals are paying for fewer valuable years than their existing contracts do. Anunoby is going into his age-29 season. Brunson and Anunoby will play their age-30 seasons this year, and Towns his age-31 season. At best, you're paying for the back half of their prime. At worst, there will be real age- and injury-related decline. If the Knicks are going to continue competing for championships, they need to acknowledge that they probably need more than they currently have to do it (especially with Robinson already gone) and that they have less financial wiggle room to pursue possible upgrades.

So where does that leave Hart, the fifth starter and the heartbeat of the team? A lot depends on what sort of extension he's willing to take. The Knicks have a bit more flexibility on this front than with Towns because he has a team option rather than a player option. The Knicks could use that option to leverage their way into more favorable terms.

Still, Hart is the oldest of the five Knicks starters. He'll turn 32 during the season. His game is probably the least likely to age well, given his inconsistent shooting and borderline reckless physicality he plays with. The old axiom is that it's better to move on from a player a year too early than a year too late. It's hard to imagine the Knicks moving Hart this season as they pursue back-to-back titles, but hesitance on a long-term extension afterward would be understandable.

There isn't an in-house replacement ready. The Knicks under two different head coaches have resisted playing McBride with the starters because of how small his backcourt pairing with Brunson would be. Landry Shamet's shooting is nice in small doses and he's improved significantly as a defender, but similar problems exist there, and durability has been a concern for him. Perhaps the best possible developmental curve for promising second-round pick Mohamed Diawara could see him turn into a starter, and he's locked into a cheap, long-term deal, but he's a long way from adequately replacing Hart.

Realistically, the Knicks would either have to stumble into a player we don't see coming or make a trade involving their precious remaining draft capital (at this point, their only tradable first-rounder is in 2033), ideally for someone on a rookie deal now. This front office has surprised plenty of times, but at this moment, Hart is still essential to New York's championship upside. The more costly Towns becomes, though, the more realistic breaking up this starting lineup becomes. You can't keep everyone in the apron era, especially if you want to maintain any level of depth.

McBride will almost certainly be the cheapest of the three Knicks we've covered thus far on his next deal. He certainly is on his existing contract. The Knicks wisely extended McBride on very team-friendly terms right after trading Immanuel Quickley, knowing that he had a bigger role upcoming. If they extend McBride before Hart, that might be a tell that they're considering repeating that process with him stepping into a starting role afterward.

In reality, though, we have to assume that Hart will be a higher priority than McBride. In that case, McBride represents an expiring contract at New York's deepest position. Not only do the Knicks have Shamet, Jose Alvarado and Kolek as viable backcourt reserves, but they have several veterans on camp deals (like Bruce Brown) fighting for a roster spot at that position as well. Meanwhile, the Knicks have very little center depth behind Towns, making McBride an obvious trade candidate to potentially fill that hole.

The tell here will be who winds up getting the final roster spot for the Knicks and how the early season goes thereafter. Say the Knicks keep a big man like James Wiseman and he proves to be playable early in the year. At that point, trading for another big becomes less of a priority. If Brown or Ochai Agbaji make the team, however, the Knicks would be left with just Towns and Andre Drummond at center unless they make a move to clear another roster spot. In that world, a McBride trade seems more likely.

#317. Suns Lock Up Oso Ighodaro with 3-Year, $29 Million Extension

Phoenix just bet on one of its own. Per Shams Charania, Oso Ighodaro agreed to a three-year, $29 million extension that runs through the 2030-31 season.

ESPN's Bobby Marks added the key piece of the structure: "To help the Suns financially for next season, Ighodaro's $2.4M team option for 2027-28 is picked up. Good deal for both sides." Translation: Phoenix keeps Oso on his bargain rookie number for one more year, and the new money doesn't kick in until 2028-29.

That works out to roughly $9.7 million a year for a guy who came into this league as a second-round flyer.

Just on Friday, Ighodaro told reporters: "Yeah, we're talking about it. We'll see what happens in the next couple days."

The timing is the win here. Picking up the $2.4 million option keeps next season's books clean while the front office works through bigger financial decisions. Oso gets long-term security, Phoenix gets one more year of a rotation big at near-minimum money, then a fair number after that, especially if he continues to progress.

The Suns acquired Ighodaro's draft rights at No. 40 from the Knicks in exchange for the draft rights to Kevin McCullar Jr., the 56th overall pick, and Boston's 2028 protected second-round pick. He's also a hometown kid, a Chandler native who led Desert Vista to a state championship.

Ighodaro appeared in all 82 games last season, starting 24, and his role expanded when a foot injury sidelined Mark Williams. In a frontcourt that got banged up, he was the one big the Suns never had to worry about showing up.

This front office keeps telling us what it wants: length, motor, and guys who can switch. Ighodaro checks all three at a backup-big price. Keeping him means the Suns don't have to overpay in free agency for that profile.

Ighodaro has been in a battle with Khaman Maluach for the Suns' starting center job with Mark Williams sidelined for the foreseeable future. He will play a major part in their rotation this season.

#318. Pittsburgh coach Mike McCarthy suffers injury during Steelers' game vs. Buccaneers

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Instead of spending halftime in the locker room, Steelers coach Mike McCarthy spent it in the medical tent after he sustained an ankle injury at the conclusion of the first half.

McCarthy was starting to make his way to the locker room when he started limping and had trouble walking. He was then assisted off the field and into the blue medical tent. He did not speak to the Steelers at halftime.

After the game, he revealed he had been stepped on, and that's why he had to go into the blue tent. However, he said he is feeling better. He told the media he delegated much of the halftime head coach responsibilities to assistant coach Joe Whitt Jr.

Despite the injury, McCarthy returned to the sideline for the start of the second half. He has also resumed his duties as the team's offensive playcaller. According to the CBS Sports broadcast team, McCarthy twisted his ankle, but it's unclear exactly when or what caused it.

Mike McCarthy (ankle) QUESTIONABLE #Steelers #NFL pic.twitter.com/EijrUvY7R8

McCarthy's injury capped off what was a lousy first half for the Steelers, who trailed 13-3 at the intermission. Pittsburgh committed several mental errors in the first half, including Darnell Washington's juggling of an Aaron Rodgers pass, which was ultimately picked off by A'Shawn Robinson. The pick set up the game's first score, a 43-yard field goal by Chase McLaughlin.

The Steelers' offense gained just 102 yards in the first half. They were just 1-of-6 on third down and 0-of-1 on fourth down.

Jalon Daniels, the Buccaneers' undrafted rookie quarterback, dominated the Steelers in the first 30 minutes. Daniels completed nine consecutive passes at one point and recorded the game's first touchdown on a short touchdown pass to Emeka Egbuka.

The Steelers went on to beat the Buccaneers 26-19 in overtime.

The Indianapolis Colts lost to the Tennessee Titans in Week 6 of the 2026 NFL season. The 2-3 Colts dropped to 2-4, while the 0-5 Titans improved to 1-5.

The Colts made a big change following the brutal loss, firing general manager Chris Ballard. Indianapolis is now looking for a new leader of this franchise.

According to Dan Patrick on The Dan Patrick Show, the Colts have made quite an interesting call already. One source told Patrick that Peyton Manning is a name to watch, as he's already been called about the GM opening.

This report from Patrick is an interesting one, and it's a whole lot more fascinating than simply hearing that the Colts will be calling Manning about the opening.

While there seems to be interest from the Colts in bringing Manning in as the team's general manager, they're also looking to get advice from the Hall of Famer on the GM opening.

MORE: Colts fans are calling for Daniel Jones benching after ugly Titans loss

But in their pitch to hire Manning, they're rumored to be offering Manning a partial ownership stake in the Colts, which would be quite an interesting situation for the former Colts QB.

Manning is still very much involved in the NFL world and could play a similar role to what Tom Brady is doing right now with the Las Vegas Raiders, acting as a key figure in the front office while also working for FOX on an NFL broadcast.

Taking over GM duties would likely take Manning away from his ESPN work, as he'd need to focus on helping the team, similar to what Matt Ryan is doing with the Atlanta Falcons.

#320. Kings' Ben Simmons suffers torn Achilles at practice Sunday, will miss entire season

Sacramento's Ben Simmons has suffered a torn right Achilles and will soon undergo surgery to repair it, the Kings have announced. While no official timetable was given, he will undoubtedly miss the entire 2026-27 season.

This is a devastating blow for Simmons, who had been out of the league for a year getting his body right and his mind in a good place. For years, Simmons had been dealing with a back issue that limited him physically, caused him to miss a lot of games, and that shook his confidence.

Taking a year off seemed to have worked. All the buzz coming out of Sacramento had been overwhelmingly positive, and Simmons, 30, was expected to be a starter on opening night. While it's just the preseason, Simmons was moving well and playing a more attacking style, averaging 10.5 points, 4 rebounds and 4 assists in 17.4 minutes per preseason game.

Two seasons ago, the former No. 1 pick played 51 games between the Nets and Clippers, averaging 5 points, 5.6 assists and 4.7 rebounds per game, while shooting 52%, all from inside the arc. He showed flashes of what he could be as a floor general and leader.

This injury also leaves the Kings and coach Doug Christie scrambling to fill a big hole in his rotation. Don't be surprised if Precious Achiuwa gets a lot of run with the starters, a group expected to include rookie Darius Acuff Jr., Domantas Sabonis, Zach LaVine and Keegan Murray.

#321. NHL Draft 2026 results, takeaways, complete list of Round 1 picks: Maple Leafs swing big, Sharks loading up

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Toronto Maple Leafs have selected Gavin McKenna with the No. 1 overall pick in the 2026 NHL Draft. One of the most dynamic playmakers in this draft class, McKenna should give the Maple Leafs an offensive boost immediately.

McKenna just wrapped up his freshman season at Penn State, and the transition from junior hockey to the collegiate level wasn't a smooth one initially. However, after a slow start, McKenna found his groove and finished the season with 15 goals and 36 assists 35 games. His 51 points ranked third in the Big Ten, and McKenna led the Nittany Lions to the NCAA Tournament, where they lost to Minnesota-Duluth in the first round.

Prior to his career at Penn State, McKenna posted gaudy numbers with the Medicine Hat Tigers in the WHL. In 2024-25, McKenna tallied 41 goals and 88 points in 56 games while helping the Tigers capture a WHL title. McKenna and Medicine Hat fell just shy of a Memorial Cup title, losing to the London Knights in the championship game.

It might be a bit much to ask McKenna to ride shotgun alongside Auston Matthews right out of the gate, but he has the skill to make an instant impact. Can McKenna land among the best No. 1 picks of this century? If he can, that would be a huge boost to a Toronto offense that finished in the middle of the league last year.

Midway through the first round, the St. Louis Blues flipped two of their first-round picks (No. 15 and No. 29) for Mason McTavish in a trade with the Anaheim Ducks. McTavish, the No. 3 pick in the 2021 draft, underwhelmed last season. Armed with four first-round selections in this draft, the Blues are making a low-risk bet on a bounce-back.

Throughout the pre-draft process, Reid was considered among the top two or three prospects in the 2026 class. Between his size and offensive skillset, Reid has everything an NHL team could want in a modern defenseman. In 38 games with the OHL's Soo Greyhounds last season, Reid notched 18 goals and 30 assists from the blue line.

Despite all that, Reid slipped to No. 7 overall on draft night. Perhaps even more shocking than the slide was the fact that Reid was the fourth defenseman off the board. There wasn't necessarily a consensus top defender in the draft, but it would be nearly impossible to find anyone who had Reid outside the top three at the position. After pending restricted free agent Jason Robertson reportedly turned down their $120 million contract offer, the Seattle Kraken needed some good news, and they got it when Reid fell into their lap on Friday night.

After acquiring the No. 9 overall pick in the William Eklund trade, the Sharks entered the night with two top-10 selections. San Jose shopped the No. 9 pick in hopes of adding a player who could help the team immediately, but nothing came to fruition, and that may have been a blessing in disguise.

After taking another dynamic offensive playmaker in Ivar Stenberg at No. 2 overall, the Sharks selected defenseman Keaton Verhoeff with the ninth pick. An enormous presence on the blue line, Verhoeff gives San Jose another blue-chip prospect on defense alongside Sam Dickinson. The Sharks would probably like to find immediate help on defense before the 2026-27 season, but Verhoeff will be able to grow with other young stars like Macklin Celebrini, Willi Smith, Michael Misa and Stenberg.

Then, the night only got better for San Jose as it used the No. 27 overall pick to jump up to No. 21 and grab defenseman Ryan Lin. Depending upon where you looked before the draft, Lin was considered a top-15 pick among some industry professionals. The Sharks prospect pool was already as deep as the Mariana Trench, but it's even deeper now, and they have the brightest future of any team in the NHL. It may not be long before San Jose is a perennial Cup contender.

The Blues entered the first round with four selections, and it would have been shocking if they didn't trade at least one of them. After reportedly striking out on a deal for Jason Robertson that included three of those picks, St. Louis used two of them to add Mason McTavish from the Ducks. The Blues needed some center help, and they had picks to burn, so that deal made a lot of sense for them.

McTavish was once considered a top prospect in the Ducks organization after the team selected him at No. 3 overall in 2021. However, he's fallen behind other young stars who were drafted after him, and McTavish will now get a fresh start in St. Louis. McTavish has flashed offensive upside with a 20-goal and 52-point campaign in 2024-25. The issue is that offense fell off last year, and his defense failed to improve. With McTavish on the ice at five-on-five, Anaheim allowed 3.17 xGA/60, which was 25th on the team, per Natural Stat Trick. If Jim Montgomery can get McTavish to play even average defense, this trade will have been worthwhile for the Blues.

#322. Miami Dolphins Trade Deadline Primer: The Top Candidates To Buy and Sell

Miami Dolphins General Manager Jon-Eric Sullivan has already shown a willingness to sacrifice short-term talent for long-term assets. Last offseason, the Dolphins dealt Jaylen Waddle to the Denver Broncos in a move that helped build one of the league's largest collections of draft capital entering the 2026 NFL Draft. As the Nov. 10 trade deadline approaches, the question becomes whether Sullivan has another move or two up his sleeve. National analysts have identified several Dolphins as potential trade candidates, with three names appearing more often than the rest: Austin Jackson, Joshua Uche and Zach Sieler.

Alain Poupart, Sports Illustrated: "Jackson is scheduled to become a free agent after the season and he's got a low base salary that would make him attractive financially to other teams."

Carter Bahns, CBS Sports: "Tackles are always in demand. He would be an affordable half-season rental."

Anthony DiMoro, Heavy: "With offensive lines such as the Philadelphia Eagles decimated either by departures or injuries, Jackson immediately steps in as a starting right tackle for the majority of offensive line-starved teams in the NFL."

Kyle Crabbs, Yahoo Sports: "Given his durability concerns and lack of a low end contract, Jackson has the makings of a perfect insurance rental at offensive tackle for a contending team." Potential buyer: Jaguars, which is currently without standout tackle Anton Harrison.

It's easy to see why Jackson has emerged as the consensus favorite to be moved. Starting-caliber offensive tackles rarely become available, and Miami has already spent much of the season evaluating younger offensive linemen. If Sullivan is looking for the cleanest path to adding draft capital, Jackson may be it.

Alex Kay, Bleacher Report: "Parting with a late-round pick to bolster the defensive front with a player who recorded 11.5 sacks as recently as the 2022 season is worth the risk." Potential buyer: Ravens

Dan Graziano, ESPN: "He's a seven-year veteran who's playing well for a team in the first year of a significant rebuild. If the Dolphins get the opportunity to turn this signing into a useful draft pick, it's not at all hard to imagine them jumping on it."

Uche presents the opposite dilemma. Unlike Jackson, there appears to be a real argument for keeping him: He has played well, fits the age profile of a player who could still contribute when Miami is ready to compete again and likely wouldn't command a massive contract extension. The question becomes whether the Dolphins value a future draft pick more than continuity in the pass rush.

Poupart: "Sieler is coming off his best performance of the season and he remains a solid, at times very good, interior defensive lineman, but he will be 32 at the start of the 2026 season. That could be a problem for Miami, though not for a contender looking for D-line help."

Antwan Staley, Athlon Sports: "With no guaranteed money remaining on his contract after the 2026 season, the Dolphins could release Sieler next offseason. Ideally, they'd like at least an early Day 3 pick, possibly from a contending team that needs interior defensive help."

Jason La Canfora, Casino.org: "While Sieler is now in his 30s, he continues to draw double teams at the line of scrimmage despite limited help around him. As Miami seeks to accumulate draft capital, Sieler becomes a prime trading chip."

Sieler is arguably Miami's best trade chip, but he's also the player who would be hardest to replace. While most rebuilding teams listen when contenders come calling about veterans in their 30s, moving one of the locker room's most respected veterans would send a signal that Miami is prioritizing future assets over short-term competitiveness.

While a handful of Dolphins have surfaced in trade speculation, those three names consistently appeared across multiple national outlets. It's worth noting that trading Sieler would result in a $10 million dead cap for 2026 and a $24+ million dead cap for 2027. A Jackson trade would result in a $4.5 million dead cap for 2026 and $14 million in 2027. Trading Uche would result in a dead cap for 2026 of just $600,000. (These stats courtesy of Spotrac.)

None of these players surfaced as frequently as Jackson, Uche, or Sieler, but each has factors that could make him expendable if Miami receives the right offer.

Justin Carter, Fansided: "With Rodriguez and Brooks both playing 90 percent or more of snaps, Gay's 50 percent snap share can be replaced by getting Jackson Woodard or Liam Anderson on the field more."

James Brizuela, Yahoo Sports: "Tolbert may not be utilized in the correct way with the Dolphins, but he could be a strong rotational option for another team that needs a boost to their wide receiver department."

Carter: "Anderson ranks 30th among safeties in PFF grade. He's only allowed two receptions all season and ranks first among safeties in yards allowed per reception."

While most trade deadline discussion has focused on the Dolphins as sellers, Miami could just as easily explore opportunities to acquire young talent. The roster remains one of the league's youngest, and rebuilding teams sometimes use the deadline to take chances on players whose value has dipped elsewhere. The Dolphins have only $6 million and change in cap room for 2026, which limits who they might be able to bring in. Just the same, here are a few names to keep an eye out for:

One of the most discussed trade targets this season, Thomas is two years removed from a 1,200-yard, 10-touchdown rookie season that earned him a Pro Bowl nod. He's young (24) and still on his rookie contract, which as a former first-round pick includes a fifth-year option. His affordability and potential could cost a Day 2 pick in the 2027 draft, making him a more expensive target than others on this list.

Back in the offseason, the Miami Herald's Barry Jackson reported the team was interested in then-free agent Jennings, who ended up signing an $8 million one-year deal with the Vikings. The 29-year-old has been a dud in Minnesota this season (2 receptions for 9 yards), but the previous two years Jennings caught 15 touchdowns and 1,600 yards for the 49ers. Adding him would cost the Dolphins maybe $2 million the rest of the season but give the team a reliable possession receiver already familiar with Bobby Slowik's offense.

The Dolphins are already in need of defensive line help, a need that will become even more pressing if they trade Uche. Maybe they can rehab another veteran lineman in Solomon Thomas, who has 18.5 sacks and 145 tackles over a 10-year career. Now, it's possible he's washed up, but at low salary ($1-2 million) and acquisition costs, he might be worth a look.

Two years off a 1,200-yard Pro Bowl season, Jeudy is languishing with the Browns (12 receptions for 150 yards) and ranks fifth on the team in receptions. The 27-year-old could probably be had for a Day 3 pick, and the Dolphins would only owe him about $1 million for the rest of the season. Jeudy has a non-guaranteed $22.9 million salary for 2027 that would need to be restructured.

Whether the Dolphins ultimately buy, sell or do some combination of both, the deadline should offer another glimpse into Sullivan's long-term vision. Last offseason he was willing to move a popular player like Jaylen Waddle in exchange for future assets. If a contender comes calling for Austin Jackson, Joshua Uche, Zach Sieler or some other veteran, we'll see whether that philosophy still applies.
