#323. Vikings poised to be aggressive at trade deadline as Colts face potential fire sale

With the NFC up for grabs and the Vikings sitting at the top with a 5-0 record, all signs point to Minnesota general manager Nolan Teasley being aggressive ahead of the Nov. 10 NFL trade deadline.

Bring Me The Sports senior Vikings writer Will Ragatz believes running back, guard, tight end, and safety are the four positions Minnesota is most likely to scan the market for.

"The Vikings are back from their bye week, as one of the NFL's last three unbeaten teams, and indications are they intend to be active before the Nov. 10 trade deadline," says Ben Goessling of the Minnesota Star Tribune. "If they find the right partner, they could look to bolster their roster for a possible playoff run."

Fellow local insider, Alec Lewis of The Athletic, also sees Minnesota being active, writing that Teasley, per anonymous team sources, "is open to pursuing a bevy of ideas at the trade deadline."

The point here is that more and more insiders believe the Vikings will be active.

Goessling believes the biggest needs are offensive line, tight end, and running back, though he isn't ruling out adding a pass rusher. Lewis is also honing in on tight ends, running backs, and guards or centers, while also not ruling out pass rushers and safeties.

Related: 6 intriguing running backs the Vikings could trade for before the deadline

Stephen Holder, who covers the Colts for ESPN, thinks Ballard's firing could indicate a fire sale is coming.

#325. Chiefs Week 6 snap count analysis: Andrew Armstrong steps up

Welcome to Arrowhead Pride's weekly snap-count analysis!

Let's take a closer look at the Kansas City Chiefs' snap counts in the 22-6 win over the Los Angeles Chargers in Week 6. The starting lineups are courtesy of NFL Game Stats and Information, and the snap-count data comes from Pro Football Focus' premium stats.

Starters (offensive): LT Kahlil Benson, LG Kingsley Suamataia, C Creed Humphrey, RG Trey Smith, RT Jaylon Moore, QB Patrick Mahomes, WR Andrew Armstrong, WR Xavier Worthy, RB Kenneth Walker, TE Travis Kelce and TE Noah Gray

Starters (defensive): DE George Karlaftis, DT Chris Jones, DT Khyiris Tonga, DE Felix Anudike-Uzomah, LB Nick Bolton, LB Drue Tranquill, CB Christian Roland-Wallace, CB Mansoor Delane, CB Nohl Williams, S Alohi Gilman and S Chamarri Conner

Inactive: TE Jared Wiley, QB Garrett Nussmeier (Emergency third QB), DB Jadon Canady, DE Jack Pyburn, OT Diego Pounds, LT Josh Simmons (Back), WR Rashee Rice (Hamstring)

With wide receiver Rashee Rice (hamstring) ruled out on the final injury report, the Chiefs elevated second-year wideout Andrew Armstrong from the practice squad. He lined up on the opening snap, marking his first career start.

It was the first of 42 snaps Armstrong played on offense, starting alongside Xavier Worthy (51) and Jalen Royals (45); he caught a 13-yard pass on one of the two passes thrown his way.

Armstrong spent 12 snaps in the slot and 14 snaps on the perimeter of the offense, signaling the use of Armstrong's blocking near the line of scrimmage on run plays. He lined up for 15 run plays, nearly as much as Worthy (18) and Royals (17).

I don't need a PFF "run-blocking" grade to know Armstrong was an impactful blocker. With an offense built around running back Kenneth Walker gashing defenses, the question becomes whether Armstrong deserves a spot on the active roster, maybe in favor of the return specialist Nikko Remigio.

After right tackle Jaylon Moore entered concussion protocol late in the first half, backup Joshua Ezeudu took over on the right edge and stayed there for the rest of the afternoon. He played 30 snaps, 17 of them on pass plays.

PFF faulted Ezeudu with one pressure and a hurry, so he kept Mahomes clean in his first time in the lineup for the Chiefs' offense. After the preseason, he was traded to Kansas City from the New York Giants after spending most of his career at left guard or tackle with Big Blue. It will be interesting to see whether the lineup shifts moving forward, even if left tackle Josh Simmons (back) isn't ready for Week 7.

Also noteworthy is third tight end Jake Briningstool, who played the most snaps (10) he has since Week 1 and made an impactful block to spring running back Kenneth Walker for the 33-yard touchdown run in the first quarter.

Second-year defensive end Ashton Gillotte played the fourth-most snaps among the team's defensive linemen on Sunday, on the field for 52% of the defense's snaps.

In that time, he registered three pressures: a hurry, a quarterback hit and a sack that broke the seal on the Chiefs' four-sack game. He earned two "Stops," tackles that count as failures for the offense.

It was Gillotte's biggest timeshare in the Chiefs' starting lineup this season, and his most impactful performance. He, along with rookie edge rusher R Mason Thomas (five pressures), was constantly in the backfield on Sunday afternoon and is a positive indicator for the pass rush moving forward.

#326. Ranking No. 1 NHL Draft picks since 2000: How Gavin McKenna compares to Sidney Crosby, Connor McDavid

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

On Friday night, the Toronto Maple Leafs will make a franchise-altering decision with the No. 1 overall pick in the 2026 NHL Draft. Barring a shocker, that selection will be Penn State winger Gavin McKenna, and the Leafs can only hope he follows in the footsteps of other No. 1 picks in the 21st century.

For the most part, the consensus draft boards have gotten it right when it comes to the top prospect in each draft since 2000, although there have been a few notable selections. Players like Sidney Crosby and Connor McDavid have exceeded the hype they received going into their respective drafts.

More recently, Macklin Celebrini and Matthew Schaefer have delivered on the expectations of a No. 1 overall pick, even if they don't have long track records. Can McKenna make it three straight instant superstars at the top of the draft?

As we get set to watch McKenna walk across the stage in Buffalo, let's take a look back on how each No. 1 pick in the 21st century has panned out. We included McKenna in the mix to provide a baseline of what fans could expect from him as a rookie in 2026-27, even if we won't know his true ceiling until he hits the ice.

Let's give NHL general managers some credit. It's rare to find a complete whiff at No. 1 overall, but this was one of them. Yakupov played just 350 career games, totaling 62 goals and 74 assists. He did, however, give us one of the most preposterous celebrations in a regular-season game of all-time. For that, he will be remembered forever.

There's a reason you rarely see goaltenders get drafted this early. That position is incredibly volatile, and it's tough to project exactly how goalies will develop. DiPietro was certainly a cautionary tale in that regard. The Islanders selected DiPietro after a dominant freshman season at Boston University, but his career never really got off the ground due to injuries and poor performance. DiPietro won just 130 games in 318 appearances before retiring.

It's very easy to see why Power went No. 1 overall in 2021. His combination of size (6-foot-6) and mobility was -- and is -- incredibly tantalizing. Still, Power hasn't ascended to the status of a top-pairing defenseman, let alone a true No. 1 option. There's hope that it can still happen. Just look at Power's teammate, Rasmus Dahlin, who took a few seasons to hit his stride. For now, though, Power hasn't quite lived up to the hype.

Johnson had a long and successful career, but he never justified the Blues selecting him at No. 1 overall in 2006, especially with future Hall of Famer Jonathan Toews going just two picks later. St. Louis traded Johnson to Colorado just three seasons into his tenure with the Blues. Johnson was a reliable defender who played over 1,000 games, and he won a Stanley Cup with the Avalanche in 2022.

Things just haven't panned out for Lafreniere, who has yet to top 57 points in six seasons, after being considered the top prospect in 2020. Lafreniere is a productive second-line winger, but that's not what the Rangers were hoping for, and his name has come up in trade rumors over the last year. Tim Stutzle, Lucas Raymond, Jake Sanderson, Anton Lundell and Seth Jarvis all came off the board in that first round.

When Slafkovsky was struggling to find his footing in the NHL earlier in his career, it was easy to forget how young he was. Following a breakout season, the 22-year-old Slafkovsky is back on track to become what the Canadiens expected when they selected him at No. 1 overall. The young Slovakian potted 30 goals and added 43 assists in 82 games, and he was part of a dynamite top line in Montreal. Now, the goal for Slafkovsky is stringing a couple of great seasons together.

This feels like a fair baseline for McKenna, at least to start. Last season, he overcame a slow start at Penn State and finished with 15 goals and 36 assists in 35 games. As is the case with many rookie forwards, McKenna will have some work to do on his game without the puck, but there's no doubt that he can make magic happen when the puck is on his stick. He should make all the misery Toronto endured throughout the 2025-26 season worth it.

Ekblad moved around quite a bit as I was writing this list because -- while he hasn't necessarily played up to the level of a No. 1 pick -- he was a defensive stalwart for a team that won back-to-back Stanley Cups. The issue for Ekblad is that he hasn't ever really been a true star defenseman, which is what you're looking for at the top of the draft. That said, he's been a steady presence for Florida, and the team eventually got the end resulted it desired with a couple championships.

He hasn't played up to the level of a No. 1 pick, but Nugent-Hopkins has been a staple in Edmonton's top six for a long time. The result of that longevity is 1,031 games and 804 points -- which includes a 104-point campaign in 2022-23. Judging him by the standards placed on a No. 1 pick, Nugent-Hopkins has underwhelmed, but he's far from a bust.

After posting absurd numbers at the junior level, Bedard was thought to be the next big superstar, but that hasn't come to fruition yet. Bedard has posted solid offensive numbers, but his defense has been a problem, and he's really struggled at the faceoff dot. There's still plenty of time for Bedard, 20, to develop into a true superstar, but Chicago needs to give him adequate help on the wing.

Hall's journey has been a wild one. His career got off to a very good -- but not great -- start with the Oilers. Then he was traded to the Devils. His first year in New Jersey was something of a disappointment, but he rebounded to win the Hart Trophy in 2017-18. That was followed by declining performance in brief stints with the Sabres, Coyotes and Bruins. By the time he was with the Chicago Blackhawks, it looked as though Hall's career was coming to an end. After being a throw-in to the Hurricanes in a three-way deal for Mikko Rantanen, Hall made a resurgence and nearly won the Conn Smythe Trophy while helping Carolina win the Cup in 2026.

Unfortunately for Nash, he played on one of the NHL's worst teams for the first decade of his career. True superstars are able to transcend the state of a team, and Nash wasn't quite able to do that. Still, he was one of just a handful of stars to emerge from a weak 2002 draft class, and the Blue Jackets were right to select Nash at No. 1. Nash won the Rocket Richard Trophy in his second season with 41 goals, but he was only able to top that number once in his career.

On the heels of Connor McDavid in 2015 and Auston Matthews in 2016, Hischier didn't garner as much buzz, but he's developed into a two-way stud at center. Not only is Hischier capable of hitting 30 goals every year, but he's also a perennial Selke Trophy candidate. Hischier may be more than halfway down the rankings, but New Jersey shouldn't be disappointed with its selection atop the 2017 draft.

At his peak, Kovalchuk was one of the most exciting players in the league, and it's a shame he was stuck on the Atlanta Thrashers for most of it. From 2001 to 2012, Kovalchuk led the NHL with 406 goals. His puck skills were elite, and his quick release was among the filthiest in the league. If Kovalchuk had a bit more talent around him early in his career -- and if he didn't take a five-season hiatus to play in the KHL in his latter years -- his trophy case would have a lot less room.

The more I wrote, the further I dropped Tavares. There's no question that Tavares has displayed incredible longevity. Tavares has played 1,266 games in his career and has been a high-impact player for 17 consecutive seasons. The issue for Tavares is that, while he's been a strong two-way player for most of his career, he lacks individual awards and Stanley Cup rings. In fact, he's never even been to the conference finals. Tavares isn't the type of No. 1 pick who was able to put an entire franchise on his back.

Somewhat of a late bloomer, Dahlin's career has really taken off over the last few seasons, and he was a Norris Trophy finalist in 2025-26. Dahlin weathered the storm on some putrid Sabres teams early in his career, and he's evolved into one of the game's best two-way defensemen while leading Buffalo to its first playoff appearance since 2011. I expect Dahlin to be in the Norris Trophy conversation annually for at least the next five years as his star continues to rise.

Hughes has the talent to be considerably higher on this list, but durability concerns keep him down at No. 10. He's missed at least 20 games in each of the last three seasons, but Hughes has been very productive when healthy. Since the start of the 2021-22 season, Hughes is tied for 10th in the NHL with 1.21 points per game. The last time he played anything resembling a full season was in 2022-23, when he posted 99 points and finished eighth in Hart Trophy voting. Can he stay on the ice over the next few years?

Fleury was a difficult player to place on this list for a couple of reasons. For starters, evaluating goalies is tougher than evaluating skaters because so many external factors affect the final numbers. Secondly, Fleury endured ups and downs in his career. In 2008 and 2009, when the Penguins made back-to-back Stanley Cup Final appearances, Fleury was outstanding. He was a key reason Pittsburgh lifted the Cup in 2009, but he wasn't in goal when the team won its next two championships in 2016 and 2017. But Fleury also had a second act of his career with the Vegas Golden Knights, where he backstopped the team to a Final and won a Vezina Trophy. For all the peaks and valleys, Fleury ranks second all-time in games played (1,051) and wins (575).

Maybe I'm jumping the gun, but I don't care. Schaefer was just that good as a rookie in 2025-26. He entered a pretty undesirable environment and thrived right out of the gate. At just 18 years old, Schaefer tallied 23 goals and 59 points from the blue line while posting solid five-on-five metrics. Schaefer is on the fast track to superstardom, and there's at least one Norris Trophy in his future.

If you thought putting Schaefer in the top 10 was premature, you might think the same about putting Celebrini in the top eight, but there is no doubt about his star power anymore. Like most of the players ahead of him on this list, Celebrini has completely flipped the outlook of a franchise that was dead in the water when he arrived. Last season, Celebrini tallied 115 points as a 19-year-old, and that number was nearly double his next closest teammate. Did I mention he also led the Olympics with six goals?

Matthews is the only player on track to give Alex Ovechkin a run for his money on the all-time goals list. No player has more goals than Matthews' 428 since he made his NHL debut in 2016, but he's not a one-trick pony. The most underrated part of Matthews' game is his defensive progression throughout his career, and he was named a Selke Trophy finalist in 2024. Although he now has a gold medal on his mantle, Matthews still lacks a Stanley Cup -- or even a conference finals berth. If he can put together a breakthrough postseason, Matthews would jump a spot or two on this list.

As things stand today, Kane is the greatest American hockey player ever. Few players in this century can rival Kane's ability to put the puck on a string and freeze opponents at will, and that quality has made him one of the best playmakers of his generation. Before Kane arrived, Chicago spent a decade as an also-ran, but that changed quickly with No. 88 in the fold. With Kane leading the way, the Blackhawks won three Stanley Cups in six seasons from 2010-15, and he captured a Conn Smythe Trophy in the process.

He's been overshadowed by Ovechkin for most of his career, but Stamkos belongs in the conversation as one of the best scorers in league history. Since he entered the NHL in 2008-09, Stamkos ranks second behind Ovechkin with 624 goals, and he just tallied 42 at the age of 35. Getting to 700 career goals certainly isn't out of the question for Stamkos. In addition to the scoring, Stamkos captained the Tampa Bay Lightning as they made four Stanley Cup Final appearances -- and won two championships -- from 2015-22.

Not every No. 1 overall pick shoots to stardom immediately. MacKinnon is a great example of that. Through his first four seasons, MacKinnon profiled as a very good player, but he hadn't lived up to the pre-draft expectations. Then, in 2017-18, something clicked and MacKinnon's career launched into the stratosphere. Since that year, MacKinnon has piled up 936 points, which ranks second in the NHL over that span. Plus, he's added a Stanley Cup, a Hart Trophy and a Rocket Richard Trophy to his resume.

Ovechkin is the greatest goal-scorer in NHL history, and he's the only player ever to top 900 career goals. Ovechkin also holds the record for most Rocket Richard Trophy wins with nine. Since the award was first handed out in 1998-99, no other player has more than three. For years, the biggest knocks on Ovechkin were his lack of defense and his inability to win the Stanley Cup. The former prevents him from being any higher on the list. The latter was resolved in 2018, when he led the Capitals to their first Cup while leading the playoffs in goals (15) and winning the Conn Smythe Trophy.

McDavid is the most talented player on this list. His combination of speed, skill, vision and hockey IQ is unmatched by anyone else in the 21st century. In terms of his production, the numbers are off the charts. McDavid is on pace to hit 1,628 points by the time he plays his 1,000th game. The only hole in McDavid's resume is, admittedly, a big one. He still hasn't won the Stanley Cup, but that's no fault of his own. McDavid has 156 points in 102 career playoff games, and he became the sixth player in NHL history to win the Conn Smythe Trophy as a member of the losing team in 2024. McDavid will eventually break through for a championship, but for now, the wait continues.

When a player gets labeled as a "generational" prospect, this is what you expect. A three-time Stanley Cup champion and two-time Olympic gold medalist, Crosby almost single-handedly reversed the fortunes of a moribund franchise in Pittsburgh. On top of that, Crosby played a major role -- along with Ovechkin -- in reviving the NHL following the 2004-05 lockout. His trophy case features the Hart Trophy (2x), Conn Smythe Trophy (2x), Rocket Richard Trophy (2x) and Art Ross Trophy (2x). Crosby has been an elite all-around player for more than two decades now, and he's easily a top-10 player in NHL history.

#327. Ben Simmons sustains Achilles injury during Sacramento Kings practice

SACRAMENTO, CA – The Sacramento Kings were excited to enter the 2026-27 regular-season relatively injury-free but the team received a massive blow just a few days ahead of the regular-season opener.

Recently signed forward Ben Simmons sustained a torn right Achilles tendon during a live drill in practice on Sunday, Oct. 18, the Kings announced.

"An MRI revealed the torn right Achilles tendon and Simmons will undergo surgery. Further updates will be provided as appropriate," the Kings said.

ESPN reported that the injury is suspected to be a season-ending one for Simmons.

Simmons was making his highly anticipated return to the NBA after signing with the Kings, filling out their final open spot, a person with knowledge of the team told USA TODAY Sports. Simmons signed a one-year, $3.5 million contract with the Kings, according to ESPN.

Simmons' deal with Sacramento gave him a fresh start in the league as he worked his way back into the feel, and conditioning, of the game.

"Coming to work hard, play the game I know how to play," Simmons told USA TODAY during training camp on what he brings to the Kings. "Communicate, and just lead. Lead how I know how to. So it's been good. We're locked in, focused."

Simmons has missed time throughout his career due to chronic back problems and a series of leg injuries. He took time off last year, missing the entire 2025-26 season to rehabilitate his body from his lingering injuries. He has also battled through mental adversity throughout his career.

Simmons, 30, was entering his eighth NBA season and his first season with the Kings. He was named NBA Rookie of the Year for the 2017-18 season and was twice named to the NBA's All-Defensive first team (in 2019-20 and 2020-21) as a member of the Philadelphia 76ers. He was also named third team All-NBA in 2019-20.

He has career averages of 15.8 points, 8.1 rebounds, 8.2 assists, 1.7 steals and 0.9 blocks per game.

Despite the agonizing diagnosis, Simmons remained positive and determined in a statement he posted to his Instagram story Sunday evening.

"I've faced challenges before that tested me mentally, physically and emotionally, and I've found a way through every single one of them. This injury is another chapter in my journey, not the end of my story," Simmons wrote.

"It's never easy being away from the game I love, especially after everything it took to get back here. But if there's one thing I've learned, it's that adversity doesn't define you. How your respond to it does.

"I've been knocked down before, and I've always found a way to get back up. This time will be no different."

There were shades of the three-time NBA All-Star during the Kings preseason games. Simmons averaged 5.0 points, 4.7 rebounds, and 5.6 assists per game in the preseason.

He was projected to make his way into the starting lineup, playing alongside Darius Acuff, Domantas Sabonis, Keegan Murray and Zach LaVine. The team felt that his acquisition would add versatility to their roster where Simmons could defend every position on the floor, making Sacramento a bigger team.

However, he won't be back on the court in the immediate future and may miss his second consecutive season.

ESPN just featured Simmons in an E60 documentary titled "Being Ben" that premiered Sunday afternoon. The documentary, hosted by ESPN senior writer Marc Spears, follows Simmons, going behind-the-scenes and discussing in-depth Simmons' thoughts and emotions upon his return to the NBA.

Health has been a major concern for Simmons throughout his NBA tenure.

He came into the NBA as a bonafide star, coming out of LSU where he averaged 19.2 points, 11.8 rebounds, 4.8 assists, two steals and nearly a block per game as a freshman in 2015-2016.

He always has been looked at as a guy who can do a little bit of anything and everything on the floor. After the 76ers selected him with the No. 1 overall pick the 2016 NBA Draft, Simmons missed the entire 2016-17 season after rolling his ankle in his first practice, fracturing in his right foot and ankle – which did not heal throughout the season.

Simmons then played nearly every game for Philadelphia in his next two seasons earning three consecutive All-Star nods before injuries began to mount again after the 2020-21 season.

First was the fiasco when the Sixers lost a 2021 Eastern Conference semifinal series to Atlanta Hawks in seven games that was infamous for Simmons passing up a wide open layup or a dunk under the basket with 3:30 remaining in the game as Philadelphia trailed 88-86.

During the offseason, Simmons asked for a trade, held out from the team and didn't appear for training camp, stating he was away dealing with his mental health. He ended up missing the entire 2021-22 with a back injury in addition to the mental health hurdles and trade holdout.

Simmons was eventually traded to the Brooklyn Nets in February 2022. He returned the next season but was limited playing only 43 games as he dealt with a number of knee injuries and lingering back issues.

His back issues continued into the next season in 2023-24, where he appeared in 15 games with the Nets before being shut down with continued back pain, eventually required surgery.

During the 2024-25 season, Simmons played 33 games with the Nets before he was waived. He signed with the Los Angeles Clippers in February 2025 but appeared in only 18 games as he struggled with his physical health and athletic mobility. He became a free agent after that season and sat out the entire 2025-26 season to rehab his body.

He felt like he was back, signing with Sacramento in the offseason amid optimism his injuries were behind him.

With Simmons' now out indefinitely, the Kings have a decision to make ahead of their season opener regarding their starting lineup. Sacramento begins the 2026-27 regular season with a game against the Clippers in Los Angeles on Wednesday, Oct. 21.

Here is their projected starting lineup following Simmons' injury:

A case could be made for either the 2019-20 season or the 2020-21 season with the Philadelphia 76ers.

In 2019-20, Simmons' third full season with the team, he led the league in steals and finished fourth in Defensive Player of the Year voting. Simmons made the All-Defensive first team and the All-NBA third team and earned his second All-Star nod. He averaged 16.4 points, 8.0 assists, 7.8 rebounds and 2.1 steals while shooting 58% from the field.

In 2020-21, his final season with Philadelphia, Simmons was the runner-up for Defensive Player of the Year behind Rudy Gobert, made the All-Defensive first team for the second consecutive season, finished 12th in MVP voting and was an All-Star for the third season in a row. He averaged 14.3 points, 7.2 rebounds, 6.9 assists, 1.6 steals while sooting 55.7% from the field.

#330. Brady Tkachuk excited to be reunited with brother Matthew on Panthers: 'I just couldn't believe it'

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

FORT LAUDERDALE, Fla. -- When Florida Panthers general manager and president of hockey operations Bill Zito made the trade to acquire Ottawa Senators captain Brady Tkachuk on Sunday, he united arguably hockey's most polarizing brothers in South Florida.

Known for their loud personalities on and off the ice, Brady and his older brother Matthew will continue to be a thorn in opposition's sides. The only difference is they'll be doing while fulfilling a childhood dream of playing together in the NHL.

With how close the Tkachuks are as a family, it shouldn't be a surprise to hear Brady found out he was traded while in the company of his family on Father's Day.

"I was off my phone for five minutes when it happened, we were doing family pictures," Brady Tkachuk said at Tuesday's introductory press conference. "From then on I just couldn't believe it. I know I'm gonna need a couple days after this just to regroup and think about everything that has happened."

Their dream will soon be a reality when the 2026-27 NHL season starts next October, but for a while, the Tkachuks thought the idea would be nothing more than that: a dream.

The first time the sibling-duo took the ice together in a competitive setting was February 2025 at the 4 Nations Face-Off for Team USA. When the United States took on Canada in the preliminary round of the tournament, Brady and Matthew had both hardcore hockey fans and casual watchers of the game on their feet when they both dropped the gloves with their Canadian counterparts mere seconds into the highly-anticipated contest.

A year later at the 2026 Winter Olympics, the Tkachuks helped bring home the first men's Olympic gold medal for the United States since 1980.

After winning one of sport's most prized possessions together, the notion of Brady and Matthew joining forces in the NHL picked up steam, from hockey fans, again.

https://t.co/I00CZBESRE pic.twitter.com/lRGWszOrDc

"I think you can always dream about it," Brady said. "I don't think we ever thought it could be a reality until we got to the Olympics. I think our only dream as a kid was just to make the NHL… I don't even think we ever talked or considered what it'd be like every single day."

Luckily for the Tkachuks, and the Panthers, the man who could bring the brothers together in the NHL wasn't too far from them in Milan.

Zito was one of Team USA's assistant general managers for both the Olympics and 4 Nations tournaments. Seeing how his star Panthers forward Matthew complemented younger brother Brady on the ice was one thing, but it wasn't everything. Zito saw how the two interacted with their fellow American teammates every day for three weeks in the village.

"They had like a hot stove central setup in their rooms," Zito said. "The Hughes brothers and the Tkachuk brothers literally were the place to hang out for the entire Olympics. So, when the players would go back, it would be to go there. Their awareness in tandem with their authenticity of 'yeah, come on in, let's hang out,' that's next level."

When the Tkachuks share the ice in Florida, they'll be just the 16th set of brothers to play together on an NHL team since 2005.

Brady, 26, and Matthew, 28, are both on major chapters in their lives away from the rink. The brothers have started their own families, with Matthew's wife Ellie giving birth to their first child in mid-April, and Brady's wife Emma giving birth to their second child later in the month.

Knowing his kids will be able to grow up around their family made Brady put into perspective how unique and exciting his new opportunity in Florida really was.

"That was the first time it hit last night, [when I was] flying together with my two kids and Matthew's daughter," Brady said. "All of us together. That was where we're like 'holy cow, this is real and this is what's going to be everyday life.'""That's something that was really important. To have our kids grow up together, be close. Something that we find that's going to be really special for our family."

NHL players are extremely meticulous, sometimes robotic when it comes to their day-to-day operations during the season. Pasta and chicken three hours before the game. Left skate on before the right. Stick tape must go heel-to-toe. Players find a sense of comfort in normalcy. Brady's new normalcy will involve Matthew.

"We've talked about little routines we're gonna have in the morning," Brady said. "We like to get to the rink -- both of us -- really early. So, little breakfast, coffee and hanging out in the morning before guys get there.

"At the end of the day I know it's exciting, but I think for me, it's the excitement to be a part of this whole entire group. It's a special group, and I know of course [I'm] always going to have that personal relationship with Matthew and he's going to be a great guide into introducing me to a lot of things."

#331. Baltimore Orioles hire Jared Banner as general manager to work alongside team president Mike Elias

The Baltimore Orioles have hired Jared Banner as general manager to work alongside team president Mike Elias.

The Orioles announced the move Monday. Banner was the assistant GM of the Chicago Cubs, taking on that role in 2024. He's also been a vice president of special projects and vice president of player development for the Cubs.

"When I first heard Mike's vision, I knew it was something I wanted to be a part of," Banner said in a statement. "The Orioles are a storied franchise with a passionate fanbase, a historic ballpark, and an organization full of talent."

Banner's arrival comes with Baltimore's front office under increasing pressure to reverse the team's decline the past couple seasons. Elias appeared to have built the Orioles into a force when the team won 192 games in two seasons from 2023-24. Since then, Baltimore has managed only 75 wins in 2025 and 79 this year.

"Jared has been one of the rising talents in our league for some time, now," Elias said. "He has demonstrated success running multiple different departments and has worked alongside some of the best people and front office talent in the league across multiple stops. He is a perfect fit to grow, evolve and improve the Orioles' baseball operations."

Banner is a Brooklyn, New York, native. He played baseball at Amherst College and was a fellow in the baseball operations department of the Boston Red Sox in 2007. He spent 11 years with the Red Sox, working in player development and amateur scouting before becoming assistant director of player personnel in 2013.

He was Boston's vice president of player personnel in 2017-18 before becoming executive director of player development of the New York Mets. Then he joined the Cubs in late 2020.

#332. Kings' Ben Simmons sustains torn Achilles tendon in practice, will undergo surgery

Ben Simmons' comeback might be over before it even began. The Sacramento Kings guard sustained a torn right Achilles tendon during practice, the team announced Sunday.

Per the Kings, Simmons suffered the tear during a live drill in Sunday's practice, with an MRI confirming the injury. The team said he will undergo surgery, but did not provide a return timeline.

ESPN's Shams Charania reported that the injury is expected to be season-ending.

Simmons reacted to the injury in a story on his Instagram, saying that he would be back.

"I've faced challenges before that tested me mentally, physically, and emotionally, and I've found a way through every single one of them," Simmons wrote." This injury is another chapter in my journey, not the end of my story. It's never easy being away from the game I love, especially after everything it took to get back here. But if there's one thing I've learned, it's that adversity doesn't define you. How you respond to it does.

"I've been knocked down before, and I've always found a way to get back up. This time will be no different."

Simmons, whose NBA career has been heavily hampered by injuries, was hoping to make a comeback this season. He signed a one-year, $3.5 million deal with the Kings last month after going unsigned last year; previously, his last contract was with the Los Angeles Clippers in the 2024-25 season.

The 30-year-old Simmons, who was expected to be a backup point guard to rookie Darius Acuff Jr., played in all five of Sacramento's preseason games. Simmons started in the Kings' preseason loss to the San Antonio Spurs on Friday, playing 26 minutes and scoring 14 points.

The deal with the Kings was reportedly a non-guaranteed deal, with the guard able to earn $1 million by making the opening night roster. However, because the injury is significant, Simmons will receive his fully salary regardless, per ESPN's Bobby Marks.

Sacramento opens the regular season on Wednesday against the Clippers.

Simmons, the 2016 No. 1 overall pick, started his career strong with the Philadelphia 76ers, but a holdout in his fifth season led to him being traded to the Brooklyn Nets. He played limited games in Brooklyn due to multiple back injuries and eventually surgery for a herniated disc; he signed with the Clippers partway through the 2024-25 season after being waived by the Nets.

#334. So was LeBron James overrated? We asked that question on our cover in 2003, and we have our answer

So was LeBron James overrated? We asked that question on our cover in 2003, and we have our answer originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

Twenty-three years ago, before he had ever suited up for an NBA game, Sporting News posed a question on its cover that has lived on in infamy —Is LeBron James overrated?

Our 2003 cover pops up on social media every so often and is sure to trigger a viral response every time. Over the course of his career, LeBron has gone 23-0 against us. Entering Year 24 and his first with the Sixers, it is looking like he will only add to the longest active winning streak in the league.

King James has more than lived up to his draft hype coming out of high school, breaking a plethora of records and putting forth a compelling argument as the greatest of all time. And he's still pretty good at the age of 41. While he's no longer the best player in the league, we still have him firmly in the top 25 in our top 150 starter rankings.

We've written hundreds of positive things about LeBron over the ensuing years, but that spicy headline is the one that probably gets remembered the most. With his career winding down, now is as good a time as ever to look back at how much crow we deserve to eat, along with what exactly LeBron did to make all of his doubters look bad.

MORE: SN's expert predictions on 2027 NBA champs, MVP, and more

Here are two inside baseball tidbits about how headlines work across news.

Betteridge's law of headlines is an adage that was created in 2009 by Ian Betteridge, a British technology journalist. His observation noted that any headline which ends in a question mark can be answered by the word no. That certainly applied to our LeBron headline, "Is LeBron James overrated?"

The second thing to know about headlines is that oftentimes it's an editor rather than the writer who came up with it.

Bob Hille, who is still with Sporting News as a Senior Editorial Consultant, was a part of the headline-writing process for the story back in 2003.

"I feel bad for [writer Sean Deveney] because the cover oversold what the story was about," Hille said. "We brainstormed cover lines to be both honest and provocative to stand out on newsstands. In GOAT hindsight, we probably leaned too hard into provocative. Or put another way: Is LeBron overrated? Um, no."

MORE: Best NBA power forwards for 2026-27: Ranking all 30 starters

When our story came out, the LeBron hype machine had been in full force for over a year. Sports Illustrated had called him "The Chosen One" on their cover 15 months earlier, when he was still a junior at St. Vincent–St. Mary High School in Akron, Ohio.

Instead of focusing on LeBron, Deveney, a long-time Sporting News NBA expert who now writes for Heavy.com, wanted to shed some light on the other top prospects in that draft.

"There was never any doubt that LeBron was going to be the No. 1 pick, but there were legitimate people (as I recall, Chad Ford of ESPN was among them, as well as a scout, Tony Ronzone) who were saying that Carmelo Anthony and/or Darko Milicic could be just as good if not better," Deveney told me via email. "And that was my focus was comparing those two to the hype and circumstances that surrounded LeBron."

"Obviously, Darko was a bust, there's no other way to say it. But Anthony was at least close to equal with James by most measures in his first season."

Before you kill Deveney for thinking that Milicic was a top prospect, keep in mind that Pistons' GM Joe Dumars validated his intel by taking Milicic No. 2 in the draft a month later.

MORE:Can 76ers win title with LeBron James? What needs to go right, what could go wrong in Philadelphia

How could anyone have doubted LeBron's future success? He was a legendary high school player that sold out arenas and consistently dominated under the brightest lights. It didn't take a professional scout to see that he was a man among boys. But he did have some legitimate weaknesses in his game.

"Two aspects of James's game the most often questioned are his shooting and defense," Deveney wrote back in 2003. "His shot is subpar, and because of that, he probably will struggle early in his career. He must work on it."

That shooting critique turned out to be somewhat right, until it wasn't.

LeBron was a good-not-great 3-point shooter in high school, connecting on 36.0 percent of his attempts. As a rookie in the NBA, he shot just 29.0 percent from 3. He was so transcendent at everything else that his lack of shooting didn't hold him back, with the exception of some key moments.

MORE: LeBron James high school stats, records foreshadowed NBA GOAT career

During the 2007 Finals, Gregg Popovich's Spurs team swept LeBron's Cavs by taking advantage of that shooting weakness. Pop told his players to sag off LeBron, resulting in him shooting just 4-of-20 from 3. LeBron's shaky outside shooting showed up again in 2013, when Popovich used that same strategy against the Heat. Again, LeBron's team lost the series.

LeBron was able to prolong his career and win several rings in part by becoming much better as a perimeter shooter. Through his first eight seasons, LeBron hit just 32.9 percent from deep. He hit 35.9 percent of his 3's from Year Nine onward, and topped over 40 percent from deep twice.

Sagging off from LeBron is no longer a viable strategy. In particular, the pull-up 3 has become a real weapon for him. He deserves a ton of credit for working hard at that aspect of his game to transform a weakness into a strength.

MORE: 'He is insane at Madden': LeBron James opponent explains NBA legend's world-class skill in NFL video game

The other question mark about LeBron surrounded his defense. As Deveney wrote, "He never had to play the defensive stopper's role against someone with comparable skills, so his defense is an unknown, not a negative. He has the tools to become a very good defender, just as Garnett, Bryant, and McGrady have."

Deveney's assessment doesn't look bad, even with the advantage of over two decades of hindsight. It is extremely difficult to project defense from a 17-year-old. But Deveney saw a Kevin Garnett-level of potential, and LeBron delivered.

LeBron hasn't been a plus defender over the last several seasons. For most of his career though, he was elite, making six All-Defensive teams. Defensive Player of the Year is the one major award that has eluded him, but he has finished runner-up twice and has seven top-10 finishes in his career. He will go down as a remarkable two-way force.

Perhaps the most iconic play of LeBron's career was his chase-down block in Game 7 of the 2015 NBA Finals, helping to win the game and title in dramatic fashion for the Cavs.

MORE: SN 140 Moments: No. 10 - LeBron James blocks shot to propel Cleveland to first NBA title

Our misses on LeBron do not look nearly as bad as our headline suggests. There were some admittedly tougher looks though when it came to Milicic, who averaged 6.0 points per game over a 10-year journeyman's career.

"You'd have to work out all three, at least, to compare them," one college scout told Deveney. "And my best guess is that it would be close, but James might not come out on top."

Scouts weren't the only ones to get it wrong. Scootie Penn, a former Ohio State point guard and European pro who was quoted in Deveney's story, was about as far off as possible.

"He's the real deal," Penn said of Milicic. "I have seen LeBron, and I have played against Darko. It's a tough call, but Darko is a legit 7-footer who can shoot the ball. He is tough and he is only 17. It's hard to describe the kid unless you see him."

While LeBron's maturity and future work ethic were questioned at the time, it was actually Milicic who fell victim to those pitfalls. He later admitted that he lacked the discipline and emotional maturity to succeed in the NBA, even getting drunk before practices. LeBron, on the other hand, had a level of determination that made him a foolproof star.

"I think the thing that stands out to me, and this was very early in my career, is the idea that you just did not know what kind of worker LeBron would be," Deveney said. "And you realize over time, that is true of every prospect, every top pick who comes in. You don't know the mindset, just how psycho the guy is going to be about getting better."

"It's the difference between Michael Jordan and Clyde Drexler. Obviously, Clyde is great, but he did not have the extra little chip that Jordan had. And looking back, Anthony was Drexler, and James was Jordan. But you can't tell that at age 18-20, which is why drafting is so inexact."

MORE: The case for LeBron James over Michael Jordan in NBA's GOAT debate

Deveney and everyone else knew that LeBron's physical gifts were a once-in-a-generation blessing that was going to give him a pretty solid floor. He was dominant, getting to the rim with ease and finishing with authority.

"At this point, James has more ability than any prep player who previously has made the jump to the NBA, with the possible exception of Kevin Garnett," Deveney wrote. "Even at 6-8, 240 pounds, James can handle the ball, cross up defenders and blow by anyone with his unpredictable first step. He is a first-rate passer with a flair for the exciting, and he ranks with McGrady and Kobe Bryant as this country's best finishers at the rim."

That assessment was dead-on. More amazingly, it still holds up today. While LeBron isn't nearly as spry as he was two decades ago, he's still one of the strongest guys on the floor. When he gets downhill, he remains impossible to stop. And his passing should be the weapon that unlocks all of the talent in Philadelphia.

LeBron has stood the test of time for 23 years and counting, which is in many respects a more impressive feat in basketball years than the 140 years that Sporting News has been around in the publishing industry. We've both taken our share of losses, as anyone will that lasts the test of time. But the wins far outpace them. And we're both ready to add to our legacy for another year.

#335. Falcons signing Andy Dalton, cutting Cooper Rush

The Falcons are making a change in their quarterback room.

Andy Dalton is signing with Atlanta, and he'll take up the roster spot the Falcons will open up by cutting Cooper Rush, according to multiple reports.

As PFT reported Sunday, Dalton was offered a contract by the Eagles, but he turned them down to sign elsewhere today. Now we know that elsewhere is Atlanta.

The 38-year-old Dalton was traded from Carolina to Philadelphia in March and played in one game for the Eagles, throwing an interception while Jalen Hurts was being checked with a concussion. The Eagles cut him shortly after that, but when Hurts had to go on injured reserve with a blood clot, they wanted Dalton back. Dalton had other offers.

The best offer came from the Falcons, who have already played four quarterbacks this year: Rush, Michael Penix, Jack Strand and Tua Tagovailoa. If Penix stays healthy, Dalton will stay on the sideline, but that's a pretty big "if," and Dalton may just become the fifth quarterback to play for the Falcons this season.

#336. The Lakers appear to be really high on Adou Thiero

Injuries not only robbed Adou Thiero of his rookie season, but also the Lakers of getting a chance to really integrate him into their team.

As a team that lacked athleticism on the wing last season, Thiero was the ready-made solution already on the roster. However, most of his season was spent either rehabbing and recovering from various injuries or getting up to speed in the G League.

However, that hasn't dampened the team's excitement for Thiero entering his sophomore campaign. Evidenced by his playing time this preseason, the team still has a lot of belief in him.

If you read between the lines, they're also signaling some of that belief as well. On a recent episode of "The Zach Lowe Show," Dan Woike of The Athletic spoke about the Lakers' pursuit of Jonathan Kuminga this summer. In doing so, he also expressed how high the team is on Thiero.

"Another ceiling raiser for them is Adou Thiero. Part of the reason, I think, why they weren't totally bent out of shape about losing out on Jonathan Kuminga, I mean they were interested but it wasn't a full-press recruitment, I would say…The version of Kuminga they wanted, they didn't want the 'I think I can be T-Mac' version. They wanted, like, 'Is there a way I can be some sort of discount Aaron Gordon?' Hyper athlete who can space the floor a little bit and defend and run in transition and be a monster.

Adou Thiero is one of the best athletes in the NBA. Adou Thiero didn't play a lot last season because of a knee issue. A knee issue that kept him out of the NCAA Tournament in college. A knee issue that pushed him down a lot of draft boards. A lot of teams had him red-flagged. He's been healthy for most this preseason…He's a guy that gives them a level of pop and athleticism that, really, no one else does."

Seeing how much more controlled and impactful Thiero has been this preseason should give the Lakers even more hope that Thiero can be a meaningful piece of the team this season. It certainly seems like he's going to get the opportunity to do so once the season starts.

On a team with plenty of wings, Thiero's incredible athleticism sets him apart. If he can add some of the other skills along the way this season, then the Lakers could be looking at a new, young piece of their core.

#337. Masai Ujiri tells an outrageous story about LeBron James' unique work ethic

Masai Ujiri tells an outrageous story about LeBron James' unique work ethic originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

Masai Ujiri might be with the Denver Nuggets now, but he still has memories of what LeBron James did to his Toronto Raptors team in the 2010s. It was a decade when the Eastern Conference was dominated by James, as he made the NBA Finals from 2011 all the way to 2018 with two teams.

However, it was during his second stint with the Cleveland Cavaliers that he dominated against Ujiri's team. It got so bad that Toronto became known as LeBronto by people in NBA circles.

As the architect of the Raptors teams in the 2010s, it was tough to have awesome regular season campaigns be shot down by James in the postseason. It became so bad that people have forgotten all of those impressive Raptors seasons.

LeBron was truly the dominant force in the Eastern Conference back then. That notion was further strengthened when he left the East to play for the Los Angeles Lakers. In the first year he was not in the East, the Raptors won the championship in 2019.

MORE: Kevin Love goes viral for taking a shot at Kyle Lowry's Raptors getting dominated by LeBron James

Since then, Ujiri has had many memories involving James. However, he has told a story about how he was impressed by seeing James work out early in the morning, which was a glimpse into what makes him such a good player.

"LeBron was in the gym, running on a treadmill backwards, and his trainers were not even there yet. It's 5:30 in the morning; what is happening here? His guys come, and he does this incredible workout for an hour and a half, and that's not in front of anybody," Ujiri said about James' work ethic while on One 4 Africa.

"What he does with himself in preparation, his mindset, and how much he loves this game. I got my ass kicked by that guy, I hated that guy with a passion."

That early morning was proof that Ujiri needed to know that he was facing off against one of the greatest players in NBA history. Even if he's 41 now with the Philadelphia 76ers, he is likely working out like that, which should still spell trouble for the rest of the league.

#338. 5 up, 5 down from Miami’s 43-35 rivalry win over Florida State

The Miami Hurricanes dug deep and found a way to get past a scrappy Florida State team on Saturday night 43-35. With that kind of scoreline, there certainly were plenty of players who had oustanding performances, while there were plenty who did not.

As usual, I'm going off of my memory/observations compared to what Pro Football Focus has graded as their top and bottom five players with at least 20 snaps.

And to the individuals who have commented that PFF's rankings are wrong/worthless/dumb/etc., well, folks, that's kind of what I'm evaluating when I do this. As in, do I believe these grades are supported based on what I saw? There has to be a reference point to compare their performances against, so that's it.

I had to throw Mallory in there as the first player off the list, as he really should have been higher, and I have to seriously question these rankings where he's not in the 80s. He ran incredibly hard and productively. He cut well, followed his blockers, and ran over guys. I did not see any serious mistakes from my eye in the sky in the press box, even though he got tagged with a 30.2 passing game mark (??). Couldn't NOT mention Mallory here, and his grade baffles me. Should be far higher and way up there on this list.

Toney and Fitzgerald, self-explanatory. Warriors, ballers, game changers. Miami doesn't win without both of them. Fitzgerald left with a shoulder injury that even Cristobal said after the game he was concerned was serious. He came back in and called game. Toughness x 10. Two of three who should be at the top, along with Mallory.

Lightfoot led all players with EIGHT QB pressures. I feel like the pressure wasn't what it should have been tonight across 60+ minutes, so it's nice that someone was pushing the pocket, and who else but Lightfoot. Scott and Blount both had their impact, as Scott was very active inside with eight tackles, second most on the team, and Blount added one of the Canes' two sacks of Ashton Daniels with a second-best four QB pressures. So, both certainly had their moments, even if perhaps without the splash factor. Certainly impactful though.

Gotta say I don't get Congdon and Okunlola being at the bottom. The issues I primarily saw came on defense from scheme, pass rush, coverage, and some iffy personnel decisions (i.e., Thornton single deep safety with JJ Dunnigan rushing on the Duce Robinson 75-yard touchdown, where Dunnigan is a ballhawk and Thornton is a missile). I did not see the left side of the offensive line being the primary underachievers in the ballgame. And Congdon had a terrific seal block on the first Fletcher touchdown. Sorry, don't agree with those marks. I can't say I recall much without a rewatch on Mueller, so I am going to refrain from judgment there.

Zechariah Poyser was on track to be the lowest graded player at 37.6, but he was (properly) ejected for targeting after just eight snaps. Day finished with three tackles but was credited with two missed tackles by PFF. Still, he did not allow a catch on one target per PFF, so I'm not sure why the grade was so low. Micahi Danzy skied over him to grab the first miracle Hail Mary in double overtime, but it was wiped out by a holding call. Despite the secondary struggles, this is a mark I don't particularly get.

Just off the cut line was Damon Wilson II, who finished with no tackles, no sacks, and three QB pressures in 25 snaps and drew the controversial holding call in double overtime to wipe out the score. On replay, he appears to get his jersey grabbed and yanked downwards towards the ground, so despite some whining, it appeared to be a justifiable call. Still, Miami needed more from its star edge rusher throughout the night, who was truly skyrocketing after the Clemson win. Not enough of a factor, and being near the bottom was justifiable to me.

#339. Warriors finalize roster by waiving three players bound for G League

It was always going to be a longshot for Dalen Terry to make the Golden State Warriors roster. After Saturday's roster moves, his best chance might be a spot on the Santa Cruz Warriors.

Terry was waived, along with 26-year-old forward Tyler Burton, and Australian Alex Toohey, a Warriors second-round pick from 2025. All three are candidates for the G League squad.

Burton played 12 games at the end of the season for the injury-decimated Memphis Grizzlies. Toohey played just two games for Santa Cruz last season before undergoing knee surgery in December, a procedure he's still recovering from. Terry had a big preseason game against the Portland Trail Blazers, putting up 23 points, eight rebounds, nine assists and four steals while most of the team didn't make the trip. However, he has too much NBA experience to sign a two-way contract, so there's really no spot for him on the roster.

The last spots on the roster still belong to Georges Niang and Brandon Williams, who will have his contract partially-guaranteed when he's on the opening night roster. Niang and Charles Bassey each have partially-guaranteed deals, though waiving them wouldn't open up much money to sign a replacement. Bassey figures to be a necessary part of the rotation, particularly while Kristaps Porzingis remains out.

It didn't appear that there was a real competition for roster spots during training camp, though Williams impressed by scoring in double digits in his first four games, before sitting out the final game with back soreness. The Warriors remain quite close to the salary cap apron, which limits their options, and the team seems focused on staying afloat until Moses Moody and Jimmy Butler can come back from their own knee injuries.

Could there be a change in the team's two-way contracts, which currently belong to Graham Ike, LJ Cryer and Malevy Leons? It really depends on who might become available during league-wide roster cuts, but the Warriors tend to value continuity, which favors Cryer and Leons. Like Bassey, Ike might play a lot out of sheer necessity, given the fragile center rotation.

The roster appears set. Santa Cruz looks like they have a nice roster as well. Dalen Terry, we'll always have Portland.

#340. CBS Sports grades Falcons' Week 6 loss to Chicago Bears

The Atlanta Falcons got out to another slow start on offense and were unable to overcome it in their 31-23 loss to the Chicago Bears on Sunday. Despite trailing by 24 points in the fourth quarter, the Falcons managed to at least make things interesting with a late run.

Atlanta put together back-to-back touchdown drives and had the ball in scoring range with a chance to tie before the team committed its third costly fumble of the day.

Truthfully, the Falcons weren't even competitive for much of the game - wasting a decent effort by the defensive front-seven, which collected five sacks on Caleb Williams and held Chicago to just three yards per carry on the ground.

As is appropriate, the Falcons have earned a poor "C" grade for this week from John Breech at CBS Sports.

"This game got ugly in the early going thanks to a Falcons' secondary that just couldn't figure out how to slow down the Bears' offense, especially during a first half in which Caleb Williams threw for 197 yards... One problem for Atlanta is that Michael Penix melted down while facing constant pressure. For the Bears, Williams did a good job of extending plays, but Penix couldn't do the same for Atlanta, and that's a big difference between the two quarterbacks. The Falcons also melted down on special teams with Zachariah Branch losing two fumbles -- one on a muffed punt and one on a kickoff -- that led to 10 points for Chicago..."

The culprits are many, beginning with a rough outing for the offensive line and highlighted by two back-breaking fumbles by rookie return specialist Zachariah Branch.

That said, there were some bright spots. Jahan Dotson (three catches, 87 yards, one touchdown) had his best game yet as a Falcon, Kyle Pitts scored twice and Gervon Dexter and Brandon Dorlus were disruptive up front.

However, Michael Penix's numbers (19/33, 225 yards, three touchdowns, no interceptions, 108.8 passer rating) were a bit misleading. While he played well in the fourth quarter, Penix proved completely helpless under pressure.

All the Falcons can do is play better, but that won't be easy with the undefeated 49ers coming to town this week.

#341. Jazz fan survey reveals who they want to start | Utah Jazz Reacts

In this week's Utah Jazz Reacts survey, I asked Jazz fans who they would prefer starting: Ace Bailey or Jaxson Hayes. That assumes Keyonte George, Darryn Peterson, Lauri Markkanen, and Jaren Jackson Jr. are locked into the starting unit. Here's what Jazz fans said:

It's pretty clear that a majority of Jazz fans want to see Ace Bailey starting over Jaxson Hayes. Obviously, this changes the starting lineup dynamics, but from what we've seen in Preseason, it is probably a better dynamic with Bailey starting.

So what are those dynamics? Well, the philosophy of starting a big next to Jaren Jackson Jr. is that it will help with his lack of rebounding and his high foul rate. It should also help defensively by adding size. At least that's what I assume after listening to Will Hardy's latest comments about what Tony Bradley brings to the table ("a lot of size").

My only issue with that is that we've seen Jaren Jackson in foul trouble all preseason while playing next to Jaxson Hayes. On top of that, the Jazz also lost the rebounding battle in their latest preseason game against the Suns, where both teams played their main rotations through three quarters, one of the longest stretches of the season.

We've also seen what looks like a leap from Ace Bailey. He's shooting 45% from the field, but that would be higher if he wasn't shooting just 27% from three, something we know should improve. But it's far from just the shooting that Bailey brings. Bailey is playing 23 minutes per game at the 3 and averaging 5.3 rebounds per game. He's also averaging 1.5 assists, 1.8 steals, and 9.5 points, with a 14.1 net rating, the clear best among the Jazz's main rotation players. The next closest are Svi Mykhailiuk at 9.8, Lauri Markkanen at 5.2, and Keyonte George at 1.5.

At this point, Utah hasn't seen a center like Hayes play next to Jaren Jackson Jr. and either improve his deficiencies or help the team win more. So it's time to run Ace Bailey at the three and let Hayes come off the bench if Jaren Jackson gets into foul trouble, which he likely will.

You can always adjust again if you need to, but at this point we've seen enough of what we get with Jaxson Hayes starting and Ace Bailey playing off the bench that it's time to give Bailey a chance to start. It might be what unlocks everything for the Jazz this season.

Right now, FanDuel has the Jazz at 37.5 wins, and this change might be what pushes them over.

#343. Can Nets ‘shock the world?’

While NBA pundits and others, including fans of the New York Knicks, either ignore the Brooklyn Nets or alternatively dismiss any chances of success, the players and their coaches legitimately believe they can, as Julius Randle said, "shock the world." Some might roll their eyes at that prediction or the more specific one that Brooklyn can win 50 games this season and think it's ill-conceived optimism at best, maybe a casual comment at the least. It is not. It's the driving force, the mantra, for the youngest roster in the NBA at 24.3 years of age. They believe it!

Now that Las Vegas sportsbooks put their season win total at 24.5, only four more than last season, and ESPN predicted they'd win 18 games, two fewer than last season, the reporters who cover the team day in and day out have their opportunity. The New York Post's Brian Lewis and the New York Daily News's C.J. Holmes published their season previews this weekend, the Post as part of a 20-page NBA supplement dominated by their take on whether Jalen Brunson and his Knicks can repeat. We should have ND's annual reporter's roundtable ready to go before Wednesday night's opener at Barclays Center.

In general, Lewis and Holmes are not as pessimistic as the national writers, but no where near as optimistic as the Nets players. In different ways, they look at a 30-win season as something reasonable.

For Lewis, the more intriguing questions are how much further will the team travel on its path to contention … and what the roster looks like after 3:15 p.m., Eastern time on February 11, the trade deadline.

He recites what Sean Marks said back on Media Day on September 28,

"Yeah, it's exciting that we've been able to add this youth to this team, watch these guys develop," the Nets GM for the last decade said. "We've always said over the course of the last couple of years, we're looking for the next Nets. Who are those guys? So we have a training camp and another year to figure this out as we build.

"We've kept flexibility over the last couple of years and know that we're poised when the time is right. [It's about] having a foundation. There's certainly some players here on this roster that will be Nets long term. That's exciting. … [To] see how they develop over the course of this next year is going to be really important. And it's not just the young guys; it's everybody we brought in. Jordi [Fernández] has always harped on developing a 28-year-old or developing a 31-year-old, it doesn't matter. They've all got to show that this is an opportunity they're going to be given, and how can they develop and take their games to the next level."

There's no numerical goal in Marks assessment. The tank may be over but the rebuild clearly is not … and while the GM may be setting goals internally, he's not providing them publicly. His mantra remains development and that's not limited to just the eight players on rookie deals, the second rounder on a tw0-way but also the 31-year-old Randle and the 28-year-old Porter Jr. (On two occasions when he's discussed MPJ's contract extension, Marks pointedly credited Fernandez's role in putting MPJ in the right place within the Nets offense.)

Randle is both the most senior Net player at 32 (on November 29, six days after his return to Minnesota) and easily the most accomplished — three NBA All-Star selections and two All-NBA teams plus Most Improved Player while playing for the Knicks.) He also said recently that he is at the peak of his game.

"Yeah, I feel like I'm the best I've ever been in my career. And I'm in a perfect situation to play my best under Jordi," Randle told Lewis. "I think accumulation of wisdom and continuing to improve every single year, I feel like I'm at my best version of myself that I've been in my career, and I'm excited to be able to utilize that under Jordi and help this team the best way I can.

"Sean brought me here because of that, because it was time to win. … That's what it is. … I'm not here to lose. I don't think anybody's here to lose this year," Randle told The Post. "We're playing to win. That's as simple as I can put it."

Egor Demin and Mikel Brown Jr., of course, are what the average Nets fan is most excited by. They're not only the highest ranking Nets draft picks in back-to-back drafts since Ed O'Bannon and Kerry Kittles in 1995-96. They're also symbolic of the Nets overall strategy: build organically through the draft. As Lewis writes of Brown Jr., he is a rare combination…

As a Louisville freshman last season, Brown joined stars Steph Curry and Trae Young as the only college players since 2008 to have a 30 percent assist rate, 84 percent foul shooting, 35 percent free-throw rate, and high 3-point volume (over 14 attempts per 100 possessions). That rare intersection of elite passing, volume shooting, and on-ball juice teases a potential All-Star. But there are going to be turnovers and rookie growing pains. Brown is going to have to get bigger, stronger, hone his shot selection, and learn when to settle for safe rather than the high-risk home run pass.

Marks adds that MBJ doesn't play or act like a rookie.

Demin too presents something new and interesting. After proving that he can shoot the three despite the preseason narrative that he couldn't, his job now is proving he can go for the more traditional two, testing the lane and going to the line.

The lithe Russian wasn't just a poor driver as a teenaged rookie, but an unwilling one. But added muscle and a more aggressive mindset have put Dëmin in a position to level up. He's bigger, stronger, and getting downhill more. After going just 1-for-4 on 2-point baskets in summer league as a rookie, Dëmin came back a year later and went 22-for-29. The disclaimer is that it was just Summer League. Dëmin got extended looks at point guard in camp with Brown sidelined, and attacked the paint, but, again, that's only preseason.

Then again, in limited action, the two 20-year-olds have displayed a great deal of chemistry. And Nolan Traore, who quite frankly looked like he was the fourth youngest player in the NBA last year, also looked so much better.

Lewis also treats at MPJ departure before or at the trade deadline as a given. After all, if he isn't extended and the Nets have until June 30 to get it done, he'll be a free agent days later. Marks & co. certainly don't want to get noting in return. But on the other hand, this isn't about helping a team like Detroit or Golden State make a playoff push in return for more picks. The Nets currently have a total of eight firsts in 2027, 2028 and 2029.

The Nets' leading scorer is 28 years old and set for unrestricted free agency, which means he's going to be a prime trade candidate. The Aug. 11 deadline came and went to extend Porter and still have him eligible to be moved at the trade deadline. General manager Sean Marks has said he wants to see Porter show consistency, leadership, and defense. It also remains to be seen how the Nets perform, and what kind of offers Porter will draw.

The Daily News' Holmes doesn't commit to a win prediction, but argues getting from 20 to 50 wins (which would be the second highest total in Nets NBA history) would be extraordinary.

Beating the market would take 25 wins. A meaningful step would look more like 30. Reach the Play-In, and the season gets discussed differently. Getting to 50 would demand all of it at once: the veteran partnership working, the young players growing quickly, and the defense holding up without (Nic) Claxton.

He focuses a lot of his preview on how Randle and MPJ will work together. He thinks they can as do the players.

"We understand each other's games really well and how we can really complement each other," Randle told reporters. "We're two guys that obviously can both really score the ball, but we do it in very different ways."

Porter has described the same possibility from the perimeter. When Randle pulls a defender into the paint, Porter has room to shoot if the ball comes back out. That one possession obviously can't account for 30 additional wins, but Brooklyn doesn't need a historic leap to benefit from it. More paint pressure and higher-percentage looks for its best shooter could lift an offense with plenty of room to grow.

One reason for the optimism, as Holmes writes is that MPJ is as good as it gets in making a 3-pointer while heavily guarded. Just nine percent of Porter's 3-point attempts were classified as wide open, the lowest share among 307 players who took at least 100 3-pointers. One the other hand, over the past seven seasons, Randle ranks fourth in the NBA in assists leading to 3-pointers, behind only Nikola Jokić, Giannis Antetokounmpo and Luka Dončić. Heady company.

"We understand each other's games really well and how we can really complement each other," Holmes quotes Randle. "We're two guys that obviously can both really score the ball, but we do it in very different ways."

There was a little of that in preseason. Who knows, maybe Fernandez was hiding how much he'll be using said combination. Every smart coach does hide some plays. Despite that, the Nets did lead the league in preseason offensive rating. Over last season with Noah Clowney starting 60 games at power forward, Brooklyn ranked dead last. As Holmes wrote, "Last season gives the Nets little room to pretend the climb is short."

Still, the optimism is there. "And it's going to take day by day, step by step," Brown Jr. said when he first mentioned Randle's "shock the world" quote to reporters. In the meantime, it'll be "just getting 1% better every day."

#344. Colts fire GM Chris Ballard

The Colts have made a major change in the wake of Sunday's loss to the Titans.

Owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon announced that they have fired General Manager Chris Ballard. Ballard had been in the job since 2017 and made the playoffs twice in his first four seasons, but have not been back since 2020 while cycling through a number of different quarterbacks.

That led Irsay-Gordon to say this offseason that improvement was needed, but Sunday's loss dropped the Colts to 1-5 on the season and became the final act of his tenure.

"I am grateful to Chris for his years of service to the Colts and for everything he poured into this organization," Irsay-Gordon said in a statement. "He cared deeply about our team and our community, and we wish Chris and his family all the best. As I said at the start of the season, the sense of urgency has never been higher. Our standard is to compete for championships, and I believe a change in leadership is necessary to meet that standard. Making this change during the season was a deliberate decision. Waiting would only delay the important work that needs to begin now. We will conduct a thorough search for our next general manager and take the time necessary to identify the right leader for the future of this organization. I also want to be clear: this decision does not change our goals for the season. We have a lot of football in front of us, and I expect us to compete, improve, and win football games."

Head coach Shane Steichen remains on the job, but he's clearly on thin ice moving forward with Ballard already gone.

That record puts them in second place in the NFC North, 1.5 games behind the 5-0 Minnesota Vikings and a half-game up on the 3-2 Detroit Lions. Both of those two teams were idle in Week 6, but the Packers have a chance to make some significant movement in the division next Sunday.

Week 7 brings the Packers their third game against an NFC North opponent this season, as they will travel to Detroit to play the Lions in the late Sunday afternoon time slot. However, the books are giving the Lions a reasonable advantage in this game thanks to it being played on their own home turf. Prior to 2025, the 2020 season was the last time Green Bay went 2-for-2, when they won similarly high scoring games in weeks 2 (42-24) and 14 (also 31-24).

That opener was a wonderful introduction. Carter scored 17 points in 25 minutes against Cleveland on 5-of-9 shooting. He went 6-of-6 at the line, putting a ton of pressure on the rim. He also added five rebounds, three assists, and two steals. He showed a lot of the promise that made him a lottery pick for Sacramento two seasons ago.

His audition was unfortunately cut short after one game, but this lone performance was strong enough and his potential is too much for Boston to pass up on.

Joe Mazzulla pointed to Carter's ceiling as the reason for the deal. "You see the talent, the impact that he could have, and you want to be able to invest in that," he said.

Carter is on his third team in four months. Sacramento took him 13th in 2024 and traded him to Atlanta in June. The Hawks then waived him in September to get down to 15 players. Mazzulla said Carter has talent and has shown flashes as a pro, but he needs to put his head down in Boston. So far, that's exactly what he's done.

"Came in with a great attitude. Did what we asked him to do," Mazzulla said.

The Celtics have a lot of options in their development pipeline, but the team uses their G League affiliate in Maine about as well as anyone in terms of investing in young talent and guiding their growth. The two-way deal gives Boston more control of Carter's trajectory. He'll fill the team's third two-way slot alongside Dillon Mitchell and Amari Williams.

Carter can also remain available when the Celtics need depth throughout the year, like we saw with Williams last season.

This is a second draft opportunity for both sides. Carter gets a change of scenery, and Boston takes a shot at a player with real NBA skills that has more room for growth.

Boston has already hit on Neemias Queta, who came off the Kings' scrap heap as well. Ron Harper Jr. went from an Exhibit 10, to a two-way, to a three-year extension. Carter could have a similar journey in store for him.

He's a smart and tenacious defender, and Mazzulla called him "really impactful on the defensive end of the floor." The shooting is a question mark. He shot 27.4 percent from three over his first two seasons. He has other skills worth betting on, but if the jumper comes along, he could find a home here like Queta, Harper, and others have.

Mono will delay that, but Boston's guard room is in good shape with Derrick White, Payton Pritchard, and Mike Conley all healthy. While the Celtics might need Carter at some point, getting him healthy and sharpening his tools in Maine is the short-term focus.

The Celtics see the vision with Carter, and hopefully this is just a brief delay before it starts coming together once he returns.

#347. Davante Adams suffered non-contact leg injury late in Sunday's loss to Cardinals

The slumping Rams may be scrambling to find help at receiver.

Veteran Davante Adams suffered a non-contact injury to his left leg late in the game. He pulled up when running into the end zone on a pass route, reached for his left knee, and hobbled off the field for attention.

The Rams had only one more offensive play, a go-ahead touchdown that did not last.

Coach Sean McVay wasn't asked about Adams's apparent injury during the post-game press conference.

Last year, Adams missed the final three games of the regular season with a hamstring injury (and still led the NFL in touchdown catches).

For the season, Adams has 30 catches for 480 yards and four touchdowns. The bulk of the production came in Week 2 vs. the Giants (195 yards) and Week 3 at the Broncos (137). In the other four games combined, he has 148 total receiving yards.

Still, they need him. Puka Nacua, who missed the two games (hip/groin/pre-hernia) in which Adams went off, is their top target in the passing game. On Sunday, Nacua had six catches for 80 yards, including three for 62 on the Rams' final drive of the game.

Beyond Nacua and Adams, the Rams have Konata Mumpfield, Jordan Whittington, Tutu Atwell, C.J. Daniels, and Alex Bachman at receiver. They may need to find someone else, depending on whether and to what extent Adams will miss time.

The question becomes whether they're willing to eff them picks in an effort to acquire a receiver via trade before the deadline arrives in 22 days. And the situation will invite even more scrutiny of the decision to invest their bonus first-round pick from last year's trade with the Falcons on a quarterback and not a receiver — especially since it was obvious that they don't have much depth behind Nacua and Adams.

#348. Chris Ballard fired after Colts lose to Titans

On Sunday, the Indianapolis Colts lost in embarrassing fashion to the previously winless Tennessee Titans.

On Monday, general manager Chris Ballard lost his job.

In a statement from owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon, she outlined how the "sense of urgency has never been higher" in Indianapolis, and that the "standard" for the Colts is to compete for championships. Irsay-Gordon then indicated that a "change in leadership is necessary to meet that standard."

Sunday's loss to the Titans dropped the Colts to 2-4 on the season, two games behind first-place Jacksonville.

Ballard took over in Indianapolis for the 2017 season, after starting his personnel career as a scout with the Chicago Bears, before moving to the Kansas City Chiefs first as the Director of Player Personnel, and later as the Director of Football Operations.

The organization made the playoffs twice during his tenure, losing in the Divisional Round following the 2018 season, and losing in the Wild Card Round after the 2020 season.

Indianapolis had a 72-82-1 regular-season record, and a 1-2 playoff record, under his leadership.

Head coach Shane Steichen remains on the sideline, for now.

#349. Colts fire general manager in first major leadership move of NFL season

Indianapolis Colts owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon promised changes to her team's leadership structure if results were not different after back-to-back 8-9 seasons.

That has now happened six games into the 2026 campaign, as general manager Chris Ballard was fired Monday, Oct. 19.

"Our standard is to compete for championships," Irsay-Gordon said in a statement announcing the move, "and I believe a change in leadership is necessary to meet that standard."

The final straw for the regime was a 26-20 home loss to the previously winless Tennessee Titans. The defeat dropped the Colts to 2-4.

Irsay-Gordon said making the decision during the season was deliberate.

"Waiting would only delay the important work that begins now," she wrote in a statement shared by the team.

Irsay-Gordon added: "I also want to be clear: this decision does not change our goals for the season. We have a lot of football in front of us, and I expect to compete, improve and win football games."

Ballard had been the general manager since 2017 and was dealt the sudden retirement of Andrew Luck before the 2019 season. The team made a pair of playoff appearances during his tenure but had not returned to the postseason since 2020.

The Colts started 8-2 in 2025 but lost their final seven games of the year to finish below .500. A late-season injury to quarterback Daniel Jones, who tore his Achilles, was a low point of the losing streak as their playoff chances dissipated.

The Colts entered Week 6 with the 23rd-ranked passing offense in the league. The team's defense, in coordinator Lou Anarumo's scheme for a second season, was the true downfall of the team, however, and entered Week 6 ranked 27th. Indianapolis finished 72-82-1 during Ballard's tenure.

The Colts held the No. 4 overall pick in the 2023 draft and used it on Anthony Richardson, seen as a developmental project at the next level after showing raw talent at Florida. Injuries and inconsistencies were factors in Richardson never panning out and, at times, led to him being the team's third-string quarterback in recent campaigns.
